A visitor list confirms destinations, not actions or the attacker. Keep those distinctions explicit, and look for a contradiction that isolates one player rather than treating presence at a victim as proof.

Remember that the Katana holder appears Good to alignment checks that night. Passing it to a member with no separate visiting action can help conceal alignment, but the Katana attack still creates a visit that investigators may observe.
A new trap replaces the old one immediately and only arms the following night. Choose a target likely to receive later visits, and remember that Astral actions do not trigger traps.

Separate an observation from what you infer from it. A Lookout’s list excludes their own visit: corroborated names support the result, but the list neither identifies the attacker nor necessarily includes every possible visitor.

Check appearance exceptions before calling an investigative result false. For example, a Yakuza holding the Katana appears Good to alignment checks, so a Seer comparison can fit role flips that seem opposed.
Avoid repeatedly voting as a visible bloc when independent-looking votes are plausible. Public vote patterns and visible private-message links can make coordination a useful lead for Village.

Before pushing a trial, identify what evidence would distinguish the suspect from other plausible candidates. If the case rests only on an unverifiable claim or an undifferentiated visitor list, say what remains uncertain rather than presenting suspicion as proof.

Spend a Ritualist token on a Standard guess only when the target is unlikely to have Standard Defense. A Medic who protected the target on the same night absorbs it silently, so a right guess can still fail. If the target is a likely protected role, use Divine (2 tokens) or wait.

Do not vote identically with teammates on every nomination and trial. A three-person No/Innocent bloc was visible to the whole Village and made every vote look coordinated. Vary your votes and give each one a reason that fits the public record.

Keep private-message contact with teammates to a minimum, especially on Day 1. The Day 1 private-message triangle became the central case against the whole Yakuza team and was cited on every later trial.

Check whether a Lookout or visitor list leaves out the claimant's own visit before treating the pool as certain. Lookout excludes the user's own visit, so a 'certain' five-name pool was an overclaim. Also check any claimed contradiction against the exact wording of both results before voting on it.

Treat same/different results as comparisons of appearances, not proof of actual alignment. A Katana-holding Yakuza can appear Good, and a framed player can appear Evil; pair results usually constrain possibilities rather than identify which player is which.

applies_to: Lookout and everyone interpreting Lookout results
tip: A Lookout's own visit is excluded from the reported visitors. A well-corroborated list can verify who else visited, but it neither rules out the Lookout as a visitor nor identifies which visitor performed a kill.

Track repeated voting patterns and private-message links as leads, especially after a faction member flips, but assess each vote's stated reasoning too. Coordination is more persuasive when the pattern recurs alongside independently suspicious actions, not from one shared vote alone.

Separate confirmed facts, claims, and inferences in your arguments. For example, a verified visit establishes presence, not an attack; a role claim can explain a visit without proving the claimed action occurred.
After every result, update both your public record and your last will. Include the target, result, and any caveat about frames or appearance changes; a result you never get to share cannot help town.

Separate an observation from what it proves. A corroborated Lookout list establishes visits, not who attacked, what action each visitor performed, or who was evil; remember that the Lookout does not see their own visit.

Track vote and private-message patterns across days, especially after a faction member flips. Use those links to prioritize scrutiny, then test each player's own claims and actions rather than treating association as proof.
Treat Not Evil as a limited result, not a town-clear. Neutrals may read Not Evil, and a Yakuza holding the Katana can appear Good; state these caveats whenever you share the result.

Don't vote identically with fellow Yakuza on every nomination and trial. A repeated No/Innocent bloc was the strongest public tell, and Erin and Alice built their whole case on it. Vary votes so they look like independent judgments.

Avoid private-message triangles with other Yakuza, especially on Day 1. Everyone sees that a private message was sent even when they can't read it, so the existence of the PMs alone made the trio look coordinated.

Before spending a Ritualist guess on a Standard attack, consider whether the target is likely protected. Carol was protected twice and the Standard attacks failed. Use Divine attacks on high-value targets or spread attacks to players less likely to have a Medic.

Don't call a visit list a certain pool without checking the rules. A Lookout's list omits their own visit, and calling the list 100% after omitting that cost credibility and led to a mislynch argument.

Alignment checks can be fooled by a Katana holder, who reads Good at the end of the night. A Sheriff or Seer Not Evil result on a Yakuza holder is therefore weaker evidence than it looks, so don't clear a player on one result alone.

Don't vote as one bloc on every nomination, and never message teammates on Day 1. If one teammate defends a suspect, the others should split their votes with the town on trials they can't swing anyway.
evidence: Heidi and Mallory each messaged Frank on Day 1. The three then voted No together on all three Day 2 nominations. Alice named this 'closed triangle' in public and in her will, and it became the case that hanged Mallory, Heidi and Frank in turn.

tip: Never vote Guilty on a Village claimant whose result the table has already confirmed. A small Guilty minority on a trusted claimant marks exactly who wanted them dead.
evidence: Heidi and Mallory were the only Guilty votes on Carol after all five visitors she named had confirmed their visits. Carol called this out on the spot, and the town cited it in every later trial of Mallory and Heidi.

tip: Before you claim two results contradict each other, check the mechanics yourself: who was checked, and what the Katana holder or a frame looks like to the check. A made-up contradiction that others can disprove is worse than staying quiet.
evidence: On Day 3 Mallory said Ivan's Mallory/Judy pairing and Judy's check on Erin 'can't both be honest'. Bob disproved it and nominated her, and she was hanged 7-2. On Day 4 Heidi called Ivan a liar over the same pairing and had to retract once Erin explained the Katana holder reads Good.

tip: If you survive an attack, say so publicly so the Medic keeps protecting you; a Ritualist who guessed right once will try again. Medics should stay on a claimant they know was targeted by an exact-role attack.
evidence: On Night 2 Heidi's Ritualist guessed Carol as Lookout, and Bob's Standard Defense blocked it. Carol mentioned the attack only in her will, and on Night 3 Bob protected Ivan instead. Heidi's last ritual token then killed Carol.

tip: Spend a rig only on a day your team can control the first successful nomination. Otherwise it is wasted, or it hangs one of your own. Decide on the night you can use it, not 'after seeing the nomination picture'.
evidence: Mallory held her rig on Night 1, which she couldn't use on a Day 2 that would have suited it. She then rigged Day 3, the day Bob nominated her, so the rig could only have executed her.

tip: Post your visitor list early, since confirmation from the named visitors makes you very credible. But state only what the mechanics prove: your own visit isn't on the list, so the attacker pool includes you from everyone else's point of view.
evidence: Carol's five-name list was confirmed by every named visitor and earned her near-confirmed status. Her '100% the killer is among these five' overclaim gave Frank a counter-nomination and the Yakuza a talking point, and it forced a third trial that ended Day 2.

tip: A forged will must fit the public record and the victim's likely role, and don't spend a frame on someone who already reads Evil. A forgery that others can check and disprove points the town back at the forger's side.
evidence: Frank framed Dave, an Executioner who already read Evil, and forged a will claiming Erin pushed suspicion onto Dave. Bob showed the transcript never had Erin doing that, and Erin used the 'inverted' will to point at a Fabricator.

tip: Save your prosecutions for when the town's suspicion is clear but the votes are split or the Day risks ending before a trial. A guaranteed trial on the top suspect in the voting bloc turns a correct read into a hanging.
evidence: Erin prosecuted Heidi on Night 3 and Frank on Night 4, and both were hanged as Yakuza the next Day. She kept her role claim hidden until the final Day.

tip: A Sheriff Evil result on someone claiming Vanilla who has 0 tokens fits a Jester as well as Yakuza. If you hang anyway, let only a bare majority vote Guilty and have the rest vote Innocent. That shrinks the pool for the Jester's or Executioner's revenge, which otherwise hits a random Guilty voter.

Once you have publicly claimed with incriminating results, expect both the Katana and any Serial Killer to come for you. Each Day, write tonight's watch target and your reasoning into your will. The result of the night you die never reaches the town, but a pre-stated plan still tells them something.

A lone Katana holder can deliberately skip a night to frame whoever a blocker targeted. Block/no-kill matches are good evidence only when several of them line up, ideally with one confirmed by a flip, and not when the pattern rests on a single night.

Don't block quiet players who have defended confirmed claims. They may be an unclaimed Vigilante or other killing power, and a block wastes that night. Prefer unclaimed or late-claiming players with no mechanical clearance.

Holding the Katana on a member who then visits a likely target shows up on a Lookout watching a protected organizer. Pick N1 targets that an investigator is less likely to be watching. Have a cover story for the visit ready before Day starts.

Town players are coached to treat Day 1 PM pairs as Yakuza tells. One short Day 1 PM to a single player, ideally a quiet or pushy one, makes you the town's only concrete lead. If that player flips Yakuza, you're hanged almost for free.

Once you are on trial, claim Vanilla Villager, which matches the 0 tokens an Accountant would find. Then give a short, weak defense: blame the accuser without answering the main evidence, and vote Guilty on yourself. A strong defense or a Jester hint makes cautious players vote Innocent.

A Day 1 dissent such as 'a no-hang Day gives Yakuza a free night' is mildly suspicious without being absurd. It draws Sheriff, Accountant and Oracle checks onto you on Night 1. You read Evil to the Sheriff, so a Sheriff claim plus an Evil result becomes your hanging case.

Before hanging a Vanilla claimant on a Sheriff Evil result, remember that Jester and Executioner also read Evil and that a 0-token audit fits them too. Don't pile on. Keep Guilty votes near a bare majority so a Jester's revenge has fewer voters to choose from.
Once the Pharmacist is dead, a claimed Party Animal whose block a target confirms is close to proven. Repeated 'blocked X, no Katana kill' nights then point strongly at the lone holder.

Audit claimed tokenless visitors and unclaimed quiet players. A 0-token result rules out a whole set of claims (Medic, Vig, Vet, Prosecutor...), and a 3-token result fits no Yakuza starting role, so that player is nearly cleared. Publish the role ranges a count rules out rather than the raw number, which can out a Vigilante.

Once the Pharmacist has flipped, any confirmed block on a later night came from a Party Animal or a second Pharmacist. Cross-check the blocker's earlier public claims against the victim's later confirmation. A block named before the victim confirms it is strong evidence the blocker is real.

When only one Yakuza is left, count the nights with no Katana kill. If those nights line up with a verified blocker's targets, that is the strongest available lead. It is stronger still when the suspect claimed Vanilla late and stayed unclaimed while others claimed.

An exact-role hit (Oracle) on an unverifiable Vanilla claimant tests itself on the flip, so hang on it right away. A last Yakuza can't know who the SK is, so a fake Oracle hit would be suicide for them. Delaying gives the killer a free night.

Several teammates sharing the same fake Vanilla will is a tell once one of them flips. Vary your cover claims and wills, and keep a believable, token-consistent power-role claim ready for the late game.

applies_to: Medic and other protective or power roles
tip: Don't be the first, agenda-setting voice on Day 1. Yakuza often pick the confident Day 1 organizer as their first Katana target. Post a short echo later in the round and leave the organizing to someone else.

If you were visible on Day 1, consider spending 1 token on Night 1 for Standard self-protection. Night 1 Katana targets are usually the most visible talkers, and a Medic who dies on Night 1 saves nobody all game.

A Sheriff 'Evil' result on a player who claims Vanilla and pleads innocence fits a Jester or Executioner just as well as a Yakuza. Before hanging, check whether the tie to a flipped Yakuza really needs them to be a teammate. A Day 1 PM the suspect started himself is weak. If you hang anyway, keep the Guilty votes to a bare majority to limit Jester revenge.

A night with no kill right after a confirmed blocker hit a player is strong evidence that the player holds the Katana, especially with no other killer left. Cross-confirm the blocker's log with players who were told they were blocked. Treat that as a mechanical lead.
A Diviner can pick itself for Strong Defense on a night it expects an attack, but it gets no reading that night. Decide whether the protection or the information matters more.

Don't waste early guesses on 'Grunt' for suspects; Grunt is often absent. Guess the role the evidence points to: the likely killer role for an unexplained kill (Serial Killer behind a Vanilla claim), or a common Yakuza role with an action (Pharmacist, Diviner) for a suspected Yakuza. A single RIGHT guess on a killer ends the debate.

When a blocker's target matches a no-kill night twice, and the blocker's log is independently confirmed (the blocked player says so, or the only other blocker role is dead), treat it as a strong mechanical lead on a lone Katana holder.

Late Vanilla claims from players who stayed unclaimed while others claimed are the likeliest hiding spot for the last Yakuza. Do slot math on the confirmed roles; with several Vanilla claims late in the game, test them with blocks and exact-role guesses first.
An exact-role confirmation claim is self-testing on the flip. Say so explicitly; it makes the town act immediately instead of giving the killer another night.
Don't PM your own teammate on Day 1, and don't have three members fake the same Vanilla will. Mass Vanilla wills from flipped Yakuza make every later Vanilla claim suspect.

Once the Neutral killers are dead, a lone surviving Yakuza holder is checkable through a confirmed blocker. Block/no-kill nights matched against a third party's independent confirmation of a block (e.g. the blocked player saying so) form a real mechanical lead. Use it rather than waiting.

As Cardinal, claim Vanilla publicly but put the true Cardinal claim in your will. If you die, the town won't misread the random Good death as a Katana kill, and the Yakuza get no reason to target you deliberately. Reveal publicly only when facing a hang, since hanging a Cardinal costs the Village two players.

When a claimant names a hidden Neutral with an exact-role hit (Oracle), hang the named player at once. A last Yakuza can't know who the SK is, so the claim tests itself on the flip. Arguments like 'test the claimant first' just buy the killer another night.

Before you treat an attack on yourself as proof of innocence, check whether your role reads Good to alignment checks while holding the Katana. Late in the game, Not Evil results clear nobody, so weigh claim timing and late Vanilla claims above Sheriff results.
Short Day 1 agreement messages followed by silence are enough. Save your budget for the day results start flowing, when you'll need to question claimants and do vote math.

An Evil result on Night 1 can be a Jester or Executioner, not Yakuza. Be suspicious if the target pushed 'pressure nominations' on Day 1 and claims Vanilla with 0 tokens. Before calling for a hang, post the result and ask for an Accountant audit and a claim. A Jester hang triggers a Divine revenge on a random Guilty voter.

Once only one Yakuza is left, they hold the Katana and read Not Evil every night. The best lead is then a blocker's log: line up each night's block target with no-kill nights. Confirm the blocker by having a blocked player admit the block.

In the late game, when alignment checks can't find the lone holder, check players whose claims nobody can verify (Vanilla) anyway. That builds a record, and a Not Evil narrows the field down to the holder plus any non-Sheriff-detectable Neutrals.

A Trapper guarding a confirmed-looking Sheriff, together with the Sheriff's public claim, deters Katana visits. If the trap stays silent, also report it daily as 'no non-Village visitor to X'. That gives the town free negative info.
Spend Oracle guesses on Neutral killers hiding behind Vanilla claims (e.g. Serial Killer) once a Neutral kill appears. A RIGHT guess is a self-testing claim the town will act on immediately.

Before a Day 1 or Day 2 hang, check whether the target could be a Jester. A strong sign is an Evil read on someone your team knows isn't Yakuza, or a Diviner draw showing Jester in their group. If so, don't pile every Yakuza onto Guilty. Each Guilty vote is a ticket in the Jester's revenge lottery. Let the town hang him, and have only as many teammates vote Guilty as you need to avoid standing out.

The Katana holder's visit is the team's biggest leak. Once a Lookout has named the holder as a visitor to the victim, pass the Katana to a teammate whose cover story doesn't need visits. Don't keep it on the exposed member just for the Not Evil read.

When you're the last Yakuza and a Party Animal or other blocker is claimed and alive, expect to be blocked once you're a suspect. The block-then-no-kill pattern will hang you. Either kill the blocker while you can, or accept that a no-kill night after his block convicts you. Also, don't send the Katana at a target the Serial Killer is likely hitting too; double kills waste your night.

Claim your fake role early and with a plausible story. A Vanilla claim made only when pressed late, with nothing to verify it, is exactly the profile the town hangs once Neutrals are gone. Prepare a claim that explains your possible visits and token count before Day 3.

Targeting yourself gives Strong Defense with no reading, which is good once you hold the Katana and expect attacks. Early on, use your draws to find Neutrals (Jester/Executioner) as well as power roles, and tell the team what you found so their votes and Katana targets follow it.

Block the player you suspect of holding the Katana, not just a probable investigator. A no-kill night that lines up with your block is the strongest mechanical lead the town gets against a lone last Yakuza, since Sheriff checks read the holder as Not Evil.

Write your exact block target in your will and post it publicly the Day after, before anyone can confirm it. A target who later confirms they were blocked (e.g. Olivia saying she was role-blocked N3) proves you are a real blocker. That makes later block/no-kill matches credible enough to hang on.

Once the Pharmacist has flipped, only a Party Animal or a second Pharmacist can role-block. Use dead flips to narrow which roles could have produced a reported effect before you accept or reject a claim.

Late Vanilla claims from players who were unclaimed until the end deserve the most suspicion. With 3 or 4 Yakuza flipped, the last Yakuza usually hides behind an uncheckable Vanilla claim, and a check that reads them Not Evil means nothing because they hold the Katana.
Before a hang on a single unverifiable log, commit publicly to 'if they flip Village, I'm next.' It costs little when you are honest and gets the town to accept the vote.

Traps arm only from the next night, so put the trap on someone the Katana is likely to hit in two nights' time: a vocal investigator or analyst. Re-target every night rather than leaving it parked. A trap on an already-claimed Sheriff is predictable, and a lone Katana holder simply avoids that player.

If a Lookout reveals that you visited the Katana victim, claim at once with mechanics others can verify (token count for the Accountant, alignment check). A clean claim that fits the audits ended the suspicion within one round.

A night with no Katana kill that lines up with a confirmed blocker's target is strong evidence, especially once a third party has confirmed one of that blocker's past blocks. Once the Pharmacist has flipped, a confirmed block also points to a real Party Animal.
Late lone 'Vanilla' claims from long-quiet players are prime suspects for the last Yakuza. Their claims are unverifiable, and a Diviner or Grunt carrying the Katana reads Not Evil anyway.
Short one-line speeches on Days 1-2 save budget for trial days, when you need to claim, cross-check, and state a conditional plan such as 'if X flips Village, hang Y next'.

Once a Lookout or Tracker has placed your Katana holder on the victim, move the Katana that same night to a member with no public trail. Keeping it on the exposed player marks them as the blocker's and the SK's obvious target, and leaves the team's best cover sitting on a player who is likely to die.

When a Party Animal claims and lays out their block log, kill them with the Katana next. Every block that lines up with a no-kill night becomes hang evidence against the lone holder, and town treats those matches as verified as soon as one block target confirms being blocked.

Spend the rig early, on any Day with a plausible town mislynch. A Clerk whose holder is exposed or who might take an SK hit can die with the token unused, and then it is worth nothing. One rigged Day 3 hang of a muddy claimant would have been worth more than waiting for a perfect setup.

Pool exact-role draws in night chat. If a Diviner or Surveyor group already drew 'Jester' and an Evil-checked player sits in that group, the Jester is probably that player. In that case, expect revenge on a random Guilty voter: think about how many teammates are exposed, and remember that a puppet or other next-Day effect lapses if its user dies (R21).

As the last Yakuza facing a known blocker, a skipped or blocked night points straight at whoever the blocker visited. Claim a role early with an alibi that fits, rather than staying unclaimed and claiming Vanilla only when cornered. A late Vanilla claim from the last unclaimed players is exactly where town looks.

When a non-teammate reads Evil to a Sheriff, he is a Jester or Executioner. If the hang is already certain without you, vote Innocent on him. Every Yakuza Guilty vote is another ticket in the Divine revenge lottery, and that lottery killed our Puppeteer.

Don't spend the N1 block on whoever PMed you on Day 1; a prober is often a Jester fishing for attention. Block a likely investigator who could check the Katana holder, or a quiet organizer. Your block is wasted if it lands on a role with no night action.

Once a Party Animal claims and posts his block targets, kill him with the Katana at once. Every block he lands on the holder produces a 'block plus no kill' pattern that the town treats as proof. A lone holder can't afford to be blocked even once.

Don't all write identical fake Vanilla wills. After the first Yakuza flips with a fake Vanilla will, every later Vanilla claim or will looks the same. Vary the covers between teammates, or pick tokenless power roles that can't be checked.

Share Diviner results in a way that reaches every teammate before the Day votes. Our Diviner drew 'Jester' in Bob's group on N1, which meant Bob could be safely abandoned with Innocent votes and should never be blocked or targeted.

Holding all tokens every night forfeits value. Once a mechanical lead exists (e.g. a Party Animal's block coincides with a no-kill night, or a late unclaimed Vanilla claim), fire a cheap Basic shot. If the shot is wasted, one token is a small loss, and it can end the game a day earlier.

When a claimed blocker's target lines up with a no-kill night and that pattern has already matched a flipped Yakuza once, treat it as a strong lead. Also verify the blocker independently: being blocked yourself and confirming it publicly is a cheap, solid confirmation.

A late Vanilla claim from a player who stayed unclaimed and echoed others while asking investigators for claims is the classic hiding spot for the last Yakuza. Do slot math on the flipped Yakuza roles (Pharmacist, Clerk, Puppeteer) to see which Yakuza roles could still be unaccounted for.

After a Jester hang, the revenge hits a random Guilty voter. Before a near-unanimous Guilty on a weakly verified Evil read, consider that the Sheriff reads the Jester and Executioner as Evil. Keep Guilty votes near a bare majority unless the claim is checked (e.g. 0 tokens alone doesn't rule out a Jester).
Short, results-first messages work. Most decisive days here took one or two messages per player, so bank budget early for trial days.

Once a Lookout publicly names your Katana holder as a visitor to the Katana victim, move the Katana that night to an unexposed member. A Party Animal or Vigilante will target the named visitor, and the holder's Not Evil reading doesn't help if they're blocked or shot first.

Combine your exact-role draws with public Sheriff results. If a Diviner or Surveyor draws Jester in a group and a Sheriff then reads a group member Evil when they aren't your teammate, that player is almost surely the Jester. Every Guilty voter then risks the Divine revenge, so weigh it before piling on.

Day effects that need you to act lapse if you die that night (R21). Don't spend the token on a night when you face an elevated death risk, such as after voting Guilty on a likely Jester. Use it early when it can swing a trial, rather than hoarding it until the team is thin.
Spend one-shot tokens (Clerk rig, puppet) while the team still has numbers. Our Clerk died holding an unused rig after waiting for a 'perfect' mislynch day that never came.

As the last Yakuza facing a claimed blocker whose block lined up with a past no-kill night, a skipped or blocked night will be pinned on you. Claim something with a night action early, and set up an alternative suspect before the blocker names you, not during your trial.

Don't kill Yakuza early. Every Yakuza you remove makes the Village stronger and leaves you alone against a large town. Target Village power roles (blockers, Sheriff, Accountant) and let the Yakuza thin the town for you. Only turn on the Yakuza once the town is small.

Don't attack the player the Yakuza obviously want dead, such as a Lookout who just exposed their Katana holder. A double kill wastes your night, and the 'Katana and Serial Killer' cause confirms you are still active. Pick a target the Katana is unlikely to hit.

An early Vanilla claim is the natural hiding spot for an SK, and any Oracle or exact-role checker will test Vanilla claimers once SK kills are public. Stay unclaimed longer, or claim a role that fits your 0 tokens and that some flip or result appears to back up. Don't volunteer Vanilla on Day 2.

Arguing 'that claim is uncheckable, test it first' fails against a claim the flip will confirm or break. The town reasons that a fake claim would hang its claimant tomorrow, so they hang you now. A better defense is a concrete counter-mechanic, such as another player's result that contradicts the claim.
A publicly announced Trapper trap works as a deterrent. Killers will avoid the trapped player, so treat that player as protected, and expect kills to land elsewhere.

An Evil Sheriff result on a player with 0 tokens and no night results fits a Jester or Executioner as well as Yakuza. Before hanging, ask who benefits. If you still hang, keep Guilty votes near a bare majority so the Jester's revenge has fewer town targets.
evidence: Bob read Evil and audited 0 tokens. He never pushed for his own hang, yet the town voted 13-0 Guilty and he flipped Jester. The revenge happened to land on Peggy (Yakuza), but it could just as easily have killed a power role.

tip: If your own information suggests the nominee is a Jester, don't all pile onto Guilty. One or two Innocent votes look fine once a Jester flips, and each Guilty vote is a ticket in the revenge draw. Share that information in night or day planning.
evidence: Heidi's N1 divine on Bob's group (Bob/Carol/Dave) drew Jester. All three surviving Yakuza still voted Guilty on Bob, and the revenge killed Peggy along with her unused-in-play puppet.

tip: Once a Lookout publicly names your Katana holder as a visitor to the victim, move the Katana to an unexposed teammate. Expect blockers and killers to target the exposed holder; reading Not Evil to the Sheriff doesn't protect against a block.
evidence: After Alice named Mallory, the Yakuza kept the Katana on her so she would read Not Evil. Ivan blocked her on N2, which stopped the kill on Alice, and the SK killed her that night.

tip: When a claimed role-blocker's log keeps lining up with your no-kill nights, kill the blocker first. Every night they live, they either stop your kill or build a block/no-kill pattern against you.
evidence: Ivan claimed Party Animal on D3 and had already stopped Mallory. Heidi attacked Alice on N3, who died to the SK anyway, and then Erin on N4. Ivan blocked Heidi on N4, and that no-kill night got her hanged.

tip: A blocker should hit the most suspected possible Katana holder each night and publish the full log. Two blocks followed by a night with no kill, confirmed by a blocked player, make a strong mechanical case.
evidence: Ivan blocked Mallory on N2 and Heidi on N4, and neither night had a Katana kill. Olivia confirmed she was blocked on N3, so the town trusted Ivan's log over Heidi's 'second Pharmacist' defense.

tip: Spend guesses on roles that matter if right, such as Serial Killer on an unverifiable Vanilla claimant, rather than repeatedly guessing Grunt on players likely to be another Yakuza role.
evidence: Erin wasted N1 and N2 on 'Grunt' guesses (Bob was a Jester, Mallory a Clerk). On N3, Erin guessed Serial Killer for Rupert, who had claimed Vanilla early. It was right and led to his hanging.

tip: Don't volunteer a Vanilla claim early when nobody has pressed you. An unprompted, uncheckable Vanilla claim becomes a natural target for exact-role checks.
evidence: Rupert claimed Vanilla on D2 during Bob's trial without being asked. Erin later said she guessed him as SK because 'the SK had to be hiding behind' an unverifiable Vanilla claim.

tip: A day PM between two players proves nothing about alignment until both have flipped. Don't treat 'PM'd a flipped Yakuza' as confirmation of anything.
evidence: The town's whole case against Bob rested on his D1 PM to Niaj, and Bob was a Jester, not a teammate.

tip: Yakuza will kill a Cardinal to get a second Good death from the Divine Attack, so a Cardinal should not stay a silent, unprotected target. Name a trusted checker in your will and ask for protection early, since a claimed Cardinal can't prove the role.

A Not Evil result on the Katana holder is not clearance, since the holder reads Good that night. Before hanging on an Evil or Not Evil result, check whether the checker could have been visited by the Katana, and whether the result matches revealed Yakuza roles such as Clerk, Diviner or Mortician.

When one player PMs several others and then pushes a nomination before any night result, record who was PMed and who followed. An Executioner pushing a target looks exactly like a Yakuza bloc, so require a checkable result before voting Yes.

A death reported as cleaned by a Mortician hides the role, so a missing role is not evidence. Track which Mortician clean matches which death, and treat a Mortician claim as checkable only when the clean target's outcome can be tested.

A Katana kill on a Cardinal is worth two Village deaths, since the Cardinal's death gives a random living Good player a Divine Attack. When you hold the Katana, check for a Cardinal before picking a weaker target.

Never publicly announce a trial vote and then switch at trial without a stated, checkable reason. Ivan's 'I'm voting Guilty' followed by Innocent gave the Village a concrete lead and got him hanged on Day 5.

A Clerk rig executes the nominee, so it is a kill tool, not a save. Plan it in night chat for a Day when the Village's likely nominee is a Good player, and don't let the token sit unused while a teammate is being pushed toward the rope.

An Executioner who privately asks several players for Yes votes on one target before any night result is pushing their own win path. Test whether the target matches their goal and ask them to name one thing they verified.

Executioner revenge after a hanging is a random Divine Attack on a Guilty voter, and that voter can be a Yakuza. Before voting Guilty on a Neutral's push, check whether that vote could expose a teammate to the revenge.

applies_to: Yakuza who hold a Yakuza-listed role such as Mortician, Clerk or Diviner
tip: Those roles read Evil to the Sheriff. Claiming one publicly invites an Evil check that the Village can use to hang you, so claim a role whose result cannot be checked against your alignment, or keep quiet about it.

Before killing a claimed Cardinal, count the Divine Attack its death triggers on a random living Good player. It can be worth two Village deaths, but only if your own claimed role will not be the next thing the Village checks.

When one player pushes Yes or Guilty privately before any night result, check whether the target matches a Neutral Executioner's target. A private push that lines up with one trial's target is a lead, not proof, so ask what they verified.

Before voting on a trial, ask whether the accuser's check came from a single source. A lone Sheriff result is weaker than several results that agree, so require at least one independent check before a hang.

A Not Evil result on a player who later proves to be a Katana holder tells you nothing, because the holder reads Good that night. Post such results with that caveat and don't use them to clear anyone.

When an Archivist or other list is public, check each claimed role against it daily. Roles on the list that belong to Yakuza (Clerk, Diviner, Mortician) make a Good claimant of that role suspect, which lets you test claims against each other.

Before voting on a nomination, ask who gains if this player hangs, and check that before the Day-1 or Day-2 push starts. An Executioner's early push for one target, backed by private messages before any night result, is a signal to test first.
Ask a player who pushed for a nomination what they privately verified, and treat repeated pressure without a new result as a lead on the pusher, not a check on the target.
Trial votes count against the revealed total, so a player who announces Guilty and then votes Innocent gives the Yakuza a free save. Ask them to explain before the trial, not after.

A Cardinal's death gives a Divine Attack to a random living Good player, so a Yakuza Katana kill on a Cardinal can cost the Village two players. Village should protect a claimed Cardinal when possible, and Yakuza should count that as a double kill.

applies_to: Archivist or any Village player holding an archive or survey list
tip: Mark each listed role that is unclaimed and belongs to the Yakuza (Clerk, Diviner, Mortician, Ballot Stuffer) as a suspect slot, and check each new claim against that list every Day. Do this before the first nomination, not after one.

Before hanging on a single power result, ask whether any second source checks it. Dave's Sheriff results were the only checks, and the Village hanged three players on them. Accept the risk only when the claimant has survived or been protected, and say so in your vote reason.

When one player pushes a nomination through private messages before any night result exists, treat that as a possible Executioner or Yakuza lead. Ask what they verified themselves. A neutral Executioner won by getting its target hanged, which the Village did on Day 3.
Claim early, post a result each night, and keep the result in your will. Public results and wills made the claims checkable and the Village's slot math possible after several deaths.

applies_to: Surveyor, Diviner, Archivist and any group-based investigator
tip: Group results only narrow a role to a candidate set. Intersect the sets across nights and post the surviving candidates, not a single claimed conclusion. Two overlapping trios can rule out a claim faster than any one result.

Pick a target early and privately ask voters for a Yes before any night result exists. A Village that trusts visible PM clusters and vote pushes will hang the target without evidence, which wins the Executioner the game.

applies_to: everyone, especially Yakuza and Village players tracking a Cardinal
tip: A Cardinal's death gives a Divine Attack to a random living Good player. Killing a suspected Cardinal can cost the Village two players, so count that before choosing a Katana target, and treat a dead Cardinal's death as a second death to plan for.

A Sheriff result on a Katana holder reads Not Evil by design. Discount Not Evil results on players who may have held the Katana that night, and only trust a Sheriff's Evil results on players with a matching revealed role.

A Standard Katana hit on a player that a Medic protects every night just fails again. After one failed hit on a protected target, switch to a different target or kill the Medic first, instead of retrying the same player.

Settle a fake claim before the first trial. Bob's Vanilla lie on Day 1 never explained the Sheriff's Evil result, and he was hanged. A lying teammate with a power-role claim needs an answer ready for the first contradicting result.

A winning Executioner leaves the game, and their revenge kills a random Guilty voter from the trial the following night. Before a Guilty vote on an Executioner's target, count that cost. Repeated Yes pushes on one target before any night result are the pattern to test.

Don't build a Yes-vote coalition by private message before any checkable result. Sender and recipient of every PM are public, so a Day 2 PM asking two players to vote Yes on your target became the case against you. Argue for your target in public on one concrete point, and PM only to share information.

A Cardinal's death is a second death: at the start of the next Day a random living Good player takes a Divine Attack. Count that victim into your vote math and survival plans before treating a Cardinal as a safe or unsafe lynch. The Yakuza used this on Day 4 to take Erin.

Cross-check claims against the archive's role list. Clerk, Diviner, Mortician, Ballot Stuffer and Wiretap are Yakuza roles, so a Good player claiming one of them is lying, and a Yakuza claiming one is exposed once the list is public. Use this to test claims instead of repeating suspicions.

Don't claim a role the public archive lists as Yakuza-only. Carol's Mortician claim got her hanged on the list alone, and her clean results on Dave (who survived) gave the town nothing to check. Stay quiet or claim a Village role the list doesn't mark as Yakuza.

Never announce 'I'm voting Guilty' and then vote Innocent without a new check. Ivan's public flip gave Judy and Olivia an easy nomination and hanging on Day 5. If your read changes, say the new check before the vote, not a repeated argument afterwards.

Never publicly announce a vote you won't cast. I posted that I was voting Guilty on Carol, then voted Innocent, and that mismatch became the lead that got me nominated. Keep your stated stance or say nothing.
Lock the Katana holder and target before the Day ends, not during the night. Late target switches cost a whole night, and the Medic kept covering the old target while the team argued.

A Night 1 Evil result on a player who claims Vanilla is the most checkable claim in the game. Demand a one-sentence answer and a second check early. Bob's silence hanged him on Day 3 with no independent confirmation.

Standard protection on a claimed investigator every night was decisive: the Katana failed on Dave twice. Keep protecting the same investigator while the threat persists, and stay alive to protect again.
Use Ballot Stuffer tokens on the trial that is actually close rather than holding them. I kept both tokens unused, and the trials that mattered were decided by more than the extra vote.

Rate a power claimant as credible only after a result matches a revealed role (for example, a Sheriff Evil on a Clerk or Mortician, both Yakuza roles) or survives a Katana attack. Treat a Katana holder's Not Evil as no evidence.
If you announce a vote such as 'I'm voting Guilty', don't flip without naming the new fact in the same post. An unexplained flip becomes the case the town hangs you on.
Spend prosecution tokens on your strongest lead while the Day's Yes pool is stuck, rather than holding them. I kept both tokens unused, so no trial was forced while the Yakuza kept the Katana alive.
Before reading any alignment check, record who held the Katana that night from the public holder announcements. A holder reads Good, so a Not Evil on them tells you nothing about their alignment.
When a PM cluster pushes a Yes vote before any night result, ask each partner publicly what was said, then vote on their answer rather than on the pattern alone.

Vary your protection target. Repeating Standard protection on one player for several nights made my pattern predictable, and the Katana holder switched to hitting me on Night 4. Once you are claimed, consider spending a token to self-protect on nights when a kill is likely.

A Katana holder reads Good, so a Not Evil result on a Yakuza holder proves nothing. Dave's Not Evil on Grace and on Ivan were both consistent with a Yakuza holder. Weigh alignment results only after checking who held the Katana that night.

Count independent sources before weighing a claim. One Sheriff's three results all came from one role, and repeating them on several Days is still one check. Ask which results could be false, and which ones are supported by a second source such as a revealed death or the Archivist's list.

A player who pushes a nomination before any night result, then asks others for Yes votes in private, is a coordination signal. Ask that player to name what they verified before anyone votes, and watch whether the same bloc votes together on later trials.
Repeated lines like still no reads cost budget and add nothing. Short posts that name one check, one claim, or one question are more persuasive and leave budget for trials, where votes are decided.

Before voting Guilty on a single hard check, ask which other checks would have to be false for it to be wrong, and whether the same source produced every related claim. Demand one result that can be tested against a later night's outcome.

Pushing for Yes votes privately before any night result (as Heidi did with Dave and Niaj) is a strong coordination signal. Ask the pusher to name one verified fact on the record, and treat the answer as a lead on their side, not just a dodge.

When a Mortician claim is public and a Katana kill follows a clean, check whether the clean was on a real target. Mortician claims are cheap for Yakuza, so weigh them against Lookout and Medic visit logs instead of trusting them outright.

A token given to a player with a Medic role is only useful if you know which Medic is real. Before handing a token, verify the claimant against a second source such as a Lookout visit log or a surviving protection result.
Switching votes publicly after announcing a stance (Ivan's Guilty then Innocent) gets punished by the table. If you must switch, announce the reason before the vote, not after it is noticed.

A Katana holder reads Good to Sheriffs on the nights they hold it, so a Not Evil result on a suspect proves little. Before using a clean result, check the Yakuza night summaries to see who held the Katana that night.

Cross-check archive or survey lists against alignments. Clerk, Diviner, Mortician and Ballot Stuffer are Yakuza roles, so a Good player claiming one is lying or misclaiming. Use this as a mechanical lead before a Guilty vote.

Do not hang on one unrebutted check. Bob and then Carol were both hanged on the same Sheriff source. Before a Guilty vote, ask for a second independent source or a result a later night can test, and vote on evidence rather than on who pushed the nomination.

Private Yes requests for one target before any night result signal a target-driven push. Ask who gains if that target hangs, since a Neutral Executioner wins only through one specific hanging, and whether the requester has verified anything.

Spend watches on players most likely to be Katana holders or victims, such as suspected Yakuza, rather than on a claimed protector. Two of my four watches on the Medic showed nothing useful, while a watch on a Yakuza suspect would have shown holder visits.

Never fake-claim or truthfully claim a role that exists only on the Yakuza side (Mortician, Clerk, Diviner, etc.). Agree a safe Village fake claim in night chat before a neighbour-based survey or slot math can corner you. Pick one that fits the unseen archive slots and matches your token count.
evidence: Frank's Night 2 survey (Carol, Dave, Erin contain a Sheriff) forced Carol to claim. She said Mortician, and Olivia immediately noted that a Good player can't be a Mortician. Dave's Night 3 Evil check finished her, with 6 Guilty to 2 on Day 4.

tip: The Cardinal's curse hits a random living Good player, so killing a confirmed Cardinal is a two-for-one for the Yakuza, not something to avoid. Re-read death-trigger roles to see which side they actually punish.
evidence: On Nights 2-3 the Yakuza first avoided Alice as 'dangerous'. Grace corrected this, they killed Alice on Night 3, and the curse killed Erin, the Archivist.

tip: If a teammate's hang is mathematically certain, bus them all the way, Yes and Guilty. Never publicly announce Guilty and then vote Innocent: a lone, futile Innocent next to a flipped Yakuza is the easiest lead the town will get.
evidence: Ivan said 'I'm voting Guilty on Carol' but voted Innocent, and she was hanged 6-2 anyway. Once Carol flipped, that switch was the whole Day 5 case against him, and he was hanged 5-1.

tip: Free Standard protection on a claimed investigator works early. But once you are claimed and the investigator's protector is obvious, spend a token to protect yourself or rotate targets. Tokens you never spend do nothing.
evidence: Mallory saved Dave from the Katana on Night 2, then guarded him again on Nights 3 and 4. She died to the Katana on Night 4 holding 3 medic tokens, one of them just handed to her by Niaj.

tip: Post every result with its target in your first speech after getting it. Attach the Katana caveat to every Not Evil. A string of results that later match flipped roles becomes the town's backbone.
evidence: Dave posted Bob Evil (Clerk), Grace Not Evil (she held the Katana), Carol Evil (Mortician) and Ivan Not Evil (flagged as a likely holder) promptly. Every Village vote from Day 3 on rested on his record.

tip: Pressure your target from Day 1 so they make a weak claim. Then attach yourself to the first hard result against them, keep repeating it, and stay calm when your vote-soliciting PMs are questioned.
evidence: Heidi's Day 1 pressure pushed Bob into a Vanilla claim. She then hammered Dave's Evil result. Her PMs drew suspicion, but Bob was hanged on Day 3 and she won.

tip: When a Katana kill follows a Yakuza hang, the holder must be one of the remaining living players. Combine a Not Evil-while-holding read with flipped players' voting partners to find the last Yakuza instead of chasing PM traffic.
evidence: After Mallory's Night 4 death, Judy linked Ivan's Innocent vote for Carol to Dave's Not Evil on him. That got the right hang on Day 5, while Ivan's deflection onto the Heidi-Judy PMs failed.

tip: Treat 'withheld then mirrored' claims as the strongest behavioral tell. When someone is pressured for a result and only produces one after an opponent's claim is public — and it conveniently mirrors that claim — weight that sequence far above the claim content itself. A real investigative role leads with results; a faker builds them backwards.

Trackers and Lookouts should announce their target choice publicly at the end of each day ('tonight I track X, result posted tomorrow'). This commits you before results exist, makes your later reports unfakeable-by-retrofit, and turns your death into verified information since your will and statements can be cross-checked.

Medics don't receive feedback on whether their protection stopped an attack. Never say 'I saw' or claim confirmation — say 'my protection is consistent with their survival.' Vigilantes: one well-reasoned shot on a contradicted claim beats saving tokens; two confirmed evil flips can swing the whole game, but coordinate targets the day before so your shots aren't wasted on claimed protectors.

Always demand that every living player name a specific strongest suspect with reasoning each day, even if they decline to nominate. 'No case, no nomination' repeated for days is free cover for evil. Forcing ranked suspicions creates a voting record that can be checked against flips later — and it flushed out real cases multiple times.

Don't fake-claim protective roles against a living real protector — duplicate Medic claims with identical protection histories create an unwinnable 1v1 the town can afford to resolve by hanging both. Instead, claim roles whose actions are invisible (Vanilla, or an investigative whose 'results' you keep private), and use Fabricator frames to make real Village investigative results look compromised.

Katana votes need a majority. If a teammate is inactive or never votes, a two-person Yakuza can't reach agreement, and no attack happens. Pass the Katana to the most reliable member early, and don't count on a passive teammate's block or vote in your plan.

Don't fake-claim a role whose actions a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict. Example: claiming Medic after a Lookout saw you visit an attacked player forces a 1v1 that a Vigilante can resolve by shooting you. Prefer claims with no visits (Vanilla), or kill the info role before making the claim.

A Katana attack that fails while the attacker gets no block notice usually means protection, or that the target has innate Defense (SK/Arsonist). Track which players survived attacks and flag a possible neutral killer. A hidden Arsonist or SK who claims Vanilla can quietly survive into the endgame.

Voting No on a nomination of an exposed teammate, or voting Innocent with them as a block, creates a pattern a Vigilante will act on. Spread out your votes, and sometimes vote with town against a teammate who is already doomed, to protect your own read.

When the Vigilante is unidentified and still has shots, prioritize killing the likeliest Vigilante early, before the Lookout or other talkers. Each Vigilante shot on a Yakuza costs you more than any information role does.

Separate suspicious behavior from mechanically disproven claims. Delayed results, awkward wording, and duplicate role claims justify questions, but do not establish a lie. Before executing, identify what evidence distinguishes deception from an honest mistake, framing, or a Roleplayer.

Use Basic shots against strong suspects without known defense to preserve tokens for additional targets. Prioritize contradictions grounded in a player's own claimed knowledge—for example, claiming to know someone attacked while later treating that same person as a possible genuine protector.

A visit identifies a destination, not an action or alignment. Tracking a Medic claimant to their claimed patient cannot distinguish protection from a Katana attack. Also, killing an attacker at night does not cancel their simultaneous attack.

Ask surviving claimants for a compact night-history table: night, target, result, and attack/block notices. After repeated nonanswers, stop spending discussion on the same question; compare independent evidence and alternative explanations. Evasiveness is a concern, not automatic proof of evil.

Keep hostile Neutrals in the suspect pool after Yakuza deaths. A Not Evil Sheriff result or a plausible Vanilla claim does not exclude an Arsonist or Serial Killer, and eliminating all Yakuza does not guarantee a Village win.

Before trusting a visit-tracking result, cross-check it against independent public claims (e.g., a Lookout's watch log); a tracker's visit reports are only as strong as the corroboration, so cite the exact target and result early rather than letting others force you into defensive promises.

Explain your reasoning for every nomination or Yes vote in one concrete sentence on the day it happens; vague or delayed justifications and 'I'll answer tomorrow' deferrals were repeatedly read as dodging and drove several executions.

applies_to: Village roles facing a Medic or Sheriff counterclaim
tip: When two players claim the same role, avoid mirroring the other's wording or protections; check whether a claim is independent before it is used as a tiebreaker, since copied claims made the Medic dispute impossible to resolve.

Coordinate protection and tracking targets through private messages only when you can disclose them later; the public PM graph was used as evidence against several players, and secret target-picking by one player looked like coordination.

Avoid spending the day repeating agreement or 'no nomination' statements; give specific reads or a question with a deadline, because the stall rule and the small living group meant unanswered suspicion and empty turns eventually decided who was hanged.
Leading the day with an early, confident investigative report against your target forces them into a defensive posture where any delayed counterclaim appears reactionary and retrofitted to town.

When an unverified Sheriff claim appears on Day 2 with an Evil check, consider the possibility of an Executioner push before rushing a Guilty verdict, particularly if the accused player genuinely fights to survive rather than acting like a Jester.
Publicly acknowledging private messages and providing brief, consistent summaries prevents opponents from using public PM notifications as ammunition to allege suspicious backroom coordination.

applies_to: Yakuza / anyone fake-claiming a protective role
tip: Before counterclaiming a role, assume the real holder is alive and will claim the identical night history. A duplicate claim makes it a coin flip, and any later flip of the real role exposes you. Prefer a role with an unverifiable history, or a claim of Vanilla. Then explain your visit as something no living player can contradict.

applies_to: Fabricator / any evil player with a fake will
tip: Keep your last will in sync with your current public claim every day. A will that contradicts what you said publicly (e.g. Vanilla vs Medic) proves the lie on death and hands town free info.

Don't publicly accuse someone and then vote No on their nomination. The mismatch between your read and your vote is exactly what Vigilantes and townies punish. If you must save someone, frame it consistently from the start.

Verify that every teammate actually submits night actions. An idle Pharmacist across multiple nights wastes blocks that would have landed kills or broken tracks. Pick redundant plans that still work if one member does nothing.

When a Lookout or Tracker is publicly active, pass the Katana to a member who has no claimed role and no reason to visit. Also kill or block the info role first. A visible visit to the attack target is the main way evil gets caught.
Medics never receive success feedback on protection; avoid claiming you 'saw' an attack stopped. Explain survival by inference only, and state that plainly when pressed.

Tracker and Lookout results only show visits, not alignment or intent. Before treating a visit as evil, check whether the visitor could be a protector, a framer, or a Katana holder, and whether the visit fits a known role's night action.

Fabricators and Arsonists can fake protection or role claims and push wills; a will that names the wrong role or contradicts public history is itself evidence. Track which claimed roles conflict with each other and weight claims by checkable consistency.

Avoid private-message clusters right after claims or votes; get the content of DMs summarized publicly early, since unexplained side channels became the main suspicion source and cost players credibility.

Avoid hanging a likely protector on a tie. When two claimants of the same role exist, collect independent evidence (a direct observation, a different role's result) before any vote, since failed nominations and wrong hangs both drained Village power roles.

every publc message you send is a commitment device - if you say 'no nomination until X answers', the entire table will hold you to it and use that constraint against you when the moment comes. pick commitments you can actually enforce.

your only real power is pattern-matching across days, so keep a running private tally of who voted what on each trial and who changed position and when. do not rely on memory in the heat of a trial. i lost my own trial partly because i could not crisply cite the vote-symmetry data that would have countered Bob's framing.

tracking the same player twice in a row is almost never the right call unless you expect them to change targets. a no-visit result on a stay-home Yakuza tells you nothing, so prioritize targets who are *claimed* to have night actions - that way a mismatch is informative rather than ambiguous.

when two players make identical role claims, the tiebreaker is almost never the claim text itself. it is who answers follow-up questions first, who answers them without being asked twice, and whose story requires the fewest assumptions about other roles. in this game i correctly identified Grace as real Medic but for the wrong reason - i anchored on Frank's flip rather than on Grace's consistent protection narrative. next time, build the positive case for each claimant before the flip tells you the answer.

a player who has been silent for many days and then suddenly produces a concrete read on someone is worth scrutinising hard - the silence itself is not guilt, but the timing of the pivot is a signal. in this game Bob went from four days of 'no nomination' to naming me as top suspect the moment the board state changed, and i flagged it but did not push hard enough before the vote.

Submit your role-block every night. I skipped it on nights 1-4 while teammates built plans on it, so kills failed and the plan collapsed. If the plan relies on you, act or say clearly in the chat that you won't.

Confirm the Katana vote explicitly in the night chat each night. A mismatched or missing vote cancels the attack entirely, and holder/target must have majority agreement. Reply with the exact agreed holder and target.

Don't keep voting No on nominations of a teammate's victim or on the same side as exposed teammates. Once a teammate flips Yakuza, everyone who defended or voted with them gets scrutinized, so distance yourself early and cast votes with town majorities.

Avoid wasting Yakuza votes on Innocent for a likely-Village power role. My Innocent on Judy got flagged later. Also, a late-game Vanilla claim with no reads gets targeted, so build a few concrete public reads early.

Executioner and Jester claims warp Day 2 trials. An early fake Sheriff Evil result against a counterclaimant can be an Executioner trying to get their target hanged. Treat the target as likely Village and the claimant as suspicious.

Never withhold your night result to bait a counterclaim. A real Sheriff who sits on an Evil result looks like a fake, and that cost me the game. Post the target and result the moment someone challenges you, or in your first speech after the result.

If someone claims Sheriff and says you are Evil, consider Executioner or Jester as well as Fabricator. They read Evil to Sheriffs and gain from your hang. Counter with your result and the possibility that they are a neutral, rather than only calling them a liar.

Do not hang a Sheriff claimant on a delayed-answer argument alone. Early hangs on 1v1 claims often hit Village power roles or feed an Executioner. Prefer waiting a day, since the one-day delay is cheap.

On Night 1, investigate a player who is likely to make a public claim or is already prominent, and prepare to disclose the result right away. An early Sheriff result is worth more as public information than as a hidden bait.

Cross-check claims against independent visit data such as Lookout and Tracker results. Players whose results are verified by a second source are probably real. Contradictory duplicate claims are best resolved through those sources rather than through speech style.

A delayed counterclaim is suspicious, not decisive. Before executing a Sheriff claimant, test both reported results against framing, duplicate roles, Roleplayers, and Executioner incentives. A confident first accusation can be deliberately engineered to make a truthful response look fabricated.

Separate observations from actions and alignment. Tracking confirms destinations; watching identifies visitors. Neither distinguishes protection, framing, or a Katana attack. Ask what competing explanations a proposed investigation would actually eliminate before treating tomorrow's result as a tiebreaker.

Prioritize contradictions between a player's own accepted premises over awkward wording. Someone who claims to have protected an attacked target and accepts a complete two-person visitor list cannot also excuse the other visitor as merely a second protector without revising a premise. Ask explicitly which premise they reject.

Before a dangerous night, put your strongest current contradiction and any important private reply into your will. Wills update only at the beginning of the day, so later discoveries should also be shared promptly with another player or publicly; private evidence dies with you otherwise.

Choose watches for likely visitors, not just trustworthy targets. An exposed investigator or probable kill target can reveal both attacker and protector. Repeating a watch on a quiet player may produce less actionable information than watching someone whose visitors can test an unresolved claim.

Douse players likely to still be alive on ignite night, not active killers or today's lynch targets. Dead douses are wasted nights. Before each night, count living non-you: you need that many successful douses plus one ignite, and you cannot enter a three-player day with zero living douses.

Ignite is a Strong Astral attack, so it is invisible to Lookout and Tracker but loses to Strong Defense: attack must be strictly higher. A Medic who can still spend a token on themselves survives ignite. Douse is an ordinary visit. Never douse on a night a confirmed Tracker has publicly committed to tracking you.

A permanent no-info Vanilla claim becomes the default hang once real power roles are cross-confirmed. Build a specific, checkable behavioral record early, and have a visit-explaining soft claim ready before the field shrinks to you versus two corroborated Village roles.

At three alive, two Yes is a majority and a wrong hang cannot be undone; at two, one No blocks every trial. Do not wait to be the only unconfirmed player opposite an allied pair. Force doubt between the confirmed roles while you still have douses banked.

Weight a night claim by whether an independent result already confirmed the same destination, not by how often the player repeats it. Corroborated visit info is real; it still does not prove alignment or what the visit did.

As Executioner, fake-claim Sheriff early and give an Evil result on your target with a simple, believable reason. If your target answers late, many players will read their counterclaim as retrofitted.
evidence: Erin claimed she investigated Judy and got Evil, with a plausible reason ('last to speak, carbon-copy answer'). Judy held back her real result and then gave a mirror Evil result on Erin. The town hanged Judy 8–4 and Erin won.

tip: When two players claim Sheriff and accuse each other, remember that a Jester or Executioner also reads Evil to a Sheriff. In that case, each claimant's Evil result on the other can be true at once. Don't hang a claimant on 'who sounded better'. Hold the trial until there is a way to tell them apart, or check the claims mechanically.
evidence: Judy's Erin-Evil result was real, since Executioner reads Evil. Frank and Carol raised the Executioner possibility, but the town still hanged Judy. That gave Erin the win, and Erin's revenge killed Alice.

tip: When someone counterclaims your role or accuses you, lead with your concrete target and result right away, and keep your last will up to date. If you withhold results and then reveal them later, it looks fabricated, and a stale will hurts you after death.
evidence: Judy dodged several requests before naming her result on Erin. Her will still said 'no investigation results yet', so voters read her result as made up after the fact.

tip: Actually submit your agreed night action and your Katana vote every night. If one teammate goes inactive, the kill fails and teammates lose protection.
evidence: Ivan was asked again and again to role-block Mallory, Grace and Dave, and did nothing on N1–N4. On N4 he voted no holder and no target, so Bob's kill on Carol never happened. If Ivan had blocked Grace on N1 or N2, those Katana kills would likely have landed.

tip: Don't make a fake role claim that a confirmed info role's results can contradict. Once you accuse someone, keep your votes consistent with that accusation.
evidence: Frank fake-claimed Medic even though Mallory's Lookout result put him on Dave, which set up a 1-v-1 against the real Medic. He then voted No on Grace, the player he had called the Katana attacker. Carol shot him that night, citing exactly this contradiction in her will.

tip: Stay hidden and shoot players whose votes contradict their own stated reads. Claim publicly only after your shots confirm you, then use that credibility to push the town and to ask the Medic for protection.
evidence: Carol shot Frank on N3 and Bob on N4, both Yakuza, based on their vote inconsistencies. She claimed on Day 5, and her last shot on N5 killed Ivan even though the Katana killed her the same night.

tip: Protect the likely Yakuza targets: vocal analysts early, then claimed investigators. Free Standard protection on the same target night after night can carry the town.
evidence: Grace protected Alice on N1 and Dave on N2, and both Katana attacks failed. That kept Dave, the Tracker, alive long enough for his tracks to confirm Mallory's and Grace's claims.

tip: Don't douse forever. Ignite once the douses would swing the endgame, and in the final three make a real case instead of passively refusing to nominate.
evidence: Niaj doused Ivan, Frank, Heidi, Bob and Carol but never ignited. At three players he gave no reads, and Dave and Grace hanged him 2–1.

tip: After a teammate flips, don't immediately lead a push on a quiet Villager who argued against your fallen teammate's opponent. A Vigilante will read that as protecting the flipped player.
evidence: Bob drove the hang of Heidi on Day 4 right after Frank flipped Fabricator. Heidi died Vanilla, and Carol shot Bob that night, citing that push as her reason.

tip: Account for the Katana exception before clearing anyone: its holder appears Not Evil to Sheriffs investigating that same night, even if they die that night. Treat a result on a suspected holder as potentially misleading, not definitive.

Separate confirmed facts from interpretations, and verify details against the public ledger before making accusations. In particular, check who sent a private message—not just who received it—before using message history as evidence.

Treat a credible investigative result as strong evidence, but not infallible proof: consider role distortions such as Roleplayers, then weigh the result alongside flips and other checkable information. Make your vote reasoning explicit so later players can reassess it.

Coordinate Katana assignment and attack decisions with the Sheriff exception in mind. The holder's same-night Sheriff result can appear Not Evil, so use that cover carefully and anticipate how the attacker's identity and death pattern may draw scrutiny.

Agree on public-language boundaries as well as night actions. Never accidentally claim insider knowledge of a faction action—describe a death as a Katana kill, not “my Katana,” unless you intend to reveal your role.

Make forged wills mechanically plausible and consistent with what other players could have observed. Before submitting one, check whether its claimed action, target, and timing create useful doubt without contradicting later evidence.

If a partner is accused on a credible investigative result, challenge the result with a specific, plausible alternative rather than relying only on “it’s unverified.” Keep your voting and defense choices credible across the whole day.
Treat votes and private-message patterns as clues, not proof. Check the public ledger carefully—including who sent each message—and weigh those clues against confirmed flips and role mechanics.

Agree on a night plan that accounts for both the Katana attack and each member’s role action. Prioritize threats who can produce repeatable, checkable information, and use role-blocks to stop the most consequential action rather than automatically targeting the most obvious claimant.

Keep claims and accusations consistent with the public ledger. Message senders, votes, revealed roles, and announced deaths are checkable; a single factual contradiction can outweigh a plausible-sounding story.
Treat vote patterns as clues, not proof. Compare them with confirmed flips and specific behavior, and distinguish a weak or cautious vote from evidence of shared alignment.
Make claims concise, specific, and revisable. Extra explanations create more chances for contradictions; when you do make a factual claim, give enough detail that others can verify or challenge it.

Don't spend Night 1 with no protection. A Katana is a Standard attack, so Standard Defense on yourself or the most-threatened player blocks it, and a Medic with no protection is an easy Katana target. Keep one token for a Strong protection later.

Before voting on or accusing someone, check the claim against the public ledger yourself, including who sent each private message. Several accusations this game were built on reversed senders or unverifiable claims.

Don't execute on a single unverified investigative result when a counterclaim exists. Ask for corroboration first, and treat a Sheriff result as possibly coming from a Roleplayer or distorted information.

Name a concrete, checkable behavior for every nomination and vote. Long rounds of weak reads and 'no nomination from me' gave the Yakuza time to pick off Village roles unchallenged, so set a deadline for committing to a target.

Keep the Katana holder's public story consistent with what a Village player would know. Grace's 'my Katana' slip about a death before the cause was revealed exposed the holder and drew suspicion onto the whole team.

A Lookout only sees who visits the target, not what the target does. A Katana or other attacker is visible only through the victim's death and the attacker's visit, so when a Katana death occurs, check whether your watch target was the attacker before assuming they were safe. Consider watching suspected attackers, not only the most suspicious players.

Before accusing someone of a specific action, such as who messaged whom, re-read the public ledger for the sender and recipient. Erin's false claim about who messaged Carol was easy for others to disprove and damaged her credibility at the decisive trial.

A single investigative result that contradicts a later Roleplayer claim is not proof either way. Compare it against the other results and the actual trial outcomes, and avoid executing or accusing anyone on one unverified result unless other evidence supports it.

Watch for players who repeatedly vote Innocent together on suspects, especially when those suspects are later revealed as Yakuza. A consistent voting bloc is stronger evidence than any single vote, and Village should track these blocs across trials rather than judging each vote in isolation.

Do not let a loud bandwagon on one player substitute for a checkable case. Ask what specific behavior or fact supports each vote and whether the accuser's claims survive a quick check. Pressure and repeated nominations can push the Village into executing its own members.
Keep a ledger of exact public facts—especially who sent each private message, each vote, and what a role result actually says. Check accusations against it before treating them as evidence.

Treat nomination votes and trial votes as separate decisions. A Yes to a nomination only puts someone on trial; reassess after hearing their defense, and vote Guilty only if the evidence supports execution.

applies_to: Village investigative roles and their allies
tip: Calibrate investigative claims against possible interference or misleading results, such as a Roleplayer or Fabricator. Seek corroboration, but update decisively when a result is confirmed by a flip.

Separate a confirmed fact from an inference: a Katana death does not identify the holder, and sharing a vote with a revealed Yakuza is suspicious but not proof. State how strong each piece of evidence is.

Agree the Katana holder and attack target in chat before night closes, and avoid having the Katana holder be the one publicly named by a claimed Medic or Sheriff; the Katana holder should keep a low public profile on Day 1 and avoid the early push pattern that draws suspicion.

A forged last will is a strong tool only if it is consistent with the public record; a fake Medic will claiming protection of a player who was never a target can be checked against role-block results, so pick forgeries that cannot be disproven easily.

Verify claimed night results by cross-checking multiple roles (e.g. Lookout visits versus Sheriff results); a single unverified claim should not drive an irreversible execution, and claimed roles should be tested by asking for details that only the true role would know.

Votes on trials are public and become alignment evidence; avoid being the lone or paired Innocent voter alongside a player later revealed as Yakuza, and consider voting Guilty on a flagged player early to avoid looking aligned with them.

Role-blocking a Medic or Sheriff only works if the blocker acts before results resolve, and a blocked Sheriff still reveals to the block-maker; plan which Yakuza will be publicly exposed by which tokens and vote-trading before the Night 2 attack.

Hold tokens for claims you can cross-check, not one-sided accusations. Spending shots on unverified claims left me with no tokens when the Yakuza's Katana chain was still running, and Yakuza can role-block a Vigilante at night to waste the shot.

Before accusing someone, check their claim against the public record (vote history, message ledger, death reveals). Erin's Day 3 accusation reversed who messaged whom, and that error discredited her and cost the Village credibility.
Do not treat voting-pattern pairings as proof of alignment. Yakuza coordinate and can make innocent-looking votes, so judge each vote by the reason given and whether it can be checked.

Count factions explicitly each day. When the Yakuza hold the Katana and Village players keep trading eliminations, verify who is still alive and who could be Yakuza before executing or shooting; the Yakuza won with a Grunt and a Pharmacist still alive.

Claim a Village role that the Village cannot easily verify, such as Roleplayer or Sheriff with a contestable result, and use it to sow doubt on Village investigators. Coordinate votes publicly in ways that look like independent reasoning.

In the endgame, weigh hard links to flipped Yakuza over unverifiable claims. Examples are voting alongside confirmed evils on a key trial and receiving private messages from them. A claim that cannot be checked, such as Roleplayer, should not erase that pattern on its own.
evidence: Carol voted Innocent on Bob together with Bob and Grace, and both had privately messaged her on Day 1. Her post-hoc Roleplayer claim got her acquitted 1-3, and the Village lost two days later.

tip: Know who actually visits whom. A Katana attack is a visit from the holder to the target, so a Lookout watching the holder sees nothing. Do not build a case on a 'contradiction' that is really a misread mechanic.
evidence: Heidi called Erin's Night 1 result (nobody visited Grace) a contradiction of Grace killing Dave. In fact it was fully consistent, and the misread helped get the real Lookout hanged.

tip: At low player counts, a mislynch is often game-losing. Do not hang a role-claimer whose claim is consistent with the flips over a minor factual slip, especially when a stronger suspect is still alive. Ask what each faction gains from the hanging before you vote.
evidence: Erin's Lookout claim matched Heidi's shot on Grace. She was still hanged 3-1 for reversing who messaged whom, leaving Carol versus two villagers with a kill and a block.

tip: When you fake-claim, build the claim around information your team already created, such as your Fabricator's frame target. Then pivot pressure onto whoever voted against you. A tailored fake result that 'explains' your suspicious vote is very hard to disprove.
evidence: Carol claimed Roleplayer with 'Alice = Evil', matching Bob's Night 1 frame on Alice. She then immediately nominated Erin, the sole Guilty voter, and won the trial.

tip: Never phrase things from your hidden perspective in public. A slip like 'my Katana' hands Vigilantes and voters a free target.
evidence: Grace opened Day 2 with 'Dave died to my Katana in the night'. Heidi shot her that night with a single Basic token.

tip: Don't publicly hint at your role or its tokens on Day 1, especially a protective role, since it marks you as the first kill. If you have to signal, do it subtly or through a last will.
evidence: Dave said twice that he was 'holding my Medic tokens'. The Yakuza killed him Night 1 and role-blocked him to make sure.
