tip: Pair your role-block with your kill on the same target, or on the player most likely to shoot or protect. When the Pharmacist also holds the Katana, block the Vigilante every night; because the Pharmacist is block-immune, they can't be stopped.
evidence: Night 1: Carol blocked Dave while Grace killed him. Nights 3-4: Carol blocked Heidi, so both Vigilante shots fizzled, while Carol killed Frank and then Heidi.

tip: Don't announce when or whom you plan to shoot while a role-blocker may be alive. Telegraphing your intent lets evil block or kill you first.
evidence: Heidi said 'I'm deciding tonight' on Day 4. Carol simply blocked and killed her.

tip: Never publicly announce your night target before dawn; announcing targets gives the Yakuza free information about which players are threats and lets them block or hit you.
Do not vote Guilty on a player merely because they have no verifiable result; missing information caused by a block is not evidence of lying, so require a concrete reason before casting a trial vote.
Track who initiates private-message clusters and who repeats the same explanation; a coordinated triangle that pushes nominations early is a stronger signal than any single claim.

Before nominating, check whether the nomination pattern (who nominates, who votes Yes) matches a Yakuza bloc; avoid joining a push that has no new information, since such pushes are how Yakuza get a Village member executed.

A role-blocked night gives no result and no verifiable information; plan to use an alternate verifiable source (such as a Lookout or a claimed Medic who protected you) and ask for corroboration early rather than waiting for results that may never come.
Keep faction coordination concise. Private-message notifications are public, so repeated DMs among the same teammates create a visible pattern even when their contents are hidden.

Avoid piling onto a teammate’s unsupported push or matching their vote without an independent-sounding reason. Simultaneous votes are revealed, and coordinated pressure can become stronger evidence than the original target’s claim.

Plan attacks around role-block risk: the Katana attack is an action and can be stopped by blocking its holder. Coordinate who holds it with the rest of the night plan, and prioritize targets whose removal meaningfully reduces the opposing faction’s options.

Keep claims and public explanations consistent with the information you could actually have. A believable, limited account is usually safer than repeated claims that invite checks or require others to corroborate them.

applies_to: Lookout, Tracker, Sheriff and other information roles
tip: Log every night result the moment it posts and compare it against public claims before trusting any claim; avoid announcing your own future night targets, since that hands the Yakuza free information.

Do not cast a Guilty vote or push a nomination on suspicion alone; a vote you cannot justify with concrete evidence later looks coordinated and damages your credibility, as Bob's and Heidi's votes did.

Track who pushes early nominations and who repeats their DMs or votes; a small coordinated bloc (like Dave, Bob and Heidi) is a strong lead, and it's worth noting that the Yakuza tend to vote together.
Coordinate shots and protections privately with a trusted villager rather than publicly, and avoid revealing your role or intended targets to the whole table until you have verified information.

Remember that a role-blocked action leaves no result and no visit, so a missing result is not evidence of lying; check for block notices first and only treat contradictions between verified accounts as meaningful.

Remember that private-message contents are hidden, but the sender-recipient pattern is public. Keep coordination purposeful and restrained; a conspicuous triangle can become stronger evidence than anything said in the messages.

Before pushing a trial, identify the concrete evidence and explain why it supports the vote. Repeated nominations or matching guilty votes without new evidence make teammates look coordinated and can create a clear voting record for opponents.

Use framing and will-forging for specific, plausible purposes. Framing only affects investigative results that night; a forged will only replaces a target’s will if they die that night. Make forged evidence consistent with public claims and likely checks.

Reassess the night plan as new claims and threats emerge. The Katana attack, role-block, and other actions can all matter, but a predictable attack can be countered by protection or expose your priorities; weigh the target’s threat and likely defenses before committing.
Don’t spend turns restating settled points. Make each public message add a read, evidence, or a specific question, then let the day move toward a decision.

Treat each shot as a scarce resource: prioritize strong, converging evidence—such as a confirmed faction mate plus suspicious voting—over a single suspicious vote or behavior. Choose attack strength only as high as needed for the likely target and defense.

Separate facts from inferences. A role reveal or an independently confirmed action is stronger evidence than a pattern of private messages, a claim, or a vote; use those weaker signals to guide questions, not as proof by themselves.
Avoid publicly announcing future night targets. That gives opponents actionable information and can make your results easier to interfere with; share resolved results and feedback instead.
Compare voting behavior and explanations across players, but assess each person individually. Coordinated-looking votes are a useful lead, not automatic proof that every voter shares an alignment.
Keep discussion focused: once a point has been answered, seek new evidence or let the day move on. Repeating plans and arguments wastes turns and can expose useful information.

Protect the player with the most credible, most-targeted role early, but vary or hide your protection pattern; repeatedly protecting one player who is publicly announced makes you an obvious target and reveals your focus to the Yakuza.
Avoid repeating the same talking points for many turns; long loops of identical accusations waste the day and let the Yakuza blend in while the village stalls without new evidence.

Do not vote Guilty on a player merely because they lack verifiable results; a blocked or silent investigator produces no output, so demand concrete reasons before voting, and track who pushes nominations without new information.
Pairing up on early private messages and co-nominating creates a visible voting bloc that the village can trace; coordinate less conspicuously and split votes across different trials.

Share claims and night-result plans with a trusted partner privately rather than publicly announcing future targets, since public target announcements hand the Yakuza free information and invite Katana strikes on the claimed role.

Don't vote Guilty on a player just because they lack verifiable results; missing info from blocked nights is not evidence of guilt. Demand concrete reasons before voting, and be wary of a pair or trio pushing the same nomination.

Track who initiates coordinated private-message clusters and who co-nominates. Repeated early DMs among the same three players, followed by joint nominations, were the strongest signal of a Yakuza bloc in this game.
Avoid pushing the same nomination or trial repeatedly with the same allies; a visible voting bloc gets exposed when a Village role reveals or a Vigilante shoots one member.
Do not announce your intended night target publicly; it hands the Yakuza information for blocks and kills. Share only resolved results, and stay consistent about who you checked.

Before a trial, agree privately with other Village members on a concrete test, such as which votes to watch and which dawn results would change your vote, so the village votes together instead of drifting.

Private-message activity is publicly visible even when message contents are not. Keep coordination purposeful and restrained; a conspicuous cluster of messages can become a lasting lead for the Village.

Treat a failed Katana attack as evidence that the target may have defense or protection. Avoid blindly retrying the same target; reassess likely protectors and choose a different target or a stronger attack if available.
Make public claims and explanations consistent with your actual behavior. Weakly supported votes or shifting rationales can become powerful alignment evidence once another player is confirmed.

Night actions resolve simultaneously. Killing a Vigilante on a night they shoot does not stop that shot, so account for the possibility that a confirmed or suspected attacker will still act that night.
Don't send visible private messages to your teammates on Day 1. Use the night chat for planning. If you must DM, also message villagers so the pattern doesn't single out your team.
evidence: Dave DMed Bob and Heidi repeatedly on Day 1, and Heidi and Bob DMed each other. Carol, Erin, Grace and Frank named the 'Dave/Bob/Heidi DM triangle' all game, and Carol's and Frank's last wills pointed to it.

tip: Don't all vote the same way on a weak push against a claimed power role. Spread your votes, or let a non-teammate lead. A bloc of Guilty votes is evidence the town can use once one of you flips.
evidence: Dave and Bob nominated Alice on Day 3, and Dave, Bob and Heidi all voted Guilty while every villager voted Innocent. After Dave flipped Fabricator, Bob was hanged 4-1 on that vote record alone.

tip: Hold your shots until the evidence concentrates, then shoot the strongest lead with the cheapest attack that will work. A confirmed flip gives the town far more than the token costs.
evidence: Erin held fire on Nights 1-2. On Night 3 she used one Basic token on Dave, who started the DMs and led the Alice push. He flipped Yakuza, which led to Bob's hanging and later her Standard shot on Heidi.

tip: Protect a claimed investigator every night, and keep your own role hidden as long as you can. Once you claim Medic, you become the next target.
evidence: Frank's Standard protection saved Alice from the Night 1 Katana. After he claimed Medic privately and Alice acknowledged it in public on Day 3, the Yakuza killed Frank that night.

tip: Don't use forged wills or fake 'Vanilla' claims that will be contradicted by a role reveal. A will that is proven false on death confirms suspicion of your teammates. Save the forge token for a night when the target is actually likely to die.
evidence: Dave spent his only forge token on Night 1 on Alice, but Frank protected her and she survived. Later Dave's own will claimed Vanilla, and his Fabricator flip exposed it, which made Bob's identical Vanilla claim easy to reject.

tip: Treat survived attacks and repeated role-blocks as evidence that a power-role claim is real. Evil rarely spends a blocker and the Katana on a fake.
evidence: Alice survived a Katana hit and was blocked every night. Grace and Frank read this as Yakuza hunting a real Sheriff and voted her Innocent, which kept the true Sheriff alive.

tip: Remember that the Katana holder appears Not Evil, and framing exists. A Not Evil result on someone who is heavily implicated by votes should not clear them.
evidence: On Night 4 Alice checked Heidi and got Not Evil because Heidi held the Katana, even though Heidi was Yakuza.

tip: Don't publicly announce your night targets. It tells the Pharmacist whom to block and tells the killers where to strike.
evidence: Alice announced checks on Dave and then Heidi, and Bob blocked her every night. Carol announced she would watch Heidi, so the Yakuza moved the Katana to Dave and killed Carol on Night 2.

tip: Vary your public defenses across the game; the Yakuza's repeated 'Innocent on the one-draw trial' pattern and identical Village claims made the lone Yakuza easy to track.
Check the Jester's revenge and R1 interaction before voting: a Jester hanged by a three-player majority can still cause a win, so count which factions remain before any trial.
Keep the Katana holder's night votes and actions aligned with the chat plan each night; missing or changing votes wasted attacks.
Track each Arsonist-style douse count against visits: four ignitions require four prior douse visits, so a claimed no-visit player can be tested by that arithmetic.
Don't rely on a single vote-mismatch accusation; check the ledger for who actually voted what before nominating, since several accusations this game rested on misread votes.
Before any trial, work out what the hang does under R1 (Jesters excluded) and who wins if it passes. Stakes change the whole vote, and several players argued the R1 point without checking it.

A douse is a visit, so a Lookout on a doused target shows the douser. Count backwards from ignition victims: an Arsonist needs one douse visit per victim before igniting, so a claimed zero-visit Vanilla cannot have killed four people.

A Vanilla claim with zero visits is incompatible with holding a multi-kill plan. Pick a claim that fits your visit history, or lie about visits consistently, because a visible contradiction gets you hanged.

Strong self-protection costs 2 tokens, so a Medic with one token left cannot cover themselves against a Strong attack. Keep a token reserve for self-protection or pick protection targets that don't leave you as the only open kill.

Volunteering a side-observation on Day 1 (such as watching private messages) makes you the obvious target for the Yakuza and the table. Keep Day 1 remarks to concrete, neutral reads and save info-pattern talk for after you have a reason to raise it.

Don’t make your Jester goal too obvious by repeatedly voting Guilty on yourself or openly begging to be hanged. That can make players avoid executing you. Keep a plausible alternative explanation for suspicious behavior so others have a reason to vote Guilty.

Know exactly when your win is secured: a daytime hanging wins, regardless of how the game ends afterward. Don’t let another player scare you away from a trial with a false claim that a faction win check will erase your Jester win. Treat revenge as a separate effect: it targets a random living Guilty voter on the following night.

A visit result establishes a destination, not what action happened there. Eavesdropping, protecting, blocking, dousing, and attacking can all involve visits; compare the result with role mechanics and other evidence before concluding what the visitor did.

Separate nomination votes from trial votes, and calculate the actual majority from living players. A Yes vote only starts a trial; it does not commit that voter to Guilty. Don’t rely on an opponent’s promise about a future vote when the current vote and incentives are observable.

Treat an anonymous role sample as a constraint on a group, not an identification. Keep every eligible person in the set—including players who die that night—and seek an independent check before turning a probabilistic result into a guilty verdict.
Keep a verified vote ledger and distinguish nomination votes from trial votes. Check the record before accusing someone of a mismatch; a factual error can undermine an otherwise reasonable case.

applies_to: Investigators and anyone interpreting their results
tip: Check each role’s exact visit rules before drawing conclusions from a Tracker or Lookout result. A visit shows a destination, not the action performed, and no visit may mean no action, a role-block, or an Astral Visit.

Plan claims around what other players can observe, especially visits and attack outcomes. A counterclaim introduced only after an observed visit—and an earlier failure to mention a supposedly important action—can be more damaging than the visit itself.

Recalculate living players, strict-majority thresholds, and the consequences of a hang before relying on anyone’s promises or rule interpretations. Evaluate a Jester’s hang win, the faction end check, and revenge separately; one does not automatically erase the others.

Account for Neutral killing roles like the Arsonist early. When Katana kills stall or role-blocks explain missing kills, do not assume Town has total control; quiet nights can indicate an Arsonist quietly dousing targets for a mass ignition.

In endgames with a confirmed Jester and an evil killing role, understand the Jester's exact incentives under Rule R1. Executing the killer immediately ends the game in a Town victory and seals the Jester's loss, so Town cannot expect the Jester to cooperate without a concrete compromise.
A tracking result of 'visited nobody' does not clear a suspect: role-blocked players, Vanilla players, passive roles, and Astral actions (such as an Arsonist igniting) all show as visiting nobody.

When an Arsonist is suspected, publicly cross-reference visitor counts and Lookout logs against player claims immediately to identify who made untracked visits corresponding to douses before ignition occurs.

applies_to: Yakuza and anyone making a fake role claim
tip: Keep a claim consistent with what you have already said publicly. If you invent a night action to explain a caught visit, account for why you didn’t mention it earlier—especially if you previously endorsed another player’s claim about the same event.

Reconstruct possible actions night by night, and distinguish a visitor’s destination from the action they performed. An Eavesdropper visiting someone who later burns does not prove they doused them; a Lookout reports a visit, not its purpose.
Factor likely role-blocks into Katana-holder choices. A blocked holder cannot carry out the Katana attack even if the Yakuza agree on a target, so consider moving the Katana to a less exposed member.

applies_to: everyone, especially Neutral players negotiating at endgame
tip: Check the written win conditions before trusting an opponent’s claim about what a vote or death will do. A promise to help you later may be a stalling tactic, and an opponent’s faction often benefits if you believe their version of the rules.

Eavesdrop targets that send no PMs yield nothing; if the whole table is silent in private, spend the night on a visit that a Lookout or Tracker can read as a real action, or claim the role early so your visits are not read as attacks.

When a Lookout claim and a Medic claim are both live, check the Lookout's visitor lists against the Medic's protection log before trusting either; a claimed Medic who never reports a night's protection is a red flag.
Do not let one Jester who self-nominates become a repeated trial; once a Jester is confirmed by an Oracle, stop voting Guilty on it and focus the trial pool on remaining claimed roles.
Count the nominations needed for each day against living players; with three alive a two-vote pass is enough, so a single town vote plus a Jester can force trials and must be anticipated.
A Neutral Arsonist's douse can be invisible to Lookouts on a Standard-protected target; treat a Medic who protects the same person every night as a suspect for stalling, not as proof of innocence.

applies_to: Investigative roles and everyone weighing their results
tip: Treat group-sampling results as evidence about the group, not an identification of a particular player. State the uncertainty clearly and avoid turning a plausible inference into certainty without independent support.

applies_to: Everyone, especially Trackers, Lookouts, and players evaluating Arsonists
tip: A visit result establishes a destination, not the action performed. Check the role’s mechanics before inferring intent: for example, dousing is a visit, while igniting is Astral and cannot be seen by visit-based abilities.

Keep nomination votes and trial votes distinct: nominating someone only starts a trial, and a Yes vote is not a Guilty vote. Use the revealed vote record rather than memory, and compare trial votes with players’ stated positions.

Test claims against the full action and death ledger, including token use, visits, protections, and timing. A confident explanation or a role claim that fits one event is not proof; look for contradictions and consider plausible alternatives.

applies_to: Everyone, especially when deciding whether to hang a Jester
tip: Separate a Jester’s win from the faction end check: a daytime hanging fulfills the Jester’s win condition even if the game ends immediately afterward. Revenge is a separate effect on the following night, so check whether the game will still reach that night and who would be a Guilty voter.
Check the public ledger before making a case based on votes. Quote the exact trial vote and correct your own mistake promptly; a mistaken accusation can undermine otherwise sound reasoning.

A visit result establishes who went where, not what they did. Lookout and Tracker evidence can fit several actions, and visiting nobody does not establish a player's role or alignment. Treat an action as Astral only when the role rules explicitly say so.

Keep results at their actual strength: a random role sample or an alignment check is a lead, not an identified culprit. Account for framing, appearance modifiers, and the fact that night actions and results resolve simultaneously before narrowing the suspect pool.

Spend attack tokens in proportion to confidence. Prefer a well-supported target over a shot based mainly on a missing kill or a suspicious vote pattern, and account for the target's possible Defense and the attack level you can afford.

Independently calculate the result of each endgame vote: who is alive after the death, whether a faction win triggers, and whether a Jester's revenge can follow. Evaluate promises by incentives—an Arsonist has strong reason not to create a Jester revenge threat that could kill them.

Before endgame votes, check each role’s win condition and the order of win checks. A Jester’s win is earned by being hanged; don’t assume a later faction win erases it, and distinguish nomination votes from the Guilty votes needed to execute.

Use exact-role guesses to test claims that could change a trial, but state precisely what the result proves: a correct role guess confirms the role, not the player’s faction, actions, or every other claim.

Treat visit reports as evidence of destination, not purpose. Combine them with role mechanics: for example, an Arsonist must visit to douse, while a Lookout or Tracker alone may not identify what the visit did.

Do not rely on a promised future vote when the promiser’s incentives point the other way. Evaluate the immediate vote and what happens after each possible death, including any revenge attack and its eligible targets.

Protection gives no feedback, so a Medic should track which nights a Strong-protected target was actually attacked; use the no-death nights and the Lookout visitors to test whether a Strong protection really lands before spending the last token.

A public Lookout or Tracker report that names a visitor is the strongest evidence in a late game; when a Lookout and a claimed Arsonist conflict, ask the claimed Arsonist for the exact nights of their douses before a trial, rather than letting a Jester-adjacent vote decide it.

When the only living non-Jester threat is a Neutral Arsonist, a Jester who promises Guilty votes for a trial is a manipulation; the Village should not rely on the Jester's promise and should nominate and vote the threat directly while the trial math still works.

Check the win-check rule carefully before arguing that a hang ends the game: a Neutral left alive after a hang changes which factions remain, and players repeatedly argued the wrong outcome of an execution.
Watch for a player who repeatedly nominates a Jester or Executioner-type target and then votes against their own trial; the mismatch between nomination and trial votes is the clearest public tell.

In late-game scenarios where an evil killing role and a confirmed Jester hold kingmaker leverage, flatly refusing to grant the Jester a trial guarantees they will ally with evil to avoid an instant game loss. Town must negotiate revenge targets rather than giving ultimatums.

When an Arsonist ignites multiple players at once, immediately calculate the minimum number of douse visits required across previous nights; players with conflicting public visits or proven non-visiting roles can often be mathematically eliminated.

As a role-blocker, successfully blocking the Katana confirms an evil player, but town should execute that player by day rather than tying down the blocker indefinitely, freeing protective and disruption roles to address other threats like Neutral killers.

In endgames with a confirmed Jester and a killing Neutral, realize that Rule R1 causes the game to terminate immediately with a Town win if the Neutral is hanged. Because of this, the Jester will never vote Guilty on the Neutral if it guarantees an instant Jester loss; Town must evaluate taking the 50/50 gamble on Jester revenge rather than repeatedly stalling into night attacks.

When an Arsonist ignites N players at once, calculate the minimum N douse nights needed. Players confirmed visiting someone outside that burned pool on those nights (such as a Medic protecting a non-ignited target) can be mathematically eliminated from being the Arsonist.

Remember that Jester wins immediately upon daytime hanging, even if the revenge attack subsequently hits or ends the game. However, if you help Town execute the final evil player before you are hanged yourself, Rule R1 immediately ends the game with a Town win, permanently locking in a Jester loss.

Treat a publicly claimed, high-value exact role as a time-sensitive attack opportunity. Check whether the guess is reliable enough to justify spending tokens, and choose attack strength with likely protection in mind; a Divine Attack can still kill through Standard Defense.

Use role-block notifications as actionable team information. If the Katana holder is blocked repeatedly, reassess the holder, likely blocker, and target instead of repeating a plan that keeps getting canceled.
Prepare counterclaims and supporting details before a visit or result exposes you. A late claim that conflicts with what you said earlier can be more damaging than the original evidence.

When in an endgame with an outed Jester and Town, emphasize Rule R1 to the Jester: executing you immediately ends the game with a Town victory, locking in the Jester's defeat on the spot. Convincing the Jester that keeping you alive is their only mathematical path to staying in the game guarantees their defensive vote.

Douses remain on targets until ignited or removed by death. If an ignition fails due to Strong or Standard Medic protection, the player remains doused, allowing you to ignite them on a subsequent night once protective tokens expire without needing to re-visit and re-douse them.

Adopt a proactive Vanilla Villager persona early on by consistently supporting legitimate town wagons against confirmed evils. Building an unblemished voting ledger buys credibility in the late game when investigative roles try to isolate the killer by elimination.

After a multi-kill ignite, the Arsonist must have visited every victim on earlier nights. The prime suspect is a living Vanilla/no-action claimant nobody has watched, not a player with an explained visit. Point a Lookout or Tracker at unverified Vanilla claimants early, especially once Neutral killers are possible.
evidence: Rupert claimed Vanilla and was never tracked or watched from N1 to N5; he doused four players unseen and ignited. On Day 6 the town hanged Grace for visiting two victims, though her eavesdrop visits were already explained. Rupert's 'no visits' story was the real contradiction, and Grace and Mallory both raised it.

tip: Give the Katana to the member with no night action of their own (Wiretap, Grunt), and move it if the holder becomes exposed. Don't let a visiting role hold it and then fake a protector claim that overlaps one you've already endorsed.
evidence: Frank (Diviner) held the Katana all game while Alice (Wiretap) had no action. Olivia's Lookout saw Frank visit Heidi on N2. He had endorsed Mallory's Medic claim on Heidi on Day 3, so his Day 4 'second Medic' claim collapsed and he was hanged 10-2.

tip: When kills keep failing with no announced save, assume a role-blocker and kill them, or move the Katana. Once a Party Animal claims to be blocking your holder, kill that Party Animal before any information role.
evidence: Niaj blocked the holder on N3, N4 and N5, and from Day 4 publicly claimed to be blocking Frank and then Alice. The Yakuza aimed at Judy twice anyway and lost three straight kills; Alice died on N5 while blocked.

tip: Save a 2-token Divine guess for a publicly claimed power role who is likely to be protected. A confirmed claim removes the risk of a wrong guess outing you, and Divine Attack goes through any protection.
evidence: Heidi claimed Surveyor and Mallory protected her on N2, which stopped the Katana. Peggy's Divine Surveyor guess killed Heidi anyway without exposing Peggy.

applies_to: Village (endgame with a Jester and a solo killer alive)
tip: Passing a Jester's self-nomination is free, because you can still vote Innocent at trial. Pass it early so the solo killer must publicly vote on the hang he promised. A solo killer can't afford the revenge risk, so his promise will break, and exposing that wins the Jester's sympathy while you still have votes to spare.
evidence: On Days 8-9 Olivia and Mallory voted No on every Carol self-nomination, though Rupert and Carol voted Yes each time. Rupert's promise to vote Guilty went untested until Day 10, when he voted Innocent three times. By then Mallory was dead and Olivia (still doused) burned that night.

tip: Claim Vanilla, never visit anyone an investigator is watching, and redirect suspicion onto players with visible visits. In a small endgame, recruit the Jester with a promise to hang them, backed by the true fact that your death ends the game with them alive. That keeps the swing vote on your side.
evidence: Rupert pushed Grace on her visits to burned players, got her hanged on Day 6, then kept Carol voting No/Innocent on him for three Days with his Rule R1 argument until he ignited the last villagers.

tip: Don't vote Guilty on yourself in a trial that is clearly going Innocent, and don't openly invite the rope. Repeated self-Guilty votes make the town and an Oracle read you as Jester, so your later fake claims are discounted and nobody will hang you.
evidence: Carol's Day 1 surrender and self-Guilty votes led the town to call 'Jester bait'. Judy guessed Jester on N3 and was right, which voided Carol's fake Sheriff 'Evil' result on Olivia. From then on the town refused every Carol trial.

tip: Before using 'math' to clear a player, list every way the facts could fit. One observed visit does not use up a player's whole night history, and checking only N2 clears nobody of N1, N3 or N4 douses.
evidence: On Day 6 Olivia 'cleared' Mallory because Mallory visited Heidi on N2, though that only ruled her out of an N2 douse. Grace correctly objected, but the false clearance helped send Grace to the gallows.

tip: After a faction member flips, separate nomination votes from trial votes and revisit the nomination dissenters—even if they later voted Guilty. A later vote does not erase an earlier signal.

Prefer a shot supported by a concrete link to a flipped Yakuza, such as a shared No vote on their nomination, over a weak behavioral read. Use the lowest attack level that will kill an ordinary target so you preserve tokens.

Separate true alignment from what an investigation reports. A flipped role establishes true faction, but a frame or role-specific exception can explain a conflicting result; don't treat a claimed result as proof that the exception occurred.
A visit report identifies a visitor and destination, not the action. Combine it with the target's death, the visitor's claimed role and action, and swap mechanics before attributing an attack.

When two investigators conflict on one target, check which one's result is exposed to a Katana or Fabricator frame before weighing their pair results; a pair result that depends on an unverified first result inherits its uncertainty.
Post your own night target and visit in your first speech after the night, before the conflict escalates; players who keep deferring their visit info look like they are hiding a visit.
Vote No on a nomination only with a stated reason you can defend on trial; a lone No that later flips to Guilty after a new claim looks like a read-follows-vote pattern and reads as Yakuza.
A visit-watch result is strongest when it shows the same player as the only visitor to a victim, and a Smuggler swap would appear in that watch; use that to rule swap defenses in or out early.
Once a Yakuza is hanged, expect the remaining Yakuza to mirror the same vote; track which players voted No with the flipped members and check their next-night actions against those votes.

applies_to: Yakuza teammates facing a likely doomed nomination
tip: Do the nomination and trial vote math together. If a teammate cannot be saved, voting Yes and then Guilty gives you a consistent public position; voting No and then Guilty creates a conspicuous split for town to revisit.

Forge a will only when its details are plausible given what the target has said and what their role might be. An exact-role claim that conflicts with the flip can make the will obviously fabricated and waste the confusion you intended to create.

After a failed Katana attack, treat protection or innate Defense as likely and change the plan rather than retrying blindly. Also anticipate that a Lookout on the victim may identify the holder as a visitor, so prepare a consistent explanation for that visit before the day begins.

Have every living teammate submit the same Katana holder and target. Coordinated votes prevent a missing majority from canceling an attack, and night chat is the time to settle the plan and cover stories.

Treat wills as evidence, not ground truth: a Fabricator can frame a player and replace their will on the same night. A will that conflicts with the revealed role should not be used to accuse its named target without independent support.

applies_to: Investigators and anyone interpreting their results
tip: Keep appearance-based results conditional. A Seer's pair reports whether players appeared to have the same alignment that night; framing can change that appearance. Resolve relevant exceptions before assigning an alignment to either player.
After a Yakuza flips, review nomination votes as well as trial votes. A later Guilty vote does not erase an earlier No vote that helped protect the teammate from being put on trial.
A visit identifies a destination, not the action performed. Use other evidence—such as a Katana holder needing to visit their target—and account for swaps before deciding what a visit proves.

Keep your target and completed result in your will, clearly labelled as a result rather than a plan. Still expect that a Fabricator may replace the will, so avoid treating a public will as guaranteed authentic.

Do not let the holder be the lone visitor to a victim while a Lookout is alive. Judy's watch on Grace showed only Carol, and that single visit got Carol hanged. Pick a victim no Lookout watches, or cover the visit with a second Yakuza visit or a swap.

Swap tokens are the only self-defence: swapping yourself with a harmless player redirects a kill aimed at you. I died to a Vigilante with 2 swap tokens unused, so spend them on a night when a kill on you is likely rather than hoarding them.
Confirm the holder and target in night chat each night, and check whether a Lookout could watch the target before committing. A cheap watch check prevents a predictable lone visit.
A Vanilla claim collapses as soon as your visit is watched. If your role has a visit, prefer a claim that explains the visit (for example a Party Animal block) before a Lookout reports it.

When a Seer or Sheriff result conflicts with another claim, first check whether the claimant's result was reported as 'as appeared' (Fabricator frame, Ex-Con, Katana holder reads Good); then ask which claims could be false and post the night's visits so Trackers and Lookouts can cross-check before any trial.

A Lookout's 'only visitor' report on a Katana victim is strong evidence, but check Smuggler swaps: a swap aimed at the victim would show the swapper visiting the victim, so a lone visitor who denies a swap is more reliable than a visitor who says they were swapped.

Do not reverse a No vote on a nomination without a stated reason; when the nominee's claim changes after nomination, that switch is a concrete point to vote on, and it is worth naming in the speech before the trial.

Keep night chat plans short and avoid debating the framing target at length in public-facing messages; the Yakuza here kept sending the same Katana plan in every chat, which made the Night 3 choice predictable.

Remember that a Katana attack is a Standard attack: a Medic's Standard protection on the target makes the attack fail, so a successful Katana hit on a protected Medic-claim target is informative about who the Medic really protected.

A DIFFERENT result compares the alignments as they appeared that night, not necessarily true alignments. Before drawing a faction conclusion, account for framing and other appearance modifiers; state conditional possibilities when the result cannot distinguish them.

applies_to: Seer and everyone using investigation results
tip: Treat pair results as constraints, not identifications. A DIFFERENT pair says one differs from the other, but without a known alignment it does not reveal which player is Good, Evil, or Neutral. Combine it with independently established information and avoid claiming more than it proves.

When sharing a result, give the exact target or pair, whether it was chosen or random, and what the result does and does not establish. Correct an overstatement promptly and keep the correction consistent in your public claim and last will.

When a role flip clarifies an alignment result, say exactly what it establishes. Dave flipped Tracker, so if my Sheriff claim was true, his N1 Evil result required a frame; I should have stated that directly rather than repeatedly presenting it as merely possible.

Explain both what a result rules out and what it does not. Ivan reading Not Evil ruled out his later Ex-Con claim if my check was genuine, but did not clear him: a Katana holder can read Good, and some Neutrals read Not Evil.
Separate observed visits from inferred actions. A Lookout establishes who visited, not why; combine that result with the death, claims, swaps and other visitors before drawing a conclusion.

applies_to: Village players after a Yakuza flip
tip: Use a No vote on a teammate’s nomination as a lead, not a verdict. Check what information was available at each vote: Carol’s No on Ivan’s nomination and Guilty vote after his defense were worth scrutinizing, but the change itself needed context.

Before the team commits a Katana attack, check whether the target is a Medic who can self-protect; a Standard hit on a Medic with a token fails, so pick targets whose protection is already spent or unknown.

Avoid unnecessary Yakuza-chat agreement loops that just repeat 'Ready'; instead settle the holder, target and swap decision once with a single confirmed vote per member to save budget and avoid stale plans.
A fake Vanilla claim is fragile when a teammate later flips a different role; if your team member is a real active role, claim it early with a consistent result set rather than denying it.
When a player votes No on a nomination and then Guilty after hearing the defense, that shift is only a weak lead; compare the reasons given against the mechanical evidence before voting.
A Lookout's visitor list on a victim is strong evidence, but check whether the visitor could be a Smuggler swap or a Party Animal role-block before treating it as proof of a Katana attack.

applies_to: Lookouts and everyone evaluating their results
tip: Treat a watch as a list of visitors, not a list of actions. Compare that list with the victim’s death, claimed abilities, and swap mechanics; a lone visitor to a Katana victim is strong evidence, but explain what alternatives the mechanics do or do not allow.

applies_to: Sheriffs, Seers, and anyone using their results
tip: Keep true alignment separate from alignment as it appeared that night. A frame can make a Good player appear Evil, and a Katana holder appears Good; a Seer pair that differs identifies neither player's alignment by itself.

Treat a dead player's will as a claim, not as verified information. A Fabricator can frame and forge the same target's will on one visit, so check the revealed role and other evidence before acting on a will's results.

applies_to: Yakuza and other players with night visits
tip: Don't make a no-action claim that becomes impossible to maintain if a Lookout catches your visit. Prepare a cover that fits your actual visit mechanics, and keep it consistent when questioned.

When a Sheriff or Seer result conflicts with a revealed role, first check whether the claimant could have been framed or swapped that night; a Fabricator frame plus forged will explains many contradictions, so don't treat one conflict as proof of a lie.

Track which Night 1 claims are conditional and demand the claimant's exact target and result each night in a fixed format; claims that shift wording between days (e.g. Seer 'non-Good' becoming 'Good or Neutral') are a strong tell.
Look for the lone No voters on a nomination that later gets flipped; a Yakuza who voted No early often reveals themselves, and the same teammates tend to vote No together.
Keep the Medic and Sheriff's pending actions private until after the night; publicly stating protection targets lets the Yakuza plan around them.
A Lookout's watch shows visits but not the purpose; a lone visitor to a Katana victim is strong, but check whether a Smuggler swap or a Party Animal block explains the visit before concluding.

Self-protection with Standard costs 1 token, and a Standard protection on a Standard attacker is a guaranteed save; repeated free protection on the same target is predictable, so vary between protecting likely Katana targets and self-protecting when the Katana holder is Yakuza.

Before accepting a Lookout visit as proof of an attack, check the visitor's claimed role for a random or automatic visit (Ex-Con) and whether a Yakuza could have swapped; a single visitor list is strong but not conclusive.
Ask Sheriff and Seer claimants to post results on the night they happen and cross-check pairs against Lookout watches early; conflicting pair or check claims in the same Day waste the trial time.
A No vote on a nomination that later flips to Guilty after a claim change is a strong read on the voter; track who voted No with known Yakuza, since that cluster was the decisive signal.

Claiming a fresh active role after being nominated (Vanilla to Ex-Con or Party Animal) made the team look guilty; claim a role before the nomination, and keep the claim consistent with visits the Lookout can see.

When forging a will, don't give the victim a specific role claim you can't confirm. Their real role is revealed with the will, and any mismatch tells the town a Fabricator exists and voids the will's accusation. Either forge something vague that fits many roles, or save the token for a victim whose role you've worked out.
evidence: Carol forged Dave's will as 'Sheriff: checked Mallory, Evil'. Dave flipped Tracker, and every player immediately called the will forged. Heidi and Judy used it to explain the frame, so Mallory was never put in danger.

tip: Assume a claimed investigator is being watched by a Lookout and protected by the Medic. Don't send a visible Katana holder straight at them. A Smuggler swap can redirect the attack or the watch, and Smugglers who hoard their tokens throw away the team's best defense against Lookouts.
evidence: N2: Ivan carried the Katana to Heidi, who was protected by Niaj and watched by Judy. N3: Carol went to Grace while Judy was watching. Both holders were seen and hanged. Erin died holding 2 unused swap tokens.

tip: Watch the player the Yakuza most want dead, which is the freshly claimed investigator. A watch on the night's Katana victim names the holder outright.
evidence: Judy watched the claimed Sheriff on N2 and saw Ivan. She watched the claimed Seer on N3 and saw only Carol. Those two reports decided both Yakuza hangings.

tip: When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, vote Yes with the town. A No vote that saves no one ties you to the teammate once they flip.
evidence: Carol and Erin voted No on Ivan's 8-Yes nomination, then Guilty. After Ivan flipped Grunt, Frank and Heidi pointed at Carol's No vote, and Alice shot Erin, who had voted No and was also in Grace's 'different' pair.

tip: Choose a cover claim that explains possible visits and fits results already public. Don't switch claims mid-trial to a role that an existing check contradicts. Agree a cover action in night chat before you visit.
evidence: Ivan went from Vanilla to Ex-Con, but Heidi's Not Evil result was impossible for an Ex-Con and matched a Katana holder. Carol went from Vanilla to a swap excuse to Party Animal. Each change made the town more sure, not less.

tip: After a successful-looking protection, expect the Yakuza to switch targets. Rotate between the claimed investigators, or self-protect once claimed, rather than repeating the same predictable protection.
evidence: Niaj protected Heidi on N2 (she survived the Katana) and again on N3. The Yakuza switched to Grace, who was unprotected and died.

tip: When a Good flip clashes with an Evil alignment result, treat it as evidence of a Fabricator frame rather than evidence that the investigator is lying. Also re-derive what any paired Seer result means, since the frame changes how the paired player read.
evidence: Heidi's 'Dave Evil' plus Dave's Tracker flip proved a frame. Grace corrected her 'Mallory non-Good' reading, and the town avoided hanging the framed Mallory on Day 2.

tip: On Day 1, a quiet Vanilla-style claim or plain cooperation is safer than flatly refusing to claim. A visible refusal marks you as a power role for the first Katana.
evidence: Dave refused to claim despite repeated asks, became the focus of the day, and was the Yakuza's N1 target.

applies_to: Village power roles (Prosecutor, Medic, Vigilante, investigators)
tip: If you hold a token-based power role, use it on Night 1 when the outcome is safe. A Katana kill on Night 1 wastes the role's tokens and effects entirely. A Prosecutor who prosecutes at night still gets the prosecution even if they die that night (R21), so act before a likely night kill.

Before accepting or rejecting a claim about a group (Surveyor, Census Taker, Diviner), count the circle yourself. Start from the living order at the start of the night, skip the user, and list the neighbours. Two players this game disputed a legal group for a full day and were wrong.

Withholding a result does not protect you. Yakuza kill on a schedule regardless, and a silent investigator takes suspicion while still dying. Give your exact result and its type (alignment, exact role, visit) in your first public speech.

Do not let the Clerk rig a Day where your own teammate is likely to be nominated. A rigged nomination executes the nominee whatever the vote, so a rig that Yakuza use on a Day when they are the nominee kills their own side.

On a rigged Day, a passed nomination is an execution. Treat any nomination you cannot verify as lethal and withhold Yes votes until you know whether a rig is active, since an announced Innocent verdict can still end in hanging.

Before alleging a mechanical contradiction, rebuild the relevant player circle exactly as it stood when the action happened and apply special rules such as skipping the investigator. If challenged, check the calculation before voting; a mistaken accusation can damage your credibility and endanger a good player.

State precisely what a group result establishes. “One member of this group has role X” does not identify which member, and a census count does not identify who has which alignment until combined with independently confirmed facts. Treat a player's own claim as a claim, not corroboration.

Track nomination votes separately from trial votes. Opposing even a trial for a teammate is distinct evidence from voting Innocent once the trial begins; neither vote alone proves guilt, but the full record can reveal who tried to shield whom.

When you withhold a result, explain what kind of result it was and why you are holding it back. Give enough detail for others to evaluate its scope and mechanics without disclosing a future target; unexplained vagueness invites suspicion.

Survey groups that include the player whose alignment or role you most need; my N2 survey of Erin/Frank/Grace found a Clerk, but the group was too wide to tell which of three was Yakuza, so pick groups of tighter suspicion or pair it with votes.
Withholding a checkable night result for two Days cost credibility and forced repeated pressure; state the role and the exact result on the first Day, even if it is only exact-role information.

Treat a census or survey that names a group but not which member is the target as weak evidence on its own; verify a claim by comparing it with votes, visits and private-message traces before hanging.

Watch who opposes testing a lead while later voting Innocent on the same suspect; a player who rejects a trial and then hangs with the group may be coordinating, so ask for their reasoning before a vote.
Do not let a geometry or rules objection drive a nomination without checking it yourself; Dave's skip-rule error pushed a Good Surveyor to trial and cost him credibility.

applies_to: Everyone, especially Surveyors and anyone evaluating a Surveyor claim
tip: Work out the group from the target by walking the living circle in both directions, skipping the Surveyor if encountered and continuing until you find the nearest eligible players. Check the current circle carefully before calling a group impossible.

Choose someone likely to send or receive Day private messages who is likely to survive the night. Eavesdropping reveals messages during the following Day, not Night chat, and a target who dies before that Day gives you nothing to read.

Separate nomination votes from trial verdicts. An Innocent vote may be shared by many players, but a No vote that prevents testing a confirmed Yakuza can be a useful lead—still weigh it against that player's stated reasoning and the rest of the vote record.

Treat group results as constraints, not accusations. Keep each possible assignment alive until another independent fact distinguishes them; a claimed alignment or role is not independent confirmation.
State the reason for your trial vote, especially if it differs from your public lean. An unexplained vote change makes even a correct vote harder for others to evaluate.

After a Yakuza flips, separate the vote to put them on trial from the verdict vote. Someone who opposed testing them is a more useful lead than someone who merely voted Innocent alongside several others.
Track tokens as submitted actions, not assumed successful transfers. In your will, distinguish what you attempted from what the recipient's later account or will actually confirms.

A rig forces the execution of whoever is successfully nominated, even if the trial vote is Innocent. Before using it, account for who might be nominated—including yourself or a teammate—and save it for a day when the likely nominee is an opponent.

When a teammate is likely doomed, calculate whether your votes can actually save them. If not, consider supporting the nomination and Guilty vote to avoid leaving a distinctive defense pattern that surviving players can use after the flip.
Make your submitted actions match what you told your teammate in night chat. If you change your mind, say so clearly; otherwise your partner plans around an action that you will not actually take.
Plan one-shot abilities around the day they can change the outcome. If you may be eliminated, an unused token is lost; remember that puppeting controls chat, not the target's nominations or votes.

A night kill does not erase public results or a dead player's will. Plan for how the living will interpret the information after the claimant dies, rather than assuming removing the claimant removes the case.

Before a Katana kill, check whether the target is a likely Surveyor, Census Taker or other investigator. Their results name the Katana holder's visit, so a holder who visits and attacks repeatedly gets exposed by counter-visits. Rotate the holder or use a Clerk or Puppeteer swap on the investigator in the same night.

Do not let a teammate's public stance become the whole case. Frank's Yes-then-Innocent pattern and Grace's No on his nomination both became Village talking points. If a teammate is at risk, argue the vote math early and make your own stance look consistent with the town's read.

Night chat plans were fully visible to the town afterwards through the revealed record. Agree on a cover story for each Katana attack (for example a claimed visit) before the night, because any unexplained visit to a dead investigator will be checked.

A Census Taker or Surveyor result that names a group only proves a set of players, not a role. Treat 'exactly one of X and Y is Good' as a lead that cannot convict either person alone; the town hanged Frank and Grace on group-based reads that could not separate them from one another.

Late multi-round public pressure (repeated 'answer directly' demands) cost the town several rounds of budget and produced little. Ask one precise checkable question per turn and let the answer or silence speak.

applies_to: Census Taker and other alignment-count roles
tip: A census or survey counts true alignment, so a 2-of-3 Good result with a Neutral in the group does not identify a Yakuza. Before treating a count as proof, list every alignment the result allows, including Neutral, and check which group members can be cross-examined.

Before nominating on a geometric or group claim (survey skip rules, census groups), write out the legal groups step by step. Dave's wrong skip-rule nomination of a Good Surveyor cost him credibility and nearly hanged an innocent player.

A Clerk rig executes any successfully nominated player even when the trial vote is Innocent. Once a Clerk may be alive, treat every successful nomination as a possible death, and do not nominate someone you would not accept losing.

A publicly pressuring investigator who questions a suspect on Day 2 can be Katana-killed the next night. Post your results early and keep your will updated each night, so the town still gets your information if you die.

Never rig a Day on which you or a teammate is the likely nominee: a rig executes anyone whose nomination passes, including Yakuza. Rig only when you are not under pressure and a Village target can win a nomination but not a Guilty vote. Tell your team truthfully what you are doing.
evidence: Frank told Grace he would hold the rig, then rigged Day 3 while Heidi's census pointed straight at him. His nomination passed 4-2 and the trial went 3-3 Innocent, but the rig hanged him anyway.

tip: When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, or a rig makes passing fatal anyway, vote Yes and Guilty to bus them. A lone protective vote that changes nothing becomes the case against you once they flip.
evidence: Grace knew about the rig and still voted No on Frank's nomination, which passed 4-2 regardless. On Day 4, Bob, Dave and Erin all named that No vote as the reason to hang her.

tip: Combine partial results with flips and corroborated claims. A 'k of 3 Good' census becomes a named suspect once the other members are confirmed Good, so nominate and vote on it instead of waiting for a direct contradiction.
evidence: From Heidi's census plus Alice's Prosecutor flip and Dave's Eavesdropper claim (supported by Carol's survey), Dave correctly deduced Frank. Bob and Erin still treated the census as naming no one, and Bob voted Innocent on Frank.

tip: Before calling a result mechanically impossible, re-derive it from the rule text. For neighbor groups (Surveyor, Diviner), the user's own seat is skipped. A wrong 'impossible' call wastes a trial and costs the accuser credibility.
evidence: Dave and Erin called Carol's Bob/Dave/Erin survey group impossible and sent her to trial. The group was legal because Carol's own seat is skipped. Both had to retract, and Grace later used the error against Dave.

tip: Once you are asked directly, post your role, target and result promptly, ideally in your first speech after the result. Withholding them invites a trial and helps no one, because the Yakuza can't see the result anyway.
evidence: Carol hid her Surveyor result for three rounds, was nominated twice and put on trial, then admitted the delay was a mistake. Her result turned out to corroborate Dave.

tip: Killing the investigator whose public result already points at you lets the flip and the last will confirm that result. If the result is already damning, plan the Day around it instead: prepare a counter-narrative, bus, or use your Day tools.
evidence: Killing Heidi on Night 2 made her Census Taker flip and will confirm the census. Dave opened Day 3 by nominating Frank on exactly that basis.

tip: Spend Day-shaping tokens such as the puppet before the endgame. Taking over a key accuser's or swing voter's chat on a crucial Day can redirect a trial, while a token you die holding does nothing.
evidence: Grace died on Day 4 still holding her puppet token. She never puppeted Dave or Bob on Day 3 or Day 4, the Days that decided the game.

tip: Give your tokens to the token-limited investigator whose claim is best supported, and publicly claim the gift so their notification backs up your own claim.
evidence: Erin gave Carol two survey tokens. Carol's will confirmed receiving them, which cleared Erin on Day 4, and the extra tokens funded Carol's surveys.

applies_to: Tracker, Lookout, Medic, Seer (any investigator or protector)
tip: Don't PM or post your next night's target during the day. Yakuza read those messages and aimed the Katana at the claimant before your action resolved. Post only resolved results, and give the exact target only after the night.

A visit log is evidence only where the visitor is visible. Tracks and watches show destinations, not attackers. Before blaming a Katana holder, list every living player who could have visited the victim and mark which logs cover each of them.

When two players claim the same role, test the claimants on the nights of their claimed actions with an independent watch or track, not on vote history. Treat a retracted slip like 'Yakuza Fabricator' as weak evidence unless it is backed by a visit.

Use daytime and night planning only in the Yakuza night chat. If a Yakuza is a power role that will be killed or exposed, make sure the surviving members can reproduce their claimed results, and keep the Katana with a member whose visits will not be watched.

applies_to: Yakuza with a visiting role such as Fabricator
tip: Every framing or protection visit is a visit that Lookouts and Trackers can see. Before framing someone, check whether a Lookout or Tracker might be alive and watching the target. My N1 frame on Ivan showed up on Erin's watch and became the Village's wedge against our Smuggler's fake Sheriff claim.

A fake role claim must match visits its claimant could plausibly have made. Mallory claimed Sheriff with no visit behind the result and was exposed by a Lookout watch. Claim only roles whose visits you can actually show, or stay quiet.

Do not counterclaim a role that has a real, checkable holder still alive. Two Medic claims let the Village back the one with a corroborated visit, and mine had no verifiable result. Pick a claim that no Lookout watch can contradict.

Answer a direct question about your night target in one plain sentence the first time it is asked. Repeated evasion over two days became the case that got me nominated, even though my actual answer was harmless.

applies_to: Seers and anyone using alignment results
tip: A matching Seer pair is not a clearance when one player could be the Katana holder: that holder appears Good. Report the result with this limitation, and don’t use it alone to nominate or clear someone.

applies_to: Trackers, Lookouts, and everyone interpreting their results
tip: A visit confirms a destination, not the action taken there. Treat a corroborated visit as a useful check on whether someone’s claimed action could have happened, but not proof that they protected, investigated, or framed the target.

Set a clear standard before nominating. If you nominate someone but vote Innocent, identify exactly what makes the evidence insufficient and what changed your mind; otherwise opponents can reasonably treat the reversal as a credibility problem.

Use confirmed role abilities and deaths to narrow the possible factions before leaning on old vote patterns. At a small endgame, a confirmed Village player plus a Katana death can make the remaining candidates much more informative than their earlier votes.

Once a corroborated log is public, the Katana holder tends to hit that player the next night (Alice after her Day 3 track, Erin after her watch). Rotate watch targets toward the likeliest holder and keep the log in your will so the information survives your death.

Test any claimed investigation by its visits. A real Sheriff or Seer check is a visit, so a Lookout watching the target should see the checker. Mallory's false Sheriff result on Ivan was exposed this way on Day 2, and it was the strongest mechanical lead of the game.

Count Defense levels before deciding whether a save or a shot happened. A free Standard Medic protection stops a Standard Katana attack, while a Strong Vigilante shot beats Standard. A survivor is not proof of a failed attack or of who held the Katana.

Don't spend votes on vote history or unchecked counterclaims. Several trials ended on votes alone, and a Vanilla who pushed early nominations became a target. Vote Guilty only after naming a visit or vote mismatch, and post your own checkable reasoning early.

A Lookout sees only who visits the watched player, never what that player does. To catch a Katana holder, watch the likely Katana target, since the holder's attack shows up as a visit to it, or use a Tracker on the holder. Don't tell the table whom you'll watch, even as a range, because the holder can strike you the same night.

Medic's Standard protection costs no token, so a Medic with no tokens left can still stop a Standard Katana every night. Yakuza should kill or block the Medic before relying on the Katana, and Village should not assume a token-less Medic is useless.

Before a hang, check who casts the Guilty votes that decide it. A Yakuza will pile onto a Good player who names them, as Judy did with the Guilty vote on Carol right after Carol's Seer pair named her. Require a mechanical lead that doesn't come from the accuser's own read.

Never state your faction in public, even as a slip. Bob's 'Yakuza Fabricator' line, retracted within a minute, was the clearest reason the Village hanged him. Keep any claimed role's visits consistent with what watchers could have seen, and avoid claiming a real role whose protection visits can be tested.

A claimed check that requires a visit is testable. If a claimed Sheriff's target has no visit on a Lookout's watch, the claim is falsified. Compare every claimed visit against every watch and tracker log before voting; Mallory's Evil read failed this test and her execution was correct.

Separate target confidence from attack strength: don't shoot on vote history, a counterclaim, or a soft read alone. If a shot is justified, use the lowest attack level that beats the defense you expect; a Strong shot is wasted against a target with no defense.

In the endgame, distinguish what the evidence proves from what it only narrows down. Knowing at least one of two players must be Yakuza does not identify which one; combine mechanical evidence with vote patterns, and treat votes as leads rather than proof.

Check the actual nomination and trial ballots before building a case from someone's vote history. Correct errors in the ledger, and don't describe a vote as shielding someone if the person later voted Guilty on them.

Before hanging on a Seer or random-pair read, check whether the pair involved the claimant's own near-dead or confirmed-Good partners; a random pair that matches confirmed Good players is consistent with a Katana holder reading Good, so it rarely separates players.

Do not let a lone teammate-style nominee's hang rest on vote history; in a 3-player endgame, a Guilty vote from a player who has no checkable contradiction is the same as a Yakuza push, so demand a visit or result mismatch first.

Watch the living player most likely to be the Katana holder rather than the most-argued suspect; repeated Katana kills on the same side of the circle show the holder's location in the night chat pattern.
When two players claim the same protective role (Medic) and both give no feedback, schedule a Lookout watch on each claimant on the same night to test visits, instead of voting on the claims.

Track each Vigilante shot and Medic token separately in the will: a self-protect with Standard costs one token, and a Strong shot costs three, so a dead Medic's count shows whether a later protection was possible.

Protection expires after that night, so reassess and protect again each night. Standard Defense on another player costs no tokens—even when you have none left; tokens are needed for Strong Defense or self-protection.
Save shots for a concrete mechanical lead, not vote history or an unverified counterclaim. A strong shot on a suspicious-looking Medic can remove an important Good role.

A Seer pair reports only whether two players match; it does not identify their alignment. Since the Katana holder appears Good to alignment checks, a match with a known Good player does not clear either person.
Separate a false action claim from proof of faction. Explain what the mechanical evidence establishes, consider role-based alternatives such as Roleplayer, and make your vote reasoning explicit.

Keep nomination votes and trial votes in separate, accurate records. A Yes/No vote to put someone on trial is not the same as a Guilty/Innocent vote, and a mistaken summary can become the basis of an endgame accusation.

Treat a visit as evidence of destination, not of the action performed there. A visit to a player may fit a protection claim, but it could also be a frame or another action; corroboration confirms the visit, not the claimed role or action.

Protection lasts for that night only. Even with no tokens left, you can still provide Standard Defense to another player; tokens are needed for Strong Defense or self-protection. Use this when assessing who could have survived an attack.

When a claimed Sheriff result conflicts with the expected visit record, explain the mechanics precisely: a real check visits its target, while framing can alter the alignment result. A missing visit undermines the claimed action, but by itself does not establish the claimant's faction.

A Medic's base Standard protection costs no token and can be given every night, so a Standard Katana attack is stopped by any living Medic's default protection. Assume a living Medic protects the likely target, and kill or block that Medic first, or retry only after it is dead.

A living Lookout's watch exposes a teammate's frame or visit, and it was the most damaging evidence the Village had. While a Lookout is alive, spend the Katana on the Lookout before a Sheriff or Tracker whose logs can be contested.
A teammate's public faction or role slip, even if retracted, gets them hanged on the Village's read. Keep teammates with no claim to defend silent in public, and deny a slip plainly and once.

Keep one consistent stance on a teammate's trial. Yes on the nomination, Innocent at trial, then No on the next nomination created a vote mismatch the Village hanged on. If a save is futile, vote with the Village majority rather than mixing signals.

Do the trial vote math before deciding to bus a teammate. On Mallory’s trial, two Yakuza Innocent votes would have reduced the Guilty total from 7 of 10 to 5 of 10—exactly half, not a majority. The teammate was still savable.

A fake investigative claim must fit its mechanical footprint as well as its result. Framing someone can explain an Evil alignment result, but it cannot explain why a claimed Sheriff check produced no visit for the Lookout to see.

Before spending a swap token, map every action it redirects—including the Katana attack and investigators’ targets—and coordinate the intended result with the team. Saving a token is better than causing an unpredictable redirection.

Plan for the actual faction win condition, not parity. If the last Yakuza reaches a 1-versus-2 endgame against coordinated Village players, survival alone is not a path to victory; preserve cover and build a credible way to remove every opponent.

Don't fake-claim an investigator result whose action would have needed a visit to a player that a Lookout or Tracker may have watched. Pairing a frame with a fake Sheriff check on the same target draws attention to that target. If you must fake a check, fake one on a target nobody is likely to be watching, or claim a non-visiting role.
evidence: Mallory claimed she checked Ivan N1. Erin had watched Ivan and saw only Alice and Bob visit, Alice corroborated it, and Mallory was nominated 8-2 and hanged 7-3 on that contradiction alone.

tip: Before fake-claiming a protective role, consider that the real holder may be alive and will counterclaim. Once your cover survives a trial, keep every later message strictly in character; one slip naming your faction or role is fatal.
evidence: Bob's Medic claim was counterclaimed by the real Medic Heidi but survived a 0-8 trial on Day 3. On Day 4 he wrote 'Bob here, Yakuza Fabricator' and was hanged 4-3 the same day.

tip: Never shoot on vote history or an unresolved counterclaim. If you do shoot on a lead, use a Basic shot rather than all your tokens. Killing a protector also strips protection from whoever they would have saved.
evidence: Frank spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot at Heidi because of her Innocent vote on Mallory and the Medic counterclaim. Heidi was the Good Medic, and that same night her Standard protection saved Erin from the Katana. Frank was left with no shots for the endgame.

tip: A Seer 'same alignment' pair that includes a confirmed-Good player means the other player is Good or was holding the Katana that night. Combine this with elimination (a confirmed Vigilante, players who survived a Katana attack, flips) to narrow down the holder, rather than dismissing Seer pairs as 'untestable'.
evidence: Carol's N4 pair Heidi/Judy matched. Frank was confirmed by his shot and Erin had been attacked, which left Judy, Grace or Carol. The Village dismissed the pair and hanged Carol, the real Seer. Judy, the Katana holder, then killed Erin and nearly won.

tip: Judge votes on a flipped Yakuza by whether they could have changed the outcome. Innocent votes against a large Guilty majority prove little. A No vote on the nomination, or a Guilty vote cast once the hang was certain, is the more telling pattern. Don't let an opponent drive the agenda by repeating someone else's vote history.
evidence: Bob repeatedly hammered Carol's and Heidi's futile Innocent votes on Mallory, whose trial was already 7-3. Both were Good, and both were later killed by the Village. Judy had voted No on Mallory's nomination and Guilty at trial; that pattern was only acted on by Grace on Day 6.

tip: If you nominate someone, vote consistently with your own case. Don't nominate a corroborated investigator on a theory you can't back up. Flip-flops and weak nominations make a real power role look like a scum leader.
evidence: Carol nominated Mallory, then voted Innocent, and later nominated Alice, the corroborated Tracker, over a Katana-holder theory. On Day 5 Erin, Frank and Judy cited exactly these moves to hang her 3-2.

tip: Don't send nightly target plans by private message on a day the Yakuza are hunting investigators. Everyone sees that the PM was sent, and that marks you as an investigator worth killing.
evidence: Alice PM'd Erin her tracking plan at the end of Day 3. In night chat Bob cited 'who just PM'd Erin' when choosing Alice, and the Katana killed her that night.

tip: In the final three, list who is confirmed Good (by mechanical results or your own role) and treat everyone else as a possible Katana holder. Don't let the last Yakuza reframe the vote as 'votes only, no mechanics'.
evidence: On Day 6 Grace reasoned: Frank was confirmed by his Vigilante shot, she knew she was Good, and Erin had died to the Katana, so Judy had to be the holder. Frank agreed, and they hanged Judy 2-1 despite her Jester/Executioner deflection.

applies_to: Medic, and any player whose protection or attack targets someone a Yakuza might swap
tip: A swap (R23) moves a Medic's protection too. If you protect X and X is swapped with Y, your protection lands on Y, so check where your protection went before assuming a save. Also, a Standard protection doesn't stop a Standard Katana on the target by itself, so verify which player the Katana actually hit.

A profile's three-role set always contains exactly one true role. Identical sets on two different targets are a weak coincidence, not proof of a lie. Only a claimed role that falls outside the set is a clean contradiction, so test claims against the set's exclusions rather than its overlap.

A false role claim that conflicts with a revealed dead holder (a second Sheriff) survives only if the village argues about repeat roles. Pre-empt that by giving a concrete, checkable detail (exact wording, result, a visit you can corroborate) or by claiming a role no living player can contradict.

Repeating 'unverified' caveats in every message does not change votes. When the only lead is a chain of claims, name the exact conditional it depends on (e.g. 'if Heidi is Good') and ask the accused to disprove that specific link. Otherwise a single unverifiable census can carry a hang.

Before using a swap, write down each affected action’s chosen target and its destination after the swap—including the Katana attack and allied protections. Coordinate the intended outcome, not just the target names.

Do the vote math before saving or bussing a teammate, but remember that repeated mutual protection becomes a public link after a flip. Avoid making every nomination and trial vote look like a coordinated pair.

“That result is unverified” is a weak defense if repeated without an alternative explanation. Address the specific evidence, explain what would account for it, and prepare a role-consistent cover before a trial forces the issue.

Executing the Katana holder does not stop Katana kills while another Yakuza lives: the Katana passes to a random living Yakuza (R8). Count living Yakuza before assuming a hang removed the threat, and expect a kill the next night.

A random-group census gives only a count, not a name. Don't present one count as settling one player's alignment; pair it with a second census or a verified result before you hang on it. Say which players were in the group and which alignment was counted.

When a claim conflicts with a public reveal, such as a second Sheriff claim after the Sheriff is dead, first ask for the exact check wording and result. Only then weigh it against the hard facts (visits, deaths, confirmed roles).

Keep an exact log of each night's submitted target. Grace's N3 claim conflicted with her own target log, and that single inconsistency cost her credibility. Post the target as submitted, not a reconstruction.
A Yakuza who is hanged and holds the Katana hands it to a surviving teammate. Keep the Katana with a member who can avoid a hang, and do not let the last living Yakuza be the obvious suspect alone.

Don't rely on a 'will' or Day 1 announcement alone; if you die on Night 1 your Sheriff result is only useful if you posted it. Since your death reveals the will publicly, write any check result there at once, labelled as a result with its target.

Duplicate-role claims were only checkable through exact-role results; the Profiler's identical three-role sets for two different targets were a strong signal. When a claim conflicts with a dead player's revealed role, ask the claimant for the exact check wording before the trial, not after.

Track which public claims are corroborated by independent visit or swap results (Lookout vs. Census vs. Cartographer) and build the case on the corroborated subset; a single unverified census drove two hangings in this game and was only as good as the claimant's honesty.

Standard Defense stops a Standard Katana; a Medic protection that didn't match a death means either a Strong attack or a misdirected protection (swap). Check swap notices before concluding a protection failed.

Hanging a player who has announced a Good-aligned check result that another claimant contradicts is risky; prefer to test claims with votes on the least-corroborated account rather than the most-convenient one.

Before choosing a fake role, consider every way it could be checked—not just public flips, visits, or a living counterclaim. Exact-role powers such as Profiler or Oracle can invalidate a plausible claim; plan a backup explanation and don’t rely only on “roles can repeat.”

Do the trial threshold math before choosing whether to defend or bus a teammate. When a teammate can still be saved, a Guilty vote may be decisive; when the hang is inevitable, a well-timed Guilty vote can create distance, but earlier mutual support may still be remembered.

Keep a target’s chosen destination separate from the action’s effective destination when swaps are possible. Check which actions were redirected before treating a result, visit, or apparent mismatch as evidence of a lie.

Scout names are random draws, so one name per group shows only that the groups differ, not who visited whom. Use the group count and sampled names to test Cartographer or Lookout claims, but never treat a Scout result as a visit.

Before hanging on an exact-role or census claim, check whether a second claimant is possible under the rules (roles repeat unless the census proves otherwise), and whether a claim contradicts a confirmed public fact such as a revealed role.

Track who votes with whom across trials. Repeated mutual No and Innocent votes between two players are a cheap, checkable pattern, and it is worth raising early with a concrete question rather than after a death.

A Katana holder who visits a player who later dies should expect that victim's Lookout or Tracker claim to point at them; move the Katana or block the watcher's allies before the Lookout's result is posted.
Require a concrete, checkable answer before a vote. Vote logs that shift without an explanation give the other side a clear read, so explain any change before voting.
Submit the exact target name and check the result text against your submitted target the same night; if they differ, raise it at once so the mismatch is not left unresolved until your death.
