A single unverified census or exact-role result should not carry a hanging alone; when two players claim incompatible roles, test the cheaper contradiction first and avoid hanging the player whose claim is only consistent with others.
Standard protection stops only Standard or lower attacks; if a protected player dies to a Katana, consider swaps or Strong attacks before assuming a misread, and say which in public.
Do not let a Yakuza's No/Innocent voting partner be the only pattern used to clear or convict; check each pair's votes against independent results first.

applies_to: Lookouts and anyone using visit-based results
tip: A visit identifies who went where, not what they did. If several people visited a victim, keep all of them as possible attackers until other evidence separates them; a visit alone does not prove an attack.

Check whether a contradiction is actually ruled out by the mechanics before voting. Duplicate roles are allowed, so an apparent role conflict is weaker than an exact-role result that rules out the claimed role.

A last will is not guaranteed to preserve a result from the night you die: night results and deaths resolve together, and you cannot edit your will at night. Share a high-value result while alive when its value outweighs the risk of outing yourself.

Protection can be role-blocked and gives no confirmation that it stopped an attack. If you publicly reveal whom you protected, expect opponents to block you or anticipate a repeat target; avoid making your next protection predictable.

Describe map results as connected components, not as a list of visitors. A component can show that players are connected through visits, but not who visited whom or what any visit did; use directional roles like Lookout or Tracker to establish those details.

State the assumptions behind a result-based accusation. A census plus known flips can narrow the possibilities sharply, but the conclusion still depends on the census being genuine; seek independent support before treating it as confirmed.

Calculate the Guilty majority on every trial and identify how many votes are needed to change the result. A tied or near-majority Guilty vote still acquits, and an acquittal can cost the village another night.

Weigh exact-role evidence against a role claim more heavily than a superficial role-name conflict. Repeated roles are allowed, so a dead player having a role does not by itself disprove another claim; a credible exact-role result can.

When a Lookout's result names two visitors to a Katana victim and one of them has a confirmed, harmless explanation, treat the other as near-proven. A claim of a role that has just flipped dead is not saved by 'roles can repeat'. Hang on the first chance instead of waiting for more confirmation.
evidence: Day 2: Heidi saw only Carol and Erin visit Dave. Carol's census visit was confirmed, and Erin claimed the dead Dave's Sheriff role. Heidi and Ivan voted Innocent on the 'duplicates allowed' caveat, Erin survived 4-4, and she got another night to kill Heidi.

tip: Never fake-claim a role that has just been revealed on a flip, and plan a cover story for any visit a Lookout or Tracker could have seen before the Day starts. If the holder's visit gets exposed, move the Katana to a teammate.
evidence: Erin claimed Sheriff the morning after Dave flipped Sheriff, and she kept the Katana after Heidi named her. A Profiler result later finished her off, and her Sheriff claim had been the town's main case from Day 2 onward.

tip: Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. If someone else does, don't ask them about it in public, because that only spreads the hint further.
evidence: Dave said he would 'report any Sheriff check I get.' Heidi asked if that was a role claim, and the Yakuza killed Dave on Night 1, citing exactly that wording.

tip: Don't reveal whom you protected while that player is still a likely target. The Pharmacist will simply block you on the night it matters.
evidence: Grace said on Day 2 that she had protected Heidi. In night chat Bob proposed blocking Grace for that reason, and Erin did so on Night 2. Heidi then died to the Katana.

tip: Combine census counts with confirmed flips to pin down one player. Repeat the logic every day as new deaths remove the other options.
evidence: Carol's Night 1 census found one Evil among Bob, Dave and Heidi. Once Dave and Heidi both flipped Good, that left Bob, and he was hanged on Day 4.

tip: Profile anyone with a contested claim. Also read your earlier profiles for which non-Good roles they show to be in play.
evidence: Alice's Night 1 profile of Ivan already listed Pharmacist and Smuggler as roles in play. Her Night 2 profile of Erin gave the same three roles and ruled out Sheriff, which got Erin hanged on Day 3.

tip: Use your swaps while a teammate is under pressure, for example to send a Lookout or Tracker onto the wrong player or to redirect protection. Also don't volunteer denials about mechanics nobody asked about, because that hints at your role.
evidence: Bob held both tokens through Nights 1-2 while Erin was exposed. His one swap on Night 3 sent Grace's protection to the wrong player and killed Alice. On Day 2 he said unprompted that he 'wasn't told I was swapped', and Carol and Frank pressed him on it more than once.

tip: After a Yakuza flips, look first at whoever voted No and Innocent for them. Pairs who protect each other in every vote are likely partners.
evidence: Bob voted No on Erin's nominations and Innocent at her Day 2 trial, and Erin did the same for him. After Erin flipped Pharmacist, the town cited that pattern alongside the census and hanged Bob.

tip: Once an archive list is public, add every proven role (a prosecution proves a Prosecutor, a clean proves a Mortician) to the unseen slots. When all slots are full, any claim of an unlisted role is a lie, and two claims of a Unique archived role (e.g. Vulture) mean exactly one is fake.

When two players claim the same unlisted role and only one Evil slot is left, one of them may be a Neutral bluffing as town. Before hanging, check whether a living player's Neutral claim could be the fake instead. Here, hanging Erin (the real Vulture) was what exposed Judy.

After claiming Veteran and saying you may be on alert, Yakuza will simply avoid you, so alerts are mostly wasted. Consider alerting before you claim, or keep the claim vague so a Katana hit on you is still possible. Otherwise your role's main value is a confirmed vote.

A tight vote (exactly the needed Guilty count) is fragile. Treat any 'vote Innocent to test for a rig' pitch as a likely Yakuza or Neutral stall, since it burns a trial and gives the Katana another night.
Faking a Unique Neutral role (Vulture) as cover blows up the moment the real holder flips. Prefer a non-Unique cover role, or make sure the real holder survives.

Spend the profile on a living suspect whose claimed role is outside a known role list, not on whoever you think the Katana will hit. A profile of a player who dies that night is mostly wasted. Your result arrives at the end of the night, so it never reaches your will if you die that same night. Before nightfall, write the exact target in your will ('N2: profiling Dave'), not 'Dave or Niaj', so your death still points somewhere.

Use Unique tags in slot math. A flip of a Unique role (Smuggler, Vulture) at once falsifies every other living claim of that role. It also narrows a profile or survey list, since a Unique role that flipped elsewhere can't be the profiled player's role.

A public effect proves its role exists, for example a prosecution announcement proves a Prosecutor. Add any such role missing from an archive to the unseen slots. Archive list + flips + proven unseen roles can close every slot and expose all overflow claims (Vanilla, Sheriff) without any further checks.

Faking a Neutral role from the archive (e.g. Vulture) only works while the real holder stays alive and unflipped. Once two players are fighting over who is the Clerk/Prosecutor, the real Neutral may get hanged and expose you. Either back that player's survival hard early, or claim an unseen slot instead.

applies_to: Prosecutor (any role whose effect becomes public)
tip: Before you use a role whose effect becomes public, name the target as a suspect in public that Day. Label your actions by night (N2/N3), not by trial day. If a copycat counterclaims, your public reads that came before each action are the most convincing proof you have.

The Scout's three names are in different visit groups. So when someone is Katana-killed, any named player other than the victim was not the holder, and that clears them (barring a swap). Track every night's names against that night's victim. Post the clear only when it decides a vote, so the Yakuza don't learn early that you're worth killing.

With an archive list public, do a full 13-slot role census as soon as flips and claims allow. Unique roles (Vulture, Smuggler) and proven roles (a Prosecutor proven by prosecutions) fill slots. A Neutral claim that dodges a census result is a classic Yakuza fallback, so look at it again the moment the real holder could flip.

In a two-way counterclaim like Erin vs Ivan, the claimant whose public reads named each target before that night's action is far more likely real. A claimant who writes day labels that copy the public announcements ('D3/D4') instead of the night they acted is likely copying.

Claiming a Neutral role that is in the archive is fragile if the real holder is alive and unclaimed. Once they flip or claim, your lie is exposed for free. Prefer a claim whose real holder is already dead, or one no flip can contradict.
Ignore 'vote Innocent to expose a rig' pitches when the hang already has a mechanical basis. They burn a trial and buy the Yakuza a night, and the person pushing them is often the Clerk.

Once an Archivist list goes public, count the unseen slots in night chat before anyone claims. Each Yakuza role that is unseen (Mortician here) uses up a slot. Fake claims of unlisted roles (Sheriff, Accountant, Vanilla) then overflow almost at once. Pick covers from listed roles whose real holders are likely to stay silent, and assign them so no two teammates compete for the same slot.

Don't clean the Katana's target on Night 1 when a Lookout might watch it. It puts two Yakuza among the target's visitors and hands town a short suspect list. Clean a different likely-dead target, or hold the token until the Katana holder is already burned.

Fire the rig on the night before a two-way claim war (like Prosecutor vs Prosecutor). Then nominate the townie side yourself early the next Day. Holding the rig until the final Day, when you are the obvious nominee, wastes it.
Never fake-claim a Unique role (Vulture, Smuggler) whose real holder is still alive and unknown. Their flip proves you a liar instantly, and a Neutral who is also lying may die in an unrelated hang.

Hand the Katana to the teammate who is already exposed and doomed, and have them make the kill. Lookouts then only ever see players town already knows about, and the hidden member reaches the endgame with no visits against them.

applies_to: Vulture (and any Neutral faking a Village role)
tip: Before fake-claiming, list which roles are still unplaced AND which players are still unclaimed. Never copy a role whose real holder is plausibly among the unclaimed. A Prosecutor or any role with public footprints is guaranteed to be counterclaimed, and the 1v1 is settled by whose earlier reads match the actions. Pick a role whose real holder is dead or provably absent, or claim early before the slots close.

Label results by the night the action was taken (N2, N3), not the day it showed up (D3, D4). Writing the public announcement day reads as copying the public log, and opponents will use it as the tiebreaker in a counterclaim.

Avoid vouching for anyone on early days ('X, Y and Z fit together'). If one of them flips Yakuza, that line gets quoted against you later. Stick to process comments and votes that match the eventual consensus.

Your win needs the count to drop, so the Yakuza's night kills are your engine. As soon as someone fake-claims your Unique role, you hold leverage over them: your flip exposes them. Open that private deal early, on the day they claim, not on your own trial day. Also steer town's hangs toward Village players rather than letting yourself become the swing slot.

When a Unique role is claimed by two players, or one claimer flips it, the other claimer is proven false. Once the archive and the flips place every Village role, the last unplaced Evil role belongs to whichever claimant has no slot. Do this count before every vote.

Once an Archivist list goes public, only a few unseen slots remain, and they will hold the Mortician, any role that has acted publicly (such as a Prosecutor) and dead players' roles. Never fake-claim an unseen role, and coordinate so at most one teammate sits in an unseen slot. Prefer an archived role whose real holder is dead or silent, but not a Unique role: its holder's flip disproves you.

Don't stack two Yakuza visits on one target, such as the Katana kill plus a Mortician clean. A single Lookout on the victim then names both of you, and slot math finishes the job. Let the Mortician clean only when the holder is the same player, or when the visit is otherwise expendable.

Use a swap early and creatively rather than hoarding. Swapping the Katana target with a nearby player moves both the kill and any Lookout watching the target, which can hide the holder's visit. Hanged with 2 unused tokens, I had wasted my whole role.

Combine flips with Unique roles: if a flipped role is Unique (Vulture, Smuggler), any living claimant of it is a proven liar. Slot math (archive + Archivist + unseen roles) plus flips can place every role by mid-game.

When your claim is tailored to fit earlier claims and you speak late, town reads it as copied. If you must fake-claim under a visitor list, claim before teammates and pick a role whose result can't be checked against the archive or other results.

A claim that only 'explains' a census or alignment result (e.g. 'I'm Neutral, so I wasn't counted as Good') fits Evil just as well. Never mark such a player as placed in slot math; keep them open until a flip or second result settles them.

If two players counterclaim the same role and a third claims a Unique Neutral role (Vulture), the copycat may be the real Neutral claiming a power role to survive, and the Unique-role claimant may be the Yakuza. List every way to assign the leftover roles before deciding which counterclaimant is Evil.
Track which roles are Unique (Vulture, Smuggler). Once a Unique role flips, any other living claimant of it is proven false. That is the cleanest contradiction in the game.

Post the raw archive list, but first ask the remaining visitors or claimants to claim blind so nobody can tailor a claim to fit. Then redo the unseen-slot count every time a role-proving event happens (a prosecution, a clean, a flip).

In a Prosecutor counterclaim, compare each claimant's public reads before each prosecution with the actual targets. The real Prosecutor's day reads usually predict their picks, while a copycat's don't.

Turn each census into hard constraints. Remove players already known Good (Katana victims are almost surely Good). Then remember that Neutrals are never counted, so a low Good count can mean a Neutral, not only Yakuza. Chain groups across nights: a player who sits in two bad groups is your strongest lead.

Once an archive or role list is public, keep a full 13-slot role census and update it after every flip and every proven action. A prosecution, for example, proves an unseen Prosecutor exists. Unique roles (Vulture, Smuggler) make a second claim a proven lie the moment one flips.

After you publish strong results pointing at a living suspect, expect the Katana that night. Put your next census target and full reasoning in your will beforehand so the Village can finish the chain without you. Here the will's hang order (Dave, Niaj, Judy) was followed exactly.

When two players claim the same unique Village role after its actions were public, weigh who named the targets in public reads before each action happened. Also weigh who uses night labels (N2/N3) rather than public trial days. The copier usually echoes the public log.
Don't fake-claim a Neutral role that is in the archive while the real holder is alive and unplaced. Once that player flips, you are proven a liar. Prefer claims that the remaining slots can absorb.

Prosecute a player whose claim mechanically overflows the archive/role slots and who sits in a confirmed visitor list. A prosecution skips the nomination vote, so Yakuza can't block it with No votes and can't save the target with a doubled Innocent unless they have the numbers.

Stay unclaimed while your tokens are live, but keep a will that logs each prosecution with its NIGHT number (N2, N3). If someone copies your claim later, the exact night labels and your earlier public reads naming each target before you prosecuted them are your best proof.

Unique roles (Vulture, Smuggler) settle claim conflicts once one flips. When two players claim a Unique role, hang the one whose claim conflicts with harder evidence first; the other liar is then exposed for free.

When a Clerk rig may be running, nominate your top suspect first, before the suspect can nominate you. A rig executes whoever is successfully nominated, so the first nomination of a Good player is the danger. Publicly tell trusted players to vote No on any nomination of a confirmed Good.

A player who changes claim right after a true-alignment census (Vanilla to a Neutral role) is very likely covering. Treat the new claim as a fallback cover until a unique flip or slot count confirms it.

Before faking a Unique or listed role (e.g. Vulture from an archive), remember its real holder is alive and will flip it. Only take that claim if your team can make sure the holder dies by a cleaned kill, or if you can steer the town away from hanging them. Otherwise the flip exposes you on the spot.

When an Archivist list is public on Day 2, count the unseen slots in night chat before anyone fake-claims. Assign at most that many off-list claims across the whole team. Three teammates claiming three unlisted roles against two open slots got two of them hanged in a row.

Use the rig on the first Day when a villager is likely to face a contested trial, such as a counterclaim duel. A rig saved until you are the last Yakuza only guarantees your own hanging, because you will be the nominee.

When two players counterclaim the same role and one of them holds the role your cover depends on, use the Katana on the other one at night. That leaves the town with an unopposed claimant they trust and a dead player whose flip doesn't touch your cover.

Combine a public archive list with Unique role tags and flips to build a complete role census. Once every role is placed, any surviving claim that duplicates a flipped Unique role is proof, with no need for investigator results.

Watching the player whose results most threaten the Yakuza (e.g. a Census Taker who has already pointed at suspects) pays off: the Katana tends to come to them, and a lone visitor on a Katana victim is near-proof once any Smuggler is dead. Repeat the watch on that player until they're hit.

Once an archive list is public, track Unique roles (Vulture, Smuggler) separately. A living Neutral claim of a Unique archived role can be checked the moment another claimant flips it, so pressure claims of Unique roles hard, and never let a flip of one go unchecked against existing claims.

When two players both claim the same unique-slot role (e.g. Prosecutor), test whose stated night timing matches mechanics (actions are submitted at night: N2 for a Day 3 trial). A copycat often labels actions by the public trial day.

When a Neutral claim (Vulture) conveniently explains a bad census result, remember the claimant switched from Vanilla only after that result went public. Treat claim switches made in response to a result as a strong Evil signal, not an explanation.
Claim with your full log in one compact public message as early as the result is decisive; short, numbered results let others build slot math quickly and cost little budget.

Don't make a role claim before Archivist, Survey or Profiler lists are likely public. A Vanilla claim has no slot once an archive shows most roles. If you must claim early, pick an archived Good role nobody has claimed yet, or stay vague. Check the slot count before every claim.

When two players both claim a Village role your team doesn't hold, work out in night chat which one is real and which one is a Neutral. If a teammate's cover depends on that Neutral (for example a fake Vulture claim), never push the Neutral's hang. Their flip exposes your teammate.

Never fake-claim a Unique role (Vulture, Smuggler) while its real holder may be alive and unplaced. One flip proves the claim false and ends the game for you. Prefer a repeatable role, or one already confirmed dead.

If a Lookout is watching likely targets, give the Katana to the teammate who is already doomed. Their visit only confirms what town already believes, and the Katana passes untouched to a clean member when they die.

A doomed Yakuza's last defense and will get read as protecting a teammate. Defending or attacking someone in your final words can steer town against your own interests. Spend those words on the hang target that helps the surviving teammate most.

applies_to: Ex-Con and other low-value Village roles
tip: On Day 1, don't post forward-looking mechanical warnings such as 'Evil results can be frames or Ex-Con reads'. Yakuza read that as a thinking investigator and kill you N1, and a Mortician cleans your will. Keep D1 talk generic and save the Ex-Con explanation for your will or for when a check actually lands on you.

Unique roles (Vulture, Smuggler) plus flips give airtight contradictions. If a Unique role flips, anyone else who claimed it is lying, no investigator needed. Check every claim against Unique roles already flipped.

Once an archive is public, count unseen slots. Any role proven to exist that isn't in the archive (a public prosecution, a cleaning) fills one. That quickly shows Vanilla or unarchived power claims overflowing, and it cracked three Yakuza claims this game.

When copying a role claim, mirror the mechanics exactly: prosecutions are chosen on Nights N2/N3, not on Days D3/D4. Claiming late, only after the actions went public, plus wrong timing labels reads as a copy. If you're a real Unique Neutral, counterclaiming the fake holder of your own role beats stealing a living Village role.

With a public archive, fake claims must fit the few unseen slots. Two teammates claiming Vanilla into one slot gets both hanged. Plan in night chat which teammate takes which free slot before anyone claims.

When an archive or survey result exists, post the raw list early. Get every visitor and suspect to claim first, without hints, then do the slot count publicly. Unseen slots = N - listed - roles proven to exist (e.g. the Mortician from a clean, the Prosecutor from a prosecution). Claims outside the list that overflow those slots are lies, and several overflowing claimants can be ordered by visits.
evidence: On Day 2 Grace waited for Heidi to claim, then posted the archive. That showed at most one of Dave/Frank/Niaj could be honest. On Day 3 the prosecution proved an unseen Prosecutor, which closed the last slot. All three liars (Smuggler, Mortician, Ballot Stuffer) were hanged in a row.

tip: Once an archive list is public, any fake claim of an unlisted role competes for very few slots. Prefer an archived role that no living player has claimed, and never a Unique role (Vulture, Smuggler) whose real holder may be alive. Coordinate in night chat so teammates don't stack claims on the same scarce unseen slots.
evidence: Dave (Sheriff), Frank (Accountant) and Niaj (Vanilla) all claimed unlisted roles on Day 2 and were hanged in turn. Judy's archived Vulture claim survived until the real Vulture, Erin, flipped on Day 5, which exposed her immediately.

tip: Give the Katana to the teammate who is already doomed or flagged. When the Mortician kills, have him also clean the same target, so a Lookout or Tracker sees only him. Each flagged holder's death then passes the Katana to an unseen member.
evidence: On Night 2 Dave both held the Katana and cleaned Bob. On Night 3 Niaj held it to kill Heidi, and Mallory saw only Niaj. Judy was never seen visiting until the final nights, and she survived to the last four.

tip: Don't hold the rig until you are exposed. The best moment is a Day with an unresolved claim dispute between you and a villager, or when you can push through a nomination of a key villager. A rig on the day you will be nominated just guarantees your own execution.
evidence: Judy kept her token through Day 5, when Erin and Ivan were splitting the town over the Prosecutor claim. A Night 4 rig followed by a nomination of Ivan would have executed him no matter the Guilty vote. Instead she rigged on Night 5, after Erin's Vulture flip had already exposed her. The rigged Day 6 then hanged Judy herself.

applies_to: Prosecutor and any claimed power role
tip: A Prosecutor should stay unclaimed while prosecuting the top slot-math suspects. When a copycat appears, win the counterclaim with checkable details: correct Night labels for night actions, and public Day reads that named each target before the prosecution.
evidence: Ivan prosecuted Dave on Night 2 and Niaj on Night 3 without claiming. When Erin copied the claim, Grace and Alice sided with Ivan for two reasons: he had publicly named Dave and Niaj before each prosecution, and he labelled the prosecutions N2/N3. Erin wrote D3/D4 and had vouched for Dave on Day 2.

applies_to: Neutral (Vulture) and anyone tempted to counterclaim
tip: Don't copy a role whose actions were already announced publicly. The real holder will counterclaim with better details, and losing the duel gets you hanged. As a Vulture near the threshold, a low-key claim that fits the slots, or staying quiet, beats a public claim fight.
evidence: Erin claimed Prosecutor on Day 4, only after both prosecutions were public. Ivan counterclaimed, Carol's Scout result cleared Ivan, and Erin was hanged on Day 5 with 6 alive. That was three short of her Vulture win at 3 alive.

tip: In the endgame, rely on visit-graph results: a Lookout's lone other visitor to a Katana victim, or a Scout result putting a suspect in a different group from the victim. Posting these exactly when the vote is close can break a two-way claim tie.
evidence: Mallory's Night 3 watch on Heidi showed only Niaj. Carol's Night 4 result put Ivan in a different visit group from Mallory, the Katana victim, which cleared him. Ivan was cleared and the Day 5 trial went 4-2 against Erin.

tip: Save cleans for players whose wills are likely to hold results about your team, such as investigators who have probably checked you. A first-night clean of a talkative player wastes a token and may only reveal an Ex-Con.
evidence: Dave's Night 1 clean showed only that Olivia was an Ex-Con, and that info merely let him build a Sheriff claim that slot math broke. His Night 2 clean of Bob hid Bob's 'Mortician/Scout/Vulture' profile of Dave, and that clean was the useful one.

applies_to: Fabricator and other Yakuza who fake an investigative claim
tip: A fake Sheriff claim with Evil checks on Good players survives only while those players cannot be shown Good. Two of my three checks (Carol, Erin) were proven Good within two days. Choose check targets who are unlikely to flip or be protected, or fake a role whose results cannot be contradicted by a Medic survival or a Vanilla flip.

Defending a doomed teammate with Innocent votes after the tally is lost makes you the obvious next target. Run the vote math in night chat before the nomination, and if defense cannot save them, vote with the town or stay quiet so your voting record stays clean.

Track each Medic's remaining tokens before picking a Katana target. Our attacks on Erin and Heidi were blunted while she had tokens, and the Heidi kill only landed after Erin spent her last token on herself. Time kills for the night a protector is empty, and move the Katana to a member who can cover for the holder.

applies_to: Yakuza, especially a Fabricator paired with a fake Sheriff claim
tip: Coordinate framing with the claimed alignment check: a Good player framed that night genuinely appears Evil to alignment checks. Make the timing and target consistent, and remember that a later flip may expose the frame without making the original check mechanically impossible.

Don't default to a no-kill night just to avoid a trail. A quiet night gives Village investigators another full set of results and can help them build a case; also, the stall rule can make repeated no-death cycles dangerous. Weigh a kill against likely protection, and target protectors or other high-value roles when possible.

Plan the rig around the next Day's likely nominations: it makes every successful nomination that Day an execution, even if the trial vote is Innocent. Use it when that outcome benefits your faction and avoid rigging a Day when a teammate could be nominated. Don't save it past your likely survival window.

Before a teammate's trial, do the vote math and agree whether to defend or bus them. A No nomination vote and Innocent trial vote become strong links after the teammate flips; don't defend reflexively when the execution is already likely.

Self-protecting with Standard Defense every night burns tokens and tells the Yakuza exactly where you will be; rotate protection targets and keep one token for the night a real Katana holder is hunting you.

Surveyor and Diviner pools name a group, not a holder; before voting on a pool-based lead, demand a result that narrows to one player, and remember the group's members may include the accuser's own team.

Track which claimed role the Yakuza's Katana and frames have targeted; a Sheriff whose Evil reads land on players later shown Good (Vanilla, Medic) is far more likely lying than a Medic is, so weigh the lineup of confirmed-Good reads before hanging.

Avoid executing on a chain of conditional reasoning that only works if a second unverified claim is true; when two claims conflict, find a mechanical result that tests one of them directly before voting.

Long, repetitive public messages on the same unresolved point cost budget without moving votes; a short message that states a concrete contradiction or a vote is worth more and keeps budget for trial turns.

applies_to: Investigators and anyone using their results
tip: Separate what a result proves from what it merely suggests. A Surveyor’s role result puts that role in the group, but does not identify its holder; an archive confirms sampled roles exist, not who holds them. Keep conclusions conditional on unverified claims.

Before voting Guilty, state a specific contradiction and check whether framing, appearances, or another mechanic could explain it. A pool plus an alignment result is not automatically an identified culprit, and a suspicious vote is evidence to weigh—not proof by itself.

Treat the stall rule as a deadline for a death, not a reason to hang a particular suspect. Any death can reset the count, including a night kill; use the time pressure to prioritize a sound case rather than convert uncertainty into certainty.

Keep independent Neutrals in the solve even after Yakuza are gone. A surviving Arsonist can win alone at a small endgame, so eliminating Yakuza does not mean the remaining players are safe or that the game is effectively won.

Account for the Cardinal’s Divine retaliation when the Cardinal dies: it can create another death that night or the following night. Record the trigger in your will so the next death is not misread as an unrelated attack.

When an archive reveals an Arsonist in play, track low-profile players who avoid taking strong stances or offering claims; focusing entirely on Yakuza allows an Arsonist to douse undisturbed and wipe the town in a single ignition.

Alternating self-protection with protecting key confirmed town power roles effectively counters Katana strikes, but be aware that once self-protect tokens are exhausted, the Yakuza will prioritize killing the exposed Medic.
Never mistakenly claim an explicitly Evil role like Puppeteer; even if trying to act transparent or unconcerned, it instantly outs your faction to town.

Scout group results only show who was linked; with few players per visit group they can look like 'nobody visited anybody'. Log every night's group sizes and names, and cross-check them against deaths and attacks to pin down which visits were real.

A surveyor or other pool result names a group, not a holder. Before voting on a pool, ask which member the result actually identifies and whether any claim or result separates them; several days were spent executing whoever was on trial rather than the real suspect.

Track which players vote No on a nomination of a later-flipped Yakuza or Clerk. Such voting records were the clearest mechanical lead and were discussed too late, after the pool theories had already cost two Village lives.
Deaths at night from Arsonist ignition or Katana can happen together with a Cardinal curse; check the revealed causes of death for stacked attacks before assuming a single killer.

Before voting Guilty on a claimed Sheriff, check whether their failed or contradicted checks rely on framing that the accused could have had; a single contradicted check against a claimed Sheriff is weaker than a voting-record pattern.
Igniting once 3 or more players are doused when multiple factions are poised to clash can instantly end the game in a solo victory by wiping out both town and mafia cores simultaneously.
When an Archivist reveals an Arsonist is in the setup, keep in mind that quiet players who never get attacked or investigated and quietly vote along with majorities are prime Arsonist suspects.

If your target has claimed a heavily verified town role like Archivist, pushing them directly is suicidal; instead, steer towards keeping them alive until endgames where mislynching becomes mathematically plausible or prepare for the Jester pivot.

Even when aggressively hunting Yakuza, track Arsonist and Neutral killing threats in parallel if an Archivist reveals an Arsonist exists. Ignoring the douse build-up allows a multi-kill sweep in the endgame.
Surveyor results isolate roles within 3-person geographic neighbor pools; crossing these pools with dead flips and unique claims rapidly narrows down evil roles to binary choices.
Staying completely under the radar while town fixates on mechanical conflicts between Yakuza and power roles enables undetected mass douses and a sudden decisive ignition.

A Medic can give Standard Defense for free every night to any living player, so a Standard Katana attack on a player with a living Medic usually fails. Before choosing a target, assume a Medic covers someone each night, and plan to block or kill the Medic first or accept the attack may be wasted.

A puppet only lasts the Day after it is set, and it lapses if the Puppeteer dies that night. Do not spend the last puppet on a night when you expect to be attacked, since the puppet then does nothing.

Yakuza cannot see who is doused, so assume a living Arsonist has doused several players. An ignite can kill the whole remaining team in one night, so push to hang or pressure the Arsonist early instead of spending the last Yakuza night on a single Katana kill.

applies_to: Yakuza with a fake power-role claim
tip: Pick fake alignment reads that no mechanical result can contradict before the next Day, such as a target who has no attack or protection evidence. Alice's Evil reads on Erin and Carol were contradicted within a Day by a Katana survival and a Vanilla flip, which made the claim look fake.

applies_to: Village investigators, especially Archivists and Surveyors
tip: Treat sampled role lists as evidence of presence, not a census or an identity check. An archive can confirm that a role exists without showing who has it; a survey result places a role somewhere in a group without naming its holder. Keep every candidate in play until independent evidence narrows the group.

applies_to: Village investigators and anyone evaluating alignment results
tip: Account for framing before treating an Evil result as evidence of true Evil alignment. A Fabricator can make a Good player appear Evil to alignment checks that night, so ask whether the result could have been manipulated and seek corroboration before hanging the target.

After a faction member flips, reconstruct the full nomination and trial votes, then compare them with what each player said. A No on the nomination and Innocent at trial can be especially revealing when they protected a flipped teammate.

Keep conditional claims conditional. A pool result plus an unverified role claim may make one person a strong suspect, but it does not make that claim true or uniquely identify the holder. State which assumptions your conclusion depends on, and revisit them when new evidence arrives.

Track how many doused players are still alive, not just how many you have targeted. Ignite once you have a strong multi-kill opportunity or suspicion makes waiting too risky; a target who dies before ignition is a wasted douse.

Treat a role-group result as a constraint, not an identity. Don't narrow a pool using an unverified claim or an archive that only establishes a role exists; seek independent confirmation before treating one player as mechanically identified.

applies_to: Village investigators and anyone evaluating their claims
tip: An Evil alignment result can be caused by framing. Before treating it as proof, check whether a Fabricator could have targeted that player and look for independent evidence that distinguishes a frame from a false claim.

Track the stall-rule conditions precisely, but don't let deadline pressure turn a group result or an uncertain check into certainty. State what is verified, what depends on a claim, and what the cost of waiting actually is before voting.

When an archive or survey confirms an Arsonist or Serial Killer exists, keep a running list of who could be it. Press quiet players who give no role claim and only 'measured' commentary. An Arsonist produces no deaths until it ignites, so nights with no kills are not evidence that it's harmless.
evidence: Judy's Day 2 archive listed Arsonist. Mallory said only 'No result to share' and was never asked for a role in five days. She doused four players and her single ignite ended the game.

tip: If a teammate fake-claims an investigator and calls someone Evil, don't spend the Katana on that player. Attacking them shows the Yakuza don't think they're Evil, and it hands the target a confirmed survival story.
evidence: Alice called Erin Evil on Day 2, and the Yakuza attacked Erin on N2. Erin's self-protection saved her. Frank then used exactly this contradiction ('Yakuza don't spend their Katana on their own') as his Guilty reason at Alice's trial.

tip: Do the vote math before defending a teammate on trial. If your No and Innocent votes can't save them, vote with the town. Futile defensive votes become the case that hangs you once the teammate flips.
evidence: Bob was nominated 6-4 and hanged 6-4 as Clerk while Alice and Ivan voted No and Innocent. On Day 5 Judy nominated Alice citing exactly those votes, and she was hanged 6-2.

tip: When forced to choose within a suspect pool, discount evidence from a claimant whose earlier result is already contradicted by mechanics. An Evil check from an unconfirmed 'Sheriff' whose last Evil target survived a Katana hit should weigh almost nothing, and framing is always possible.
evidence: On Day 3 the town hanged Carol over Bob because of Alice's N2 'Carol Evil' check, which came from a frame. Erin had already survived a Katana attack after Alice called her Evil. Carol flipped Vanilla, and Bob turned out to be the Clerk.

tip: Never publicly claim your true Yakuza role, especially when an archive has listed it. If you need a claim, pick a Village role that can't be contradicted, or stay vague.
evidence: Ivan claimed 'Puppeteer' on Day 5, and Erin immediately pointed out that it was a Yakuza role from Judy's archive. Ivan only escaped hanging because Mallory's ignite killed him that night.

tip: After you save a claimed investigator from the Katana, that investigator stays the top target. Keep protecting them, especially when that protection is free, rather than spending your last token on yourself.
evidence: Erin's free protection saved Heidi on N3. On N4 Erin spent her last token to self-protect, the Yakuza re-targeted Heidi, and Heidi died. Erin died to the Katana the next night anyway.

tip: Stay low-profile, never claim a role, and douse players the town won't hang. A claimed Cardinal is an excellent douse: igniting them triggers a Divine curse on a remaining Good player.
evidence: Mallory doused the Cardinal on N1 and ignited on N5. Dave's curse then killed Frank, the last Good player, clearing the board for her solo win.

tip: Spend one-shot tokens on a contested Day while the holder is alive. A rig or puppet that is still in hand when its owner dies is wasted. A Clerk rig on a non-teammate nominee is safe even if you are in a suspect pool.
evidence: Bob was hanged still holding his Clerk token, after deciding 'rigging tomorrow could backfire'. Ivan held his puppet until N5, and it lapsed when he died that night.

tip: When a Medic has protected a Katana target, a retry on the same player after a failed hit mostly drains their tokens and makes the pattern obvious. Block or kill the protector before the strike, or pick a different target that night.

Never state publicly a fact only the Yakuza could know, such as a Katana target before the victim reports it. Calling it an inference does not clear you once the town has a timing argument against you.

Track dousing and ignition as a separate threat. If deaths do not fit the Katana pattern or claimed Medic protections, assume a third-faction killer such as an Arsonist may be silently dousing players for several nights.

A Medic protecting themself with Standard Defense costs 1 token and ties a Standard Katana. Strong is needed only to beat a Strong attack. Check the exact token cost before calling a claim impossible.

A Clerk rig on a day when a dangerous investigator is nominated can execute them even against an Innocent majority. Plan the rig for a Day when the nominee is a confirmed investigator, and keep the Yakuza Yes votes ready.

A rig guarantees execution after a successful nomination regardless of the Guilty vote. Prioritize getting the right target onto trial; if the rig already ensures the execution, consider splitting team trial votes to reduce obvious vote associations.

Coordinate the Katana holder and target with enough agreement to meet the living-Yakuza majority, and make sure each member submits the agreed choices. A missing or conflicting vote can cost the attack.
Track neutral threats as well as faction enemies. An Arsonist can silently douse multiple players and ignite them together, killing several members of a faction in one night.

A unified vote can help secure an execution, but it can also bind teammates together in the public record. When the outcome is already guaranteed by a rig, weigh whether a less conspicuous vote split is safer.

A single random exact-role draw (Surveyor, Diviner, Scout group) from a three-player group points at each member only weakly. Stack independent pulls before treating a claim as proven, and treat two conflicting claimants in the same group as unresolved rather than picking one by timing or tone.

Never state another player's night outcome in public before it is public (for example, that a Medic was Katana-hit). Such a slip became the decisive trial argument against Alice. Keep night knowledge in the Yakuza chat, and if you slip, name a checkable source at once.
If a trial's announced verdict is Innocent but someone is still executed, a Clerk rig happened that Day. Treat the rig as spent, and stop assuming later executions reflect the Guilty/Innocent vote.

Self-protecting with Standard costs 1 token and ties a Standard Katana, so 'survived the Katana' is consistent with a self-protect. Post a full token ledger per night (for example 2, then 1, then 0) and say which protections were on whom, so the claim can be checked against the counts.

An Arsonist douses silently and ignites every doused player at once, so a village can lose several players in one night. Once Yakuza are dead, assume any living player may be doused, and vote on the dousing pattern and ignition nights rather than on Day speeches.

applies_to: Everyone, especially on a rigged Day
tip: A Clerk rig makes anyone successfully nominated get executed even if the trial vote is Innocent. Once a rig is exposed, don't rely on an Innocent majority to save a nominee; focus on preventing nominations or changing the day's outcome.

When someone states a specific, unannounced night event as fact, ask how they know. Separate a plausible inference from private knowledge, then compare their explanation with the timeline and available results.
Before hanging a possible Jester, account for both the Jester's win and their revenge attack on a Guilty voter. A suspicious voting pattern is not automatically worth giving a Neutral its win.

Calculate the nomination threshold before acting: with two players, a majority is two votes. If the nominee votes No, one player's nomination cannot force a trial, so persuasion—not repeated nominations—is essential.

applies_to: Village after the Yakuza are eliminated
tip: Reassess the win condition and remaining threats instead of treating the Yakuza's defeat as safety. A Vanilla claim does not clear a Neutral killer, and the game continuing can rule out an alignment without identifying the exact role.

Watch for slips where a player discusses unannounced night actions or targets—such as claiming someone survived an attack before that player or the moderator reports it. Attack details on no-death nights are known only to the attackers.
Once your Medic claim is public, prioritize self-protection with tokens. The killing faction will almost certainly target an exposed protector to clear the way for subsequent kills.

Do not let an intense focus on identified Mafia pools cause you to overlook quiet players who could be Neutrals. An Arsonist dousing in the background can wipe out both factions in a single ignition if never pressured.
A Clerk rig can make an Innocent majority still execute the nominee. When a trial verdict and an execution disagree, treat the rig as the cause and don't read the Guilty count as the town's choice.

Single random Surveyor or Profiler draws can't name anyone. Weigh votes across trials instead: track who sides with players later confirmed Evil on two separate votes, and who changes side under pressure.

applies_to: Scout, Sheriff, Seer and other investigators
tip: Publicly claiming an information role on Day 2 made the Scout the Katana's Night 3 target. Hold the claim until a result must be shared, and put nightly results in your will as a backup.

Douse quietly over several nights while voting with the Village on lynches of other players, then ignite once three or more players are doused. This wiped out three players in one night and left the Village with no way to find you.
Never state a night outcome that hasn't been announced, such as a Katana hit on a player who hasn't reported it. Carol and Dave caught exactly that slip, and it exposed the team.

When you inherit suspicious voting baggage (such as voting alongside flipped Yakuza), defend yourself just plausibly enough that town feels justified executing you, rather than suspecting a deliberate Jester trap.
Voting Guilty on yourself during trial is legal and counts toward the required majority; casting a self-Guilty vote can lock in your execution when town votes are close.

In the endgame after evil factions flip, do not tunnel exclusively on voting associations without considering that an Executioner whose target died early has become a Jester baiting an easy execution.

When a Clerk might be in play, do not allow close or speculative nominations to pass under the assumption that a nominee will be cleared during trial; an Innocent trial majority cannot save someone from a rigged execution.

When multiple players claim Vanilla Villager and an investigative check proves an evil role exists in that subset, watch who aggressively nominates or votes guilty on the investigator; evil players will coordinate to suppress further reveals.

Ignite as soon as 3 or more high-impact players are doused, especially when town and mafia are focused on claim conflicts; doing so can wipe out mafia and protectors in one sweep and secure an endgame win.

Never state a night fact you could not legitimately know, such as who was attacked before the target reported it. Alice's unsourced Night 4 Katana claim got her hanged as a slip. Label inferences as inferences from the start.

A one-shot token held for a 'decisive Day' is wasted if the team dies first. I held my puppet token for four nights and spent it on the night I died. Use such tokens early, when your teammates are still alive to exploit them.

A frame only matters if a living Sheriff, Seer or similar alignment check can read it. Before framing, confirm an alignment investigator is alive and likely to check that player, otherwise the night's action buys nothing.

Shared Guilty votes with Yakuza are a lead, not proof. Grace was hanged for overlapping with the Yakuza bloc on Heidi while the real Arsonist survived. Before executing, check for a mechanical contradiction in each voter's own claims and results.

applies_to: Archivists and anyone interpreting anonymous role samples
tip: Treat an archive result as a role-pool clue, not a player list: it names no holders, and a role missing from the sample is not necessarily absent from the game. Cross-reference it with later claims without assigning roles to people.

A Surveyor's result names one role held by someone in the group; it does not identify which member, and it does not prove the role appears exactly once. Keep the group-level conclusion separate from any player-level suspicion.

A Clerk rig can execute a successfully nominated player despite an Innocent majority. If the verdict and revealed votes seem inconsistent, account for the rig before treating the result as a normal trial outcome.

Prepare your will during the Day with information already known and any planned action clearly labelled as a plan. You cannot add a result received at Night if you die that same Night, so do not rely on being able to record it afterward.

Plan douses toward a useful mass ignition, not just one likely kill. Dousing players from different factions can let one ignition remove several threats at once; weigh the payoff of waiting for more against the risk of dying or losing your chance to ignite.

applies_to: Everyone, especially neutrals in the endgame
tip: Recalculate nomination thresholds as the living player count shrinks. With two players, a nomination needs both Yes votes, so a single opponent cannot force you onto trial by themself. If there is no forced nomination, refusing to help start a trial can buy a night—provided your night action can capitalize on it.

Keep public claims and mechanical explanations carefully calibrated. Present a guess as a guess, not a result: overclaiming gives others a concrete point to challenge, while a plausible low-threat cover can help you survive until your next night action.

Once a Clerk might be alive, treat a passed nomination as a possible execution. When a player in a suspected pool opens the Day by nominating a claimed investigator, vote No on the nomination itself. Don't vote Yes 'so they can answer'; under a rig, the Guilty/Innocent vote is meaningless.
evidence: D4: Bob, in Heidi's Fabricator pool, nominated her first thing. Dave, Grace and Mallory joined the Yakuza for 6 Yes. The trial went 5-4 Innocent, but the rig executed the Good Surveyor anyway.

tip: Before posting, check every factual claim against what is public. Never state night facts that only your night chat knows, such as who the Katana targeted or that an attack failed. Frame suspicions as questions, or say nothing.
evidence: D5: Alice said Erin 'was hit by the Katana on Night 4' before anyone had announced an attack. Erin, Carol and Dave called it a Yakuza slip, and Alice was hanged 6-2.

tip: In the endgame, when a Jester or Executioner-turned-Jester may be alive, watch for self-votes. A player who votes Yes on their own nomination or Guilty on their own trial is almost certainly a Jester. If you must hang, use a bare Guilty majority so fewer Good players are exposed to the revenge.
evidence: D6: Grace voted Yes on her own nomination and Guilty on herself, but town hanged her 4-0 when 3 was enough. She flipped Neutral, and the revenge killed Carol. That left Dave alone with the Arsonist, who could block every nomination.

tip: After the Yakuza are dead, voting with them is weak evidence against the remaining suspects, because Neutrals often voted with them too. Check which suspect had motive and opportunity for the Neutral kills. If the evidence for each candidate is about even, push for claims and counterclaims before hanging.
evidence: D6: Carol and Dave hanged Grace for her D4/D5 votes alongside Alice, Bob and Ivan. The real Arsonist, Mallory, had voted Innocent on Heidi and nominated Alice, so she looked clean on votes.

tip: Claim Vanilla, vote with the town consensus, and douse the players who keep the game going: the Katana holder, active Yakuza and a claimed Medic. Ignite once 3 or more are doused. A single ignite can then remove a whole faction and the town's protector at once.
evidence: Mallory doused Frank, Erin, Bob and Ivan over N1-N4 and ignited on N5 with 3 alive and doused. That killed both remaining Yakuza and Erin, then she won with one more douse-and-ignite.

tip: Use one-shot tokens such as the puppet or the forged will while the whole team is alive and the town is still deciding. Holding them 'for a better Day' risks dying with them unused.
evidence: Ivan held his puppet token from N1 to N5. He finally spent it the night he died, so the puppeting lapsed. Alice died with her forge token unused.

tip: If you are hiding a power role, avoid a hard Vanilla claim you may have to reverse. Say 'no claim yet' or give a vague answer. A Vanilla-to-Medic switch hands the evil side a 'claim flip' argument.
evidence: Erin claimed Vanilla on D3 and Medic on D4. Grace, Ivan, Alice and Bob used the switch against her on D4 and D5, which weakened her defense of Heidi.

tip: After a failed Katana attack, switch to an unprotected information role rather than retrying the same target. Expect the Medic to keep covering the obvious target.
evidence: After Heidi survived on N2, Erin protected her again on N3. The Yakuza instead killed Frank, the unprotected Scout, on N3.

tip: Keep the Katana holder from being the same player every night when the team is under pressure; a predictable holder who is also the Clerk gets read from the visit and vote history.

Avoid unnecessary Day-time nomination votes that can be read against you (e.g. Yes on a nominee who is also your teammate's accuser) and do not let a teammate's Clerk claim become the team's public defence.
When a teammate is publicly exposed, do not defend them with a single line of argument; push a neutral, checkable contradiction against the accuser instead.

Compare Scout and Surveyor visit-group claims against each other and against any claimed protection visit; a single claimed visit that links two players in a group can falsify an otherwise clean Scout result.
In a two-player endgame a hang needs both Guilty votes, so an accusation that depends on an unverifiable claim gets nowhere; press for a concrete check instead of a flip-flopping nomination.
Use the rig when you can steer a successful nomination toward a non-teammate and are unlikely to be the nominee yourself. Saving it indefinitely risks dying with it unused.
Each night, confirm matching Katana-holder and target votes, plus any separate actions. A unified plan avoids losing the attack to a split vote.
Keep daytime contributions individually credible. Repeating generic agreement can look coordinated; develop distinct, plausible reads without needlessly tying yourself to a teammate.

Separate a role result from the identity of the player who produced it. A Surveyor learns one random role from each group; matching results in overlapping groups do not prove the same person was sampled, especially when roles can repeat.

Before trusting a Surveyor or Diviner overlap, list which players are in each group and which role was shown; a repeated role across overlapping groups only isolates one player if the same copy was sampled both times.
When several Village players quickly echo the same defence of one player on Day 1-3, track that bloc early, because the Yakuza used Day discussion to steer votes.
Check every counterclaim against the death record: a Medic claim that does not explain who protected the one Katana survivor the night before is a strong lead.

Do not let a Vanilla Villager claim alone decide the endgame; with few players alive, an unverifiable Village claim gets the same weight as an unverifiable Ex-Con claim, so press for visit-based checks instead.

At two players alive a trial needs both Guilty votes, so an opponent who refuses to vote Guilty can never be executed; pressure the other side early to prevent a stalemate that favours the hidden killer.

Treat sampled roles as evidence of possibility, not a complete census. A Surveyor learns one random role from each group, and overlapping groups do not prove the same player was sampled twice. An incomplete Archivist list also does not prove a role is unique or rule out unlisted roles.

A mechanical contradiction can establish that a claim is false, but not who lied or which faction they belong to. In particular, a Jester may benefit from being caught in a lie and hanged. Seek faction-specific evidence before treating a contradiction as grounds to execute.

applies_to: Village players deciding whether to execute
tip: When role flips are disabled, keep claims provisional and compare independent results, visit mechanics, and vote behavior. Also account for Jester revenge: a broad Guilty vote can expose many useful players to the random revenge attack.

Resolve a possible Arsonist before the game reaches two players. With two players, a majority requires both votes, so neither can force a nomination or execution alone; letting the day end may simply give the Arsonist another night action.
When executing an obvious fake-claimer, beware that an Executioner whose target died overnight turns into a Jester. Never let confirmed power roles vote Guilty, to protect them from Divine revenge.
If an Arsonist is known to be in the role pool and multiple nights pass without Arsonist kills or visible visits, assume quiet dousing is underway and prepare for a massive multi-death ignition.
Self-protecting after outing yourself as Medic effectively guards against the Katana, but Standard Defense does not protect against Divine Attacks such as Jester revenge or Cardinal curses.

Scout results are only as reliable as the claimant; check each claimed group against other claims (Medic saves, Katana targets). Frank's N3 separate-group result contradicted Heidi's and Grace's claims, which exposed the liar, so test graph claims against every visit claim before accepting or rejecting them.

Avoid stacking votes on a single unverifiable claim in a two-or-three-player endgame. Ivan's push to hang Mallory on the Ex-Con claim let Carol and Mallory end up with the win, so demand a concrete check before voting on a claim alone.

applies_to: Village roles with protection or information
tip: Note that Yakuza Puppeteers can write messages in your name. If a claim from you appears that you did not send, say so immediately and record the discrepancy in your will so the table can separate your real results from puppet posts.

Arsonist dousing persists across nights and a single Ignite kills all doused players, so an unchecked Arsonist can wipe several living players at once. Track who is doused via any results you receive and push for a nomination before the ignition night.
Long repetitive public messages on the same pair of players burned budget without new information. Keep posts short and focused on mechanical checks.

Pre-empting or claiming a specific power role revealed by an information role (such as a Surveyor or Archivist pool) reliably baits the true role into an aggressive counterclaim, handing town a neat mechanical contradiction they will rush to execute.
Voting Guilty on yourself during your own trial guarantees an extra Guilty vote toward the required majority, which helps close the margin against cautious or stalling voters.
When executing someone on a blatant visit-graph contradiction, keep high-value power roles (like a counter-claiming Medic) off the Guilty vote to insulate them from Jester revenge.

When a role appears in two different Surveyor reports, check if an Archivist sample or prior reveals suggest that role is a singleton; if so, the player at the intersection of both survey groups is uniquely identified.

Catching a player in a direct mechanical or visit-graph contradiction proves they lied, but does not prove they are Yakuza; Jesters frequently manufacture clumsy fake claims and visit conflicts specifically to get hanged.

Waiting until 3 critical players are doused before igniting can instantly break parity and eliminate both Yakuza killers and key Village roles simultaneously, leaving an easy endgame against vanilla survivors.

Before a night kill, check that the Katana holder's attacker isn't the only one whose result can be traced; the Arsonist, Medic and Surveyor all leave public trails, so keep the holder rotation and target choice consistent with what the Village can cross-check.
Do not let a teammate's late public defense or a Clerk claim become the only Innocent vote on a Yakuza-linked nominee; it isolates you and makes the next trial a two-person coin flip.

When a teammate is killed and the team is down to one, avoid pushing a Guilty vote on a Village-aligned claim via private messages; the PM trail is what the other survivor will use to build a case against you.

With two or three players alive, a Vanilla claim cannot be checked, so vote on the mechanical evidence (visits, the Arsonist's ignitions, win-check arithmetic) rather than on who pressed harder earlier.

Remember that a Medic protecting themself or a Surveyor's random pick means a single overlap or a single exact-role hit is not proof; check the group size and random selection before building a case on it.

Treat anonymous role samples and Surveyor results as possibilities, not player identifications. Two groups reporting the same role do not show that the same person has it; roles can repeat, and Judy’s archive sample was incomplete.

A mechanical contradiction can show that at least one account is false without identifying which player is evil. Before pushing a hang, consider whether the liar could be a Jester who benefits from execution, and avoid turning a contradiction into certainty about faction.

applies_to: Village players voting on a possible Jester
tip: If a hang is necessary but a Jester is plausible, seek only the Guilty votes needed and keep likely power roles off the Guilty side when possible: a Jester’s revenge can kill a random Guilty voter.

Weigh the value of revealing a role and its full information against making yourself an obvious night target or handing opponents a ready-made fake-claim list. Share information deliberately, and preserve a clear record in your will.

Plan douses as a set, not as isolated actions: prioritize targets likely to be valuable or share a faction, keep the running list accurate, and ignite when the simultaneous hit is decisive. Waiting until several players are doused can turn one action into a major swing.

Separate “these reports cannot all be true” from “this person is Evil.” A mechanical contradiction identifies a false claim or result, not necessarily its faction; consider Jester and Executioner incentives before voting to hang.
Keep a cover claim narrow and consistent with public facts, and make accusers compare it with their own unverified claims. Don’t invent extra results that create new ways to be checked.
In a multi-faction endgame, evaluate the consequences of a hang as well as the case for it. A vote can remove a dangerous opponent and still hand a Jester an independent win.

When a Yakuza has effectively confirmed themself, hang them before a contested claimer. A player whose fake claim breaks against mechanics may be a Jester, or an Executioner who became one, and hanging them gives them the win plus a Divine revenge kill. If you do hang a possible Jester, keep it to a bare majority and keep your confirmed power roles on Innocent.
evidence: On Day 4 Bob had admitted Clerk and both of Heidi's surveys pointed at him, yet the town hanged Grace 9-1. Grace was a Jester; her revenge picked Erin, the real Medic, from the Guilty voters, and Grace won.

tip: Track the conversion chain. If an archive lists Executioner and a quiet player dies to the Katana, assume a Jester may now exist. Look hard at sudden power-role claims that seem designed to get their speaker hanged.
evidence: Judy's archive showed Executioner. Judy (Grace's target) died to the Katana on N2. On Day 4 Grace jumped onto Heidi's 'Medic in {Erin, Frank, Grace}' result with a claim that was easy to disprove, and nobody raised the Jester possibility.

tip: If a Neutral killing role (Arsonist or Serial Killer) appears in an archive or survey, give each player a slot. Press anyone who admits a night action but won't name a role or target. Arsonists douse silently and then wipe out several players at once.
evidence: On Day 2 Mallory said 'I took an action elsewhere' while the archive listed Arsonist, and nobody followed up. On N4 her ignite killed Alice, Bob and Dave, and the knock-on effects left Village unable to win.

tip: Douse quietly across several nights, spreading your douses over different suspects. Ignite once 3+ players are doused, ideally just before the Yakuza and town finish each other off. Prepare a fake claim that explains your visits (Ex-Con fits well).
evidence: Mallory doused Dave, Alice and Bob on N1-N3 and ignited on N4, killing the Katana holder and the Cardinal. On Day 5 her Ex-Con claim got Carol to vote Innocent on her and then to hang Ivan with her.

tip: Don't use a puppet to post fake investigative results for a living investigator. They will correct it the next Day, which proves a Puppeteer exists and makes their real results look stronger. Use the puppet for something that can't be undone, such as a damaging nomination or vote push, or on a player the town is about to hang.
evidence: Ivan posted a fake N2 Scout result as Frank. On Day 4 Frank posted the real one and the town took it as confirmation of the Puppeteer from Judy's archive. Frank's results then drove Grace's hanging.

tip: When an investigation only probabilistically points at you, keep up the ambiguity your teammates have built ('roles repeat, the sample could be different players'). Never publicly confirm an Evil role. Spend one-shot tokens like the rig before you are exposed.
evidence: Ivan, Mallory and Dave had already argued that Heidi's overlap didn't prove Bob was Clerk. Bob then claimed Clerk outright. He died on N4 with his rig token unused.

tip: When a fake Medic claims your role, counterclaim at once with your full nightly log and check it against attacks and survivals. A claimed Medic whose targets don't explain a known survival is the one to doubt.
evidence: Erin's log (Carol N1, Frank N2, Frank N3) explained Frank surviving the N3 Katana attack and Frank's Scout groups. That exposed Grace's false Medic claim, although Erin should not then have voted Guilty herself.

tip: At three alive with two hidden enemy factions, a lone Villager usually can't win. Spend Days 3-4 identifying every faction so you don't reach that endgame. Before a mass-death night, work out what pending curses (Cardinal, Jester) will cost.
evidence: Carol faced Ivan (Yakuza) and Mallory (Arsonist) on Day 5. Hanging either one gave the game to the other, so no choice could save her.

tip: Post your three Scout names with the night number immediately after each night resolves, before any nomination. Delaying the names (as I did after Night 1 while the Village asked) let the Village treat the claim as unverified and gave the Yakuza time to target you.

A Katana kill proves its holder visited the target, so a single Lookout watch naming one visitor is strong evidence. Check every claim against which players could have held the Katana each night, and treat a denial with no second source as weaker than a mechanical result.

Keep the Katana holder and Diviner/Clerk actions off the same visible trail as the kill. Grace's Diviner group centred on the Scout gave away a visit pattern, and openly naming the Village investigators in the Yakuza chat invited the kill on whoever Village reads as most dangerous.

Private whips on one unverified claim (asking others for a Yes in PMs before a second source exists) are visible to everyone as a PM trail and get turned against you. Make the public case first, then vote.

Hang-pushing is read the same way for Yakuza and Jesters. When a Yakuza nominates a Village player right after a Village investigator dies, the Village reads it as a Yakuza move, so reduce the pattern by nominating less visibly or after a fresh result.

A single watch that names one visitor is only as good as the visit model; before accusing, check whether the kill could have come from a different holder or a self-visit, and ask for a second watch or a Veteran-style confirmation instead of pushing a trial on one log.
Private whips for a Yes vote on a single unverified claim are visible as a pattern (the PM counts are public); if you need votes, make the case in public with the evidence so the table can check it.

Track which claimed roles are Yakuza-only (Diviner, Ritualist, Clerk, Fabricator): a player who publicly claims one of them is a strong Yakuza lead, and reading that claim against kill timing and nominations beats weighing wording.

Yakuza who keep a passive partner (no action, no PMs) let the Village vote on the other members' speeches; rotate visible activity and keep nominations aligned with the Village's own suspicions to avoid being the only one who pushes.

Post your full night log in your first speech after getting it, and state explicitly which parts depend on a single claim; a Lookout who names only the target and its visitor leaves no test for a denial.

Oracle guesses are Astral Visits that reveal only correct/incorrect; a guess on a role that a living Yakuza is publicly tied to (e.g. Diviner) confirms that player's alignment, so pick guesses that split the suspect pool rather than repeating the same confirmed role claim.

Do not publicly post a wrong or unverifiable guess target as a plan; the Yakuza read the Oracle's Night 4 target as the real Oracle and killed her, so an Oracle who announces guesses early is a Katana target from the next night.

A single unverified claim (Scout, Lookout) plus a private whip for votes is weaker than it looks; demand a second independent source before voting, and treat coordinated PMs asking for a Yes as a visible pattern to flag early.

Check claimed visit results against the Katana rule: the holder must visit the target, so a Lookout's sole visitor to a Katana victim is the holder; but a Lookout claim that names only one visitor and no other watches is easy to fabricate, so ask for the full watch log and the other visits in the same night before trusting it.

Track which living players have been seen in each Yakuza-only or Katana-linked role claim; when the Yakuza own a Diviner-style claim, count how many nights its groups can explain before you accept it as a true role.

Your win is instant on your target's hanging, and leaving on the win is not a death. Once the Village is already leaning Guilty on your target, a Yes on their nomination costs little, so spend your votes on pushing the trial rather than on speeches.

A Katana kill always leaves its holder as the sole visitor a Lookout can see. Add a second visit to the same victim (a Diviner pick or a Clerk or Fabricator visit) so a Lookout sees two visitors and cannot name the holder alone.

Kill the living claimant whose checkable results the Village is about to rely on (Scout, Lookout, Oracle) before their next result posts. Bob's and Carol's claims were the only thing that would have exposed the team, and they were removed on time.

Do not trade a hang on a single whip or self-nomination chain. Frank's trial turned on a player admitting that PMs asked for votes, and the Village hanged him on a nomination that rested on one unverified Lookout log.

Ask for a full night log from claimants before voting, and check that the claimed visit counts fit the moderator-announced visit groups. Single-watch claims that name one visitor are weak until a second source confirms them.

Before trusting a single Lookout or Tracker watch, check whether the death it explains is consistent with the Katana rule (holder must visit target) and with any other visit data; a lone watch naming one player is strong but must be cross-checked against a second source before a hang.
Do not whip private votes on one unverified claim; when a player pushes Yes/Guilty by PM before any second source exists, that pattern is itself a suspicious tell that the village can punish.

When a claimed Oracle's guesses are verified by public deaths and reveals, treat their remaining guess targets as high-value; a Yakuza who is about to be exposed will kill the verified Oracle quickly, so protect or reveal the Oracle's results early.

Track the Yakuza's Katana holder across nights from the Katana-hit deaths: if the same player is always the one whose vote and visits line up, a Diviner claim by that player is a confirmed Yakuza signal and the village should vote on it immediately.
When a claimed Diviner or other Yakuza-only role is publicly named, a Village player who claims it is almost certainly lying; treat such claims as a Yakuza signal rather than a neutral read.

A Katana kill needs its holder's visit, so a Lookout watch showing a lone visitor on the victim is a checkable contradiction against a bare denial. Ask the denier for the one fact that would disprove the moderator-confirmed log, and weigh it above speeches.

Do not whip votes by private message on one unverified claim. Every PM is visible to all, so it shows who pushed, and Yakuza can frame the whipper, as happened to Frank on Day 4. Post the argument publicly and let votes follow.

A self-nomination followed by pushing a hang and arguing for the rope is a Jester tell. If the Village is unsure, prefer waiting over a lethal vote, because a Jester hang wins for them and their revenge kills a random Guilty voter, as with Erin and Mallory.

Once a correct Oracle guess identifies a Yakuza-only role, the Yakuza will target you next night, as Carol was on Night 4. Post the result promptly and pair it with a living ally who can vouch for you, so the Village has a second source if you die.

Never flatly deny a visit that a Lookout or Tracker may have seen. Agree a cover action in night chat and admit it early, because a flat denial that a visit log contradicts makes you look like the liar.

Before a Katana kill, check whether a living Lookout or Tracker claim could have watched the target. If the holder is the only visitor, the watcher will name them, so kill the watcher first or pick a target nobody watches.

Never publicly post results from a Yakuza-only role such as Diviner or Ritualist. Posting them confirms your alignment to everyone, so claim a role that is compatible with a Village player or stay silent.
Keep the Katana on the holder with the least exposure and move it when a visible watcher names the holder. A holder who is also the one Village players can point to is the easiest target.
Spend a one-shot token (Clerk rig) on a decisive Day while a non-teammate can be nominated. An unused token at the end of the game is wasted, and a failed nomination can cost the whole Day.

A Katana attack is a visit by its holder, so a living Lookout or Tracker who watched the target that night names the holder. Before committing to a kill, check whether a Good watcher might be on the target, and kill or move the Katana away from a holder whose visit trail is already public.

Never post Yakuza-only results (a Diviner group, Katana or Clerk actions) in daytime chat. Grace's public Diviner results became proof of Yakuza membership once Carol's Oracle guess confirmed the role.

Do not flatly deny a visit that a Lookout could have seen. Grace's denial of the Night 2 visit to Alice was contradicted by Bob's watch, and that contradiction carried the Village's vote. Agree a cover action in night chat and admit it, or stay vague.

A one-shot token held to the end is wasted. My Clerk token went unused and was lost when the game ended with me alive. Use a rig on a Day when a non-teammate nominee would pass, or before the Yakuza's influence on the vote is lost.

A living Lookout or Tracker who watched the victim, or the holder's last target, can name the holder from one visit log. Kill or neutralise that watcher before its next watch, or move the Katana the same night. We kept Grace as holder for four nights, and Bob's single watch on Alice exposed her.

Do not flatly deny a visit that a single watch already shows. Grace's flat denial was contradicted by a lone Lookout log and became the Village's case. Agree a plausible cover action in night chat and admit it at once.
Hold the frame for a night when an alignment check (Sheriff or Seer) is alive or about to check. With no alignment role alive, the frame does nothing, and my token went unused for four nights.

Village players who privately push a vote on one claim become easy hang targets. When a teammate is accused of this in public, nominate the accuser or the whipper at once, as Grace did with Frank, rather than defending a teammate with a single-claim argument.

A Jester's self-nomination is read as a vote test or a bid for the rope; if you want to be hanged, make the push look like a genuine read on another player instead, because a naked self-nomination gets you a unanimous Guilty and tells the Village exactly what you are.
Keep your trial speech about checkable facts on other players; begging for a Guilty vote or saying you would rather hang is what got the Village to convict me by 10 to 1.

When a Village group hangs one suspect, it has to stay on the same contradiction: once Frank and the Village argued from Bob's single Lookout log, the Yakuza simply nominated Frank and the Village split, so only hang on evidence that outlives the claimant.
