evidence: Frank publicly claimed protecting Alice on Day 2, and the Yakuza attacked Heidi on N2 anyway; Frank had protected her. Bob died with both swap tokens unused, and Frank was only targeted on N4, after Bob was gone.

tip: When a teammate's hanging is clearly decided, vote Guilty with the majority. A lone Innocent vote saves nobody and becomes the first case against you once your teammate's role is revealed.
evidence: Bob was hanged 5-2 with Erin as the only other Innocent vote. On Day 5 Dave nominated Erin and cited exactly that vote.

tip: Never argue from game-end consequences that only a Yakuza could know, such as 'if I die, everyone left is Village.' Pitch to the Jester or other Neutrals with conditional reasoning that a villager could also say.
evidence: In her trial on Day 5, Erin told Grace that hanging her would leave only Village non-Jesters. Grace, Heidi, Alice and Dave all seized on the slip, and Erin was hanged.

tip: Don't let two teammates take the same safe claim, especially once an Archivist-type list is public. Three people claiming Vanilla with only one Vanilla in the list draws attention to exactly the right players.
evidence: Bob, Erin and Dave all claimed Vanilla against Carol's list, which showed one Vanilla. Carol's suspicion, though overstated, pointed at the two real Yakuza and got Bob onto Day 3's trial.

tip: Present an archive list as evidence that changes the odds, not as a count of every role. Say 'only 5 of 7 roles are sampled, so duplicate Vanilla claims are suspicious' rather than 'at least two must be lying.' Overstating it gets the point discredited even when the suspicion is correct.
evidence: Carol claimed the list proved two of the Vanilla claimers were lying, was rebutted by everyone, and retracted. Bob was acquitted 0-8 even though Bob and Erin were in fact the Yakuza.

tip: Once you have publicly claimed your protections, expect to become a target. Rotate protection, and spend a token on self-protection on the night your investigator's result has just exposed a Yakuza and you look like the next kill.
evidence: Frank announced his N1 and N2 protections, kept protecting Heidi every night, and died to the Katana on N4 with 2 medic tokens unused.

tip: Don't use up the Day's three trials on nominations nobody intends to vote Guilty on. Each 0-vote trial burns a nomination and reveals nothing new.
evidence: On Day 3, Bob, Carol and Frank were each tried and acquitted 0-8, ending the Day with no new information and no execution.

tip: Post your group sizes and name the group of three early, before any Night action could remove you; a dead Cartographer's unnamed map leaves the Village with nothing to check.
Avoid flatly denying night actions and then flipping under pressure; Heidi's no-visit denial followed by a Tracker claim cost her credibility and drew a trial.
When two Oracle or claim-based checks conflict, demand the exact role and target named in the result before voting, rather than letting the nominator's unnamed result decide.
Don't let a single unexplained nomination or withdrawal carry a trial alone; ask for a reason once, and weigh it against checkable results instead of repeating the pressure.
Track token counts and visit groups carefully: Accountant audits and Cartographer sizes can confirm or disprove a claim, so cross-check them before accepting or discounting a role.

Before a Katana or kill plan, check whether the target's role is actually a visit-reader. Oracle guesses are Astral Visits, so my plan to kill Carol as a visit-reader was weak; a Tracker or Lookout is the real threat, and Heidi's track on me was never checked.

Do not let a teammate's Guilty votes and a late role claim look like a bloc. Bob's Puppeteer claim after two Guilty votes and his hedged denial gave the town a clear lead; answer direct questions with a plain yes or no at once.

A Tracker or Lookout claim that contradicts an Oracle or Accountant result is decisive only if the exact-role check names a role and target. Demand the named role and target from an Oracle before voting, and do not let a silent nomination carry the vote.

Track who PMs whom each Day and who votes No on the nominations those players push. Grace's Day 4 PMs to Erin and Carol plus Erin's Day 3 PM to Grace were the clearest bloc signal, and the town only used them late.
Public messages cost more as rounds rise, so long repeated demands for the same answer burn budget. Post the concrete question once, then vote on the answer instead of repeating it in every round.

Naming the exact role of a player who has already publicly claimed it only tests a claim, not the player; a correct guess on a publicly claimed role checks nothing. Prefer guesses on players who have not claimed, or on roles nobody has claimed, so that a hit is real evidence.

Before nominating or voting, pin down each player's exact night-by-night actions in one reply. Hedged denials (e.g. only denying the claimed role) and flip-flopped no-action answers were the main sources of wasted days; demand plain yes/no answers per night and note the first answer as the baseline.

Track who PMs whom on the same day as a nomination and who votes No on nominations they later defend. Several days were spent on a cluster of private messages between the same few players, and a single clear pattern of PMs followed by identical votes was the most reliable public signal.

Stall and attrition math matters: with 5 or fewer players, a nomination needs 3 Yes votes, so one player's vote can swing a trial. Count the threshold for the current living count before planning a split vote.

Do not shoot on a single unverifiable public or private request from another player. A Basic shot that fails only shows Defense or protection, so plan the shot on a result the public can check, and say the plan in your will rather than acting on a PM.

Before trusting a role claim, check whether its key result names a specific target and role. Carol's N4 'Heidi is not a Tracker' named no role, which made it uncheckable, yet it drove two trials and a Vigilante push.
Weigh a single unexplained move (a nomination then silent withdrawal) against the player who made it, but ask them to answer directly once; repeated dodging is more telling than the original act.

Visit counts from Fortune Teller and visit-group sizes from Cartographer can be reconciled with tracker and audit results. Work out the full visit graph before trusting either number, since a third visitor can hide in the group.

Do not let a Vigilante be steered by private requests from a single claimant. Shoot only on a mechanical lead and keep your shot for a case you can verify, because a wrong shot at a Tracker costs you the only shooter.
A late role-claim made only after being nominated looks like a shield, and publicly contradicted claims get dropped fast. Claim early with a consistent, checkable result set.

Audit a player who claims a token role as early as possible. A token total is the cheapest exact test: a claimed Puppeteer or Mortician showing 0 tokens refutes the claim, while a Philanthropist's thrown-away token can make a true role look empty, so compare the result with other token holders before relying on it.

When a role claim has a checkable mechanical outcome (a Katana death, a failed Basic shot, a visit count), tie the claim to that outcome before voting. A Tracker's track list can fit the public numbers without proving the role, because a liar or a Roleplayer can produce consistent results.

Visit-count claims such as Fortune Teller numbers only resolve when you list every visitor first. The Katana holder's visit, an Accountant audit and a Tracker's visit all count as visits to their targets, so write out the full visitor-to-target list for the night before deciding which number is the visited count.

If you vote No on a nomination after privately urging a Guilty vote on the same player, say so publicly with your reason. Unexplained contradictions between private pushes and public votes drew the most suspicion this game and pulled the Day's attention away from the mechanics.

A flat false denial of night actions is worse than an early honest admission. Heidi's Day 4 denial, corrected only after nomination, made her look like a liar even when her tracks were consistent, so admit a real role early and keep the claim checkable.

Before a Katana kill, check whether the target is an investigator who can still act; the team killed Alice and Ivan, the two public visit-readers, and both claims were then unverifiable. Killing the one player who can expose a teammate's token use is worth more than a generic threat kill.

Never flatly deny a night action that a visit-reader could contradict. Heidi's Day 4 flat denial of Night 1-2 actions, then a Tracker claim after nomination, cost the team credibility, and Bob's hedged denial ('my Puppeteer role took no action') drew the same suspicion.

A player who nominates on a vague reason and then withdraws without answering the room gets a lasting mark. Carol's Day 3 Bob nomination was never explained and gave the town a Guilty lever for three days.

Keep the Katana holder and the swap or rig tokens coordinated before Day, and don't let the holder die with an unused plan; Frank died holding the Katana and the team lost its attack pipeline on Night 4.

Oracle guesses and other Astral Visits are not visits, so a Katana holder cannot see them; claim-based 'exposure' reasons for a target are wrong and get called out. Check the mechanic before using it as a reason.

A Basic shot only beats Defense None. A suspect with Standard innate Defense (Arsonist, Serial Killer) or Medic protection survives it, and the target learns a Vigilante is alive. Before shooting, check whether the suspect could have Standard Defense and whether the lead is strong enough to spend a token and reveal the role.

A claim that gives a role and a target but whose result names no role or target (such as a bare 'not a Tracker' check) verifies nothing. Demand the exact role guessed, the target, the night number and the result in the same post, and discount checks that first appear after a nomination.

An Arsonist can douse players silently over several nights and then ignite, killing every doused player at once (Frank and Judy died together on Night 4). When a living Arsonist may exist, track who was visited and expect a mass death once two or more players are doused.

A nominee who flips a story under nomination (for example, denying any night action and then claiming a role) is a real contradiction, but check whether their public numbers actually fit before hanging them. A lie can be panic while the claim is true. Ask for a plain yes or no answer and note whether it was given.
Do not move toward a shot or nomination on one unverifiable result passed privately. If a player PMs you to act on their word, bring it into public chat and wait for a second source before acting.

Douse early and quietly, but count the ignition threshold against living players: the Arsonist's win requires being alone, so plan the ignite to clear the last Yakuza/Village rivals rather than waiting; I wasted Nights 5-6 dousing players whose votes were already the swing.

Never flatly deny a night action on Day 1-2 after you have already announced a role in the Day discussion; a flipped no-visit denial was the concrete contradiction that got me nominated and forced a fake Tracker claim.

Votes that cluster on a single role-claim (Oracle or Vigilante) can be steered by one unverifiable PM; before voting on a claim, ask the claimant for the exact role and target in public, since vague results ('Heidi is not a Tracker') checked nothing and let a pair of players drive two executions.

Do not PM teammates or leave a PM trail from a player who later becomes a suspect; Grace's PMs to Carol and Erin on Day 4 became the central case against her and the cluster read was built from PM counts.

Check whether an Arsonist's Astral ignition and a Katana attack can both kill the same player; Frank died to both on Night 4 and the will and death-cause reveal showed it, so tally multiple fatal causes before reading a death as a single-killer event.

Your two numbers are visited-count and visitor-count, unlabeled; if a Katana holder visits two players, both orders stay consistent, so don't spend credibility committing to an order. Post the raw numbers each night and let the visit-based claims (Tracker, Lookout, Cartographer groups) cross-check them.

Oracle or Accountant claims that only restate a role another living player already claimed can't check anything; prioritize claims whose result a third party can test (token audits, a Tracker's visit, a Vigilante's shot outcome).

A pair of players who PM each other on the same Day and then both push the same nomination is a bloc signal; before a hang, ask who sent what and whether the PM partner's vote matches their public stance.

Long repetitive public pleas for answers cost budget and add little; a single concrete question addressed by name, repeated only when the answer changes, works better and keeps budget for the trial defense.
Stall rule and night deaths: when the game is near a stall loss, a Village role should prioritize actions that create checkable outcomes, since a silent Night 3 cannot be recovered.

Once a Katana holder has a visible pattern of attacks, a Tracker or Lookout claim becomes a real threat; Heidi's tracks were fake, but the Yakuza team's visible Katana-holder lock made it easy for Village to track our movements. Rotate holders or hide the holder's visit pattern, and do not let one player hold the Katana for every night.

A player who flips a no-action denial to an action claim after being nominated is a strong contradiction; if you are the flipper, admit the lie early and give checkable targets in one reply, because withholding roles until a later Night reads as stalling.

Oracle-type hits on a claimant who already publicly claimed that role only confirm the claim exists, not the claimant's honesty; weigh independent checks (audits, tracks that match the visitor counts) above guesses that repeat a claim.

Visit-count pairs (e.g. Fortune Teller 2 and 3) can be resolved by counting unique visited players and visitors per night with the Katana holder included; commit early to which number is visited so the town can test it against other investigators' results.

Never let the Arsonist and Yakuza both be alive without a plan for the Arsonist; the Arsonist killed two of our Yakuza by ignition on Night 4, so when a neutral killer is alive, treat it as a third faction that can end the game.

Save a Basic-level shot for a player whose visible claim is already contradicted; a Basic shot against a Defense-None target is wasted if it fails, and a failed shot only tells you the target has innate or protective Defense.

Do not deny a night action outright when a Tracker, Lookout or Veteran could contradict it; a flat false denial that is later exposed (as the Tracker's N1-2 denial was) becomes the trial's main evidence and drives the nomination.

When a nominee's claim is only checkable through another player's unverifiable result, ask the claimant to name the exact role and target first; several votes this game turned on a result that named no role or target.

Before a Katana kill, confirm the target's trial and claim exposure; the Yakuza spent a night killing a Yakuza-cleared Accountant while an Oracle with a true hit was alive, leaving the town with confirmed roles.

Count token budgets and visit numbers explicitly against the public ledger before voting; Fortune Teller pairs (2 and 2, then 2 and 3) and group sizes can be checked against known visits and should be posted with which number is which.

Never claim your true Yakuza role when pressed for a role. If you must claim, use a prepared Village role whose token count matches yours. Answer 'did you visit anyone' with a flat, complete denial or cover story, not a role-limited hedge.
evidence: Bob, asked for his N1-3 actions on Day 4, said 'my Puppeteer role took no action.' Carol pointed out that Puppeteer is Yakuza, and Dave and Erin attacked the hedge. Bob was nominated and hanged 6-3 that Day, flipping Evil.

tip: Spend one-shot tokens on a Day when they decide something. A Clerk rig is strongest on a Day when a Village power role is likely to be nominated but would survive the trial. Swaps and puppets lose all value if the team dies holding them.
evidence: Judy's rig, Frank's 2 swaps and Bob's puppet were never used. On Day 4 Carol's nomination passed 6-3 and she was acquitted 3-6; a rig that night would have executed the real Oracle. All three Yakuza died with every token unspent.

tip: Don't vote as an identical minority bloc across trials. Split your Guilty votes, or join the majority on a trial you can't win, so the town can't read your team off the vote record.
evidence: Bob, Frank and Judy were the only Guilty votes on both Carol's and Heidi's Day 4 trials (3-6 each). Grace and others immediately asked those three to justify themselves, and Bob was nominated within minutes.

tip: A role claim whose 'results' fit the public visit counts is not verified by that fit. A liar can match their claimed tracks or watches to their own real visits. An exact-role check from an investigator with a proven record outweighs visit-count consistency.
evidence: Heidi's Tracker 'tracks' (Bob, Frank, Judy) were her real Arsonist douse targets. They fit Ivan's 2/2 and 2/3 and Alice's group of three perfectly, and that won her the Day 4 acquittal. Carol's correct N4 Oracle result (Heidi is not a Tracker) was the true signal, but it was discounted.

tip: Post past results completely and at once: the exact guess, the target and right/wrong. Never invent mechanics to justify withholding. Don't nominate without a stated reason, and don't privately urge a Vigilante to shoot. Vagueness and backchannel pushes make a real investigator look like a scum player.
evidence: Carol nominated Bob on Day 3 with no reason, though he was Evil. She claimed her Oracle target was 'exposed to the Katana holder' (Oracle guesses are Astral). She said 'Heidi is not a Tracker' about six times before naming her guess, and PM'd Grace to shoot Heidi. She was hanged on Day 6 as a real Oracle with 4 of 5 guesses correct.

tip: Pick a cover claim before you're questioned and never flatly deny visits you actually made. A claim built on your real visits (douse targets presented as tracks) holds up well, but only if you don't contradict it first.
evidence: Heidi said on Day 3 she 'took no night action on Night 1 or Night 2,' then flipped on Day 4 to a Tracker claim. That flip was cited as the 'concrete contradiction' at every later trial, including the Day 7 hanging that ended her game.

tip: When unsure, shoot with a 1-token Basic Attack. A miss against an unprotected suspect points to innate Defense (Arsonist, Serial Killer, Jester or Executioner), which is mechanical evidence for the next Day.
evidence: Grace's N6 Basic shot on Heidi failed because Arsonists have Standard Defense. On Day 7 Grace cited the failed shot alongside Carol's will, and Heidi was hanged 3-1 for the Village win.

tip: Track how many killers are left. Igniting when your doused set includes the remaining members of a faction can wipe that faction out in one night. Then keep dousing the survivors before you are suspected.
evidence: With Bob hanged, Heidi ignited on N4 and killed Frank and Judy, eliminating the Yakuza. She was later hanged before she could douse and ignite the remaining Villagers.

tip: A Scout's group results name random players, so 'separate groups' only rules out visit links between those specific named players. Build a visit graph across all nights and test each claim against it rather than treating one clean result as proof of innocence.

Fortune Teller-style two-number counts are only meaningful if you track every visit each night; when the numbers imply more visitors than the public record shows, look for the unnamed visitor rather than declaring the count impossible.

A Yakuza kill that lands on a Good player the night after a power claim is itself a clue: map who the Katana holder was each night by listing who was alive, who visited whom, and which holder claims are consistent, then vote on that set.

A Jester who keeps self-nominating is hard to convict without a result, so a nomination that a Jester wants is a cost to the Village; spend votes on checkable targets instead of letting repeated self-nominations drain the day.

Keep low-information public messages short and save budget for trial turns and key contradictions; the Village stalled for many Days repeating the same questions, which cost budget without moving any vote.

Spend early watches on players likely to act at night, such as claimed power roles or the most active voices. A no-visitors result on a quiet player on Night 1 told the Village almost nothing. Post every result in your first speech, since the Yakuza will kill the watcher whose results threaten them.

applies_to: Lookout, Tracker and anyone reading visits
tip: A visit shows only a destination. A Fabricator frame, a Tracker check and a Katana attack all look the same. Before treating one visit as a lead, ask which actions the visitor could have taken and whether a kill, a frame or a test fits the public record.

The Katana holder survives every kill, so after each Katana death list the living players who denied a visit. Check every claimed count against named visits: a Fortune Teller 2-and-1 needs one visitor with two targets, and visitors can be more than the visited players.

When a suspect keeps self-nominating for a hang, set a deadline and vote for the most mechanically supported nominee instead of stalling. Five days of 'prefer not hanging' let the Katana kill a Good player every night.

Oracle guesses are checked only at end of night and reveal only right/wrong; spend the guess on a player whose exact role would split the suspect pool, and remember a wrong guess on a Village player gives no information about who the Katana holder is.

Track every Katana kill and which living players have denied visits; a repeated Katana kill each night means one living Yakuza holder, so compare the denial list against Fortune Teller and visit counts before voting.

Vote Guilty on a suspect only when the vote would also be correct if they were a Jester; a hanged Jester wins outright, so avoid voting Guilty on a player whose only evidence is repeated self-nominations and PMs asking for votes.

Claiming a role early and posting a Night 1 result that is verifiable against the Oracle's own reveal is strong, but guess the most dangerous suspect rather than a player already exposed, since the Katana tends to target active claimants.

Flip-flopping between Guilty and Innocent in public, or voting against a stated read, gets used as a lead by every other player; announce any change of vote with its reason before the vote is revealed.

As a Neutral Executioner, I was killed by a Katana on Night 1 with no information. Early on, a Neutral with no role-specific power should share a tight will and avoid public Day 1 commitments, since the Yakuza target visible pushers first.

Track which players actually visited whom using Lookout and Tracker results plus Scout group separations; an unexplained Katana kill with a living holder is the strongest signal to test claims against, so list every night's Katana victim and check each claim against it.

Do not repeatedly self-nominate or PM players asking for votes when you are a suspected Jester; it made the Village treat the pattern as Jester-shaped and blocked every hang that could have tested the real Katana holder.

When the Village has a Fortune Teller or similar count, verify its numerical consistency (visitors must be at least as many as visited, and visits need named visitors) before using it to clear or convict; the Village spent several days arguing over unnamed counts.

Do not vote Guilty on a player for a single flipped or late vote without a mechanical link; both Erin and Heidi were hanged or nearly hanged on that reasoning while the Katana holder survived to the end.

applies_to: Village investigators (Lookout, Tracker, Scout, Fortune Teller)
tip: Post a dated, exact result the moment you get it and state the action type; claims that stay vague about night and target (Ivan's Frank/Erin/Alice shifts, Mallory's unnamed-visitor numbers) cost the Village days of stalling.

Track the Katana holder by the kill pattern: a single living Yakuza holder kills every night, so after each kill, list which living players denied night visits and eliminate them rather than debating wording.

Repeated self-nominations by one player are a Jester tell, but in a Jester-vs-Yakuza endgame the Jester's hang is a win condition, so test the Katana holder with votes on non-self-nominated suspects rather than letting the Jester force the trial order.
With 4 or fewer alive, a Fortune Teller count or Scout result is worth more than any speech; demand every living player's exact night target and visit answer in one round before any nomination.
Keep vote changes explained at the time they happen; late unexplained flips (Heidi Guilty-then-Innocent) became the main attack lines and wasted trials.

applies_to: Fortune Teller and other count-based roles
tip: Before calling a count impossible, list the minimal set of visitors it requires. A 2-and-1 count with one visitor on a kill means exactly one hidden visitor, which narrows the suspects quickly.

Two public claims that agree on one visit are only consistent, not proven, since a Yakuza Tracker can match a real Lookout by design. Test each claim against kill results and Scout separations rather than against each other.
Repeated self-nominations by one player spend the nomination and speaking budget without new information. Agree early that a repeat nomination needs a new result, then apply that rule consistently.
Announcing a planned next-night target in public gave the Katana a warning and a list. Post only completed results, and keep plans private.
When a player flips from Guilty to Innocent without explanation, press it at once in the same Day. Waiting until the next trial lets the flip become the default defence.

A Diviner group that includes a dead or known-role player is still checkable against the public record; when the Village posts its own Fortune Teller or Scout counts, match them against your own visits before denying anything, because a denial that a count contradicts is the fastest way to lose the Village.

Don't deny a night visit flatly when the Village already holds a count that includes it; I falsely denied my own Night 4 visit and then had to privately admit the count matched it, which made every later denial look suspect.

With only one Village non-Jester left, the Katana holder should avoid public accusations of teammates and let a Jester pattern carry the vote; the Jester-hang fear protected us from Guilty votes on Judy repeatedly.

Count the living majority before each trial: with 4 or 5 alive, one flipped or retaliatory vote decides the outcome, so a self-nomination by a suspected Jester can be used to test the room without risk to the Village.

A Fortune Teller's 'two numbers' claim is only checkable if the claimant names visitors; demand named visits for every count, and treat numbers that need unnamed visitors as unverifiable rather than as proof of a lie.

Clerk rigs can only be placed on the Yakuza's own night choice; a Clerk who holds a token but never submits a rig gets zero value. Decide the rig night and target early, and rig a non-teammate nominee before the trial phase rather than holding the token to the end.

Fortune Teller number pairs are a strong constraint: enumerate which visitors and targets must exist each night, then check each denial against the pair. Ask the claimant to name the visited players, not just the counts.
Keep the Katana holder unchanged and vote the same target every night, but avoid a fixed pattern of Diviner or Clerk choices that the Village can deduce from the visit counts.

A Jester whose win comes from hanging is best handled by voting on mechanical evidence rather than repeated self-nominations; a late Guilty-then-Innocent switch costs credibility and should be explained at the moment it happens.
Private messages to a Village player who later dies are revealed to all as message counts; limit them to avoid giving the Village a pair-link to a teammate.

A Fabricator framing a Village player every night is a visible, repeated pattern; framing only when it protects the team or redirects a real investigation is less likely to draw suspicion, and a frame on a Vanilla adds nothing once the Village has no tests.

Before the Katana kills a Village investigator, check whether a public result already names your team's holder; the Village kept asking who visited a Good victim and the team never produced a clean answer, so agree on a cover explanation for each kill in night chat first.

Once a Village player has publicly asked for a yes/no on a specific night, answer it with a bare yes or no in the next speech rather than deflecting; repeated dodges became the main lead against the team.

A Jester who repeatedly self-nominates can be tested by voting Innocent and watching whether the self-nominations continue; hanging the Jester hands them a win, so prefer tests on Katana-linked evidence over pattern reads.

Check whether a Fortune Teller's two numbers can be explained by named visitors before accepting or rejecting them; both sides in this game argued from counts without naming visitors, which stalled the Village.

A Jester who keeps self-nominating gets only one Yes from its own nominee; with three living players the Village votes Innocent, so pressure must come from a teammate-like faction or a Village player who already voted Guilty, not from repeated self-noms.

Fortune Teller count pairs only bound visitors; when a count needs more visitors than the public record shows, check the arithmetic against every named visit before accusing anyone, and ask the claimant for the named second target first.
Track each player's trial vote against their stated reason; a player who says Guilty and votes Innocent loses credibility fast, so either post the reason before voting or stay silent until the vote.

Consistent cross-checks (Tracker and Lookout describing the same single visit, Scout separating players) beat repeated demands for answers; name the claim that conflicts and the night it conflicts on.
A hanged Jester wins, so a Guilty vote on a self-nominating Jester is a gift to them; if you must hang someone, pick a player whose hang reveals alignment without handing the win.

applies_to: Fortune Teller and other numbers-based information roles
tip: Claim the role on the first Day you have a result you can post, with the night's two numbers and the candidate visitor sets. A silent information role gets Katana-killed before any count can be corroborated.

When a visit count doesn't match the named visitors, ask the claimant to name each visitor and target per night before accusing anyone. A hidden extra visitor can be the Katana holder, so a count-based claim may be right even when it looks unexplained.

Never flatly deny a visit that could be checked. When a visit count mismatches a teammate's cover story, the Village can test the denial against the numbers, so agree a cover action in night chat and admit it early.

Don't let one self-nominating player drive the day. Repeated identical self-nominations wasted about four Days; instead, force a Yes/No on a specific nominee with a stated reason, and ask for one checkable answer per round.
Repeated 'nothing new from me' posts and identical nominations burn budget and bury the record. Spend budget on one concrete question or result per round.

Read count results literally. If the Fortune Teller reports exactly one visitor on a Katana night, that visitor is the Katana holder. Any player who refuses to state their night action that day is the hang. A flat 'no' given only once on trial is not an answer that clears them.
evidence: Night 4 numbers were 2 and 1: Grace visited both Alice and Mallory. Grace refused to post her target, then denied any visit at trial. Erin and Frank had said they leaned Guilty, but voted Innocent, and Grace survived to win.

tip: In the late game, do the vote math before every nomination vote, and count the Jester as a swing voter. A Jester who wants to be hanged will gladly vote Guilty on other people. Never vote No on a nomination of your top suspect when your Yes is the one it needs.
evidence: Day 6, five players alive: Frank nominated Grace and Judy voted Yes. Erin voted No, so it got 2 of the 3 Yes votes needed. Frank, Erin and Judy would have been enough to pass it and then to vote Grace Guilty, ending the Yakuza threat.

tip: Don't spend trial slots on an obvious Jester's self-nominations. Don't vote Guilty on an investigator claimant just because evil players attack how her results look; ask them to name the contradiction concretely. Save your nominations and trials for the mechanical lead.
evidence: On Day 6, Erin and Frank voted Yes on Judy's self-nomination, and two of the three trials went to Judy. On Day 5, Frank voted Guilty on Mallory, the real Fortune Teller, after Grace and Heidi's vague 'unnamed visitors' attack on her numbers.

tip: A frame changes only what alignment checks see, but it is still a visit that a Lookout, Tracker or Scout can see. If no Sheriff or Seer is known to exist, skip framing, or frame someone unlikely to be watched.
evidence: Ivan framed Bob, Erin and Alice although no alignment checker ever appeared. Bob watched Erin on Night 2 and saw Ivan. That single visit was the lead that eventually got Ivan hanged.

tip: If you fake-claim a visit-based role, give your real visit destinations as your targets. Visit-group results (Scout, Cartographer, Lookout) can then only confirm you. Prepare the cover claim in night chat before you need it, rather than improvising targets.
evidence: Ivan first said 'I won't explain' about the Erin visit, then claimed Tracker. He named Frank as his Night 3 target, and Alice's Scout result showed Ivan and Frank were not linked. His real Night 3 visit was Alice, and switching to Alice after being contradicted got him hanged.

tip: Don't refuse to answer about your night action; have a plausible, consistent account ready from the start. Grace survived her refusal only because the Village gave her the benefit of the doubt, and it nearly cost the game.
evidence: On Day 5, Grace said 'I won't post my Night 4 target', then denied visiting at all. Mallory and Erin nominated her and she went to trial. A clean claim made early would have avoided the trial entirely.

tip: Constant self-nominations and private messages asking people to vote Guilty make you an obvious Jester, and nobody will hang you. Act like a nervous Yakuza: deflect, make one mild false claim, and let others build the case for you.
evidence: Judy self-nominated about 15 times and private-messaged five players asking for Guilty votes. Mallory called it a Jester pattern on Day 2, and every Judy trial ended Innocent.

tip: With no protective roles evident, kill each investigator the night after they claim, keep the Katana on an unclaimed member, and have every member submit the same holder and target each night. That steady kill rate wins long games for you.
evidence: Grace kept the Katana all game and killed Carol, Bob, Alice and Mallory in the order they claimed. All Yakuza votes were unanimous every night, and they never missed a kill.

tip: A Jester wins by being hanged, so self-nominating and saying you won't object is read as a hang-seeking pattern. Make the push look like a reasoned vote on the record, and keep the nomination itself for the moment the table already leans toward you.

A claimed investigative role that is killed by the Katana at night is probably the real one, since the Yakuza hit the threats they can't explain away. Use the night kill list as a claim test before voting on the claims themselves.

Keeping the Katana with one holder every night and hitting the most active claimant was never contested, because nobody could prove protection or a visit. Rotate the holder only when a Lookout or Tracker has named it.

Repeated demands to name a night or a visitor, with no deadline, stalled Day 2 and Day 3 for several rounds while the Yakuza kept killing. Set one concrete question per round and vote on the answer, or nominate on the first clear contradiction.

Once a Village player has claimed a role, have your teammates test that claim with a vote against it before it is confirmed. Their answers to direct questions then carry more weight than the claim itself.

Post your watch result with the night and full visitor list the moment you get it, and when a rival claims the same role, watch the player who accused you or the most likely Katana target, since a watch on a player with no suspicious links tells you little.

Killing a self-declared Lookout or Medic makes the table read the claim as real. Only Yakuza who reliably know the Katana holder's targets should rely on that, because visit-based watches can still expose the holder.

Before a hang, check whether the nominee wins by being hanged. A player who pushes Yes on others, then nominates themself and says they won't object is a Jester tell, and a Village hang on them hands the Jester a win.
Repeated demands like 'name the night' cost budget without adding information. Ask once, concretely, then make a short contradiction-based case that the table can vote on.
A player who survives a Standard-level attack should name the protection at once. Vague wording like innate Defense reads as a Neutral threat and invites a hang.

An archive with no target is not a visit, but the result list of 9 roles is only useful if you can line up its fakes against claims; track which roles have already been publicly claimed and which are still hidden to find the fake slots quickly.

When two players claim the same role and one visit result names a single visitor with no night given, demand the night and the full visitor list immediately; a claim that cannot be checked should be weighed against the Katana death pattern rather than endless demands.

The Katana holder who kills the real Lookout or Archivist-style information roles early gets a free read on the Village; kill claimants whose information is hardest to verify, and keep the holder fixed to avoid tipping the table.
Nominating yourself or saying you won't object to a hang reads as Jester behaviour and gets you lynched; if you are a real Village player, avoid that pattern because it hands the Yakuza a free trial.

Post a plain, checkable claim early (for example a Medic self-protect with a specific night) rather than a vague 'innate Defense', since vague claims invite a hang on silence and the table votes on the unexplained part.

A profile returns a three-role list where exactly one is true, so two profiles on the same target with overlapping lists narrow things only if their intersection is small; a single profile never confirms a claim. Spend tokens on players whose claim conflicts with a visit result, not on a claimant you want to confirm.

Track which claims are testable at all. Archivist and Profiler-style information is mostly untestable, so an accusation built on it wastes Days; ask for visit-based or vote-based contradictions and give the table a concrete night to check.

The Yakuza pattern of killing the active claimant or the Lookout worked well: the Katana killed the two most vocal claimants and the Village spent its Days on untestable nominations. Keep the holder fixed and avoid self-nominating Jester bait to waste Village votes.

Pushing for your own hanging while claiming to be a helpful Village player is a legible pattern; a Jester who self-nominates after pressing for a hang gets voted by the table. Stay quiet on the trial record instead of asking for a Yes.

Late-game, when the Village is down to two or three players, a Guilty majority needs only a few votes; each Day the Yakuza can force a hanging by splitting the Village's votes, so keep track of who is still alive before every nomination.

Don't leave Ritual tokens unused for four nights. Spend them on guesses at the strongest unexplained claimants, such as a Medic or Lookout, using a Divine attack when a Standard one would be blocked by protection. A wrong guess exposes you, but a right one removes a key Village role and makes the Katana's job easier.

Use swap tokens to redirect a known protection. If the Village has a Medic who self-protected or protected a target, swap that protected player with an unprotected one so the Katana lands on the weaker target. Holding two swap tokens for the whole game gives no value.

Plan the rig for the Day the Village is most likely to nominate a teammate or a key Yakuza-suspected player. Passing the rig earlier, while Village votes are split, can also remove the main threat. An unused Clerk token gives the Village an extra trial for free.

Agree early on a rule for when to use role actions. The team's silent no-action nights let the Village spend three Days arguing over claims, which helped us, but at 5 alive we had no reserve plan when a claimant was nominated against us. Discuss one contingency per Day in night chat.

When two players claim the same unique-looking role and results conflict, check which claim has a visit result that can be cross-checked (for example a Lookout watching a player who confirmed they took no action). Push for the night and visitor list on the first Day, not after several Days of repeated demands.

Smuggler swaps resolve before any attack (R23). When the Katana target is likely protected, swap the target with an unattacked player so the attack lands on them instead, and say nothing publicly about it. Don't sit on two unused swap tokens for four nights.

Unused ritual tokens are wasted. A Standard guess on a claimed role that is hard to test (such as a Lookout or Medic) either kills a real role or costs one token and stays hidden if wrong. Decide early on a guess plan instead of only passing.

Kill the most-accused claimant only when the Village has no checkable result on them. Each night we killed the loudest claimant, and the Village's Lookout-versus-Lookout fight kept the real information unresolved. Keep a pre-agreed rule for choosing targets so the team doesn't drift.

A self-nominating player who keeps saying they are a 'fair target' is often a Jester. Quietly nudge the Village toward hanging that player, since a Jester hang wins for them and the Yakuza lose no one. Don't push that nudge too hard, or it reads as Yakuza steering.

A Medic self-protect with a Standard token explains a Standard-level survivor. Before voting, ask the survivor directly for the attack type and whether they were protected. Silence after that question is weak evidence, so don't hang on silence alone when a clear claim is available.

Ignite as soon as 2 or 3 doused players are still alive and a Strong ignite would kill a real threat. Dousing night after night without igniting let the Yakuza pick the kills and got me hanged on Day 4 with zero kills.

Don't switch a survival story under trial pressure. My innate-Defense explanation was replaced by a Medic claim when hanging was near, and the table read the switch as a lie. Choose one story early or stay quiet.

Watch for Jester tells: a player who pushes a Yes on a rival, then self-nominates and repeatedly says they are a fair target or won't object is often a Jester seeking a hang. Test that pattern before following the crowd.

Track which claimants the Katana hits each night. The Yakuza kept one holder and targeted the most active claimants, so a claimant who dies to the Katana is likely real, while a claimant who survives is worth a visit-based test.

Unspent shot tokens are worth nothing. Yakuza kill the last unexplained non-Yakuza player with the Katana, so spend a shot on the strongest mechanical lead before the Katana reaches you rather than holding all three for a lead that never comes.

Two players claiming the same role is a conflict, but a claimed result with no night or detail is not yet a contradiction. Ask once for the specifics, then move to checkable visits and vote records instead of repeating demands for days.

Surviving a Katana hit can come from protection or innate Defense (Arsonist and Serial Killer have Standard Defense). Treat a survivor's claim as a test to check, not as proof they are a real Medic or other Village role.

Track who benefits from each nomination and kill. Yakuza pushed silence-based nominations against Village claimants, and the Village hanged or lost several of its own claimants that way. Before voting, ask whether the vote helps the Yakuza.
Repeated 'no new result, still no nomination' messages burn budget and add nothing. Spend the budget on one concrete check or contradiction per round so the table has something to vote on.

A lone Lookout claim with one visitor, denied by that visitor and unconfirmed, becomes a lynch target. Post the full result with night and visitor list once, then point to contradictions in other claims. Repeating a demand for the night every round reads as stalling and gets you nominated.

A player who self-nominates while saying 'I won't object' or 'I'm a fair target' may be a Jester seeking a hang. Hanging them wins them the game, so before a Guilty majority, check whether the nominee wins by being hanged and consider a different action.

Keep the Katana with one holder who never claims or draws attention, and make no daytime PMs between teammates. Target claimants whose results conflict with yours, and let the Village argue over unverifiable claims while you vote the same way every night.

Each round, post one new check, such as a new contradiction or a direct question with a deadline. Repeating the same accusation or 'not nominating yet' costs budget and makes your messages look like filler.

A player who pushes a Yes on a Village-looking nominee, then nominates themself and says they are a fair target who won't object, may be a Jester. Before any hang on pressure, check whether the nominee wins by being hanged, because the Jester won this game that way.

When Yakuza are a minority of the living, count the exact Guilty majority needed before the vote. Let Village players make the public case against a Village nominee and keep Yakuza Guilty votes aligned with the visible majority, so the Yakuza bloc never stands out.

After a Katana hit fails, switch targets rather than repeating the same kill. A self-protecting Medic is hard to see from the outside, and a survivor's claim can come out later and reshape the Village vote.

Do not hold the rig as a backup token until the end. Spend it on a Day when the Village would otherwise fail to execute a Village player, because an unused token does nothing once the game is decided.

Repeated demands for the same answer, like naming a night, spend budget without adding information. Short posts that name one concrete contradiction are more useful in later rounds where the multiplier is higher.

A player who self-nominates, keeps saying 'I'm a fair target / I won't object', or begs to be hanged without a claim is very likely a Jester. Vote No on the nomination and Innocent at trial. A Jester hang wastes the Day and its revenge kills a random Guilty voter.
evidence: Alice repeated 'I'm a fair target' for two Days, then nominated herself. She was hanged 6-2 and her revenge Divine Attack killed Dave, the Profiler. Frank, a Yakuza, had openly called the Jester read and still voted Guilty.

tip: When two players claim the same investigative role and one result is unverifiable, check for a Roleplayer before calling it a Yakuza lie. If an Archivist, Profiler or Surveyor result shows 'Roleplayer', the duplicate claimant with the oddest result is probably it. Discount that player's results instead of spending the Day hanging them.
evidence: Carol's archive showed both Lookout and Roleplayer. Ivan, a Roleplayer with fake role Lookout, got a false 'Carol visited Erin' result. Carol even said 'liar or Roleplayer' once. Yet the table spent all of Day 2 on Ivan, and the Yakuza killed Bob, the real Lookout, that night.

tip: Check that a 'contradiction' is real before using it to hang someone. Repeating an impossible demand creates false certainty and burns budget. Use your messages to share results and do role math, not to echo the same question.
evidence: For dozens of messages, players demanded Ivan 'name the night' of his Erin result when only Night 1 had passed. Heidi was the only one who pointed this out. 'Grace, name the hit' was also repeated for rounds by nearly everyone. Meanwhile nobody analyzed the archive list.

tip: Use your shots before the Yakuza reach parity. Holding all tokens is the same as being a Vanilla Villager. Mid-game, a Basic shot on the most suspicious claimless voice is worth the risk. Good targets are players who push nominations on 'silence' or always echo the consensus.
evidence: Heidi took no action on Nights 1, 2 and 3 and died on Night 4 with every token. That left the Yakuza 3 of 5 on Day 4 with nothing to slow them. Judy had led weak nominations of Carol and Grace and would have been a reasonable shot.

tip: Profile decoys are drawn from roles actually in play, so publish all three names. Evil roles among them (Smuggler, Ritualist, Arsonist) tell the table what threats exist. Overlap across two profiles narrows the true role. Post each result in your will at once, and profile unclaimed players rather than re-testing an active claimant.
evidence: Dave profiled Carol twice: Archivist/Arsonist/Smuggler, then Archivist/Ritualist/Smuggler. Both lists named Yakuza roles present in the game. The second result never reached the table because Dave died that night. Erin, Frank and Judy, all unclaimed, were never profiled.

tip: If you survive an attack with innate Defense, prepare one consistent cover claim before you're pressured. Switching stories mid-trial is fatal. Once three or more players are doused and you're under suspicion, ignite rather than waiting to be hanged.
evidence: Grace said 'innate Defense, nobody protected me', then switched to a Medic self-protect claim on trial and was hanged 3-2. Carol, Erin and earlier Bob had all been doused, but she never ignited and died with zero kills.

tip: Quiet, consistent play wins. Agree on Katana votes every night, send no daytime PMs to teammates, and echo the Village's own reasoning instead of leading. Let the Village spend its hangs on Neutrals or Roleplayers. Kill information roles and avoid players who already survived a hit.
evidence: Erin, Frank and Judy sent no daytime PMs, avoided Grace after Night 1, and killed Bob, Carol and Heidi. They joined the Ivan, Alice and Grace hangs on the crowd's own arguments. None of them was ever nominated or even seriously suspected.

tip: Once an Archivist list is public, do slot math. Match claims to listed roles and flag listed Evil roles (Clerk, Ritualist) as live threats. The players who never claim anything are where those roles hide.
evidence: Carol's list included Clerk and Ritualist, and both were real (Judy, Erin). No one ever asked who among the non-claimers (Erin, Frank, Judy, Heidi, Alice) could fill those slots. The three Yakuza simply stayed 'no role claim' all game.

tip: A Lookout's watch shows every visitor, so a claimed Sheriff or Medic who was never on the list is exposed; compare each claim against the visit list before the trial, not after.

Census or trio-based claims that each contain exactly one non-Good player can be combined to find the player common to all trios; test that claim against Katana victims, since victims are almost always Good.
Do not let a Clerk hold a rig while a Yakuza teammate is alone with a few Good players; the last-two endgame lets the Good side win via a single Yakuza vote and makes rigging a losing move.

Eavesdropper or Wiretap claims that quote a private message are risky to hear from a Yakuza-accused player; if a quoted PM is only readable by two people, ask the accused to explain the leak before voting on it.
Secret votes make bandwagons on a single claim dangerous; hang only on a concrete contradiction, not on who pushed hardest.

Census results are only as useful as the trios overlap; vary targets so trios share few names, or the single shared name becomes an unfalsifiable suspect. Consider reporting the trio result publicly with the exact composition earlier to let others cross-check.

Track which living players could have been the Katana holder each night: a Katana kill requires a living Yakuza holder, so eliminate players from the Yakuza list as each kill is explained by a visible holder move. Use this to test claims before voting.

Do not let a single mechanical argument (a missing visit, a PM quote) drive a hanging when the accuser is also a pusher. Ask who gains from each hanging, especially when a Jester is in the game, and vote on the claim that survives cross-checks.

Keep the Katana holder unchanged and attack the investigator with the most verifiable results; the Katana holder being a Good-looking Yakuza is a strong cover, but pushing a hanging of a Vanilla player right after the Yakuza count drops to two gives the Village an easy final vote.
Check the speaking order and nomination threshold each Day; with two players alive a nomination needs a majority of living votes, so an unsupported nomination can end the game in a single trial.

A player who invites a hanging ('if you think I'm the liar, nominate me') while pushing a thin accusation may be a Jester. Before a bandwagon Guilty, ask whether the nominee wins by being hanged, and vote on contradictions that aren't just awkward wording.

When a player quotes a private message, first ask who could have read it. An Eavesdropper or Wiretap claim is cheap cover for leaks, so test the quote against who could have seen it before voting on it.

A three-role profile with exactly one true answer is weak alone. Combine it with deaths (a Katana victim can't be a Clerk, for example) to eliminate options, and spend tokens on players whose role would decide a vote rather than on dead players.

Write down every census trio and check which names repeat. A name in every trio is strong evidence but can also be the framing target, so check it against independent visit lists and claims before acting on it.

Votes are secret in this variant, so bloc reasoning matters. Lay out the Guilty evidence early in the Day, while others are still deciding, rather than in a final word after the votes have mostly formed.

A Tracker's single result is only as good as the visit list it reads; corroborate your target's visit with the Lookout before counter-claiming, and watch which night you were attacked, since a Katana kill on the Tracker is a strong sign the Yakuza see you as the investigator to remove.

Census or trio-based results can be reconciled across nights: track which player appears in every trio and whether a single non-Good explains each trio, rather than assuming the common name is guilty.

With secret votes, do not treat a pile-on of Guilty votes as evidence; the hanging of Grace and later hangings were driven by early momentum from one Sheriff claim, so demand a concrete contradiction before nominating.

Yakuza who keep the Katana in one holder's hands and attack unprotected claimants each night can clear a whole investigator line quickly; the Village only survives if it nominates from the vote ledger rather than from speeches.

A Tracker's public death by Katana on the night after it claims a visit, combined with a Medic protecting someone else, is a strong clue the Medic claim is false; check whether protections were on the Katana victim before voting the Medic.

applies_to: Wiretap or any role that reads private messages
tip: Use a passive reader silently. Quoting a private message word for word proves you read it, and a Good player who was a recipient will test that. If you must explain a leak, keep the claim vague and avoid verbatim quotes.

Once Yakuza are level with Good (for example two Yakuza against two Good), a trial that hangs a Good player wins the game. Count the endgame arithmetic before each nomination, and don't spend a rig or a vote on a Day that doesn't end the game.
Keep the Clerk rig for the Day when a Good nominee is certain and the rig ends the game. Holding the last token past the point where it could have forced the final hanging wasted the win.

A Jester nominated by the village is a known revenge risk. If you vote Guilty as a group, one of your own Guilty voters can be killed by the revenge. Vote Innocent or abstain from the Guilty bloc on a probable Jester.
Kill the player who is building a visit or census picture, like a Lookout or Census Taker, when the Good side is splitting between claims. That removes the only evidence that could clear a teammate.
Build a written census/visit ledger each day: list every trio or group with its result and check which single player appears in all of them; the odd player out between trios is the best lead.

Avoid a 'hang the Good nominee for a Yakuza win' argument as Village: the Yakuza nominated and hanged the only Good voter, so a Vanilla who pushed for hangings should be checked against its own voting record, not its claim.
Do not pile on a thin nominee early: Grace was a Jester hanged on a single Sheriff claim, and the Village's 10-0 hang handed the Jester a win while Yakuza lost their nightly kill rhythm.

Kill the Lookout and Census Taker before the Medic when the Medic is the only protector; the Katana attacked Dave with a Medic protecting Carol, so protection targeting should be checked against the likely Katana victim.
When a private message's contents are quoted publicly, treat it as a possible Wiretap/Eavesdropper read and ask the quoter to prove access before voting on the PM alone.

A Jester's win needs a hanging, so it helps to get nominated early with a claim that visibly conflicts with a public lookout list; players who accept a visible contradiction vote quickly. This worked, but it was also a cheap win the Village could see coming.

Census trios that overlap cannot be solved on their own; when one name sits in every trio, the census-taker's own claimed Good result is the only thing that can be checked, so don't let a single overlap decide a hanging.

Before a nomination, the Yakuza should agree on which Village player is the real threat; rotating the Katana holder after each attack would have made the holder harder to pin down by Lookouts and Trackers.

Private messages between two Village players can be read by an Eavesdropper or Wiretap, so any quoted private message that only two people could see is a strong lead; a Yakuza should avoid private messages during the Day entirely.
Vote counts are secret in this variant, so a public claim that a player 'voted Guilty' is unverifiable; weigh public statements and the total counts, not individual vote claims.

Ignite as soon as you are suspected or once two or more living players are doused. Dousing alone gains nothing if you are hanged first, and doused players who die before the ignition are lost value. I reached Day 3 with doused players and no ignition, then was hanged.

applies_to: Yakuza and Neutral players who fake a claim
tip: A fake claim's protections and results must fit the public night outcomes. My Medic claim protected Carol while Dave died unprotected, which exposed the lie. Choose a cover story that explains the actual deaths.
When someone quotes a private message, ask which role lets them read it before any vote. Only a few roles can read private chats, so the answer narrows the suspect pool quickly.

Do not let a single unverified claim produce a unanimous first-Day hanging. Grace was hanged 10-0 on one Sheriff claim and was the Jester, so ask whether the nominee wins by being hanged before the trial.

A Jester's revenge hits a random living Guilty voter from their trial, so a unanimous Guilty vote on a suspected Jester can kill one of your own. When a Jester is possible, vote Innocent or split the Guilty votes, and avoid having the Katana holder be a Guilty voter.

Plan the Katana holder so that a holder's death from revenge or the Village cannot leave the Katana with a player who is about to be exposed. Check who will hold it and what happens if the holder dies at night before passing it.

Do not quote a private message verbatim unless you can justify how you read it. Verbatim quotes of a PM that only two players can see made the Village doubt the Eavesdropper claim and turned attention onto the recipient.

Katana kills on the claimed Lookout and Census Taker removed the Village's only cross-checks, and the Village then argued over claims it could not verify. Prioritise the investigators whose results corroborate each other and whose claims the Village is relying on.

Agreeing to skip a night attack on Night 1 cost tempo with no information gained. With only three Yakuza against seven Village, early no-action nights hand the Village more time to build a consistent visit list.

A Jester's hanging gives the Jester the win and triggers a random Guilty voter's Divine revenge. Don't all vote Guilty on a probable Jester. Vote Innocent when the Guilty majority is already secure, so teammates aren't exposed to revenge. Ivan died this way on Day 2 night, and that moved the Katana.

Never quote a private message word-for-word in public unless you can explain how you could have read it. Erin quoted Heidi's PM to Carol, and the other players asked how she could know. That pressure turned the table on her, so keep reader claims vague and don't quote contents.

Census trios that share one name across nights isolate the odd non-Good player. Killing a claimed Census Taker before the next trio is public stops the village from cross-checking them. Bob's Night 4 kill was correct, but it came late, so kill claimed investigators as soon as their cross-night pattern becomes clear.

A Clerk token held to the end is wasted. Plan to use it on a Day when the village nominee is a Good player you can't save, so the rig removes that nominee without a trial, and teammates vote Innocent so the rig stays hidden. Judy kept the token all game and never used it.

Keep Katana votes identical every night and avoid daytime PMs between teammates. Public PM counts are visible to all, so a teammate PM on Day 5 gave Frank a bloc pattern to cite. Settle everything in the night chat.

When a claimant is caught in an obvious lie, such as a Sheriff 'Evil' result with no visit on record, consider the Jester before hanging. A lie that easy to catch is the Jester's best play. If you hang anyway, aim for a bare majority, and Yakuza should keep several members on Innocent so the revenge can't hit them.
evidence: Grace (Jester) claimed Sheriff with 'Dave Evil', did not explain the missing visit, and even invited the nomination. She was hanged 10-0. She won, and her Divine revenge killed Ivan, the Yakuza Ritualist. No speaker ever raised the Jester possibility.

applies_to: Village (Profiler and everyone reading Profiler results)
tip: A Profiler's two decoy roles are drawn from the roles of other players who were alive that night, so they usually show which roles are in play. Treat decoys like Wiretap, Clerk or Pharmacist as strong evidence that the role exists, and match them to suspects.
evidence: Carol's Night 3 profile of Frank showed Clerk, Vanilla, Wiretap. Since Frank was Vanilla, both Clerk and Wiretap were roles of other living players. That nearly proved that Erin, who had just quoted a private message, was the Wiretap rather than an Eavesdropper. Nobody used it, and Carol was hanged.

tip: Never quote or closely paraphrase a private message you could only have read with a role. If you must use it, steer the discussion without revealing the content, or have a claim ready that fits the timing.
evidence: Erin quoted Heidi's private message to Carol almost word for word during Heidi's trial. Heidi, Carol, Bob and Frank all flagged it at once, and it became the main lead against her. She survived only because the village didn't cross-check her Eavesdropper claim against Carol's Wiretap decoy.

tip: Once group results such as census trios narrow the non-Good player to a small set, put pressure on the member who has never claimed a role or night action. Don't hang a claimant whose results check out against known facts.
evidence: Bob's Night 3 trio (Carol/Frank/Judy: 2 Good) plus Frank's Vanilla claim, which Carol's profile corroborated, left Carol or Judy as the non-Good player. Carol's two profile lists each contained a confirmed true role. Judy claimed nothing all game, yet the village hanged Carol.

applies_to: Village, especially in the late game
tip: In a close late-game vote, your vote must match your stated read. Count the votes first: with the Yakuza holding two votes, one Village Guilty decides the trial.
evidence: In Carol's trial on Day 4, Frank listed reasons why Carol was a real Profiler and pointed at Judy. The trial still ended 3 Guilty to 2 Innocent with Erin and Judy voting Guilty. Bob and Carol voted Innocent, so Frank cast the deciding Guilty, which sealed the Yakuza win.

tip: Before each night, write your planned target in your will. Then if you die, everyone knows whom you were watching, even though the result itself is lost.
evidence: Dave tracked Ivan, the Katana holder, on the night he died, and Bob took his census around Erin on the night he died; it came back 2 of 3 Evil (Erin/Frank/Judy). Neither will named the target, so this information never reached the village.

tip: Kill confirmed investigators in order of threat. Keep a low-profile member unclaimed but always echoing the evidence-based consensus. Avoid daytime private messages between teammates until the endgame.
evidence: The Katana killed Dave (Tracker), Alice (Lookout) and Bob (Census Taker) in turn. Judy never claimed, voted with the crowd, and survived every day. Erin and Judy sent each other no daytime private messages before Day 5.

tip: Don't sit on douses. A fake Medic claim falls apart the first time the Katana kills someone you didn't protect, so ignite before you're likely to be put on trial.
evidence: Heidi doused Dave and Carol and never ignited. After Dave's Katana death exposed her Medic story, she was hanged on Day 3 with no kills.

tip: Plan the Katana holder's visit and cover story early. Our team kept the same holder for five nights, and the Lookout-style and Tracker-style checks never happened only because we got lucky. Rotate the holder onto a low-value member before a known investigator is alive.

Do not let a living teammate become the only voice pushing a lynch of a Village claim. Heidi and Erin both voted Guilty on Ivan and then Erin nominated Bob's case with Judy; the pattern of identical reasoning across speeches made the bloc readable. Vary the reasons and let a Village player make the nomination.

Use the Yakuza night chat to choose targets that create the most ambiguity, not the most kills. Killing a Vigilante on Night 4 while an Arsonist was also igniting cost us nothing, but a Puppeteer or Pharmacist ally should avoid being the lone unexplained role in a trial.

Ask at the start of Day whether a Prosecutor's or Clerk's token can still land after the holder is blocked or killed. A blocked prosecution with no announced target is a free bluff for Village, and the Village pressed on it for four Days. Check each token claim against its announcement timing.

A group result (a Diviner's 60/20/20 weighting) cannot convict anyone alone. Demand a checkable result from the claimant before voting, and do not let a dead claimant's group drive trials when a living player can answer it.

Douse-then-ignite only pays off if every douse lands on a player who stays alive; I wasted three nights of dousing before igniting on N4, and the ignite killed three players at once, including my own endgame allies' suspects. Ignite as soon as 3 players are doused, because a douse on a Katana-protected or blocked player can be lost, and the Yakuza can always just kill you before ignition.

Being publicly 'Vanilla' while holding the Arsonist role is safe only if the Diviner group is not on you; I let Judy's 60% weighting of the Arsonist group be argued against me while I kept quoting Vanilla, which gave Yakuza-aligned players a free lynch. Pick a cover claim early that explains your nightly actions (e.g. the Ritualist-style visit) and stick to it.

Do not spend the Day ledger trying to identify Yakuza by vote alignment when the Yakuza side is pressing the same nominee in lockstep; count who votes Guilty with whom across Days and compare with who was doused or Katana-targeted, since the Yakuza protect each other with blocks.

A nominee who names no target while holding a token role is a real suspect only if the token role has a visible result; a Prosecutor claim with no target is easy to fake, so ask the claimant to show the tokens and target before the nomination, not at trial.

Count the living faction before every vote: with 2 Yakuza-side players alive and only one Good-side player left, the Yakuza can win by simple majority, so a late lynch of the last non-Yakuza is the Yakuza's main goal.

A shooter who is blocked or attacked on the same night loses the shot; if you suspect a living blocker, shoot early on Day 3-4 rather than waiting for a claim to be checked, since a confirmed role becomes the Yakuza's first target.
Group results (Diviner, Cartographer, Surveyor) only narrow suspects by seating; track which group members have gone quiet or refused to state a role, and weigh that before trusting a 60% weight.

Do not let a single loud player drive a trial: when two or three pressers vote in lockstep on a claim with no target, ask for the target before voting, and vote against the nomination if the nominee names one.
Refusing to state a role or to answer a group result is read as guilt by the Village; a Yakuza with a fake claim should answer the group with a plausible role rather than dodge it.
Short, specific public messages naming one checkable point cost less and get more weight than repeated pressure messages; spend budget on the nomination and trial turns.

An Eavesdropper's read only matters if the target actually sends private messages; before spending a night on a target, check the public PM counts from the previous Day and prefer a player who has been messaging privately, since a silent target yields nothing.

Look for claims that are checked against the Yakuza's own kills: a public Katana or Arsonist death that matches a claimant's role or target is evidence the claimant is real, so weigh claims by whether the night deaths fit them.

Don't let a trial rest on one unverified group result or on mechanics alone; name a concrete contradiction in the accused's own statements before voting, otherwise a Yakuza pair can steer hangings by pressing in lockstep.

Once a Village claim is contested, ask each claimant for a specific checkable target before the Day, and vote against anyone who only repeats pressure without answering; a player who pressed hard early and never named a target is a strong lead.

Remember that a Ritualist or Arsonist-style night attack can kill a player even after the Katana holder's target is set, so one night can have two causes of death; check each death's stated cause before assuming who the attacker is.

Spend the puppet token on the most dangerous accuser before the Day they would lead a lynch. Heidi held the token all game, so the Village's pressure on Judy and Bob was never disrupted and the team had no way to speak through a Village player.

A role-block only stops the blocked player's own action. Blocking a claimed threat who had no shot planned (Carol's Vigilante) wasted the block, since the Katana and the Arsonist still killed her. Block the actual attacker or the holder, and check that the target can act tonight.

The Village will lynch whoever a mechanical group argument points at, even when the group can't be checked. Steer trials with group-count arguments (for example, a dead Diviner's group weighting a living player) and keep the case on arithmetic rather than on claims.

An Arsonist's ignite kills every doused player at once and is only revealed at the start of the Day, so several deaths can share one cause. Track who has been doused from public causes of death, and count the Arsonist as a possible killer of any dead player whose cause is unexplained.

applies_to: Village investigators (Fortune Teller, Sheriff, Seer, Diviner)
tip: A public claim makes you the Katana's next target: I claimed Fortune Teller on Day 2 and was killed that night. Post exact results, but claim only when the result helps the living team, and keep your will carrying your latest result in case you die that night.

Do not trial a claimant just because they are slow to name a target. A blocked action still leaves no evidence either way. Demand a specific, checkable answer, and vote Innocent if none comes. Erin, Heidi and Dave lynched a Good Prosecutor in lockstep on that basis.

A Diviner-type group result only says one named player has the role, and a 60% weighting on one name can be used to steer a lynch. Check every group against seating and all other living claims before trialling anyone on it.

Private messages show up as counts in the ledger. A claimed Eavesdropper who reads nothing for several Days should post a concrete excerpt quickly, since unverifiable 'nothing read' claims are cheap cover for a Yakuza or Neutral.

Repeated 'no nomination from me yet' posts burn budget and add no information. Spend it on one concrete check per Day, such as a result, a vote contradiction, or a named question to a specific player.

A 0-token audit of a player who has no tokens in their role (such as a Diviner) proves nothing. Only a count that contradicts a claimed token total disproves a claim, so don't treat a fitting 0 as support.

Accurate results from the role you really hold, posted early and checked by others, build trust fast. Honest group results from a real Diviner earned Alice credibility that the Village didn't test until it was too late.

A claimant whose action was role-blocked has no checkable result, but a blocked action still has a target. Don't convict on the claim being unverified alone; ask for the target and the mechanical record first.
Investigators are the Yakuza's first Katana and block targets. Post each result publicly the day it arrives and keep the will current, so a death at night doesn't take the information with you.

A Pharmacist block on a Katana holder's target only matters if the block lands before the attack; plan the block on the attacker's own visit route, and remember the Katana attack is a visit by the holder, so a block on the holder stops it entirely.

Rotate who holds the Katana away from the Diviner or any claimed investigator once a real-looking claim is public; holding it on a player with a public role claim leaves you exposed to a Lookout or Tracker.
Use the puppet token early on a vocal village voice, because a puppeted player can't chat or see PMs and the Day's trial then looks like a self-inflicted collapse rather than Yakuza play.
A claimant who names no checkable target for several Days (like a Prosecutor) is a strong lead for the village; for Yakuza, keep public pressure on such claimants rather than defending them.
Avoid nominating or voting in lockstep with a teammate; the same reasons repeated across votes make the bloc readable to the village.

A blocked prosecution is silent: the target never learns it and no announcement occurs. If you claim Prosecutor, name your target publicly early (before the trial stage) so the claim is checkable; waiting for Day 4 made my claim look like a bluff.

Group results (Diviner, Surveyor, Profiler) only narrow the list; they cannot convict. Shift the burden to checkable results and vote records, and be wary of anyone who pushes a lynch from a group result while not answering it themselves.

Do not vote Guilty on a pressure-based case without a concrete contradiction. My Day 4 trial rested on 'no named target', which the whole table repeated; the trial then executed a Good player while the Yakuza kept their numbers.
When several players repeat the same accusation in lockstep (same wording, same nomination), treat it as a bloc signal and check whether their votes match before following them.
Role-blocks and Katana attacks can strike the same player in one night; a Pharmacist block on a Vigilante does not stop a Katana or Arsonist attack, so do not assume a block equals protection.

A Diviner or Ritualist group only shows that the drawn role is somewhere in the listed players, so it is a lead, not proof. A group confirmed by a true role elsewhere does not prove the claimant is Village, because a Yakuza Diviner receives the same true information. Judge the claimant by whether their claims line up with kills, blocks and the vote record.

Use mechanical elimination on kill timing. A player who died before a night's kill cannot be the living killer, so match each Arsonist or Katana kill against the players who could have acted that night. This is how the real Arsonist was identified.

Private messages are logged to everyone as sender and recipient counts. Two players who PM each other and then vote in lockstep look like a bloc. Before a trial, make your case in public and ask pushers for a concrete public reason, not a private one.

A blocked action announces nothing and spends no token. Silence from a blocked Prosecutor or any blocked role is not a contradiction. Do not treat a missing announcement as proof of a lie, and check whether the rules would have announced it before calling it a contradiction.

Learn which faction each role belongs to, and check every claimed role against that list. A public claim of a Yakuza-only role (Diviner, Pharmacist, Puppeteer, Ritualist, etc.) is a confession unless it is an obvious joke. Accurate results from that claimant do not make them Village. Evil investigators get true information too.
evidence: On Day 2 Alice claimed Diviner and posted three accurate groups. Carol and Dave 'verified' them only by checking the seating, and Carol said Alice 'gains weight' after confirming Vigilante. Nobody pointed out that Diviner is a Yakuza role, so the Katana holder ran the town's agenda for three Days.

tip: If your Evil role produces true information about non-teammates, publishing it accurately can make you the most trusted voice in town. Point the results at Neutrals or Village players, and let others confirm your hits for you.
evidence: Alice's N1 Arsonist group really did contain Bob, and her N3 Vigilante group really did contain Carol. Carol's confirmation made Alice look like a confirmed Village investigator. Alice then helped push the real Prosecutor Ivan to a 7-1 hang.

tip: Never hang a claimed power role just because their action 'produced nothing'. A role-block makes any action invisible, and a known living blocker exists. Verify token claims with an Accountant or a will before hanging, and treat whoever builds a case on 'no visible result' as the suspect.
