Require a mechanical contradiction (a result, a visit, a death cause, a vote total) before voting Guilty, and say out loud which of those you have. Even a correct hang can look coordinated if the nominator and a PM partner act together.

Private messages are visible as pairs to the whole table. A pair that messages heavily and then nominates or votes together gets scrutinized as a team. If you coordinate, do it in public, or accept that the pair becomes the suspect.

An archive's fakes are drawn from all roles, so a listed role is only weak evidence. Use the list to test specific claims: for each claimant, check whether their role is in the list and whether later deaths or results confirm it. Post the archive once, with the names of the roles you think are real, and keep the rest of your claim tight.

Unused tokens and shots are lost at death. Erin kept an Armed shot through the whole game and Ivan's last Sniper token went unspent. Decide on a trigger before the stall clock forces a choice, and fire on the first solid lead rather than waiting for certainty.

Check the attack level against the defense before trusting a save. Standard protection (Medic, Veteran alert, Diviner) does not stop a Strong attack such as an Arsonist ignite or a Vigilante's 3-token shot. Only a Strong or Divine defense does. Ivan died to a Strong ignite despite Standard protection.

Two or more deaths in one night from the same cause (for example two doused players ignited together) is strong evidence of a single Arsonist, and the Arsonist's douse targets are never revealed to Village players. Track the douse log yourself: each douse you can see is a visit from a non-Village player, and the night before an ignite is the window to watch.

A Lookout's 'no visitors' result cannot clear a Neutral or Yakuza player who simply did not visit the watched target. Treat a claim like this as untestable until the watched player is attacked, and don't cite it as a check on someone else. I wrongly used Heidi's N4 no-visit claim to vote Innocent, and she was the Arsonist.

A claimed Archivist or other list-based result can be checked later: when roles on the list are confirmed by deaths or results, the list gains weight. Dave's Night 2 archive listed Cartographer, Auditor and Sniper, and all three were confirmed as real. Use these checks to rank claimants before a vote.

Don't pre-arrange a nomination in private before the Day's public discussion. A PM of the form 'I'll nominate X if you vote Guilty' followed by a nomination in the same round looks coordinated to everyone, and it hands the target a credible defense. State the reason publicly first, then nominate.

If your claimed result contradicts your own earlier wording, correct it once, cleanly and publicly, with the exact night, target and result. Repeating 'no action', 'audit pending' and 'no submitted audit' across days gave a Village Auditor an unnecessary nomination and cost the town a Day's discussion.

State your night action once, plainly, and never describe a result as 'pending' or reword it after the fact. I gave three different Night 3 answers ('audit pending', 'no submitted audit', 'no action'), which made a harmless gap look like a lie and got me nominated. If you took no action, say 'no action' at the first mention and leave it there.

With 4 or fewer alive, a hang that kills a Village player can leave the Neutral killer unfindable and run the stall clock. Do not hang on timing, wording or PM frequency alone. Require a mechanical contradiction, and count who is still possibly the Arsonist before voting.

When two players make the same claim with identical outputs, look at who coordinated privately. Bob copied Alice's Cartographer sizes exactly and had five private messages with the dead Katana holder. Those patterns point at a Yakuza pair. A Sniper shot on the copier was correct. Test duplicates early, before the stall clock matters.

Audit the player most likely to vote in the next trial, not a quiet player like Bob (who cast no votes). A 'no votes' result from a silent player gives nothing, and the same goes for auditing someone who already has no votes.

Strong Attacks (Arsonist ignite, Sniper Strong) beat Standard protection. Once a Neutral killer may be alive, a Medic should protect with Strong or aim where the killer is likely to strike. Standard protection only stops Katana-level hits.

Standard protection stops Katana and Standard attacks only. Against a possible Arsonist ignite (Strong) or any Strong attacker, give Strong protection (1 token on others) when the threat is live. I lost Ivan to a Strong ignite on a Standard protection, and that made the Arsonist's survival clear to everyone.

Use the attack trail. A player whose Avenger trait is triggered by an attack shows that the attacker's attack would have been fatal. Doused players who die later at an ignite point to the Arsonist. Track who was doused, watched or visited, and check each claim against those trails rather than against wording.

Watch claims of 'no visitors' only weakly. A Lookout who watched a player shows no visitors when the true visit was an astral or a douse on someone else. Require a later attack on the watched player to test them, and do not hang on the claim until that test has run.

Track the stall clock (R14) from the day of the last death. With 4 players alive and no deaths for two Nights and Days, a hang must come soon. Plan the nomination and the Yes/Guilty votes in advance with stated commitments, so you do not end up with a 2-1 or 3-1 split that fails to convict.

applies_to: Village roles with a one-shot trait (Armed, Sniper, Vigilante)
tip: I held my Armed shot all game and never used it, even when the Arsonist was narrowed to two players. Use a one-shot on a solid lead (Night 5 or 6 with two suspects) rather than keeping it for a cleaner read that never arrives.

applies_to: Neutral killers (Arsonist, Serial Killer) and anyone reasoning about Medic protection
tip: Standard protection stops Standard attacks only. Strong attacks (Arsonist ignite, Strong shots, Trapper traps) go through a Medic's Standard protection. Before a Medic's protection is treated as safety, check which attack levels exist in the game. A Neutral killer should plan Strong kills against players the Medic has been protecting.

applies_to: Neutral roles that can't be checked (Arsonist, Serial Killer)
tip: Don't publicly claim a role that makes checkable night results (Lookout watches, visit reports) when your real night targets would contradict them. Claiming Lookout with watch targets I never used got me hanged on a timing argument, because the Village could only ask me to explain, not check me. If you need cover, prefer a claim whose results can't be tested before the stall clock, or stay quiet and let the Village hang someone else.

The stall rule (R14) is a real clock. Once several nights pass without a death, the Village pushes hangs on thin evidence, and nominations that would not otherwise happen become likely. A Neutral can use this: stay quiet, let the clock build, and keep the Village focused on the stall instead of on your doused players.

Ask for each player's exact night target and result early, and compare them against the public death causes. Several claims in this game (Medic, Lookout, Archivist, Profiler) were never checkable until a later attack, so the Village spent days on wording. Pick the one check that can be made tonight (a visit, a death cause, a protected target) and vote on that, not on nomination timing.

Coordinated nominations are visible. When one player nominates right after another says they will nominate if a third player commits, the rest of the table reads it as a pact. That helped me defend myself to the Village, but it also means a Village nominator who reveals a pact with a Medic gives a Neutral or Yakuza a cover story to pin on the pair.

Standard protection does not stop a Strong attack. An Arsonist ignite or a Serial Killer strike is Strong, so once an Arsonist is alive or suspected, protect with Strong (2 tokens) on the players you most need alive, and don't spend tokens on a Standard guess.

When a player's claim depends on a private PM partner, track the partner's claim too. Bob and Carol shared five PMs and copied each other's Cartographer story. Treat such a pair as a coordinated unit and test the pair's claims against shared mechanics, not against each other.

Stall-rule pressure (R14) is real when hard results are scarce. After a quiet stretch with few mechanical leads, Village should prioritize a death (a hang on the best mechanical lead) before the stall clock forces a loss, instead of waiting for certainty that never arrives.

Don't nominate on wording or timing alone. Dave's nomination of Heidi came right after Grace's PM. A nomination that rests on timing gives the nominee a credible innocence story, and it splits the Village vote, so require a checkable contradiction first.

Keep a shot or token as a trigger that can break a stall or confirm a suspect's role on a hard lead. I spent my Day 3 shot and died with my last token unused, which was a loss of tempo; a dead player's unused token is worth nothing.

If an investigator's result corners you into the same role as a live claimant, don't kill that claimant the next night. Killing the one player who contradicts you all but confirms you. Kill someone else, such as the investigator who boxed you in, and let the duplicate claim sit unresolved. Better still, agree a cover claim before Day 2 so you aren't improvising a copy of someone else's results.
evidence: Bob copied Alice's exact Night 1 sizes to claim Cartographer. The Yakuza killed Alice on Night 2, and her Avenger trait killed Carol. On Day 3 every Villager pointed at Bob as the copier who had messaged Carol, and Ivan's Sniper shot killed him that turn.

tip: Never send your teammate private messages during the Day. Everyone sees who messaged whom, and once one of you is exposed, the other is the next target. Do all planning in night chat.
evidence: Bob and Carol exchanged five daytime private messages that said nothing night chat couldn't have. On Day 3 Grace, Frank, Dave and Ivan all cited 'five PMs with the Katana holder' as their main reason to suspect Bob.

applies_to: Profiler (and anyone reading a Profiler result)
tip: Read a profile's two decoy roles too. One decoy is always the role of another player alive that night, and the other is a role nobody in the game has. If the target's claim fits one of the three, the other two tell you that exactly one of them is in play. That can reveal a hidden Neutral killer or a Yakuza role.
evidence: Erin's Night 3 profile of Dave read Archivist, Arsonist or Puppeteer. With Dave as Archivist, an Arsonist or a Puppeteer had to be alive. Since the Yakuza seemed gone, the Arsonist was more likely. Nobody said so, and the Arsonist ignited two players two nights later.

tip: Free Standard protection stops only the Katana and Basic or Standard attacks. Neutral killers (Serial Killer, Arsonist) and Vigilantes can attack at Strong. Once the Yakuza look dead, or a Neutral killer is suspected, spend your tokens on Strong protection for your most valuable ally. Unused tokens are worth nothing.
evidence: Grace protected someone every night with free Standard Defense and finished with 2 unused tokens. On Night 5 her Standard protection on Ivan lost to Heidi's Strong ignite, and both Ivan and Frank died.

tip: When the Katana is quiet and the Yakuza are probably dead, look for the Neutral killer among players who never give a role, targets or results and who answer every question with filler. Push that player to commit to checkable details early. Don't spend nominations on how a confirmed role worded a report.
evidence: Heidi said almost nothing but 'no nomination, I'll vote on hard results' for three Days, claimed Lookout only at the end of Day 4, and stated her watch targets only once on trial. Meanwhile Day 4 went on a 0-6 trial of Frank over his wording. When the Village finally pressed Heidi on Day 6, they hanged the Arsonist and won.

tip: Make a full, consistent claim early, with targets that fit the visit evidence. Being the vague one gets you hanged in the endgame. Douse players who are likely to live, not ones the Yakuza are about to kill. A non-Good player you douse is told an Arsonist exists. Ignite while the group is still big enough that you aren't one of only three suspects.
evidence: Heidi doused Carol (Yakuza, and Carol was told an Arsonist doused her) and Alice, who both died on Night 2, so those douses were wasted. Her ignite on Night 5 left 4 alive. As the only player without real details, she was nominated and hanged 3-1 the next Day.

tip: Know which attack beats which Defense before relying on a shot. Armed shots and 1-token Sniper shots are Basic and can't kill a Serial Killer, Arsonist or Jester's Defense. Once a Neutral killer is suspected, a hang is usually the only reliable kill.
evidence: Erin and Grace each held an unused Armed shot, and Ivan kept 1 Sniper token. All of these were Basic attacks, which could not have killed Heidi's Standard Defense, so hanging her on Day 6 was the Village's only real option.

tip: Post each night result the moment it exists, with night, target and exact result. Holding a result until the next Day start looks retrofitted, and it gave the Yakuza time to push a hang on the claimant.

An Evil read is not proof of a Yakuza. The Jester also reads Evil to the Sheriff. Before hanging on one Evil read, check whether the nominee could be a Jester and whether any other roles or votes explain the result.

Do not shoot a fellow Village claimant before any night data exists. An early Standard shot on a Village-looking player is taken as proof of guilt by everyone and makes the rest of the Village distrust you. Save the shot for a confirmed Yakuza read.

Do not rely on a Pharmacist block to hide a Katana visit from a living Tracker. The Tracker can still track the holder on a later night, and a Katana holder who visits victims night after night is exposed by a Tracker's track. Rotate the holder and avoid repeated visits to the same kill pattern.

Check your own stated vote before posting it publicly. A false public vote claim (Frank's Guilty post that was then corrected to Innocent) creates an extra mystery the whole table has to resolve, and it can make the trial look rigged.

Don't fire a shot at another player who claims the same role before any night result exists. Grace and I were both real Snipers, so my Day 2 Standard shot removed a Village power role and gave the Yakuza a free reason to attack my credibility. Hold shots until a mechanical lead points at a Yakuza, and use a shot only on a player you have confirmed as Yakuza.

When two players claim the same investigative role, check the claims against each other before reacting to either. Two Sheriff or Tracker claims that agree on the same visit are often both true, so a single contested result is not grounds for a hang. Demand each claimant's night target and exact result on schedule, and treat a missed promise as a lead.

Keep a running record of every player's stated night visits and every private message pair. Late in the game, a Yakuza's false no-visit claim was exposed only because a Tracker's result and a death lined up. A pair of players who privately message each other while pushing the same hang is worth reporting publicly, since it is the pattern that exposed the Yakuza pair here.

Before voting Guilty, ask whether the player on trial could be the Jester or another neutral who wants the hang. Erin pushed a hang on me and then won by being hanged, so a player who pushes hangs without new data may be trying to get hanged themselves.

A Katana holder dies on the night their victim dies, and the Katana passes only to a living Yakuza. A claim that the Katana reached you through a death is checkable against the will and death announcements, so compare it with the claimed holder's visits before accepting it.

A role-block on a Tracker or Sheriff tells the town that a blocker is alive, and a blocked investigator usually names the blocked target. Use the block only when the cost is worth revealing a Yakuza exists, and expect the town to hunt the blocker's teammates by elimination.

Do not stake a flat 'I had no visits' claim that a live Tracker can contradict. Carol's denial of an N4 visit was exposed by Frank's track, and her evasive answer under direct questioning then convinced the town. If you must lie about visits, pick a cover that a tracker cannot check, or admit a visit with a prepared cover.

Answer direct visit or vote questions in one plain line. Carol dodging the N4 question and Heidi's long defenses both read as guilt, and a dodge is harder to recover from than an honest, checkable claim.

A player who self-nominates, or pushes a hang with no new data after an unrelated nomination, may be the Jester. Erin's push on Bob and then her hanging win were the warning signs. Ask the self-nominee to explain before voting, and remember a hanged Jester wins outright.

A Sniper's shot that kills before any night data exists is a hard fact, so ask the shooter for the reason before the trial. A Village claim that fires early may be real, but an unexplained kill should be resolved before the Day 3 vote, not left open for two Days.

Don't reveal your protection target in public chat before the night resolves, and don't repeat the same target two nights running. The Yakuza read a predictable protection pattern and spent their Pharmacist block on the Medic on the two nights that mattered (N3 and N4), so the protected players died. Vary targets, and consider a one-token self-protect once a blocker is suspected.

A Sheriff's Evil read does not separate Yakuza from a Jester, because the Jester also reads Evil. Before hanging on an Evil read, check whether the nominee pushed a hang with no new data. Erin did, and the Village's 7-0 hang gave the Jester the win.

Treat a real kill by a claimed role as proof only that the role's tokens exist, not that the claim is true or that the shooter is Village. Verify claims from the investigators' results and the night-by-night visit data instead.

Post night results the same Day they are produced, and never hold them for a later Day. Holding Night 2 results until Day 3 let the Yakuza and Bob's shot set the agenda, and the delay made every claim look retrofitted.

When a Katana holder dies, the Katana passes to a living Yakuza, and a holder killed at night passes it after that night's results. In a late game, a Yakuza who claims the Katana 'passed to me' is telling the truth, so check which living players could be the new holder before voting.

A Jester wins only by being hanged, so a Day 2 self-nomination that gets just 2 Yes votes achieves nothing. Build a case that makes the Village's real suspects look wrong and gives them a reason to vote you, e.g. press a trial on someone the Village respects and let the vote fall on you. Expect the Village to hang you only once they have a mechanical-looking read against you, so keep your public Guilty pushes consistent and sound like a sincere Village player.

Cross-check investigator and tracker results against the visit they imply before trusting a claim. This game's decisive deduction was that a Tracker's Night 3 'Bob visited no one' ruled out Bob as the Katana holder, which left only the two players who denied visits. Ask every claimant for night, target and exact result on the night it happened, not at Day start.

Do not fire a Sniper shot at another Sniper claimant on Day 2 before any night result exists. Grace and Bob were both real Village Snipers, so the Standard shot that killed Grace destroyed a Village power role and locked the game into a long guessing contest. Resolve duelling claims with a vote or a pending result, not a kill.

A Yakuza claiming Vanilla Villager who stays quiet and reports no visits is hard to tell apart from a real Villager when the Village is still gathering results. Nothing in this game caught the Pharmacist or the Grunt until they were pinned by Tracker data. Keep your no-visit story consistent with what the Tracker can still show, and avoid being the only player who denies a visit the Tracker can later check.

Ask for the trial's stated votes before voting and compare them with the announced totals. Several Day 3 and Day 5 totals only made sense with hidden Innocents, and players who hung on a lone unverified claim (Alice's Evil read on Erin) lost the chance to test it. Hang only on a result that a second source corroborates.

Don't re-track the same player. I tracked Bob three nights running and got 'no visits' each time, while the Katana holder was a teammate of the players who denied visits. Spread tracks across unverified claimants and whoever denies a visit that a victim's death implies. Track the people whose statements conflict with the kills.

Before acting on an Evil read, check whether the reader's target is the player who keeps pushing hangs or self-nominated. Erin self-nominated on Day 2, pushed the Bob hang with no new data, and was the Jester. Her Evil alignment matched the Sheriff's read, and the Village hanged her on that read. A Jester wins by being hanged, so a pusher with no data is a Jester suspect.

When a Katana victim dies, list everyone who denied night visits and check those denials against the victim's visitors. Two players both said 'no visits' while one of them was the holder, and nobody tested them until too late. A single tracker track on the right person would have settled it.

Watch private message counts between two players who push the same hang. Bob and Dave's private messages were visible as counts all Day 5, and Heidi named that pattern, but the Village never acted on it. Ask the pair directly in public, and don't let a paired push go through unchallenged.

Don't fire a shot on Day 2 before any real information. Shots resolve after a random delay, so a rival Sniper with a Standard shot can kill you first and cancel your pending shot. Publicly announcing a shot also tells the other side exactly who to hit. Hold the shot until you have a result that makes the target a clear threat.

When two investigators claim, post your night results at once, with night, target and exact result. Holding them back until the next Day made both claims look retrofitted and gave the Yakuza time to pick a side.

A Sheriff's Evil read on a nominee is not proof of Yakuza, because Neutral roles such as the Jester also read Evil. Before hanging on an Evil read, check which Neutral roles could be the target. Here the Evil read was true, but the hanged player was the Jester, who won by being hanged.

Pick cover claims that fit real visits and tokens, and don't let a teammate's Katana holder visits be the only thing protecting a fake claim. The Pharmacist's blocks were publicly announced by the moderator, and each block on an investigator made the investigator look more credible to the Village.
Long, repeated 'no hanging without evidence' posts across many rounds used up budget without adding information. Short, specific questions to named players produced more useful reactions.

A teammate's night summary shows their chosen action and reason text. If the Pharmacist's block on a Tracker or Medic is aimed at the one player who could expose the holder, the Tracker/Medic's results are the team's main risk. Block the protector before the attack, and keep a plan for the case where the block is out of reach (Dave was blocked, but Frank still died).

When one Yakuza is left and holds the Katana, the Village needs only two votes to hang the last Yakuza in a three-player game. Do not let a daytime PM pressure campaign against a Village player show up as a count; the visible private-message pattern (Bob-Dave, then Heidi-Bob) exposed both sides to the Village.

A player who self-nominates on Day 2, then pushes hangs with no new data, is a strong Jester suspect. Vote-count math (for example 2 Yes on Day 5 after 4 Yes on Day 3) shows who is pushing. Check whether the nominator would gain from the hang before voting Guilty, because a Jester who is hanged wins.

A Sniper's pending delayed shot is cancelled if the shooter dies before it fires, and a Standard shot kills a Basic-defense target. A Sniper who fires before any night information exists risks public suspicion, and Grace's will framed Bob. Hold shots until a real lead exists.

A Standard protection stops a Standard Katana attack, so a Medic on a likely target blocks the holder's kill. The Yakuza then need a Pharmacist block on the Medic, and a Medic should claim and protect the likeliest target each night to force that spend.

Two people claiming the same role is not a contradiction when roles can repeat, and hand-built setups make repeats likely. Before you shoot or hang a player for making the same claim as you, ask them for something that can be checked, like token counts or results. Don't race to shoot each other.
evidence: On Day 2, Grace and Bob were both real Snipers. Each called the other fake and fired. Bob's Standard shot killed Grace, so the Village lost a Sniper and 2 tokens, with no Yakuza involved.

tip: A player who nominates themself is very likely a Jester. An Evil Sheriff read on them fits a Jester just as well as Yakuza. Don't hang them while the Katana is still killing. If you hang them anyway, keep Guilty to a bare majority and have your power roles vote Innocent.
evidence: Erin nominated herself on Day 2. Alice then read her Evil on Night 2 and declared her Yakuza, and all 7 voted Guilty. That gave the Jester her win and spent a whole Day. The revenge hit Alice, who was already dying to the Katana, so this only cost nothing by luck.

tip: At endgame parity, kill the player who still holds a day-kill token (Sniper or Vigilante) before you kill investigators. A day shot can break parity before your next night kill, and a block can't stop it.
evidence: On Night 4, the Yakuza killed Frank and left Bob alive with his last, publicly claimed Sniper token. On Day 5, at 2 v 2, Bob shot Carol, and the Village won by hanging Heidi. If they had killed Bob, the Yakuza could have blocked every nomination and won with the next kill.

tip: After a Katana attack fails, work out who the protector is from the claims and votes. Role-block them on the next try at the same target.
evidence: Alice survived the Night 2 Katana attack. Carol ruled out Bob as Medic because his shot proved he was a Sniper, so she blocked Dave on Night 3. Alice died that night, and the same block got Frank killed on Night 4.

tip: Once you've narrowed the suspects, don't announce whom you'll investigate tonight. Put your planned target and reasoning in your will instead, so it survives if you die.
evidence: On Day 4, Frank kept saying he would track Carol or Heidi and post the result on Day 5. The Yakuza killed him that night, citing that plan, and his result (Carol visited Dave and Frank) was never seen.

tip: When the Yakuza reach half the living players, they can block every nomination. Use any day-kill token right away, even on a coin flip between two suspects. Waiting for the next night's results means losing.
evidence: On Day 5 it was 2 v 2 (Bob and Dave against Carol and Heidi). Bob shot Carol instead of waiting for Night 5 results, which made 2 v 1 and a guaranteed hang.

tip: On trial, never mention night mechanics that only Yakuza know, such as who holds the Katana. And when you're about to be outvoted, defending yourself doesn't matter. Spend the effort earlier on getting rid of the token holder.
evidence: Heidi's trial claim said the Katana had passed to her when Carol died, which proved she was Yakuza. The 2-to-1 vote math had already decided her fate.

tip: Rule out suspects with confirmed facts: who was tracked with no visits, who was blocked on the kill night, and whose public actions prove their role. When only two suspects are left, pressure both.
evidence: On Day 4, Frank used his Night 3 track (Bob visited no one) and Dave's Night 3 block to narrow the Katana holder to Carol or Heidi. That was correct, and it set up Bob's Day 5 shot.

applies_to: Yakuza (especially a Grunt with no night action)
tip: A Standard Katana cannot kill a Standard-defense Serial Killer. When a Katana attack fails on a player who later shows innate Standard defense, treat them as an SK or a Standard-defense role and plan a hang instead of more Katana votes. Don't spend the team's Katana nights on a target you can't kill.

Don't use first-person action wording in a defense (e.g. 'my Katana on Carol failed'), even when repeating a teammate's claim. A slip like this got Frank hanged on the Village's read, and it's the easiest tell a Village player can get. Re-read defenses for 'my' + action verbs before posting.

Roles can repeat. Two players can both be real Kitsunes (or any duplicated role), so one conflicting claim doesn't prove a liar. Check whether both stories fit real night events before calling either one fake. Here both Kitsune charm stories matched real attacks, and the Village wrongly treated one as false.

Before a hang, reconcile every announced total with each player's stated vote. A mismatch can be a miscount or a self-correction, not a lie. Grace was executed after flip-flopping her vote claim on Dave's first trial, which turned out to be an honest miscount. Ask for the reminder explanation before the next nomination.

Wording evidence is strong when it's a first-person action from a player claiming a role that can't do it, but weak when it's a single phrase in a defense. Separate these cases before hanging. Frank's slip was real, but the same standard applied to Dave and Grace produced hangs on weaker evidence.

A visit that lines up with a death is strong evidence. Bob's Tracker result showed Dave visiting Bob on Night 1, and Bob then died to a Serial Killer that night. The Village never cross-checked that, so Dave survived to the end. When a Tracker or Lookout result sits on a victim, check the visitor first, before debating claims.

Don't hang on a single phrase or wording slip. Frank, Grace and Dave were each nominated over one word or a vote-count dispute. Good players were executed while the real killer stayed alive. Require a mechanical reason, such as a result, a death cause, or a verified vote total, before voting Guilty.

Check announced vote totals against stated votes before the next nomination. The 2-2 Dave count was used as a weapon by several players, and the Village spent days arguing over it instead of over the real evidence. Ask each voter to restate their Guilty or Innocent vote once, and then drop the topic.

Unexplained survivors are suspects. Dave survived a Standard Katana on Night 1 with no protector named, and that matched Standard Defense. Serial Killers have Standard Defense innately. Treat any player who survives an attack with no protector as a lead to test, not as a clear.

A charm on a player who later dies to the attack it swallowed is confirmed information. Only the real Kitsune has a unique charm story that matches deaths. If two players claim the same role, test each claim against the next death cause before hanging either one.

A Not Evil read on a Neutral killer proves nothing. Serial Killers and Arsonists read Not Evil to the Sheriff. Before trusting a clean read, ask whether the target could be a Neutral killer, and cross-check it against the death causes and the Standard-Defense survivors.

A player who survives a Standard Katana with no named protector probably has innate Standard Defense (Serial Killer), not a Medic. Look for the Neutral killer among the survivors of Standard attacks before assuming a Good protector exists.

Do not hang Village players on a single phrase or wording slip. Hanging Frank was right only because his phrase lined up with a real Katana night. Grace's hang on phrases killed a Village player, and the Village was then down to two living Good players. Ask for a mechanical contradiction first.

With an even number of voters a tie is not a majority, so the accused is Innocent. Count the voters before pushing a hang, and when the total reads 2-2, ask who actually voted what before the next nomination.

Posting a claim with a planned next-night target made me the target that night. Publicly stated check targets, and the claim itself, invite a Katana or Serial Killer hit. Consider holding the target back, and have a protector or a second claimant ready before you announce.

applies_to: Serial Killer or any Neutral killer
tip: Kill claimed investigators (Sheriff, Seer, Tracker) early, and keep killing the strongest remaining claimant each night. Their results are the main threat, and a Village that cannot verify claims will stall or hang its own.

applies_to: Serial Killer or any Neutral killer
tip: With two players alive, a hanging needs both votes. Vote No on every nomination and make the other survivor look like the threat. Then use the night kill on the last other player to win alone.

applies_to: Serial Killer or any Neutral killer
tip: Let the Village hang its own. Quietly backing pushes against town-looking players on weak phrase-level evidence costs you nothing, while publicly defending the accused makes you the next suspect.
Do not claim a role with first-person action wording ("my Katana", "my attacks") unless you have it. Players treat such slips as a Yakuza or Neutral tell and hang on them.
Before any hang, have each player restate their exact vote, then compare the announced totals. Unexplained extra Guilty counts are the reliable lead, not the wording of a defence.

A held swallowed attack is worthless once you die, so release it on the first night you suspect you may be targeted or exposed, and pick a target whose death you can justify. I died on Night 3 still holding a Katana I never released.

Don't spend two charms on the same player. My Night 1 and Night 2 charms both went on Carol, which gave one fact-set instead of two. Spread charms over likely targets (claimed investigators, the player who survived an unexplained attack) so each night adds information.

When two players claim the same unique-feeling role, look for a victim or third party whose own notifications corroborate one claim. Carol's N2 double-attack notification matched both Kitsune stories, so it proved the events but not who was lying. Ask for the claim that adds a checkable detail, like the exact level and cause on release.

Write down every stated vote the moment it's announced and compare it to the totals before any nomination. The Dave trial mismatch (2-2 against several 'Guilty' claims) exposed a false vote claim, but only after two hangs had been driven by wording-level reads.

Don't hang on a single phrase or wording slip (Frank, then Grace). A hang needs a mechanical fit such as a Katana victim's visitor list, a Sheriff read, or a vote count. Otherwise the Yakuza can convert hang pressure into a Village-on-Village execution.
Many turns repeated 'no nomination from me' and the same request, which costs budget without adding information. Spend budget on the one claim or vote question that moves the game.

Scrub first-person action wording from day chat. A Vanilla Villager saying 'my Katana on Carol failed' while repeating a teammate's claim was enough to get me hanged. If you must reference a night event, use the wording a Village player would use, and make sure it matches your claimed role.

Two players claiming the same role is not proof that one is lying. Duplicate roles can both be real (here, both Kitsunes were real). Before concluding that someone is a liar, check whether the role could appear twice and whether the two claims are actually incompatible.

Do not hang on a phrase or a wording slip. Frank and Grace were both executed on single-sentence readings, and the Village ended up with only Dave, the Serial Killer, left alive. Require a mechanical contradiction (a result that conflicts with a visit or a death) before a hang.

State your vote exactly once, and reconcile it against the announced totals. Several players publicly misstated their trial votes, which created a 2-2 count nobody could resolve and made every later vote look suspicious.

Before choosing a Katana target, check whether the target is a likely protected investigator. Our Katana failed on Dave (N1) and on Carol (N2, likely protected), and each failure cost us information and credibility, while the Serial Killer kept killing freely. Consider whether a Neutral killer in the game changes which targets are worth it.

A Kitsune's released attack keeps the cause of the attack it swallowed, so a 'Serial Killer' death on a later night can be a Kitsune release rather than a live Serial Killer. Before assuming a new killer is alive, check whether a Kitsune charm swallowed that cause earlier.

Two players can share a role, and two Kitsune claims can both be true. Don't eliminate one claimant on a 'they must be fake' argument. Check which claimed events deaths and visits independently match, and weigh both claims until something separates them.

A Not Evil alignment read on a player who survived an unexplained Standard-level attack is a lead, not a clearance. Serial Killers and Arsonists read Not Evil and have Standard Defense, so ask which Neutral killer explains the survival before counting the read as clean.

Check your own vote reminder before you state it publicly, and don't correct a public vote claim after the fact. A wrong stated vote that is later reversed reads as a lie, and it made me the main suspect even though I was Village.

Don't nominate on a single wording slip, and don't coordinate a hang after a burst of private messages with one player. Others read that as a bloc. Build the case on a result that lines up with deaths or visits, and state it in public chat before the vote.

Don't spend your first fox charm on an arbitrary player. Charm the player most likely to be attacked (a claimed investigator, or the player whose death would hurt you). My N1 charm on Alice caught nothing, while the N2 charm on Carol caught a real Strong Serial Killer attack, which is what made the held attack useful.

Two players can share a role claim and both be telling the truth. Kitsune Erin and Kitsune Heidi were both real. Before you call a rival claim fake, check it mechanically: a swallowed attack's level and cause must match a real attack that night on that player. Don't release a held attack (a kill) on someone you only dislike.

A Serial Killer has innate Standard Defense. A Standard Katana that fails on a player with no named protector is evidence for a Neutral SK, not for that player being Village. Use survival-with-no-protector as a lead toward the SK.

Don't convict on one wording slip or a disputed vote count. The Village hanged Frank on a phrase and then Grace on a disputed count, leaving the Serial Killer with an easy path. When only 3 or 4 Village remain, each hang on weak evidence is a gift to a Neutral killer.
Never announce tonight's night target or charm plan in public chat. I wrote 'tonight I'll lay my charm', and the Serial Killer killed me that night. A silent target keeps your night action useful.

A duplicate claim of a non-unique role is not proof that one claimant is lying. Only Smuggler and Vulture are unique. Before calling a liar or acting on it, check whether both claims can be true together, for example whether both explain the same night's events.
evidence: Heidi said Erin's Kitsune claim was false because she knew her own role. On Night 2 their two charms on Carol swallowed a Katana attack and an SK attack, which matched Carol's report of surviving both. Heidi still released her held SK attack on Erin on Night 3, killing a real Village Kitsune, and only admitted the mistake on Day 4.

tip: When a Serial Killer is alive, take any chance to hang him, even if it means siding with villagers. Your Standard Katana can't get through his Standard Defense, but his Strong Attack kills any of you. If the game comes down to you and him, you lose. Count ahead: once the SK is gone, a lone Katana holder can usually block hangings and kill their way to a win.
evidence: On Day 4 Alice voted Guilty on Dave's first trial, then switched to Innocent on the second and to Guilty on the villager Grace. That left Alice and Dave alive. Her Katana couldn't hurt him, and he killed her on Night 5. If she had hanged Dave, it would have been Alice against Grace and Heidi, with no majority for the village to hang her.

tip: A player who survived the Katana with no protector claimed, and who reads Not Evil to a Sheriff, fits a Serial Killer. Add evasion about what he did at night and you have your best hang target. Make the case early, before the SK can thin the village.
evidence: Dave survived the Katana on Night 1 and read Not Evil to Carol. He also said his results were 'my own attacks, which I'm not sharing'. Nobody pushed this until Day 4, and by then the SK had killed Bob, Carol, Erin and later Heidi.

tip: In a small endgame, every vote decides the game. Check your vote reminder before you say how you voted, cast the vote you announced, and never state a vote you aren't sure of. Village: when one stated vote doesn't match the count, the likely explanation in a 4-player game is a single misclick. Treat it as a lead and question the person, not as grounds to hang them.
evidence: Grace nominated Dave and said she was voting Guilty, but cast Innocent, so the trial tied 2-2. She first said publicly she had voted Guilty and later 'corrected' it to Innocent. Heidi, Dave and Alice then hanged her for the mismatch, which handed the game to the SK.

tip: Keep your night perspective out of day chat entirely. Don't use first-person words about Katana actions or kill results. Before posting, reread your message from your fake role's point of view. One slip like this gets you hanged even with no other evidence.
evidence: Frank, claiming Vanilla, wrote 'the Katana I aimed at Carol' and 'my Katana on Carol failed'. Grace nominated him at once and he was hanged 5-2. Dave nearly went the same way with 'my own attacks'.

tip: While you hold a swallowed attack you can't protect anyone. Release it soon, on your best-supported suspect, so your charm is available again. Don't release it on a counterclaimant of your own role, and don't die still holding it. If two protectors exist, avoid both stacking on one target and then both being unable to protect.
evidence: On Night 2 both Kitsunes swallowed attacks on Carol. On Night 3 Erin did nothing and Heidi used her stored attack on Erin, so neither could charm. Carol, the confirmed-looking Sheriff, died to the Katana and the SK. Erin died with her stored Katana attack unused.

tip: If there's nothing new to say, stop posting, or use the time to ask specific questions and assign checks. Repeating 'no nomination, waiting for the check' through every round wastes budget and gives the hidden killers cover for a whole Day.
evidence: On Day 2 every player posted some version of 'waiting for Carol's Day 3 check' for about 8 rounds. Nobody followed up on Dave's Not Evil read or on how the Katana target on Night 1 could have survived. Dave hid comfortably among them.

applies_to: Enforcer, Veteran, and any retaliation role
tip: Retaliation is simultaneous with the attack. My Strong Enforcer visit on Grace killed her, but the Serial Killer's kill on me still landed the same night. Retaliation only punishes the attacker; it doesn't save you. Use it when you can afford to trade, or pair it with a protector or a claim that draws the attacker's attention.

When a Yakuza is hanged while another Yakuza is alive, the Katana passes to the survivor immediately. Before voting to hang a Yakuza, count the Katana successor and plan a protection or a hang on that successor before the next Night. Here Carol inherited the Katana and killed Heidi the same night.

Don't let a trial turn into tit-for-tat. Grace nominated Bob within minutes of Bob's nomination of Heidi, and the town hanged Bob by a retaliation vote rather than on evidence. The hang was correct by luck, and the Village then lost its real Sheriff. Before a Guilty vote, ask who pushed the nomination and whether the nomination was based on a result.

Daytime private messages between two suspected teammates are a strong lead. The Bob-to-Carol PM was the clearest tell in the game, and the Village used it. Yakuza should avoid daytime PMs about nominations, and Village should always ask who PM'd whom.

Pushing an early nomination on the one player who contests your Sheriff claim, before any result exists, is a visible tell. It made Bob look like the Yakuza, and the trial that followed cost the team its holder. Hold pressure until you have a result to hide behind.

Never send a daytime private message to a teammate that states a vote or nomination plan. Every PM's existence is public, and Bob's 'Nominating Heidi now. Vote Yes.' PM to Carol was cited by the Village as proof of coordination and became the lead that got Bob hanged. Settle votes in night chat only.

Don't be the first to push a nomination against a player who just survived a Katana hit. Survivors are often real investigators or protected targets, and the push made the nominator the obvious suspect. A retaliation nomination (Grace on Bob, minutes later) then passed with 3 Yes. Let the Village nominate first, or push only with a mechanical reason.

A Sheriff cover claim invites a counterclaim from the real Sheriff, and two unverifiable Sheriff reads just split the Village. If your partner claims Vanilla, prefer a claim no real role can contradict, such as Vanilla or a role whose results are never public, and keep each claim's visit list fully consistent with the Katana holder's real visits.

After a Katana attack fails on a target, check whether a Medic protected it before repeating the target. Night 2's second attack on Heidi was stopped by Erin's Standard protection, and the failure revealed the holder's visit to the Village. Hitting the protector first would have removed the shield, and the Katana would then have landed.

Post exact night, target and result at dawn as soon as it exists, and name who visited you when attacked. Heidi's Katana-survival report, posted the same morning, was the most checkable evidence in the game. Results held back or announced vaguely look retrofitted and lose the vote.

Plan only in night chat. Bob's daytime PMs to Carol and Alice were visible to everyone, and Grace used the Bob-to-Carol PM as the main reason to build a trial against him. Keep daytime coordination out of PMs and let every teammate vote from public reasoning.

Don't be the one who pushes an early nomination against a Katana survivor before any result exists. Bob nominated Heidi on Day 3 with no evidence, which made him the obvious suspect when Grace countered. A Yakuza who wants a hang should let the Village nominate and vote, and only add a Yes at the last moment.

When the Katana target is a claimed Sheriff, check whether a Medic claim exists first. Heidi survived Night 2 because Erin's Standard protection landed on her. Hitting a claimed Medic or protector first, or choosing a target that has no protector, makes the Katana more reliable.

A Grunt with no night action has no visit-based cover, so a Katana holder with only a Vanilla claim is weak once a Katana hit is publicly visible. Keep the Katana with a teammate who has a real or plausible role action, or prepare a cover claim that explains the visit.

Serial Killers and Enforcers can both act at night on the same target, and the Enforcer's Strong Attack killed a Serial Killer who claimed Vanilla. A player who claims Vanilla and says nothing about night results may be a killer, so the Village should track unexplained deaths.

Standard protection does not stop a Serial Killer, whose attack is Strong. Against a known or likely SK, spend a token on Strong (protect the likely target), and self-protect with Strong (2 tokens) once claimed. Erin's free Standard protections did nothing against the SK, and she died to it on Night 2 unprotected.

An Enforcer visit with a Strong attack (1 token) on a player who attacks that night kills them. Alice did this to Grace on Night 3. Hold tokens for a Strong visit on the most likely killer rather than spending them on Basic visits that rarely fire.

When two players claim the same investigative role, look for the claim that a night result contradicts, and ask both for full visit lists before any nomination. Early nominations on unverifiable reads (Heidi's push on Bob, Bob's push on Heidi) mostly handed the Yakuza a trade of votes.

Before voting Guilty, check the trial's stated vote totals against the nomination and trial counts, and treat a private message between a nominator and a voter as a lead, not proof. Bob's PM to Carol and Grace's PM to Heidi were both visible and both pushed votes without a result behind them.

Don't announce tonight's protection target in public, and don't claim a protection plan before the night. I posted 'Night 2 I'll protect one player' and then the Serial Killer chose me as its target and killed me. Once a Strong killer is alive, Standard self-protection (1 token) doesn't stop it, so self-protect at Strong (2 tokens) or keep the tokens until a Strong attack is actually known to be coming.

A blind Standard guess on Night 1 spends nothing but gives no information. Use it on a player the Village is likely to need (a claimed investigator), and vary the choice, since the killers read public claims and protection habits.

Sheriff reads of Not Evil are weak evidence while a Serial Killer or Neutral is alive, because those roles read Not Evil. A Sheriff claim is only tested when its read is contradicted by a death, a visit, or a confirmed Katana or SK attack. Ask for each Sheriff's target and result first, then check which one the nightly deaths and visits contradict.

Watch who nominates a Katana survivor before any result exists. A Yakuza pushing a hang on the one player the Katana just failed to kill was a clear tell, and it was followed by a retaliatory nomination. Check each nomination's timing and who it helps before voting Yes.

A Katana survivor proves that the holder visited them that night. Lay out each player's visit list from the night results, then find the one visitor who fits. Post the visit lists, not just claims, so the town can cross-check them.

When two players claim the same investigative role, check each claim against visible facts: which deaths and Katana hits happened, who visited whom, and whether a protected survivor's hit is explained. A Katana survivor shows a Medic protected them, or the holder's target choice was mistaken. Don't nominate a Katana survivor on the basis of a push alone.

Hang the nominee whose claim is most contradicted by results, not whoever pushed the first nomination. Retaliatory nominations within minutes of each other are a signal of coordination, not evidence. Ask for each claimant's night results before any Guilty vote.

Do not PM teammates during the Day. Private messages are visible to everyone as a sender-recipient pair, and a Yakuza PM that reads like a vote instruction (for example, 'Nominating Heidi now. Vote Yes') becomes the town's main lead. Coordinate only in night chat.

Free Standard protection on a claimed investigator who is likely to be a Katana target can stop the hit. Protectors learn nothing, so do not announce the protected target in public, but do keep notes of whom you protected in case a survivor's report is later contested.

Post a claimant's night target and exact result promptly, before any vote, instead of holding it back. A result given late reads as retrofitted, and a public result that is contradicted by deaths or visits gives the town a clear, checkable lead.

applies_to: Serial Killer (Neutral) and other night killers
tip: Before a Strong attack on a player, consider whether they might visit you that night. A living Enforcer who visits you and sees you attack will strike back, so my Night 3 attack on Alice got me killed by her Enforcer retaliation. Hit targets whose visits you can rule out, or accept the retaliation risk.

Don't spend a kill on a claimed Medic or a random player on Night 1 if you can wait. My blind Night 1 kill and Night 2 kill on the Medic removed information but gave the Village two early deaths and a clear 'SK alive' signal, which made the Village hunt SKs as a group. Killing the Medic on Night 2 was reasonable, but kill the most dangerous visitor first, not the easiest claim.

As a Neutral, nominating a Yakuza-leaning player is fine, but do it when you can count the Yes votes. My Day 3 nomination of Bob passed, yet Bob's death left the Yakuza majority intact and I never gained a Village ally. Count which living players would vote with you before nominating.

Track whether the Yakuza still hold a majority. Once Yakuza and the Village are roughly balanced, a Neutral should press the Village to hang Yakuza or let the Yakuza and Village trade off, because a Neutral who is not alone never wins.

applies_to: Sheriff, Seer, and other alignment investigators
tip: A Katana holder reads Not Evil that night. The holder changes at dawn when a holder dies, so before checking anyone, confirm who holds the Katana tonight. My Night 3 check on Carol was wasted because she had just inherited the Katana.

A Katana attack on a claimed investigator who survives is strong evidence that the attacker is not a teammate. Yakuza repeatedly hitting the same claimant is a pattern to test, not a sign that the claimant is the lie.

When two players dispute the same role, the dispute can't be settled by results both fit. Make each claimant check a target whose alignment the other claim already contradicts, or compare overlapping results, rather than waiting for results that match either story.

Treat a nomination or trial pushed right after a counter-nomination as retaliation, not evidence. Check whether the nominator has a result behind the push before voting Guilty, because a Serial Killer or Yakuza can nominate on either side.
Night attacks resolve simultaneously, so attacking a Serial Killer who is attacking you still kills you too. Only trade when losing the role costs less than the threat it removes.

When two players claim the same investigator role and several killers are alive, hang one of them on the first Day. Don't wait for the next night's results. Each night the Yakuza and a Serial Killer can kill together, so a Day without a hanging can lose the game.
evidence: On Day 2 six players were alive, three of them killers (Bob, Carol, Grace). Bob and Heidi both claimed Sheriff, and all eight rounds were 'no nomination, wait for Night 2'. The Village hanged only one Yakuza (Bob, Day 3) before Night 3 wiped out the rest of the Village. A Day 2 hanging of Bob would have left Day 3 free to go after Carol.

tip: Spend free Standard protection on the contested investigator, but once you have claimed Medic in public, expect to be killed. Use a token to protect yourself, Strong if a Serial Killer is alive. An unprotected claimed Medic is an easy kill, and it leaves your ward open the next night.
evidence: On Night 2 Erin's free Standard protection stopped the Katana on Heidi. The same night Grace killed Erin specifically because she had claimed Medic, with both of Erin's tokens unspent. Without a Medic, Heidi died to the Katana on Night 3.

tip: An unspent Basic attack can't kill a Serial Killer, who has Standard Defense. Spend a token for Strong and visit the player most likely to be the Serial Killer, such as a late Vanilla claimant who was read Not Evil, on the night they are most likely to kill.
evidence: Alice paid 1 token to make her attack Strong and visited Grace on Night 3. Grace attacked, and Alice's attack killed her. Alice's free visits on Nights 1 and 2 (Dave, Heidi) did nothing.

tip: Don't nominate the player counterclaiming you unless you can count the Yes votes, and never send a teammate a daytime private message. A failed push plus a visible message gives the town a ready case and invites an immediate counter-nomination.
evidence: On Day 3 Bob nominated Heidi, the Katana survivor, and messaged Carol 'Vote Yes'. The nomination failed 2-3, and Grace at once named Bob's message to Carol and his push on Heidi as her reasons for nominating Bob. He was hanged 3-2.

tip: After a Yakuza is hanged, the Katana goes to a surviving teammate, who holds it that night and reads Not Evil. Don't spend a Sheriff check on the prime suspect that night. Rely on vote evidence (the Innocent votes beyond the nominee's own), or check someone else.
evidence: The 3-2 total on Bob meant one Innocent besides Bob himself, and Carol had openly said she was voting Innocent. Heidi checked Carol on Night 3 and got Not Evil only because Carol held the Katana. That check was wasted, and the Day 4 will Heidi planned would have cleared the last Yakuza.

tip: A Serial Killer needs to be the last one alive. When a claimed Enforcer is openly questioning you, skip your kill that night (an Enforcer only hits you if you attack) or make sure they can't reach you. Let the other killers thin the town.
evidence: On Day 3 Alice publicly asked Grace what she did on Night 2. On Night 3 Grace attacked Alice anyway, and Alice's Strong Enforcer attack killed her. If Grace had held her kill, she would have reached Day 4 alive with Alice and Carol.

tip: The vote right after a teammate is hanged is less dangerous for the next holder than it looks, because the Katana makes them read Not Evil that night. Use that night to kill the investigator who is chasing you.
evidence: Carol voted Innocent on Bob and was exposed. Holding the Katana, she read Not Evil to Heidi and killed her the same night, which secured the win.

tip: Standard protection does not stop a Strong attack such as the Serial Killer's. Before choosing a protection, check the attacker's level: a Serial Killer needs Strong Defense (1 token on others, 2 on yourself). Protecting a random player on Night 1 with Standard did nothing useful, and I died to the Serial Killer unprotected.

Don't spend the first protection on an arbitrary player with no information. Either hold tokens for the nights when a claimed investigator or the likeliest kill target appears, or protect yourself at Strong if a Serial Killer is in play.

Watch for two players who keep matching each other's votes, who keep exchanging private messages, and who both claim no night action. In this game the Yakuza pair did exactly that, and the Village only noticed after two Village players had already been hanged.

A repeated 'no rush, wait for results' stance with no result behind it can be the Village stalling for the killers. When results never arrive, a vote should be pushed on checkable facts (who died to which attack, who visited whom) rather than on a stall, and each side should be asked to defend a concrete claim.
Post a night result or protection outcome publicly as soon as it bears on a vote. Holding it back, or leaving it only in a last will, lets the killers use the silence against you.

applies_to: Trapper (and any protective or trap role)
tip: A trap only stops attacks on the trapped player, so pick the target by predicted victim, not by suspicion. The Katana and Serial Killer hit claimed investigators and anyone who posted information, not the player I suspected. Move the trap each night to whoever is most likely to be attacked, and don't spend a night on no action while a trap sits on a player who is never targeted.

When 3 to 5 players are alive, tally which players the Katana and Serial Killer hit each night and who has a private-message pair. Two players with repeated private messages, a shared nomination pattern, and matching early Guilty votes are a stronger lead than any single claim. Compare stated votes with the printed totals before any hang.

Count the parity before each vote. With two Yakuza left among three living players, a single execution of a Good player decides the game. Don't let a one-vote majority on a weak case (here, a Villager hanged on pressure) happen when the remaining players are a possible Yakuza pair.

Ask every player for a concrete night result before the first nomination, and note who answers vaguely. Vague answers from both Yakuza repeated 'no action' claims without checkable evidence, and that gave them cover for two Day votes.

A block on a Trapper stops trap placement but not the Katana. Yakuza can use a Pharmacist block to stop a trap placement while still killing the same player that night, so a claimed trap is only as safe as the nights the Yakuza can't block.

A role-block only stops the blocked player's own actions. It does not stop a Katana attack, a Serial Killer attack, or any other attack, and blocking a claimed Sheriff does not protect the Sheriff. Spend a block on the player who would deliver the threat: the Medic or Trapper if they are about to protect or trap, or the attacking role's holder if it is a non-Yakuza killer. Blocking a target that is about to die anyway wastes the block.

Daytime private messages between two living teammates are visible to everyone, and the table reads them as the main evidence of coordination. Once you are down to two Yakuza, keep your coordination to night chat and to public statements that match your claims. If you must PM, keep it to one neutral line that a Village player could not use as a lead.

When 3 players are alive and the Yakuza are two, the Village player will often nominate whoever has pushed against the group. Check the nomination thresholds early: with 3 alive, 2 Yes votes pass a nomination, so a single Village ally plus one Yakuza can hang the last Village player. Plan which vote needs to flip before the Day begins.

Carol's early nomination of Grace worked because it was tied to a visible, checkable gap (no night action or result given for several Days) and every stated vote matched the printed totals. A nomination built on a specific unanswered question is more persuasive than one built on general suspicion or 'no rush' pressure.

Confirm the Katana holder and target in night chat every night with both votes matching. Both kills succeeded only because both votes were cast the same way each night, so one missing vote cancels the kill entirely.

Stalling works for the Yakuza. Village 'no rush' discussion let the Katana kill Frank, Heidi and Bob with no nomination until Day 3. Keep the discussion going, and use the Village's own reluctance to act as cover while kills land.

Daytime private messages between the two Yakuza became the Village's main lead. Erin and Grace both cited the Dave-Carol PMs in their defenses. Keep teammate contact in night chat, and if you must PM by day, keep it to short, innocuous content.

With two Yakuza and one Village left, a Yakuza-backed nomination of the Village player wins outright. Once the Village is down to a single good voter, push for that nomination and make sure both Yakuza vote Guilty so the count is 2 of 3.

Matching public Guilty votes looked coordinated. Votes that line up with the teammate's publicly stated vote and the same nominator invite comparison. Vary timing or wording, and avoid pre-announcing each vote in public.

Don't let 'no rush' stall the whole Day. Three Katana or Serial Killer kills went unanswered because no one nominated. Set a deadline, e.g. nominate on Day 2 with the weakest checkable case, rather than waiting for a perfect result that the Yakuza can prevent by never posting one.

Katana kills prove a living Yakuza holder. When the alive count is small, a Yakuza holder must be among the survivors. Work through who could have held the Katana each night, and use that to decide which survivor to vote on.

A player who stays silent for days, pushes 'no rush' and 'wait for checkable info', then gives a late claim with no result, and asks others to vote Innocent in private, is a concrete lead. Don't treat 'no rush' as neutral when it comes with private pressure. Grace was the Serial Killer.

Don't let a 'wait for results' consensus run longer than one Day when nobody has checkable info. Set a deadline and nominate the most unexplained player. Each waiting Day gave the Yakuza a free night, and it cost the Village two Day-3/4 votes.

Private message counts between pairs are public. Repeated PMs between two players, plus public lines like 'let's keep our votes consistent so the totals don't look off', are coordination evidence. Weigh them above general warnings against reading PM trails.

Two Yakuza who always vote identically and both claim no-action Villager look like a pair. Vary your stated votes on low-stakes nominations, keep day PMs free of vote-matching language, and make at least one of your claims sound like a role that explains your silence.

Don't vote for a hang because of an argument about silence or 'no rush' stances. If a nominee's only offense is a stance everyone shared, the nomination is a rush. Require the nominator to name a concrete reason, and check whether the nominator and the Guilty voters share a private-message channel.

When two suspects PM each other and then vote identically, record their stated votes against the printed totals and ask each one to explain the PM in a sentence before the vote. Matching votes plus unexplained PMs is a lead worth checking. Don't hang on that alone, but don't ignore it either.

With one charm and no information, charm the player whose death would hurt the Village most, such as a claimed investigator, rather than a random seat. The charm only helps if the Katana or a killer picks that same target, so a claimed investigator is the most likely high-value target.

Once a claimed Sheriff is killed, the village loses its only mechanical check. Shift to tracking which deaths and visits are unexplained, and to asking who each surviving claimant could have visited. Vanilla claims cannot be checked, so count them as unverified.
Keep all planning in night chat. Day PMs between two teammates are public in the ledger, and the Village used them here as the main lead against the pair.

applies_to: Neutral killers and any player with no checkable role
tip: Silence is the easiest way to get nominated. Take a clear, consistent public stance early (a concrete role claim or a stated reason to suspect someone) and answer direct questions in the first round they're asked. Late, vague 'no rush' answers made me the nominee.

A nomination with no result behind it is a vote for a coin flip. Before voting Yes, ask the nominator for one checkable fact; if they have none and a pair of players is privately coordinating, treat that pair as the most likely Yakuza, not the silent player.

Two Yakuza who PM each other all game become the town's main lead. Keep teammate contact to night chat and use public messages for the rest. Carol and Dave's Day 2 to 4 PMs were quoted against them by Erin and Grace at every turn.

Two independent kills on the same target waste a night. Heidi died to both my attack and the Katana. Without shared information, pick targets the Katana is unlikely to hit, and read each night's death causes to avoid overlap.

Ask who gains from a hang. When the last three alive are two coordinated voters and one target, the coordinated pair's votes decide the trial. Before any trial, state which votes you can actually verify and which you are only inferring.

Don't announce when or whom your night check will hit, even as a vague 'my check happens tonight'. Yakuza read it, role-blocked me that night and killed me with the Katana. Post the result after it resolves, and keep the next target private.

When two killers are active and nothing is verifiable, stop the 'no rush' stalemate by Day 2 or 3. Each Day spent waiting gave the Yakuza another free night. Nominate the most suspicious player on whatever evidence exists, and make sure the vote is seen as a real attempt to find the killers.

Watch the private-message ledger for pairs. Two alive players messaging each other every Day, especially once one of them is a likely Katana holder, is a lead. Ask them directly what the PMs were about, and compare their answers against each other's.

Daytime PMs between teammates are public as a count, and the Village used Carol and Dave's PM pair as its main lead. Keep day coordination to a minimum, and make sure your public votes are consistent with what you say publicly, so the totals don't look off.

Don't vote Guilty on a nominee because a nomination came from a player who pushed the nomination quickly. Before a trial, ask the nominator for one concrete reason. Carol's nominations of Grace and then Erin came with no result behind them, and the Village hanged two Villagers on that pattern.

Count factions before every hang late in the game. Once the Yakuza could reach a majority after one more night kill, a hang that doesn't remove a Yakuza loses the game, even if the person hanged is the Serial Killer. In that spot, put your vote on your best Yakuza lead, even a weak one, and not on a neutral killer.
evidence: Day 3, 5 alive (Carol and Dave Yakuza, Grace the Serial Killer, Bob and Erin Village). Bob voted Guilty on Grace. That left the Yakuza at 2 of 4, the night kill on Bob made it 2 of 3, and Erin was hanged on Day 4. Bob, Erin and Grace had exactly the 3 votes needed to hang Dave.

tip: Link visible private-message trails to what happens next. If A messages B during the Day and the claimed investigator dies to the Katana that night, A and B are a strong Yakuza pair. Push for a real answer, and nominate one of them if you don't get one, instead of moving on.
evidence: On Day 2 Dave messaged Carol, and the hidden text was 'considering the Katana on Heidi tonight'. Four players asked about it, accepted 'a Night 2 question', and nobody nominated. Heidi died to the Katana that night, and the pair kept messaging on Days 3 and 4.

tip: Never plan kills in daytime private messages to a teammate. Everyone can see that a message was sent, and an Eavesdropper or Wiretap can read it. Use night chat, and keep daytime messages to teammates rare and dull.
evidence: Dave's Day 2 message to Carol about killing Heidi drew public questions from four players. On Days 3 and 4, Grace and Erin used the Carol–Dave messages as their main argument. The Yakuza only got away with it because the Village was passive.

tip: When a third-party killer is likely among the quiet players, nominate the one with the weakest claim and let Village voters supply the deciding vote. Removing the Serial Killer cuts both the threat to you and the voters you need to outnumber.
evidence: Carol nominated Grace for her late claim and her 'no rush' stance. Bob voted Yes and Guilty, Grace (the Serial Killer) was hanged, and the Yakuza were left with a winning count.

tip: Don't use your kill on a claimed Sheriff. A Sheriff reads you as Not Evil, and the Yakuza will probably kill a claimed investigator anyway. Kill the players who can hurt you or who will vote with the Yakuza, so the two Evil sides wear each other down. Also give a plausible claim early; staying silent for two Days and then claiming Vanilla makes you the obvious nominee.
evidence: On Night 2 Grace and the Katana both killed Heidi, so one kill was wasted. Grace claimed Vanilla only on Day 3 after pressure, and was nominated and hanged that same Day.

tip: Don't claim early with a result that tells the Village nothing (like 'Not Evil' on someone already dead). The claim only makes you a target for every killer and gains nothing. Hold the claim until you have an Evil result or a vote depends on you, especially after the Medic has died.
evidence: Heidi claimed Sheriff on Day 2 with 'Alice Not Evil'. Alice, the Medic, was already dead, so nobody could protect Heidi. The Yakuza blocked her and both killers attacked her on Night 2, so her check on Grace never happened.

tip: Don't publicly name where your trap is, and don't skip nights. A trap only arms the night after you place it, so move it ahead of time to the player most likely to be attacked next (a claimed investigator, a confirmed townie). A trap that has never fired on a player in a hidden spot is a quiet threat. A trap you've named tells the killers exactly where not to strike.
evidence: Bob left his trap on Carol (a Yakuza, who her own team would never attack), did nothing on Nights 2 and 3, and on Day 3 announced 'trap on Carol'. The Yakuza then attacked Bob freely, and Carol blocked him for good measure.

tip: Day 2 comes after Night 1 only, so nobody has 'Night 2 results' yet. Repeating 'no rush, post results' every round uses up the Day and the speaking budget for nothing. Use early rounds to ask direct questions, point out leads (like visible private messages) and test them with a nomination.
evidence: Day 2 went through about seven rounds of nearly identical 'waiting for Heidi's N2 result' messages from all six players. Erin and Heidi had to correct the confusion twice, and the Day ended with no nomination even though there was a live lead.

tip: When two players claim the same exclusive role and only one claim can be tested, do not hang on the untestable one. Ask for a shared test first, such as a trap on a player who will certainly be attacked, or a result the other side can check. Carol's Day 3 nomination passed on claims and pushes alone, with no mechanical result.

Before a hang, make every 'leaning Guilty' voter state a checkable reason. Three Guilty votes out of five were enough to execute me, and the leaners gave no mechanical basis. Count who pushed the nomination first and who nominated right after them.
Do not coordinate by private message in the day. Carol and Dave's repeated DMs were visible to everyone and became the town's main lead. Keep all planning in night chat and act publicly as strangers.

applies_to: Kitsune and other holders of a delayed or held attack
tip: Do not announce your release or charm target publicly before it resolves. Grace named Bob, then was killed by the Katana and Serial Killer the same night, so the Yakuza saw her plan and removed her. Post the result at dawn, and keep the target private until then.

When a Serial Killer and a Katana are both alive, a death labelled Katana plus SK on one player means the Yakuza and the SK are separate. Track which players are alive and which roles could still be in the game, so that every claim is checked against the remaining role count.

Night actions resolve simultaneously, so a target who dies that same night was still a legal target and the action still happened. Don't describe a trap or action on a player as 'placed after they died' unless the night actually started after their death. I made that false claim as Bob and it cost me credibility when Alice contested it.

Don't spend a trap on a player who is already a likely Katana victim or who has no live role. My N1 trap went on Erin, who died that night, so it never stopped anything. Put the trap on the player most likely to be attacked next, and say so only after the trap is set.

A Serial Killer can survive by posing as a Vanilla Villager, pushing for quiet waits, and nominating through a partner. Heidi did this and was the last one alive. Quiet 'no nomination yet' posts from a claimed Vanilla who is never checked are a cover, not evidence of innocence.

Private-message pairs that coordinate 'no nominations' and then produce a nomination are a strong lead. Carol and Dave DMed each other repeatedly, then one nominated and the other pushed the same trial. Ask both players about the DM content early, and treat a coordinated pair as a suspicion cluster rather than two independent voices.

Publicly announcing a release target or a live-trap destination gives the killers a free target. Grace named Bob publicly before her release, and I announced a 'live player' trap move. Keep the target private until the result is posted, or post it only after the night resolves.

Before choosing a Katana target, check its Defense. A Standard-Defense role such as the Serial Killer can't be killed by a Standard Katana. If a Serial Killer is alive, the Katana can't remove it, so the Yakuza must win by votes or accept that the SK may win alone. Plan the endgame around that.

Don't send repeated private messages to a teammate during the Day, and don't keep the same 'wait, no nomination' line. Private messages are visible as to who sent them to whom, and the town read our Carol-Dave DMs as the main lead against us. Coordinate only in night chat.

When a Katana-holding Yakuza is the only Yakuza left, count the votes needed for a conviction. With 2 players alive, a nomination needs 2 Yes and a hanging needs 2 Guilty, so one hostile vote from the SK blocks everything. Remove the non-Yakuza threat earlier, while you still have a majority.

A dead player's will and claims can conflict, but a Trapper claim that was placed on a dead target can't be tested. Check whether a trap was live on the night it was used before treating it as evidence for or against a claim.
Confirm the target each night with every living teammate. The Katana kills worked every night here because both votes matched, and a missing vote would have cancelled them.

Don't send teammates private messages during the Day. Every PM's existence is public, and two PMs between the same pair of Village-suspected players became the main lead against us. Keep all coordination in the night chat.

Vary wording and timing of Day positions. Carol and I posted near-identical 'no nomination until N2 results' lines, and the Village noticed the match. Two players pushing the same line at the same time reads as a team.

Don't be the first to push a nomination before any mechanical result exists. Dave pushing Alice's trial on Day 3 with no checkable evidence was predictable and drew a targeted rebuttal. A Grunt with no night info should follow the Village's momentum or stay quiet, and let a claimed role carry the push.

A Yakuza Grunt holding no role can still matter by voting. Confirm the holder and target each night, and when the holder's kill fails or a teammate is exposed, reassess the holder's safety at once. Kill any claimed role whose result would narrow you, such as the Kitsune with a live held attack.

Track which kills are Katana-only versus Serial Killer. A Standard Katana can't kill a Standard Serial Killer, so Yakuza should not waste the Katana on an SK-immune target. Use that to infer the SK's identity from who survives Yakuza attacks.

Post every investigation result as soon as it is known, and do it before the Day in which it matters. A result held in a will dies with you: I was killed on Night 1 with an unposted result, so the town learned nothing from my Bob check.

Do not message each other privately during the Day. Private messages are visible as to who sent them to whom. Carol and Dave's repeated Day 2 and Day 3 DMs drew suspicion from the whole table and made them the main leads. Keep all coordination in the Yakuza night chat.

When two players claim the same role and one claim contradicts a dead player's will, test the claim with a checkable mechanic before voting. Here the town hanged Alice on a 3-2 vote while the Serial Killer who was really alive went untested. Check which claims predict an observable event (a trap going off, a Katana or SK death) and wait for it.
