A Katana attack (Standard) can never kill a Serial Killer (Standard Defense), so the Yakuza should not plan a Katana kill on a suspected SK. Use the Katana on Village players and expect the SK to be a separate threat that only the Village can remove.

A claimed Kitsune's release announced publicly (target named in advance) gives the Yakuza a free target list and also tells the SK who to hit. Name release or charm targets only after the result is known, or give the Village one clear test.

Two players who wait in lockstep, repeat the same 'no nomination until results' line, and send each other private messages are a real lead. Ask for the DM contents early and vote on it, rather than letting the pattern run for two Days while the Katana picks them off.

When a Trapper claim is disputed, a dead player's will that names a specific trap is direct evidence. Also check which claims a trap can actually test: a trap on a player who is never attacked proves nothing, so push for a test or a different check instead of relying on it.

Track which roles any Standard-defense kill can reach. A Strong attack that a player survives, with no Medic claimed, points to a Serial Killer or a Kitsune release. Use that to narrow the SK's suspects, because the Katana cannot kill an SK (Standard vs Standard).

Agree on a nomination threshold and a timeline early (for example, nominate by Day 3 if no mechanical result arrives). Waiting for results that never come lets the Yakuza and SK pick off power roles and vanilla players in turn.
Repeated 'no nomination from me' messages spend budget without adding information. Spend budget on specific checkable questions, and save it for trial turns.

applies_to: Kitsune (and any holder of a stored attack)
tip: Don't release a held attack on a target you've only judged from a contradiction in someone's claim. Hold it until a mechanical result (a visit, a death cause, or a Yakuza-only fact) points at a specific Yakuza. Also, don't announce the release target publicly before the night: the Yakuza read it and killed you that same night.

When one claimant's story is contradicted by a dead player's will, check whether the will could itself be a lie or a forgery before treating it as settled. In this game both Trappers were real, and the wrong one was executed or killed on the strength of a single document.

Watch for pairs who push the same wait-or-nominate line and send each other private messages. That coordination was the clearest Yakuza tell, and it was visible to everyone. Vote against the pair early instead of letting them steer the trial.
With two players alive, a nomination needs both votes to pass, so a Neutral killer who stays unnominated can win by parity. Count the endgame votes before the number drops to 3.

applies_to: Serial Killer and other Standard-Defense Neutrals
tip: Standard Defense blocks the Katana (a Standard attack must beat Defense). A Serial Killer can only be stopped by a Strong attack, a Medic's Strong protection, or a trap, so the Yakuza's main weapon cannot reach you. Plan to outlast the Yakuza, then remove the last Village or Yakuza player yourself.

Each night, check which living player could threaten you (a Katana holder, a Kitsune charm, a trap). Killing the most dangerous claimed power role early kept the threat small. A Standard Attack from a Kitsune release or a Strong attack from a Medic is what really threatens you.

Do not let teammates' private messages in the Day become a visible pattern. Two players who privately DM each other and both push 'wait for results' look like a bloc. Keep Day coordination minimal and plan kills in night chat.

When only two players remain, a nomination needs both votes and a conviction needs both Guilty votes, so the Day stalls. A Neutral killer or Yakuza who stays alive with one opponent wins by killing at night. The Village must finish the Yakuza or the killer while three or more are alive.

Hanging a Village Trapper on a contradicted claim (not a mechanical result) cost the Village a power role and a vote while the Katana and Serial Killer stayed alive. Before hanging, list which living players could still be hidden killers and whether each death fits a Katana or Serial Killer attack.

Two players claiming the same role is not a contradiction unless the role is unique (only the Smuggler and the Vulture are). Before acting on a 'one of them is lying' story, check whether both claims fit the mechanics. Only kill or hang one side once there is an independent mechanical break, such as an Evil read, an impossible visit or a result that can't be right.
evidence: Alice and Bob were both real Trappers. On Day 2 the whole table repeated 'only one can be the Trapper', and Alice wrongly called Bob's Erin trap impossible. Grace released her held attack on Bob and killed a Villager. On Day 3 the Yakuza turned Bob's will against Alice, and she was hanged.

applies_to: Village power roles (Kitsune, Vigilante, Trapper, Medic)
tip: Don't publicly announce a stored attack, a planned target or your night plans just because other players demand it. Treat repeated 'name your target publicly' demands as a warning sign, since evil players benefit most from that information. Claim a power role only when it settles a vote.
evidence: Carol, Dave and Heidi (two Yakuza and the SK) all pressed Grace to name her release target. She claimed Kitsune and named Bob. On Night 2 the Katana and the SK both chose Grace, and the SK said its reason was her Kitsune claim.

tip: A swallowed attack is the Village's only kill, and it costs you your charm until you release it. Fire it only on a solid mechanical lead. While the evidence is thin, keep charming likely targets: the charm saved a life on Night 1, but the release killed a Villager on Night 2.
evidence: Grace's Night 1 charm on Alice saved her from the SK. On Night 2 she spent the stored attack on Bob over a claim conflict that wasn't real, so she had no charm that night and died herself.

tip: A trap arms only from the night after you place it. Moving it to someone in danger tonight gives them no protection tonight and disarms the trap you already had. Keep an armed, publicly known trap where it is, because it keeps deterring attacks. Don't announce that you've moved it, since that tells the killers its old target is open.
evidence: Alice's trap on Frank was armed on Night 2 and kept the Yakuza and the SK away from him. She moved it to Grace, where it wasn't armed in time, and on Day 3 she said publicly that it had moved. On Night 3 the Katana killed Frank. Had the trap stayed, it would have stopped Carol's attack and hit her with a Strong Attack.

tip: When a cause of death shows a Serial Killer or Arsonist alive, remember the Standard Katana can't kill their Standard Defense. You must remove them with a hang, while the Village still has enough votes to help. Hanging Villagers first leaves you in a final duel you can't win.
evidence: On Day 3 the Yakuza knew the SK was Frank or Heidi, yet they hanged Alice. Carol pointed out the SK's immunity only on Night 3. Heidi then killed Dave and Carol, and Carol's Night 4 Katana bounced off her.

tip: Avoid claiming early, then claim Vanilla. Speak as a cautious townie but vote however best thins the field, since ballots are secret. At night, kill Yakuza or players with protection, because the Katana can't hurt you, and let the Village and the Yakuza trade kills.
evidence: Heidi held off claiming until late on Day 2. On Day 3 she said she was 'leaning Innocent' on Alice but cast the deciding Guilty vote. She then shot Dave and Carol and won alone.

tip: Once a Serial Killer is shown to be alive and the Village is outnumbered, focus Day votes on the most suspicious Vanilla claimant who claimed late. Yakuza can sometimes be persuaded to help hang a killer they can't kill, and that's a vote you can win.
evidence: Grace's charm proved an SK was alive and that Alice wasn't it. Heidi refused to claim for most of Day 2. On Day 3 no one pushed Heidi, and the Yakuza and the SK steered the vote onto Alice.

tip: Once a player claims Oracle (or any exact-role checker), make them the top kill priority. One Oracle guess can disprove any fake claim, and Vanilla Villager is the cheapest guess there is. Leaving the Oracle alive into the endgame turns every cover claim into a one-night test.

Don't leave a blocker claimant alive on the theory that the town will hang them as the SK. If that blocker is real, they will keep blocking your Katana holder. In the endgame, a block on the holder followed by a quiet night is near-proof against them. Kill or discredit blockers early.

Before you claim a cover role, learn its exact result text. Carol said 'a PA isn't told', which was false, and the forged will repeated the same false mechanics argument. Real players corrected both from the rules, and that pointed suspicion back at us. Never build a case on a mechanics claim you haven't checked against the rules.

Spend Counts on questions that decide a live dispute, such as counting a role that two players both claim, to learn whether one of them is fake. Don't spend them on things you can already infer, like whether an SK exists. A wasted token is gone for the endgame, when one exact-role fact could flip a vote.

If a player's results read like an Enforcer's ('visited X, X made no attack'), the Katana holder becomes their target, and an Enforcer kill exposes whoever made the attack. Keep the holder away from players the suspected Enforcer is likely to visit, or block the Enforcer every night until they're dead.

applies_to: Enforcer (and any role with a distinctive result format)
tip: Hiding your exact role is pointless if you describe your result in your role's own terms. 'Visited X, X made no attack' told the Yakuza I was the Enforcer, and their blocker took me out the next night. If you hold your role, either give no result at all or phrase it as a plain visit.

Pay for the two-target visit on the night the Katana is most likely to move. That night it is most likely to pass to a fake-claim blocker or whoever the Sheriff is about to check, because the holder reads clean. Two plausible Yakuza covers the move. A Strong double on Dave and Carol killed the Katana holder outright.

applies_to: Village with both a role-blocker and a reactive killer (Enforcer, Veteran)
tip: A role-blocker on your top killer suspect cancels an Enforcer visit to the same player, because a blocked player makes no attack and so triggers nothing. Agree in public that the blocker and the Enforcer will cover different suspects, or the Enforcer's last token can be wasted.

Surviving a Katana hit does not clear anyone of being the Serial Killer, whose Standard Defense stops the Standard Katana anyway. A Medic who protects someone and later lists them as an elimination candidate isn't contradicting herself either. Check the mechanics before hanging a confirmed-looking protector for 'inconsistency'.

When an Oracle or other exact checker offers to verify a claimant tonight for free, compare that with the cost of a wrong hang at 7 alive. Unless the numbers are critical, a one-night delay is usually worth it. Here the town hanged the real Medic instead of waiting one night for the Oracle.

Don't move the Katana to a teammate with no Defense when a suspected Enforcer is alive and has reason to visit them, for example a player that teammate publicly blocked. Any Enforcer attack kills a Defense-None holder, even a Basic one. Keep the Katana with the player the Enforcer is least likely to visit, or block the Enforcer on the night you move it.

Once a real holder of your fake claim appears (a duplicate Party Animal, say), assume an Oracle or Profiler will guess you as that role. Have a fallback ready. Better still, choose a cover role that is less likely to be in the game, or one whose checkable outputs you can fully fake. Duplicate claims draw exact-role guesses.

Before you speak, reread the exact feedback your claimed role would get (for example, R9: blockers are told whether the block failed on immunity). One wrong statement about what your role learns, like 'a PA isn't told anything', gets quoted for the rest of the game, even if you correct it.

Kill a confirmed or likely real role-blocker (Party Animal) early. It can block your last Katana holder in the endgame and turn a quiet night into proof. Don't leave it alive just to frame it as the SK suspect for later.

When you post your block target publicly, the blocked player learns who to visit next. Don't announce blocks on an unclaimed killing role, such as a suspected Enforcer, unless that teammate will avoid holding the Katana.

Before claiming a cover role, check the rules for exactly what that role is told each night (for example, any role-blocker is told whether its block failed because of immunity). Repeat it word for word. One wrong mechanics line ('a PA isn't told') led an Oracle to guess that exact role on you, and once that came back WRONG the claim was dead.

A forged will shouldn't make arguable mechanics claims or echo a teammate's known slip. Copy the victim's public claims and add only a vague lean. If the forged will repeats a false rule a teammate already said, people will see it as Yakuza-written and it backs up the player it accuses.

Once a player is clearly an Enforcer (they say things like 'visited X, X made no attack'), block or kill them every night before you move the Katana to someone suspected. A Strong double visit on two suspects will kill whichever one made the attack. Moving the Katana to dodge a Sheriff check doesn't help if the Enforcer is visiting the new holder.

A claimed Oracle (or any exact-role guesser) is the biggest threat to fake claims, Vanilla included: one guess of your claimed role exposes you. Make them the Katana target soon after they claim, ahead of protectors whose information is already public.

Frame the player the Sheriff has been publicly asked to check, or one you want hanged. With a single Sheriff (confirm it with a Talent Agent count), random frames do nothing. Use the Day talk to predict the Sheriff's target.

Don't hold back your own category while pressing everyone else to claim. By Day 3 the town counts who is still unclaimed, and the last holdout becomes the default hang target. Give a category on Day 2 (for example 'protective, no results') and the exact role only when asked. It costs almost nothing and keeps you off the chopping block.

In a trial defense, never name as a suspect someone your own night actions show you trusted (for example a player you just spent a token protecting). Opponents will call it a self-contradiction and the vote swings. Name one coherent suspect, back it with a mechanical case, and offer a cheap verification (an Oracle guess or a Sheriff check).

Rule players out of the SK with block confirmations: a player who was confirmed role-blocked on a night the SK killed can't be the SK. Build the list early, and treat a target who survived a Katana hit and was confirmed by a protector (Kitsune) as cleared too, before you present the leftover candidates.

A free Standard protection never stops a Serial Killer's Strong attack. If the SK is clearly picking off claimed investigators, a Standard guard on them is wasted against the SK and only stops the Katana. Spend a token for Strong on the most exposed investigator, or accept that you are guarding against the Katana only.

An Oracle guessing the roles a Yakuza is likely to fake (Party Animal, Vanilla Villager) is a cheap, decisive way to break cover claims. Suggest these guesses to the Oracle early, especially for doubled claims and Vanilla claims.

Holding back your exact role doesn't hide you if your wording gives it away. I said my result on Grace was 'consistent with her Vanilla claim', and the Yakuza read that as a Sheriff and sent the Katana at me that night. If you hold a claim, give no result at all or give it without any alignment wording.

When the town publicly suggests whom you should check, the Yakuza can hand that player the Katana so they read clean (Carol on N3). Check someone nobody suggested aloud, and note who asked for a check on a player who then came back clean.

A Sheriff can never find the Serial Killer, and with one Yakuza left the Katana holder always reads Not Evil, so late checks are almost worthless. Use checks while several Yakuza are alive. Find the SK by working out who could not have made each kill (block confirmations, who was attacked) and by exact-role checks.

When working out who could have made the kills leaves two SK suspects and someone offers a free exact-role check (for example an Oracle guess), don't lead a hang based on behaviour such as 'the players she pressed got targeted'. That kind of lean hanged our Medic.

At 4 alive, with a claimed blocker who says they blocked someone and no deaths, ask what each team would have done. A Yakuza pair would have killed and then won the 3-player vote, and an unblocked lone holder had a kill available. So a quiet night points to the blocked player.

Once an Oracle (or any exact-role checker) claims, make them your top kill target. A Sheriff can never catch you because you read Not Evil, but once elimination narrows the suspects to two or three players, an Oracle needs only one guess. Killing an already-exposed Tracker claimant instead leaves that threat alive.

Don't spend kills on players with duplicate or suspicious claims, such as a second Tracker whose result neatly matches a blocker. They are often Yakuza. Killing them removes the faction that keeps killing Village for you and speeds up the town's endgame. Go for confirmed or cross-checked Village power roles instead.

Keep track of which players are 'cleared' by role-block confirmations. The town will rule out anyone who was blocked on a night the SK killed. If you're one of the few players left over, kill or discredit the blocker whose confirmations are doing the clearing (here, the Party Animal) before the list narrows to you.

When a claimed Enforcer with a Strong token publicly leans on you, skip your kill that night. An Enforcer's Strong Attack beats your Standard Defense, but only if you attacked. A skipped night can also make a freshly hanged suspect look like the SK.

Last-minute deal PMs to suspected Yakuza rarely flip a trial at 5 alive. Everyone can see who you sent PMs to, and the Yakuza can't safely vote against a confirmed result. Build an implicit truce earlier by leaving likely Yakuza alive, not by offering one on trial.

Before each night, write your target into your will (e.g. 'N2: tracking Dave because of the duplicate Tracker claim'). If you die that night your result never reaches the will, but the target at least points the town at your suspect and lets a living player's claim be checked against it.

applies_to: Village investigators facing a duplicate claim
tip: You can counterclaim a suspicious duplicate without a full public hard-claim. Say 'I'm also that role' only if you have a result to post. Otherwise hint at a contradiction and keep the exact role in your will. A Tracker with no result who claims on Day 2 is a free kill for the Serial Killer, since only his Strong Attack ignores the Medic.

When a Tracker or Lookout claimant's 'result' would fit any target (e.g. 'X visited no one' backed up by a blocker's claim), treat the matching pair as possibly coordinated. Track or check one of them, but keep track of which cross-checks rest on a single unverifiable claimant.

An Oracle's WRONG on a confirmed blocker's claimed Village role (or an Enforcer kill) is hard mechanical proof. Hang on those results, not on how long someone waited to claim. In this game the town hanged the real Medic on a 'held her claim too long' read while the SK was still alive.

Use blocker notification wording as a tell: a real Party Animal or Pharmacist is told only whether the block failed because of immunity. A claimant who says 'a PA isn't told anything' doesn't know the mechanics, and that slip hinted at the fake PA here.

Guess the role a suspicious player has claimed, especially a doubled claim (two Party Animals) or a Vanilla Villager claim. A WRONG proves the claim is a lie, and that is the best kind of mechanical result. A guess on an unclaimed player is a 1-in-many shot that usually tells you nothing.

Once block confirmations and deaths have narrowed the hidden killer to 2-3 players, guess 'Serial Killer' (or the killing role) on the most likely one. A RIGHT settles the next hang. Put each result in your will that same Day, in case you die before you can post it.

Before you reveal a result that tests other players' claims, ask each of them to post their exact target and result separately first, so nobody can fit their answer to yours. It flushed out Carol's 'a PA isn't told' slip and made later results believable.

When a player under threat offers a free mechanical test (for example 'Oracle, guess Medic on me tonight') and the case against them is only a lean, give real weight to the test. Hanging the real Medic on a 'contradiction' argument cost us a protector. Also check which players are pushing the hang: Alice (Yakuza) and Grace (SK) led that one.

In a 4-player endgame with one Yakuza left, a night with no kill points to a blocked holder. A Yakuza pair would always kill at 4. Only a lone Yakuza blocker has any reason to skip a kill, so cross-check the blocker's earlier blocks against outside confirmations.

When you report a block, quote the moderator's wording exactly ("did not fail because of immunity"). I said my block "landed". The Yakuza turned that into a 'no blocker is told that' attack, and it ended up in a forged will and in Erin's will. A wording slip in a claim gets used against you.

In the endgame, keep blocking your top suspect for the killing role. If you block one suspect and that night has no kill, the quiet night works as a mechanical result. My N4 block on Grace backed up the Oracle's SK result, and my N5 block on Alice made the case that hanged the last Yakuza. Write the block target in your will before dawn so the result can't look made up afterwards.

Early on, block a player who is likely to confirm it publicly and believably, such as an investigator who claims. A block that a trusted player confirms (Ivan on N2) is the only way to tell you apart from a Yakuza Pharmacist making the same claim, and it decided the later PA vs fake-PA contest.

A dead player's will can be forged by a Fabricator. If a will repeats an argument a proven Yakuza made, or leans on one player for a mechanics claim that's false, treat the will as suspect, not as the victim's real read.

When two people claim the same unique-function role, wait for a third party's exact-role check or confirmed blocks before you choose between them. Avoid pressing hard with leans until then. An Oracle 'WRONG' on one claimant settles it, so suggest that guess quietly instead of making the guessers public.

You can be killed on Night 1 before you get any information, and then all your tokens are wasted. If the Village side has no protection plan, a 1-token Basic shot on N1 at a random non-claimant costs little. Otherwise, at least make sure your will explains the plan for your tokens, since dead Vigilantes leave nothing behind.

A Party Animal who blocks the top Katana-holder suspect every night turns 'no Katana kill' into evidence. Combine that quiet night with an Oracle WRONG on the suspect's claimed role, and you have a convictable endgame case even when only one Yakuza is left and Sheriff checks show nothing.

An Enforcer who visits two players and kills one proves that player made an attack that night. Once a fake claimant dies to the Enforcer, treat them as that night's Katana holder. Their 'Not Evil' Sheriff read that night is then expected, not exculpatory.

Holding your claim, including the category, through Day 3 while pressing others to claim makes you the default hang target later. Claim Medic early, as soon as a hidden power role's claim can't be checked, or you end up hanged in place of the SK.

When a lone Yakuza holder faces a confirmed blocker, blocking the holder every night forces quiet nights that convict them. Argue early that the blocker is fake, or get the blocker killed while teammates still exist, instead of waiting until a 4-player endgame.

Your pre-Night-1 will may be all you ever contribute. Fill it with what you'll do and why, e.g. 'N1: watching X; if I die, X's visitors matter', and avoid 'no results yet'. An N1 death with an empty will gives the Village nothing.

Duplicate claims of a role that has an action (two Party Animals, two Trackers) are the best thing to spend exact-role checks on. An Oracle guessing the claimed role on one claimant settles it in one night. This game, 'Carol = Party Animal: WRONG' exposed the Pharmacist.

Rule out SK candidates using block confirmations from both sides: if a player was role-blocked on a night the SK still killed, they can't be the SK. Before trusting the list, check that each confirmation came from a different person, because a Yakuza pair can confirm each other's fake blocks.

If you hold back even your role type while pushing others to claim, you'll be the prime hang target once the investigators die. The Medic was hanged this way. Claim at least your category on Day 2 and give a check others can verify (e.g. 'I protected X').

With one Yakuza left and few players alive, block the top Katana-holder suspect every night. A quiet night after the block, plus a matching exact-role result, makes a solid case for a hang that ends the game.

Once your charm swallows an attack, release it on the very next night on your best lead. You can't charm while you hold it, and holding it publicly makes you the Yakuza's top kill target. If you wait for one more result, you'll probably die with the attack unused, as I did when I held on N3.

Announcing 'I hold a loaded attack and will release it on the top Yakuza read' tells the Yakuza to kill and block you that night. Confirm the useful fact (who the Katana targeted) without advertising the threat you still pose, or release it first and talk about it afterwards.

A Fabricator can replace a will on the night its owner dies. Post your current leans in public chat during the Day, not only in your will. A will that contradicts what its owner said in public (e.g. a lean on a player they never suspected) points to a forgery and to the Yakuza, not to the named player.

In the endgame with one Yakuza left, a quiet night after a blocker blocks claimant X is strong evidence that X is the holder. Pair it with an exact-role check (an Oracle WRONG on X's claim). With 4 alive, a Yakuza pair would have killed rather than skipped, so a quiet night rules out the 'two claimants are a pair' theory.

Ask the blockers to post their targets on their own before you reveal the result that checks them (as Ivan did). The cross-checks are then hard to fake, and they exposed the Yakuza Pharmacist who was posing as a Party Animal.

Spend your guesses on the claimed role of a suspect whose claim can't otherwise be checked: Vanilla Villager, a duplicate claim, or a claim with a mechanics slip. A WRONG result breaks the claim outright. Once the field is narrowed, guess the hidden killer's real role in case of a RIGHT.
evidence: Ivan's guess Carol = Party Animal came back WRONG and exposed the fake PA. Grace = Serial Killer was RIGHT after the elimination left Grace and Erin. Alice = Vanilla Villager was WRONG and settled the final hang. The Village got all three of its decisive hangs or confirmations from these guesses.

tip: Enforcer: once a likely Katana holder is narrowed down, pay for a double visit (and Strong if you can) on the two most suspicious claimants. Yakuza: an unclaimed player whose result reads 'X made no attack' is probably an Enforcer. Don't move the Katana to the teammate the town already suspects while that player can act; block the Enforcer or keep the holder unsuspected.
evidence: On Night 2 the Yakuza had read Bob as an Enforcer and blocked him. On Night 3 they let him act, passed the Katana to Carol, the publicly suspected PA, and Bob's Strong double on Dave and Carol killed her. Carol had called the risk 'acceptable'.

tip: Kill or neutralize a working role-blocker early, even one you suspect is a Neutral. A real blocker on your holder turns every quiet night into proof against you, and it confirms or breaks claims cheaply.
evidence: The Yakuza deliberately left Judy alive, guessing she was the SK. She blocked Alice on Night 3 and Night 5. The quiet Night 5 together with Ivan's result got Alice hanged, which ended the game.

tip: Before claiming a role, learn exactly what feedback it gets, and never describe your results in words the real role would not use. Avoid Vanilla Villager as a long-term cover when an Oracle may be in play, since it is the easiest guess to make and it can't be backed by any visit.
evidence: Carol said 'a PA isn't told whether a block landed'. Judy publicly corrected this, and the same false claim showed up in the forged will. Alice's and Grace's Vanilla claims were both broken by single Oracle guesses.

applies_to: Village protectors / anyone under elimination pressure
tip: Give at least your role type by Day 2–3, so you don't end up as the one unexplained player in an elimination. On trial, don't name as a suspect a player your own actions showed you trusted. Offer a check, and argue for the other remaining candidate.
evidence: Erin held even her category the longest and became one of the last two SK candidates. In her defense she named Frank, whom she had just spent a token protecting, as a possible SK. Frank, Grace, Ivan, Judy and Alice all called this a contradiction, and she was hanged as the real Medic.

tip: In an elimination between two players, look at who is pushing the nomination. With several killers alive, a free check offered by the nominee (an Oracle guess, say) is worth weighing against hanging on rhetoric, especially when one candidate has a mechanical tie to a dead investigator.
evidence: Grace, the SK, nominated Erin, and Alice, the Yakuza, piled on. Bob's case pointed at Grace: the SK had killed Heidi, who tracked Grace, and then Dave, who reported Heidi visiting Grace. Bob was the only Innocent besides Erin. The mis-hang cost the Village its Medic.

tip: Confirming a check partner is valuable. But don't announce that you hold a weapon aimed at 'the strongest Yakuza read'. That makes you the next Katana target, and you can't protect yourself while holding a swallowed attack. Write the planned target in your will instead.
evidence: On Day 3 Olivia announced she would release the swallowed Katana on a Yakuza. On Night 3 the Yakuza blocked and killed her and forged her will, so the release never happened.

tip: Use a pre-commit protocol for cross-checks. Ask claimants to post their exact target and feedback first, then reveal the result that tests them. That way nobody can fit their story to yours.
evidence: Ivan and Bob had Carol and Judy post their Night 2 blocks before revealing that they themselves were blocked. Frank had Olivia name her charm target before confirming he survived the Katana. These checks confirmed Frank and Olivia and helped the town trust the claims that turned out to be real.

applies_to: Yakuza, and anyone using a false role claim
tip: Choose a cover role whose visible facts match your real behavior. I switched from 'no night action' to 'Tracker' while cornered on Day 3. A Tracker holds no tokens, so one Accountant audit showed 1 token and exposed the claim. Before claiming a role, check every public check it could fail (token counts, visit results, audits) and never retract into a second cover.

Keep all teammate planning in night chat. Day PMs between two teammates are visible as existing, and four players called out my repeated PMs with Carol on Days 2 and 3. Repeated PM pairs become the town's main lead, so avoid them even when they seem harmless.

A Bloodhound's cumulative scent counts track every attack made by a group, and their counts gave the town a mechanical lead on the Katana holder. Once a Bloodhound posts scent, prioritize removing that Bloodhound over a Medic or other protector, and avoid repeatedly placing attacks inside the same overlapping groups.

Before spending a doubled-ballot token, compute the trial threshold with the actual living voters and the extra vote included. My doubled Innocent raised the needed Guilty count to 4 of 6, but four Guilty votes still passed. Spend the token only when it changes the outcome, which means your side is exactly one vote short.

A Neutral Bounty Hunter kills independently of any Yakuza plan and can kill a teammate, as Bob killed Carol. Track the claimed bounties against the attack ledger and treat a Neutral kill-claimer as a third faction in every vote count.

Plan the bounty claims around who the Village will actually hang, not just who you want dead. Bounties on Katana or Bloodhound-type targets can be lost to other killers, and a 'hang with my Guilty vote' bounty needs three Yes nominations that you cannot force alone. Recruit a nominator and a Guilty bloc on Day 1-2 before the nominations are needed.

Use token audits and role-specific mechanics to test claims. An Accountant's count can refute a Tracker claim (Trackers hold no tokens), and a Juror claim explains no kill. Ask for the mechanical check first, then vote on the result rather than on who pushed hardest.

Cumulative attack counts (Bloodhound) are only useful if you know which group was checked on which night. Post the exact group and night, and compare them with the revealed kills before anyone is nominated, so the count cannot be bent into a case against one player.

Votes are secret, so a nomination that fails at 2-3 Yes tells you the alliance is thin. Before nominating, count the Yes votes you can credibly get from public statements, and do not spend budget on a nomination you will lose.

Keep day-time coordination out of PMs. The private messages between Alice and Carol were visible to all and made them look like a pair, which became the Village's main lead. Plan in night chat only, and keep public stories consistent with each other.

applies_to: Yakuza (Smuggler, Katana holder and other teammates)
tip: Agree a redirect plan in night chat before the night. A Smuggler who holds swap tokens should say in advance which kill it would redirect and against what threat, such as a Bounty Hunter or a Medic. I held my swaps, the team's kill on Erin went through, and I was then killed by a bounty I could have pre-empted.

Cumulative scent counts (Bloodhound) reveal repeat attackers across nights. If the Katana holder keeps appearing in the same watched groups, the Village can narrow it to one or two people. Vary the holder when a Bloodhound is alive, or make sure the group members have different cover stories that explain their visits.

Avoid claims that a token count can refute. Alice's Tracker claim failed the Accountant's audit (a Tracker holds no tokens) and the team lost credibility. Prefer a cover role that matches your real token count, or pick a claim that cannot be audited, and keep the story consistent with the night-chat plan.

Test claims mechanically before voting: token audits (Accountant) for zero-token roles like Tracker, Juror and Veteran, cumulative attack counts against the Bloodhound's groups, and stated votes against announced totals. Those checks are what exposed the false claims this game, not who pushed hardest.

Do not send teammate-to-teammate private messages during the Day. They are visible to everyone (only the contents are hidden) and become the Village's main leads. Alice's Day 2 and Day 4 PMs were the strongest public suspicion against the team.

Alerts are only worth spending when a visit is likely. I spent all 3 alert tokens on Nights 1-3 and nobody ever visited me, so the tokens bought no information. Hold them for nights when a key role or a likely Katana target is exposed, or when the Yakuza have shown they are hunting claimed roles.

Use zero-token role claims to test claims. Tracker, Juror and similar roles hold no tokens, so an Accountant audit that finds tokens exposes the claim as false. Alice's Tracker claim fell this way, and it was the most useful mechanical check of the game.

Track who nominates whom against unclaimed bounties. A Bounty Hunter who still needs a kill keeps pushing one named target, so repeated nominations of the same player with no visible reason are a Neutral-killer signal worth checking.

A publicly claimed Medic or Bloodhound is the next kill. The Katana took the claimed Medic the night after she protected publicly, and then the Bloodhound. Claimed protectors should be removed early, and Yakuza should avoid public Day PMs that link them, since those became the main lead against Alice.

Day 2 was full of identical filler posts ('no nomination from me, post your names'). They cost budget and added nothing. Post only new information, a vote, or a direct question, and save budget for trials and the later rounds, when prices rise.

Once you claim Medic, you are the obvious Katana target, because the Yakuza kill the protector after a failed hit. Spend the 1 token on Standard self-protection on the nights after you claim, and keep the protection target unannounced. I had 2 tokens, self-protected on neither night, and died to the Katana on Night 2.

Don't publicly confirm who you chose to protect, or that you chose it yourself. Saying so tells the Yakuza which of their targets were guarded and which teammates are at risk, and it gives them a lead on your next move.

Cheap token audits and cumulative scent counts are the strongest mechanical tests. A Tracker or Juror should hold 0 tokens, so a 1-token Accountant audit exposed a false Tracker claim. Use cumulative Bloodhound group counts to narrow the attacker, and post audits and counts promptly, since they are decisive.

Convict on mechanical contradictions: a claim that can't explain a kill, a failed token audit, or a stated vote that doesn't match the announced total. Don't convict on who pushed hardest. Frank's trial showed that a pushy accuser can be wrong, and Alice's trial showed that a retraction after a failed audit is still a lie to judge on the numbers.

Use the public chat to fix the day's known facts early, such as who was in each scent group, what each claim says, and which claims are still unchecked. Mid-day private PMs between two suspects (Alice and Carol) looked bad to everyone and cost the Village time without producing evidence.

applies_to: everyone, especially Bloodhound and any cumulative count
tip: Write down each night's visit groups and each cumulative total as a small table before accusing anyone. Grace's counts were cumulative, so 'N2 group has 2 attacks' had to be split against N1 and against tonight's Katana and Bounty Hunter kills. I argued in circles for a day because I never built that table.

applies_to: everyone with an Accountant, Tracker or Juror read
tip: Token audits are the cheapest test of a claim. A Tracker, Juror or Sheriff holds no tokens, so any count above 0 disproves that claim. Heidi's audit of Alice's 'Tracker' at 1 token broke the claim and drove the hang. Use audits on no-token claimants early and do not spend them on people whose tokens are already public.

A Juror pair check on 1 trial vote and 1 nomination vote tells you almost nothing, since a match is expected by chance. Save it until several votes are on record, and pick the pair whose stated votes conflict, so the answer discriminates.

Daytime PMs between teammates show up as counts in the public ledger, and two Yakuza PMing a lot drew the whole table's attention. Keep the plan in night chat. When cornered, a claim with no token count to match (Tracker after the fact) gets audited, so pick a cover that fits the token and visit numbers before Day 2.

Most of the chat was repeated 'no nomination from me yet' and 'post your night names' filler that burned budget without new information. Spend budget on one specific check per turn (a count, a visit, a vote) and save it for the trial turn, where the price is lower.

applies_to: Information roles (Bloodhound, Tracker, Lookout, Sheriff, Seer)
tip: Don't publicly announce tomorrow night's track or check target. I said 'my last scent token goes on Alice tonight' in Day chat, and the Katana killed me that night. Post the result after it resolves, not the plan.

applies_to: Bloodhound and any player reading cumulative attack counts
tip: Scent totals are cumulative for the whole game. Isolate a night by subtracting the previous total, and list which players are in both groups. I spent several rounds arguing over a total that was really two separate nights of attacks.

Token counts test role claims. Tracker, Juror and Veteran-after-spending claims can be checked against an audit. A 1-token audit exposed a Tracker claim and forced a retraction, so run audits on the claims that hold tokens or none.

Choose cover claims whose visits and tokens you can actually back. Alice's Tracker claim was contradicted by an audit, and her retraction and Philanthropist switch made her look worse. Retracting a claim after a count lands is usually fatal.

applies_to: Village when a Neutral is alive
tip: Track Neutral win conditions. Bob the Bounty Hunter needed one more claimed bounty, and my death ended one. Before a Village hang, ask whether it advances a Neutral who never blocks the Village win, and whether a Neutral's bounty target is about to die.

Token counts are the hardest evidence in this variant. Roles that hold no tokens (Tracker, Lookout, Sheriff, Juror, Bounty Hunter's non-token play, Veteran once spent) cannot show a positive count, so an Accountant audit of a claimant who should hold 0 tokens settles the claim. Audit the claim that most contradicts the mechanics first, and don't waste the audit on a claim that can't be tested.

Cumulative Bloodhound counts give a group that contains the attacker. Work out which groups overlap and which players are excluded by their own public acts (an alert that caught no visitor, a token count of 0). Post the arithmetic, then ask the one player whose visits the arithmetic leaves open to answer directly, rather than pushing a vote on whoever talked most.

When a trial total exceeds the number of living voters, check for a doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) before assuming a count error. Count the extra vote for its holder and recheck whether the verdict still holds. Use the secret-vote reminder to confirm your own ballot before reasoning from totals.

Heavy private chat between two living players on one Day is visible to everyone and becomes the town's main lead. Keep coordination to night chat, and never let a public denial be contradicted by your own visible PMs. Switching a claim after being caught (Tracker to Philanthropist) was what got the Yakuza hanged here; pick one cover and defend it, or own the lie early with a checkable detail.

Announcing a planned target in public (for example Grace saying she would track Alice next night) hands the Katana holder a plan and removes any surprise. Post the result after the night, not the intended target, and keep the next night's target to yourself.

Before Day 2, pick a cover role whose token count and visits match what you will really have, and claim it once. Saying 'I took no action' and later claiming an active role, or switching claims when cornered, is close to self-incrimination. If an Accountant is claimed, never claim a role with no tokens while you hold tokens.
evidence: Alice went from 'no action' (Day 2) to Tracker (Day 3) to Philanthropist (Day 4). Heidi had said publicly that a Tracker holds 0 tokens. Her audit found 1 ballot token, which broke the Tracker claim and led to the hang.

tip: Never misstate a vote you already announced or cast. Juror, Auditor and Scrutineer results can expose it, and the announced totals limit what you can claim. If you lie about a vote, the lie has to agree with your earlier public statements.
evidence: Alice said 'I'm voting Guilty' on Frank and later claimed she voted Innocent. Frank's Juror check showed Alice and Dave voted the same way, and Dave had voted Guilty. That contradiction was the second pillar of her conviction.

tip: With one kill a night, aim it at the player whose next result will break your cover, not at someone whose data is already public. Players who have announced a claim test (an Accountant auditing claimed token-less roles) are top targets.
evidence: On Night 3 Alice killed Grace, whose earlier scents were already public and could not tell Alice from Frank. Heidi was left alive, and her token audit of Alice decided the game the next day.

tip: Once you have claimed Medic publicly, you are the next Katana target. Spend a token on self-protection that night instead of repeating your last target.
evidence: Erin claimed Medic on Day 2, protected Grace again on Night 2 with 2 tokens unused, and was killed by the Katana.

tip: Bloodhound counts cover the whole game so far. One Katana holder who attacks every night adds 1 each night, so 'two attacks in the group' does not mean two different attackers. Before you nominate on scent math, list which nights each name could have added attacks.
evidence: Dave nominated Frank on the claim that Erin's and Carol's deaths needed two attackers in Grace's Night 2 group. In fact Alice alone made both counted attacks (Night 1 and Night 2), and Carol's killer, Bob, was outside the group. Frank, who was Good, was put on trial and survived only 2-4.

tip: Don't announce tomorrow's target. The Yakuza will kill you first or plan around you. Hint that a check is coming without naming the target, as Heidi did.
evidence: Grace announced she would scent Alice on Night 3 and was killed that night, so the result never reached the Village. Heidi refused to name her Night 3 audit target, survived, and her result convicted Alice.

tip: Once you have claimed Bounty Hunter, your nominations of your own targets look self-serving and will fail. Earn trust by voting with the Village's mechanical case, and wait for real evidence against a target before pushing a hang.
evidence: Bob nominated Dave three times on Days 3-4 with no evidence. The nominations got 3, 2 and 2 Yes votes, and Dave said openly that Bob's bounty needed him hanged.

tip: Keep daytime PMs between teammates to a minimum. Everyone sees that you messaged each other, and repeated PMs while you both deny acting tie you together.
evidence: Dave, Erin, Grace and Frank all publicly asked what Alice and Carol's frequent Day 2 PMs were about. That kept attention on the scent group with Alice in it.

tip: Track the stall clock from the last death. With 2 players alive a nomination needs 2 Yes and a trial needs 2 Guilty, so a Good player who won't vote on themselves and a Yakuza who won't vote on themselves deadlock. The stall rule then ends the game for everyone. Good should force the decisive trial while 3 or more are alive, not wait for the last two.

An armed trap on the last living Good player works as a real deterrent: a Katana holder who attacks the trapped player takes a Strong Attack and dies. Place it on the player most likely to be targeted, and say so publicly so the holder has to weigh it.

When an announced trial total repeats an impossible pattern (the same voter's Guilty counted as Innocent twice), look for a Fixer flip on that voter. Check your own reminder first, then ask the voter to post theirs. Do not switch votes on a theory alone.

Treat offers to self-nominate or vote Guilty on yourself as traps unless the offerer is also committing their own vote. In a 2-player endgame, an offer to 'test' you by a self-nomination usually only costs you your vote and hands the other side the stall.

Heavy private-message traffic between two players becomes the town's main lead. Keep teammate PMs minimal and cover-story details out of them, and agree cover claims in night chat instead of daytime PMs.

Post your claim once, in full and in the past tense, with exact numbers. Don't promise results 'at dawn' or 'in Night 2' before they exist, and don't restate the numbers in new wordings. Each rewording made the town doubt me more, and the Yakuza could see me as the most dangerous claim.

A public claim makes you the Yakuza's obvious night target. Get your key result into the public record as early as possible, ideally with a second investigator who can corroborate it, so a single kill doesn't erase your information.

Keep teammate coordination in night chat only. Heavy daytime PMs between two Yakuza became the town's main lead and got Grace hanged. Give the town a plain public cover story and don't invent phrases like 'Night 2 cover' that need explaining.

Use the Katana victim's visitor list to narrow the holder: list every admitted visitor, eliminate the claimed roles with clear visit evidence, and press the unexplained visitor. Also compare announced trial totals with each player's stated vote to catch a Fixer flipping a vote, which is what exposed the Day 6 anomaly.

The stall rule ends the game for everyone after 3 Days and 3 Nights with no death. With two players left, neither side can convict without a self-vote, so plan the endgame earlier: a trial or a kill is needed before the stall clock runs out, and a trap or a Katana threat alone won't end it.

Heavy private chat between two Yakuza during the day is the biggest tell in the game. Our Carol-Grace PM traffic (dozens of messages) became the town's main lead and got Grace hanged. Keep day coordination to a single line, or move it to the night chat.

Do not let a cover story slip or contradict itself. Grace's 'Night 2 cover' phrase, followed by a denial of any Night 2 action, was the opening the town used. Agree on a plain, checkable story before Day 2, and have the teammate repeat it word for word.

A Fixer flip on an active Village voter is visible: the trial total fails to match the stated votes, and the victim's allies can infer the flip. Spend the token on a player whose vote matters only in a tied or near-tied trial, and do it on a Day when the town isn't already auditing totals.

Track the stall clock early. With three nights and three days without a death, everyone loses, including the Yakuza. Once a Village trap or Ex-Con makes a Katana kill suicidal, a 1v1 can stall to a no-winner end. Plan the last kill before the trap is armed, or make sure a trial can end the game.

Before the Katana holder dies, pick the successor and the next target together. A passed Katana can land on a player who then has no safe target, and the last Yakuza alive loses the ability to kill without triggering a trap.

Verify claims with death causes and visit counts from the night, not with elimination logic ('the holder is Carol or Alice, so Carol'). Elimination only works when the candidate set is truly closed, which it rarely is.

An Enforcer's Basic Attack fires only if the target makes their own attack that night, so visiting a player who doesn't attack is a wasted token and a public visit. Use it on the suspected Katana holder on nights the Katana is likely to be used, because the holder's attack is an attack of their own choosing. Don't spend the visit on a Katana victim or a silent player.

Once the living count is down to two, a Katana holder who can't attack without dying to an armed trap, combined with a hang that needs both votes, produces a stall. The stall rule ends the game for everyone after three nights and three days without a death. Track the nights since the last death and push for a resolution before the third one, rather than waiting.

Check each claimed role's faction against the role list. A Village claim on a role listed as Yakuza (here Talent Agent) is a mechanical lead. Also check counts against public deaths: a Talent Agent's Fortune Teller and Enforcer counts matched the deaths and were hard to refute, so verifiable public results carry more weight than leans.

Keep teammate coordination in night chat only. The Yakuza pair's 15 daytime private messages and an out-of-place 'Night 2 cover' phrase became the town's main lead and got the Talent Agent hanged. Any shared cover story needs to be agreed before Day and kept off the public record.

A trial count that doesn't match stated votes is a clue to a Fixer, but a Fixer flip lasts the whole Day. Advising a player to flip their vote on an unverified theory is a gamble. Ask for the plain, announced vote and confirm the mechanism first.

Post each audit result publicly as soon as it arrives, not at the next dawn. Dying the night after you posted nothing wastes the result, and a dead investigator's private results are never used. Log each token count against the previous one, since a drop shows a spent token that night.

Before nominating on a role-count argument, count the claimed role's uses from the start. Erin nominated Grace on the belief that Talent Agent had two uses, but the claim had three, so the 0-token audit fit. Also check the claimed role's faction against the rules: Talent Agent is listed under Yakuza, so a Village Talent Agent claim was impossible and was a strong lie signal that went unused.

Private-message volume is public metadata: every sender-recipient count was posted each Day. A pair that messages constantly and then both deny the same ground is what got Carol and Grace read as a pair. Keep PM counts low, and agree on a cover story in night chat before Day, not in daytime PMs.

When a trial total does not match the stated votes, first have every voter repost their reminder, then look for a Fixer. Carol's Fixer flipped Heidi's Guilty on Day 6, and Alice caught it from the totals. The flip lasts the whole Day, so a re-vote can be flipped again, and the town should not rely on telling players to switch votes.

A Trapper's armed trap on a likely Katana holder makes that holder unwilling to attack the trapped player. With two Yakuza-side players, this stalled the game into a loss for all three nights in a row (Nights 7 to 9 had no kills). Once the living count is small, the stall rule is the real clock; plan for it before Night 6.

An armed trap on the last Good player can freeze the Yakuza: they won't attack the trapped player, so the game stalls and everyone loses under the stall rule. Before the final few players are left, move or remove a trap that blocks the only remaining kill, or force a daytime vote while there is still a way to win.

applies_to: Juror and anyone running pair checks
tip: A Juror pair check built on one shared vote (0 of 1 or 'no shared votes') is almost no evidence. Wait for several shared votes before treating a pair as a lead, and don't let one check start a hang.

Repeated identical trial totals (for example 1 Guilty of 3 twice) suggest a flipped vote, but a Fixer's flip lasts the whole Day. Advising a player to switch their vote on a later trial is a gamble. Confirm the mechanism first (Auditor, Informant or the reminder check), or ask the player to re-check their reminder rather than changing it.

Check the faction of every claimed role against the role list. A player who claims a role the rules list under Yakuza (here, Talent Agent) as Village is making a false claim, and that is a strong lead. A Village-looking count sequence does not clear them.

Heavy daytime private messaging between two Yakuza, even about innocent-sounding topics like 'cover', becomes the town's main lead. Keep daytime coordination minimal and agree plans in night chat, as the rules suggest.

Never claim a role that the public role list places on the Yakuza side as a Village role. My Talent Agent 'Village' claim was contradicted by a public label and gave the town its main hanging argument. Pick a cover role whose faction and token count you can defend, and check it against what the table already knows.

Daytime PMs between teammates are the most visible tell in the game. Carol and I exchanged about 15 private messages and kept hitting the same 'Night 2 cover' phrasing, which made us the town's focus. Keep all coordination in the night chat, and keep daytime replies short and consistent with one agreed public story.

Before the last few players are alive, plan the endgame around the stall rule (no death for three Nights and Days ends the game for everyone). An armed Trapper on the last Good player can make your Katana kill self-destructive, so you may need to hang or force a trial earlier, while you still have votes.

Hunt the mechanical contradictions early. Night 1 counts and the Accountant audits were enough to settle who visited Bob, but the table spent several Days on lean and PM arguments instead of checking the visit counts and token audits against the deaths.

Track the stall clock (R14) from the moment the living count drops to about 3. Three quiet nights and days end the game for everyone, so with two or three players left, a hang or kill is needed every few turns. Don't spend a whole Day on a stalemate vote.

When an announced trial total is off by one from the votes you can count, check for a Fixer flip before accusing anyone. A Fixer flip lasts the whole Day, so every later trial that Day is flipped too. Ask the Day's Guilty voters to re-check their reminders and act on the mismatch.

Don't convict on elimination logic ("the holder is A or B, and A claims an outsider, so B"). Look for a visit or death-cause fit that is checkable. With only two alive, a wrong hang or a refused hang both decide the game, so get a checkable result before the vote.
Heavy private chat between two Yakuza in the Day was the main public lead against this team. Keep Day coordination to a single public line, and use the night chat for everything else.

applies_to: Accountant, Talent Agent and other info roles
tip: Info roles that visit (Accountant audits, Talent Agent counts) are the easiest to check against public deaths. Count your uses and tokens against the roles' real starting totals, and post those counts publicly before a vote, not in a retrofitted line.

Check every role claim against the faction headings in the rules the moment it appears. A player claiming a Yakuza-only role (Talent Agent, Fixer, Clerk, Diviner, and so on) as Village has broken their claim, and that is grounds to convict at once.
evidence: Grace logged 'Talent Agent (Village)' during her Day 3 trial and was acquitted 2-5. Nobody noticed the role was Yakuza until Erin did late on Day 5. In between, Dave and Frank were killed.

tip: If the totals show your trial vote counted as the opposite, assume a Fixer flipped you for the whole Day. Vote the opposite of what you want in the next trial, or at least vary your vote across the Day's trials to test it. Don't take the suspect's advice to 'vote as announced'.
evidence: On Day 6 Heidi was fixed and her Guilty showed as Innocent: 1 of 3 Guilty, three times. Alice spelled out the flip. Heidi kept voting Guilty as Carol urged, and Carol survived three trials when one Innocent from Heidi would have hanged her and won the game.

tip: In an endgame against a Trapper plus one other villager, kill the non-Trapper first. A Trapper can't trap herself and her trap lasts after she dies, so killing the Trapper lets her last action protect the survivor for good. Also remember that a Cursed villager's death can take another Good player with it.
evidence: On Night 6 Carol killed Heidi, whose final action moved her trap onto Alice. That made Alice unattackable and ended in a stall where everyone lost. Killing Alice would have set off her curse on Heidi, the only other Good player, and won that night. Even without the curse, Heidi could not have protected herself on Night 7.

tip: When two players are the clear suspects, such as a pair trading daytime private messages, spend a token to visit both. The Katana holder counts as making an attack, so covering both suspects has a good chance of hitting it. Don't die with tokens unused.
evidence: On Night 3 Dave visited only Carol, who made no attack, while Grace held the Katana and killed him. He died with all 3 enforcer tokens; visiting Grace as well would have killed the holder.

tip: Keep your trap on the player the Yakuza are most likely to attack next, usually a loud investigator who has claimed, and move it when the threat changes. Don't leave it parked on a low-value player or skip nights.
evidence: Heidi trapped Ex-Con Alice on Night 1 and left the trap there through Night 4, taking no action on Nights 2 and 3. Meanwhile Bob, Dave and Frank, all claimed investigators, were killed untrapped.

tip: After a failed trial, don't make the nominator the default suspect just for 'rushing'. Yakuza love to turn the town on whoever pressed them. Judge the nominee's answers instead.
evidence: After Grace's Day 3 acquittal, Erin, Frank, Heidi and Alice all copied Carol and Grace's line, demanding Dave explain his 'rush'. Dave was the Village Enforcer, and the Yakuza killed him that night.

tip: Save a Fixer token (or any vote-changing token) for the Day when one Village voter decides a trial. Fix the voter most likely to vote Guilty, then publicly urge them to 'vote exactly as you announced'.
evidence: On Night 5 Carol fixed Heidi, then spent Day 6 telling her to keep her announced Guilty. Heidi complied and Carol survived three straight trials with only 1 of 3 Guilty each time.

tip: Don't announce tonight's target, especially when it points at the likely Yakuza. They will kill you before the result comes in.
evidence: On Day 4 Frank announced several times that he would Juror-check Carol and Grace that night. Grace proposed killing Frank in a daytime private message to Carol, and Frank died that night with the check unposted.

tip: Anyone who claims a Yakuza-only role (Wiretap, Clerk-style or Katana-holder claims) is a strong suspect. Put them on trial early on that alone, instead of spending days debating their wording. Grace's Wiretap claim was the clearest Yakuza tell this game, and the town spent Day 2 arguing about it.

Lock in one night story early and correct errors once, in a single post. My N1 account changed three times (audit, then no action, then 'protected by someone'). Each change looked like a lie, and it made my real Auditor result easy to dismiss. Consistent, checkable claims carry more weight than explanations added later.

applies_to: Kitsune and any holder of a held attack
tip: A held attack dies with its holder. Heidi kept her Strong attack unreleased for two days and was killed without using it. Release or name the target while you're alive, even if the evidence is partial, because the charm's value disappears on death.

Use the mechanical trail: a result that doesn't match the announced count (the Day 2 flipped vote, the Clerk rig on Erin) points to a living Yakuza. Track which living players could have acted on each night, and check who was alive then. Rig, flip and Katana-holder inferences narrowed the Yakuza much faster than the pushes did.

Don't hang on a push alone. Ivan's Guilty votes on Alice, Grace and Erin, with no result behind any of them, were the strongest Yakuza-shaped pattern left at the end. Ask every pusher to state the specific result behind each vote, and treat an answer that never arrives as a lead.

Don't spend Standard protections on a guessed or claimed target every night. Standard loses to Strong attacks, and Carol died to a Strong Serial Killer on the night I protected her. Once any Strong killer is alive (an unexplained Strong hit, a Kitsune charm, or a Neutral killer claim), put the Strong token on the most likely target, or keep the tokens for yourself.

Ration tokens for the final nights. I spent my last two on a Strong self-protection on Night 4 and had none left when the Katana holder came for me on Night 5. Save at least one token for the night the last Yakuza is most likely to target you.

An Innocent verdict followed by an execution means a Clerk rigged the Day. The rig is only announced when the verdict is Innocent, so an unannounced hang with a Guilty majority hides it. Look for 'Innocent but executed' as the Clerk tell.

A Yakuza who claims a Yakuza-only role (Wiretap, Clerk, Fixer, and so on) gets nominated and loses the claim quickly. Claim only roles the Village can't check if you are sure you can defend them, and keep the claim to a single line.

Nominations cost budget that rises by round. On a late-round Day, a nomination can cost more than you have left (3.50 at round 8, against my 2.88), so use your cheap early rounds to nominate. Curt players should keep messages short, since the length part of each price is doubled.

applies_to: Investigators (Profiler, Sheriff, Seer, Auditor, and similar)
tip: Post an exact result as soon as it bears on a vote. Holding it gains nothing: I kept Erin's Serial Killer profile back until my next turn, and the Serial Killer killed me that night. Investigators are targeted by killers, so an unposted result dies with you.

A Clerk rig can execute someone even when the Guilty/Innocent verdict is Innocent. If a hanging follows an Innocent verdict, a living Clerk rigged the Day. Treat the Clerk's Day-night as a Yakuza action and look for who nominated or pushed that trial.

When a player's announced vote conflicts with an audit or Kindred-style read, first compare the announced totals with each voter's reminder. A count that doesn't fit the announced votes points to a Fixer or Ballot Stuffer, and the player who gained from the flip is the lead.
Public claims of Yakuza-only roles (Wiretap, Clerk, Fixer) make the claimant the first target for the Village. Claiming one to bluff is a losing move unless you can defend it with a checkable result.

Once you publicly claim a killing role and use it, expect to be the next Katana or Serial Killer target. I claimed Sniper and fired on Day 3, and the Katana holder killed me the next night. Hold a one-shot kill until the target is confirmed by a result that bears on a vote, not a claim backed only by a death announcement.

A living Clerk can rig the Day, so a Guilty majority is not the real lock. Once a Clerk is possible, the nomination vote is the real defence: a Yes that passes is an execution. Count who could still be a Clerk before you treat an Innocent trial as safe.

A player who repeatedly pushes hangs with no result, votes Guilty on several Village-aligned players, and never states a role late in the game is a strong Yakuza lead, even when they say they are 'waiting for results'. Build the case from the pattern of pushes and votes, not from their wording.

applies_to: Village with Kindred, Faultline or Auditor-type vote info
tip: Partial vote information (a Kindred sample, an audit of one player's votes) is strong evidence when it contradicts a player's announced vote. Compare it with what they announced and with the announced total before blaming anyone, and say exactly which contradiction you see.

Many turns were repeated 'no nomination from me' or 'vote on results' filler that spends budget and adds nothing. Save budget for the turn that carries a result, a vote, or a specific question to a named player.

applies_to: Serial Killer and other Neutral killers
tip: A failed Strong attack on a player who then survives is not proof of Defense. It can be a Kitsune charm swallowing it, so before reading a survivor as protected, check for a charm claim. Track which Kitsune claims are still unreleased, because a held attack survives its holder's trial and night until it's released.

Don't stack kills on the same target. On Night 2 my Strong attack, a Katana and a Bounty Hunter's Strong attack all hit Heidi, so two of the three were wasted. Before a night's attack, check public claims and other killers' likely targets, and pick a different living threat when one is already dying.

A rigged trial can hang someone after an Innocent majority. Erin was executed after a 1-Guilty-of-4 verdict because of a Clerk rig. When a Clerk may be alive, read each hanging as possibly rig-driven, and treat the trial count and the execution as separate facts.

When a Yakuza is hanged early, the Village's evidence against the remaining players gets thinner. Count the Yakuza left and your own path to a solo win: if it needs the last Yakuza dead, plan the kills around the Katana holder's visible behaviour and the Village's remaining checks, not around the Village's count.

Public nominations on thin reads turned into executions of Good or Neutral players. Before voting Yes on a nomination with no result behind it, ask whether the nominee could be a Neutral killer or the Village's last investigator, since the hang removes that information for good.

A Clerk rig executes the nominee even when the trial verdict is Innocent. When a Clerk may be alive, a Guilty/Innocent result does not protect anyone, so decide on the nomination itself and keep the rig in mind when reading a 'saved' trial.

applies_to: Bounty Hunter and other Neutral killers
tip: Publicly claiming a killer role on Day 3 made me the Sniper's target and I died before my bounty plan finished. Claim only when the claim wins a vote or protects a plan, and otherwise keep the role hidden and act at night.
A swallowed attack is lost if you die, and Heidi died holding it unreleased. Release a held attack on your best live suspect on a night you expect to be attacked, rather than waiting for certainty.

Nominating a claimant whose results are unverified (my Day 3 nomination of Carol) got 3 Yes and failed, which cost a Day. With few players left, nominate only on a mechanical lead, such as a contradiction in a stated vote or a count mismatch.

Lone and contradictory accounts (Alice's three Night 1 versions) drew more attention than the Yakuza-only Wiretap claim, which was the real tell. Check each claim against which roles could produce it before weighting how often someone changes their story.

Never publicly claim a Yakuza-only role such as Wiretap. The claim can't be checked, so the Village treats it as a confession. Mine got me nominated and hanged on Day 2, and the retraction didn't save me. If you must fake a role, pick a Village role whose results the Village can't easily test, and keep it consistent.

Keep all day-time coordination out of private messages. Everyone can see who PM'd whom, and a Day 2 PM from me to Ivan became the town's lead on both of us. Plan the target and holder in night chat only.

Prioritise killing whoever holds a result that would narrow you: investigators with exact-role or profile results, and any player holding an unreleased attack. Ivan's Katana kills on the Auditor and the Profiler were the most damaging events for the Village.

A Wiretap reads every Day private message, so use that to find the real investigators and the Village's private coordination before choosing a night target. I read the Alice-Heidi and Carol-Dave PMs but never used them to pick a target or to steer a vote, which was a wasted edge.

Medic protection of an investigator only stops Basic and Standard attacks. A claimed Medic who keeps protecting the same Standard target can't stop a Strong killer, so read a repeated failed protection as evidence of a Strong attacker, not as a Medic lie.

applies_to: Kitsune (and any holder of a swallowed or held attack)
tip: Release a held attack early on the best-supported suspect, rather than holding it for a 'clear' target. A held attack is lost the moment you die, and a public Kitsune claim makes you the top kill target: I was hit by three attacks the night after claiming. If you claim, be ready to release on the same Day or the next night.

applies_to: Kitsune, Good investigators and other claimed Village roles
tip: A public role claim with no checkable follow-up draws every killer at once. Before claiming, decide what you will do with the claim (who you would release on, which result you will post) and state it in the same message, so the town has a reason to back you and the Yakuza have less reason to hit you.

Survival from an unexplained attack is evidence of a live Strong killer or a charm, not of a protector. Do not demand a protector's name from a survivor who has no Defense; ask instead what night result or role could have blocked the attack, and treat a Kitsune or Medic story as checkable against the death announcements.

Avoid public claims of Yakuza-only roles (such as Wiretap or Clerk) unless you have a real plan for the day. Grace's Wiretap claim was retracted under pressure, the Village treated it as the main Yakuza lead, and the retraction did not clear her. Also rig a Clerk vote only when the nomination is already a sure hang, because the rig is announced in the will of a dead player.

Many players repeated the same 'name your result' line for several turns, which spent budget without adding evidence. Post one specific question per turn, and save budget for the trial speech where a vote can change.

Self-protection always costs a token (Standard = 1, Strong = 2), and free Standard protection can't go on yourself. Keep at least one token in reserve for your own protection once you are one of the last Village players. Spending tokens early on unattacked players left Bob with 0 tokens and no defense against the final Katana.

The Medic is the main obstacle to a Standard Katana. Once they have no tokens left, kill them first, because the Village then has no Defense to stop the attack. Sequence the kills so the protector goes before the last Village players.

A Clerk rig executes the nominee even when the Guilty/Innocent vote is Innocent (the rig is announced publicly if the verdict is not Guilty). Use it on a Day when a nominee would survive the vote, and treat an announced rig as proof a living Clerk exists.

Don't claim a Yakuza-only role publicly, even to retract later. Grace's Wiretap claim, then withdrawal, became the Village's main case and got her hanged. Stay silent or claim a Village role that fits your actions.

Private messages between two players are seen as a pair. Day PMs between Yakuza, or a PM pair that pushes one player, became the town's lead. Plan in night chat, and keep daytime contact with your partner to a minimum.

Once you hold a swallowed attack, release it at your first real lead, and don't announce publicly that you're holding it. A public 'I hold a Strong attack' makes every killer choose you, and the attack is lost when you die.
evidence: On Day 2 Heidi said she was holding the Serial Killer's Strong attack. She took no action on Night 2 and was killed by the Katana, the Serial Killer and the Bounty Hunter at once, so the attack was never used. Grace had just been hanged, and her PM to Ivan during the trial was an obvious place to release it.

tip: On the Day before the numbers collapse, hang the best lead you have. Unclaimed players whose counted votes went against a cleared player are a real case. Repeating 'I'll vote only on a result' all Day hands the game to the night killers.
evidence: On Day 3 the Village had 4 of 6 players alive. Erin and Ivan were the only ones who never claimed, and the Alice trial count (3 Guilty: Grace plus two others) pointed at both. After the failed Carol nomination, the Village spent about 6 rounds saying 'vote only on a result', which Ivan kept repeating. Nobody was hanged, and the Village then lost Alice and Carol overnight.

tip: Once any cause of death or attack report proves a Serial Killer or Arsonist is alive, spend a token for Strong Defense on the investigator who just said who they'll check next. Free Standard protection only stops the Katana.
evidence: A Serial Killer had been confirmed since Day 2. On Night 3 Bob gave Carol free Standard protection, and Erin's Strong attack killed her through it. Bob then spent both tokens on himself on Night 4, when Ivan attacked Dave instead.

applies_to: Sniper, Vigilante and other Village killers
tip: Shoot players who block the Village's win, meaning Yakuza and Serial Killer suspects. Don't shoot a Neutral that never blocks wins or has already used its attack. Before firing, ask whether this target can still hurt the Village.
evidence: Frank had openly claimed Bounty Hunter and had already spent his only attack token on Heidi. Bounty Hunters never block wins, so he was harmless. Dave still shot him on Day 3 while Erin (Serial Killer) and Ivan (Yakuza) went unshot, then died on Night 4 holding 2 unused tokens.

tip: Never name a Yakuza-only role in a claim or the ledger. When a teammate is doomed, vote Guilty on them and don't PM them during their trial. Ivan's bus vote kept him hidden all game.
evidence: Grace's ledger claim read 'Wiretap (Yakuza)', and she was hanged 8-1. Her PM to Ivan during her trial was pointed out but never followed up. Ivan voted Guilty, and nobody seriously suspected him until it was too late.

tip: While a Yakuza may still be alive, treat a Yes on a nomination as a vote to hang, because a Clerk rig executes anyone successfully nominated. Don't vote Yes 'just to get a trial'. As the Clerk, rig when few players are left and nominate early.
evidence: On Day 4 Ivan had rigged the vote, spoke first and nominated Erin. Bob and Dave voted Yes only to get a trial and then voted Innocent, but Erin was executed anyway. Ivan controlled the hang, and he would have been executed himself if the Village had voted No and then nominated him.

tip: When a player's stated vote doesn't match the count, the simplest explanation is that they voted differently from what they said. Don't assume a hidden vote-manipulating role (Fixer, Ballot Stuffer) without other evidence, and don't let that theory replace hunting the players you can actually see.
evidence: Heidi said she'd vote Guilty on Alice but voted Innocent. On Day 3, Alice, Dave and Carol all built cases on a 'living Yakuza Fixer' who didn't exist, and that pulled attention away from Ivan and Erin.

tip: Don't announce tonight's target, especially when it's a suspected killer. Post results once you have them.
evidence: On Day 3 Carol said she would use her last profile on Erin, and Alice said she would audit Erin. Erin (Serial Killer) killed Carol that night, and the Katana killed Alice, so neither result was ever posted.

applies_to: Village roles that can repeat (Auditor, Sheriff, etc.)
tip: If another player publicly claims your role with a result, back them up with your own claim and results the same Day. If you claim it days later, it looks like you copied them, and a duplicate claim with no backing is easy to shoot or hang.

Audit the players whose votes were in question (the hidden No or Innocent in the totals, or anyone who openly switched), not someone whose votes are already public. A result that only confirms a public claim looks like copied information if you're ever challenged. Bob's audit of Dave's No vote was the useful one.

When two Good-looking info claims clash (here an Oracle saying 'Seer WRONG' against a Seer whom the Katana attacked), test each one against facts known from outside. A Roleplayer's results are usually false, so an 'Oracle' whose CORRECT results all land on dead or publicly claimed players is likely a Roleplayer or a liar. Don't settle on either side too early.

Count the hidden No/Innocent votes in every total and match them to the players who claimed them. A lone No that someone admits to (Dave on Frank's nomination) next to an unverifiable 'confirmation' of that same player is a strong Yakuza tell, worth a shot or an audit.

In the endgame, a last will that points elsewhere is not enough.
