An Oracle 'CORRECT' that hits a Yakuza but names the wrong exact role means a Roleplayer (random results) or a swap. It does not confirm the claim. Check the Yakuza night actions or a Smuggler flip before you write 'checked out' in your will.

Results from the night you die never reach your will. So post any partial lead publicly during the Day, and write in your will what each possible result would mean, so the town can still use the logic.

A Mortician clean on the first night's victim often hides an investigator's will (here, a Roleplayer-Accountant who had checked the Mortician). Treat a cleaned victim's Day 1 hints as a sign of what the Yakuza feared.

An Oracle claim that gives 'CORRECT' on a role the player later flips as something else is strong evidence the claimant is a Roleplayer. Only blame a swap if the swap really fits the result: for it to work, the actual guessed role would have to be on the swapped partner. Hits that land on the right faction can be luck, so judge each one separately and don't build a trusted info source out of them.

Before Day 2 ends, find out who has Chronicler marks (or other ways to reveal a role) and hang marked suspects first. A marked hang checks itself: it turns a claim clash into a hard result and exposes the Yakuza who defended the suspect.

Once claims start, post the full archive list publicly. Claims that match roles on the list get weak support. Roles that appear once can still be fakes, so the list never clears or convicts anyone alone. Use it to test cover claims that come later, like a Seer or Surveyor.

If a Ritualist may be in play, a public claim of your exact role invites a Divine kill that no Medic can stop. Post the result in a way that doesn't reveal your role, or claim only when the result decides the vote.
Go on alert on nights when only a few Yakuza are left and you are a natural Katana target, such as a quiet unclaimed player who backed every hang. One Yakuza dying on your alert can end the game.

When you're the last Yakuza, don't attack a quiet, unclaimed player who has never been targeted. That profile fits a Veteran on alert, and Veterans spend their alerts late. Pick a target whose role is known and can't fight back (a 0-token claimant, or the obvious protector). Better still, attack someone a teammate's attack has already reached safely.

A puppet lapses if you die the night you set it up, because it needs you to act during the Day. Using the token on the last night you're likely to survive is too late. Spend it while you still have teammates to soak up the night's risk, for example on the Day after a confirmed investigator's result appears.

A Chronicler who claims publicly on Day 2 turns every later hang into a reveal. Kill them that night. If a Medic is likely on them, swap them with a decoy (Smuggler) or double up the attacks. Each mark they place costs a teammate's cover.

Don't decide an Oracle is fake or real only because its 'CORRECT' results came out wrong. A Roleplayer still chooses its own targets, so a good reader can keep naming real Yakuza and get random results that happen to agree. The targets the claimant chose are evidence of their own, apart from the results.

Arguing No on a doomed teammate's nomination before the vote makes you the next suspect, and investigators will spend tokens on you. Once a self-checking hang (a Chronicler mark) is coming, vote Yes and Guilty from the start.

Protect whoever is steering the town's hangs right now: the claimed investigator who keeps nominating, or the Chronicler whose marks expose Yakuza. The Yakuza kill the town's leader whether or not that player's results are real. Free Standard protection on these players stopped two Katana attacks without spending a token.

Count a role check that says 'CORRECT' and then flips a different role against the claimant. Saying a swap moved it only works if a Smuggler actually acted that night and the swap partner had the guessed role. Usually the claimant is a Roleplayer, and a Roleplayer's later results are coin flips even when they keep landing on the right side.

A Chronicler mark turns a disputed claim into a hang that checks itself. When a marked player is a solid lead, hang them over unmarked players, because the flip settles every claim tied to them, such as an Oracle's result or a fake counterclaim.

Once you've publicly claimed an exact role, an enemy Ritualist or Oracle can guess it for certain. Claim only when your result swings the current vote, and put the result in your will first so it outlives you.

If a Yakuza fake-claims your role (e.g. claims Medic), you don't have to counterclaim while the hang is already heading their way through other evidence. Stay hidden, let the flip expose them, and keep your full protection record in your will.

If an exact-role result of yours is contradicted by a revealed flip, the simplest explanation is that you're a Roleplayer. Before you blame a swap, check whether a swap could actually have happened. Don't build follow-up theories (like 'a Pharmacist is still alive') on results that might be random, because a false will or claim can send the town after a role that doesn't exist.

When a suspect has been marked by a Chronicler, hanging them is a self-checking test: their true role is revealed and no Mortician can hide it. Use that early to settle disputed claims, and save unmarked hangs for leads that have more support.
Late in the game, when only one or two Yakuza are left and they need a kill every night, alert on the nights you look like a likely target. One alert that catches the Katana holder can end the game.

If you confirm that another player is a Roleplayer, think before you announce it. If their random picks keep landing on players who flip Yakuza, outing them can kill the town's momentum. Keep the fact in your will so it isn't lost, and stop their claims from steering votes only once their picks start hitting town.

A Village investigator who publicly claims a role that matches the results they posted is an almost certain Ritualist hit. A 2-token Divine guess gets through any Medic, and the Katana can attack someone else the same night.

If an Oracle-type claimant reports CORRECT on a role the target later flips as something else, and nobody reported being swapped, treat the claimant as a likely Roleplayer. Don't explain it away with a Smuggler swap. A Roleplayer's random results can still land on Yakuza by luck, so judge their calls on their own merits and don't stack trust on them.

A Chronicler mark makes a hang self-checking. Steer hangs toward marked suspects, since even a wrong hang gives hard information, and a revealed Yakuza-only role also clears or exposes whoever pushed for it.

Tokens die with you. When the Yakuza are down to one or two and a suspect has a strong mechanical case that the vote can't reach tonight, fire at least a Basic shot. Don't hold all game waiting for certainty, because a protected town can still lose at the lock.
In the endgame, the Yakuza run out of safe targets and often go after quiet, unclaimed players. Alerting on consecutive late nights while staying unclaimed can kill the last Katana holder outright.

A cover result that happens to match the truth (e.g. calling the real Roleplayer a Roleplayer) gets ignored if your own flip is revealed by a Chronicler mark. Before relying on a cover, check whether a Chronicler has claimed marks; if one has, assume the marked teammate's role will come out and plan around that.

applies_to: Village info roles (especially token-auditing or investigator roles)
tip: On Day 1, don't say anything that hints at your role's mechanics, like 'claims should match token counts'. Yakuza look for exactly that kind of line when they pick their Night 1 Katana target and Mortician clean. A plain, generic Day 1 message is safer.

Any Sheriff, Tracker, Lookout, Seer, Fortune Teller, Oracle or Accountant (yourself included) might be a Roleplayer getting random results. Treat a single result as a lead until a role flip or a second, independent result backs it up. When an exact-role guess misses, ask whether any swap actually happened, not just whether one could have, before you write off the mismatch.

If you confirm someone is a Roleplayer (for example, an Oracle guess of Roleplayer comes back CORRECT), post it once their results start driving hangs. The table needs to know their calls are random, even if they happen to be landing on Yakuza right now.
Mark the most influential or suspicious players early. A marked player's hang reveals their true role, so the table can hang them with little risk, and every flip checks the claims made around them.
Save alerts for the late game, when few Village players are left for the Katana to pick from and you're one of the likely targets. One well-timed alert can kill the last Yakuza holder.

A Roleplayer's results are random, but the targets it chooses are real reasoning. If a claimed Oracle's "wrong" exact-role calls keep landing on players who flip Yakuza, follow the targets, not the role names. Don't invent a swap to explain them unless a swap was actually reported.

Use guesses to confirm or break public claims, e.g. guess a claimer's exact claimed role, or guess Roleplayer on a claimed Oracle/Sheriff/Tracker. A CORRECT on a claimed role clears that player. A CORRECT on a Yakuza-only role gives a hang with no flip needed. Don't spend a guess on a likely Village Katana target.

A Chronicler mark turns a hang into a self-checking test: the hanged player's true role is revealed even if a Mortician exists. Hang a marked suspect before an unmarked one when the leads are close, and let the flip settle conflicting claims.

Publicly claiming a role with a distinctive result (Bloodhound, Oracle) hands a Ritualist an exact-role guess for a Divine kill that no Medic stops. Claim only when it decides the vote, and give the result without naming the role if that's enough.

Late in the game, when few Yakuza remain and the Katana must keep hitting someone, alert on nights you're a plausible target. One alert visit from a lone holder can kill the last Yakuza and end the game.

Once a Chronicler has publicly claimed and still has tokens, assume their next mark goes on your most suspected member. That night, swap that member with someone else. The mark, a Bloodhound's token and Oracle guesses then all land on the decoy. Dying with unused swap tokens while marked throws the game away.

A Ritualist kill is announced with the cause 'Ritualist', so every Oracle now knows to guess Ritualist. Make the kill only when it is worth getting exposed. Afterwards, pass the Katana to a teammate and plan for an exact-role hit on you within a night or two.

If the Katana fails on the obvious town anchor (the claimed Chronicler, the trusted Oracle), a Medic is guarding it every night. Don't hit the same kind of target again. Kill the likely protector: the player who pushes hard but never claims a result. Or kill an unprotected quiet player.

A quiet unclaimed player who survives into the late game may be a Veteran sitting on alert tokens. When you are down to your last Yakuza, a Katana on them can kill the holder and end the game. Prefer targets whose roles are known to have no alert.

A Roleplayer playing Oracle gets random CORRECT/WRONG results. If the moderator's random picks keep landing on Yakuza, the town follows them anyway. As Yakuza, don't rely on 'he's just a Roleplayer' once a flip agrees with his calls. Counter his name-level hits directly.

Mark the players most likely to be argued about: an early suspect, a contested claimant, or someone who just argued against a hang. A marked player's hanging reveals their true role, and a Mortician can't clean a Day death. That turns each hang into proof that can confirm or break the claims around it.
evidence: Bob marked Carol on Night 1 and Dave on Night 2. Their hangings revealed Mortician and Smuggler, which broke their Surveyor and Medic claims and gave the town two certain kills. Without the marks, both hangings would have revealed nothing.

applies_to: Village investigators (any game with a possible Ritualist or other exact-role killer)
tip: Don't publicly name your exact role unless the vote needs it. You can give the result without the role name, or claim only once the role itself is what proves the result. A publicly claimed exact role is a free, unstoppable Divine kill for a Ritualist, and it's an Astral Visit, so no watcher sees it.
evidence: Erin claimed Bloodhound on Day 2 even though the hang was already certain. On Night 2 Olivia guessed 'Erin = Bloodhound' with 2 tokens, and the Divine attack killed her through any protection.

tip: If your result settles another claimant's role, especially by showing they're a Roleplayer, post it at the next Day. Otherwise the town builds theories on random results. If your own exact guess comes back CORRECT but the revealed role differs, treat yourself as a likely Roleplayer and don't let others explain it away.
evidence: Niaj learned on Night 2 that Ivan was a Roleplayer but stayed silent. The town then explained Ivan's misses as 'Dave's swaps', which was false because Dave never swapped, and hanged Olivia mainly on Ivan's random call. It worked only because Niaj's real guess happened to match.

tip: When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, don't be the lone public voice arguing No or 'wait and test tonight'. Hiding inside the majority is worth more than a doomed defense. Your argument also gets quoted the next Day as a delay tactic.
evidence: Dave argued No on Carol before the nomination and then switched to Guilty in the trial. Every Day 3 speaker cited that push, Erin spent her token on him, Bob marked him, and he was hanged. Grace stayed with the majority and was never seriously suspected.

applies_to: Yakuza (Smuggler, Puppeteer, any holder of one-shot tokens)
tip: Spend utility tokens once a teammate is under real pressure. A Smuggler who becomes a lead should swap himself with another player on the night a mark, track or check is likely aimed at him. Tokens you still hold when hanged are wasted.
evidence: Dave was the obvious Day 3 lead on Night 2 but held both swaps. Bob's mark and Erin's track hit him directly, and he died with 2 swap tokens. Grace saved her puppet token until the night she died, so it lapsed.

tip: Stay unclaimed and guard whoever the Yakuza most need dead: the player who just claimed a strong result or who is leading the hangs. Unchecked claims from fake protectors can sit on top of yours. Your saves speak for you.
evidence: Heidi protected Bob on Night 2 right after he claimed Chronicler, and Ivan on Night 3 while he led nominations. Both Katana attacks failed. Dave's fake Medic claim never pulled her out, and she survived the whole game.

tip: A quiet, unclaimed Veteran should start alerting once the Yakuza are few and need kills on players nobody is guarding. A lone late Yakuza attacking a silent, unclaimed player should weigh the Veteran risk, because a failed kill and a dead holder end the game.
evidence: Alice never claimed and alerted on Nights 3 and 4. Grace was the last Yakuza and attacked her on Night 4. The Standard Katana failed against her alert Defense, and Alice's counterattack killed Grace, ending the game.

applies_to: Jester or any Neutral who needs a hanging
tip: With 7 alive, a self-nomination needs 4 Yes votes, so it only works if you can line up votes before the nomination. Build the Guilty bloc in Day 2's cheap early rounds, then nominate yourself. Waiting for the Day to settle let the window close, and I never nominated.

Do not coordinate by day private message. Every PM's sender and recipient are published in the ledger, so a repeated pair (Dave->Bob twice) becomes the town's first lead. Keep all team talk in night chat, and keep daytime messages to a Villager's view.

When two players claim the same role, look for a claim that fits a visible fact it could not fit. Here a Pharmacist claimed Tracker, and the real Tracker's result showed Bob visiting Erin and Frank, which pointed to a block. A visit-based claim is a lead, not proof; check its visit list against the public deaths, protections and blocks.

applies_to: Village roles with a kill (Vigilante, Sniper, Enforcer)
tip: An exact-role kill settles a duplicate claim outright. Heidi's shot on Bob revealed Pharmacist, which exposed Bob's false Tracker claim. If you hold a kill and a duplicate claim is live, consider resolving it on the first night you can.

Your night-chat plan decides the public story. Agree on a cover that fits the team's tokens and visits, and don't coach a fabricated claim. Dave's coaching of Bob's Tracker line after the claim was visible made the town vote for him.
Keep teammate coordination in night chat. Daytime private-message contents are private, but the sender and recipient are public, and repeated messages create an obvious connection.
Prepare a simple, consistent cover that fits your real visit pattern. A Tracker can reveal destinations, including the Katana holder’s visit and any separate visit from that holder’s role action.
When a teammate is unlikely to survive a trial, consider whether publicly defending them will make you look like their partner. If your vote cannot save them, distancing may be safer than defending.

Coordinate the role-block with the Katana attack: blocking a likely protector can let the Katana kill a different target without protection. Night actions resolve together, so the block need not succeed before the attack is made.

Don't publicly promise tomorrow's results on Day 1. I said I'd post concrete info first thing tomorrow, and the Yakuza Pharmacist blocked and then Katana-killed me that night. Stay vague about your role until you can post a result that matters, and treat a loud 'I'll reveal tomorrow' as a target sign.

Don't coordinate by daytime PM. Dave's Day 1 and Day 2 PMs to Bob were visible as events and their content became the town's main lead, leading to Dave's hanging. Keep all team talk in the night chat, and avoid private coaching of a claim you have already made.

When two players claim the same unique-looking role, a duplicate claimant is often a Yakuza bluff. Check which claim has a corroborating visit or a later independent result before hanging either one. Use a Vigilante or other kill on the confirmed liar only with a real lead, and note that a shot that kills a claimant reveals their true role.

Protecting a player with no visible Katana or kill threat on Night 1 wasted a token. Guard the most likely Katana target, usually a claimed investigator or a player who has just been pushed, rather than a teammate of the Yakuza.
Once a Yakuza's PM is public and the content is coaching a claim, hang on that lead promptly, since the Yakuza will lose the next day. Waiting for more data let Frank be killed the next night.

Don't use daytime private messages to coordinate a claim or cover story with a teammate. Every PM's existence is public, and its wording becomes the town's main lead. Keep all coordination in night chat and keep day talk to what your claimed role would say.

A fake claim of a Village role must survive a duplicate-claim test. If a real holder of that role exists, their result can contradict yours. Before a teammate claims, check whether a real claimant could be in the game, and prefer a claim whose results can't be checked, or stay silent.
Phrasing like 'keep it concise and consistent' or 'don't add details' reads as coaching a false story even when it's meant as caution. Avoid giving teammates advice about what to say in public.

Katana Master and Katana Expert only help on nights you hold the Katana. Plan the Katana holder with the trait in mind. If the trait holder never gets the Katana, the trait is dead weight, so plan the holder and the trait use together.

When two players claim the same unique-looking role, the one whose result conflicts with a real role claim is the likely liar. Test the duplicate against the other claimant's result and the Katana death pattern before voting. Don't wait for proof, and don't hang on a 4-3 vote without a mechanical fit.

A Pharmacist-style role-block silently cancels a ward. If a target you warded still dies to a Katana attack, check whether you were blocked, since the result alone looks the same as a Strong attack. When the ward matters most, consider a Strong ward or a self-ward, and don't post the ward target or reasoning in advance, because a Yakuza blocker can read it.

Two Tracker claims with 'visited nobody' results don't separate a real Tracker from a liar. A blocked or no-action player also visits nobody. Ask each claimant what was blocked or swapped, and weigh a claim that matches a verifiable death pattern above one that only reports an empty visit.

Teammate PMs that coach a claim (for example 'stay low-key' or 'keep your story consistent') are strong evidence of a Yakuza pair. Get both players' exact wording in public before the vote, and don't rely on one side's paraphrase.

Before hanging on a case that depends on one side's account of a PM, ask the accused to repeat the message verbatim. A 4-3 hang on a weak case still removes a Yakuza here, but it leaves the Village with fewer players and no way to test the surviving claim.

Keep teammate coordination in night chat. Daytime private messages reveal who is talking to whom, even when the contents are hidden, and repeated messages between the same pair can draw public scrutiny.

applies_to: Trackers and anyone interpreting Tracker results
tip: A result that someone visited nobody only rules out observed visits; it does not prove they were harmless or clear them of suspicion. A role-block can also prevent their actions and visits.

A target can visit multiple players in one night through separate actions. For example, a Katana holder's attack is a visit, in addition to any visit from their own role action. Interpret each destination separately rather than treating multiple visits as a contradiction.

Put known results and the reason for your next target in your will, but post actionable results publicly as soon as you can. A result received during the night you die cannot be added to your will afterward.

A duplicate role claim is not itself a contradiction: most roles can appear more than once. Look for incompatible results or a role that is explicitly unique before treating duplicate claims as proof that one is false.

A result can be accurate without proving the claimant's role. For example, a Tracker can report that someone visited nobody because they had no action or were role-blocked; assess what the result actually rules out.

Use public PM metadata to spot connections, then ask each person separately what was said and compare their explanations. Repeated claim-coaching is meaningful evidence, but distinguish evidence of coordination from independent proof of faction.
Do not infer individual trial votes from a public stance or the secret totals. A narrow Guilty majority does not reveal who voted which way.

Treat private-message coordination as a lead worth testing: ask both players to give their accounts separately, then compare them with the public message history and each other’s claims. A duplicate claim alone may be ambiguous; corroborated coaching or story coordination is more informative.

Choose the attack level that addresses a plausible defense, not automatically the strongest one. A Basic shot would kill a Defense-None target and preserve tokens; reserve Strong for credible protection or innate Defense, or when a decisive kill is worth the extra cost.

Coordinate in faction chat rather than daytime private messages when the fact that a message was sent is public. Even private contents can be denied, but the visible contact pattern itself can invite scrutiny.

Never send a teammate private messages during the Day, least of all right after one of you makes a role claim. Everyone sees that a message was sent, and the town will make you both explain it in public. Coordinate only in night chat. If a Day 1 message is already on record, agree in night chat on a dull, matching account of what it said.
evidence: Dave sent Bob a private message on Day 1 and two more on Day 2. Erin, Frank, Grace and Heidi all asked about them, and the hanging case against Dave was built entirely on what the messages were said to contain.

tip: When asked what a teammate's private message said, never describe it as advice about your claim (e.g. 'keep my story consistent'). That reads as admitting the claim is invented. Give a bland reason that has nothing to do with the claim, and settle it with your teammate beforehand.
evidence: Bob said Dave's Day 2 message told him to keep his Tracker explanation 'concise and consistent'. Dave added 'details we can't back up'. Erin, Grace, Heidi and Alice all quoted those phrases when they voted Guilty.

tip: Pick a cover role that is unlikely to be duplicated, or one that lets you stay unclaimed, like Dave did. Don't claim the same investigator role as a probable real one. A duplicate claim draws scrutiny and keeps everyone looking at you and any teammate tied to you.
evidence: Bob's Tracker claim clashed with Frank, the real Tracker. Frank then pointed to Bob's 'unsupported duplicate Tracker claim' as the reason Dave's coaching mattered.

tip: If your team can't block a hanging (2 Yakuza out of 7 voters), don't argue for the doomed teammate or vote Innocent. Vote Guilty with the town, or at least stay quiet. Defending them marks you as the partner, and you become the next shot or hanging.
evidence: Bob argued for Dave and voted Innocent. Dave was hanged 4–3 anyway, and Heidi shot Bob that night.

tip: Once the town has hanged one half of a pair that messaged privately, shoot the surviving partner that night. Use enough tokens to get through possible protection. Don't wait for a check that a dead investigator may never deliver.
evidence: Heidi spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot at Bob on Night 2 and killed the last Yakuza. Frank's tracking result on Bob died with him, so the shot was the only thing that ended the game that night.

tip: On Day 1, don't say you'll have 'concrete information tomorrow'. It tells the Yakuza you are an investigator. Sound like everyone else until you have a result worth posting.
evidence: Carol said twice on Day 1 that she would post concrete information. Bob's Night 1 night-chat message named that as his reason to block her and kill her with a Strong Katana attack.

tip: Plan which teammate holds the Katana around your traits. Move it to whoever has Katana Master or Expert before a kill you expect to be protected. A strong trait on a teammate who never holds the Katana is wasted.
evidence: Dave had Katana Master, but the Katana stayed with Bob both nights. Dave said himself on Night 1 that his trait 'does nothing for me tonight', and he was hanged without ever using it.

tip: Don't keep offering yourself as the hang target with no reason given. The town reads that as Jester behaviour and ignores it. Try instead to look mildly suspicious in some believable way, for example a shaky claim or a vote that doesn't fit what you said.
evidence: Alice said on Day 1 and three times on Day 2 that she was 'a fair vote'. Nobody nominated her, and the town hanged Dave instead.

tip: Treat messages sent while a player is puppeted as the puppeteer's statements, not as independent evidence from that player. A later correction can invalidate the claim, but it does not by itself prove who puppeted them.

A failed Basic shot shows only that the target survived; it does not distinguish protection from Defense or reveal alignment. Avoid spending a shot on silence or as a test, since the claim can be used against you even when the shot fails.

Before voting Guilty, ask for a concrete contradiction or independently corroborated fact. A night action being unverifiable is not evidence of guilt—private night actions are normally unverifiable to other players.

Recalculate the nomination threshold as the player count changes. At three Village and three Yakuza, the Village cannot pass a nomination alone; use earlier Days to pursue the strongest credible lead rather than let the game drift to parity.

State exactly what a result establishes and what it does not. A Surveyor result identifies a role somewhere in the reported group, not which person has it; share the group and avoid treating the result as an individual accusation or clearance.

Recalculate the nomination threshold after every death. Once the Yakuza can block a majority vote, repeating unproductive discussion will not restore the Village's ability to force a trial; act on the best supported lead while that option remains.

Check whether apparent corroboration is genuinely independent. A claim or report made while someone is puppeted may reflect the puppeteer's choices, so establish who controlled the speaker before relying on their testimony.

Puppet a living Village player who will publicly claim a visible role (here Alice). Their fabricated Lookout claim pointed the town at Dave, and when the puppeted player later became a suspect, the town hanged them. Puppet the player the town is most likely to trust with a claim.

Private message counts are public, so a PM burst to two teammates right before a nomination is visible and was flagged as a bloc. Coordinate in night chat, and avoid a PM spike immediately before you push a nomination.
Spend Fixer tokens on the strongest Village trial voter when a hang is close, since reversing one Guilty or Innocent can flip a trial. Holding both tokens to the end wasted them; tokens die with you.
Keep killing the info roles (Tracker, then Profiler) in the order their results would narrow your team. Confirm holder and target in night chat so every vote matches and the Katana never misses.

A player who says they were puppeted has revealed that a living Puppeteer exists. Treat that player's claims as void and look for the Puppeteer among the players who push them, rather than hanging the puppeted player for those claims.

applies_to: Trapper (and any protective or trap role)
tip: A trap only matters if the Katana team actually chooses that player. Don't announce the trap's location in public chat early, because the Yakuza will just avoid it (their 'Dave's trap is on you' note shows they used it). Place it on the player most likely to be targeted, such as a claimed investigator, and make the claim before the first attack so the trap is credible when it stops something.

A survivor of a failed attack is evidence about the survivor. If a Basic shot on a player fails and the victim survives with no protector, that points to hidden Defense or a survival trait such as Narrow Escape. Use that to re-read the victim's team, not to dismiss the shooter's claim. Don't hang the shooter on an unverifiable claim when the survivor's reaction is the stronger clue.

Don't use 'hang the best lead rather than wait' as a reason to convict on a weak lead. When two players in private chat push the same nomination right before it happens, that pair is the lead; hang on the pair's contradictions, not on whoever has the thinnest case. An unverifiable claim from a Village-only role is not enough for a hang when a Yakuza-linked pair is visible.

When a claim is shown to be puppeted (the Lookout case), look for who had private messages with the puppeted player and who gained from the resulting nomination. That was Erin's and Carol's pattern. Treat any puppet event as a sign that one of the remaining players is the Puppeteer and rank the people who benefited first.

Post verifiable results early and with exact wording, and share them in one place. Several Village claims (Profiler, Tracker, Sheriff) went unverified for days, so the Yakuza bloc could keep the main leads contested. Agree early on who will be the trusted night-action reporter and who checks whose claim, so one contradiction can be tested quickly.

Use your one puppet on someone whose public claim or vote can redirect attention, and make the message fit what the target could plausibly know. Treat it as a temporary diversion: the target can reveal they were puppeted the next day, so don't build a long-term case that depends on the false claim staying credible.
Confirm both Katana choices and make sure every living teammate votes. A coordinated majority secures the attack; night chat is the safest place to settle the plan.

Prioritize players whose continuing results could narrow the team. A Tracker or persistent investigator can become more dangerous with each night they survive, even when their current result is inconclusive.
Avoid daytime private messages to teammates when possible: the public can see who messaged whom, even if they cannot read the contents. Coordinate during night chat instead.

Track the quiet, unclaimed player who has the most reason to hold the Katana, not the player who just got publicly accused. A Katana holder's visit to a victim is what you want to see, and I tracked Erin (who visited no one) instead of Carol, who held the Katana every night. Claim early only if your result forces a decision, because a claimed investigator is the first Katana target the next night.

A survived Basic attack on a player with no visible protector is not proof of innate Defense; it can come from a trait such as Narrow Escape. Before reading a failed shot as a clue against either side, ask what Defense or trait the target might have, and do not hang the shooter on that failure alone.

Before voting on a nomination, check which players sent private messages to each other right before it. Carol PMed Erin and Grace and then nominated Alice, which Heidi flagged, but the Village still hanged Alice 3-2 on a shot that could not be verified. A private-message bloc that pushes one nominee is a stronger signal than an unverifiable kill claim.

When a player retracts or corrects a claim, check whether they were puppeted that Day. A Puppeteer can post in a player's name, so a false Day claim can come from the puppeted player's own account. Check who was quiet or unusually active on that Day, and who gained from the claim.

Keeping the Katana with one holder and killing each claimed power role (Bob, Frank, Dave, Heidi) on the night after it spoke removed every real source of information for the Village. Kill claimants who have verifiable results rather than the loudest accuser, and keep the same holder while it is working, since a holder change gives the Village a tell.

Keep coordination in night chat unless a daytime private message is essential. Even when the message contents are hidden, the public ledger shows who contacted whom, and a cluster of messages around a nomination can expose a team connection.

Use a cover claim whose results fit the actual mechanics, and explain its limitations before opponents can frame them as contradictions. A Sheriff result of Not Evil on the Katana holder is plausible, but explicitly does not clear that player.

Prioritize killing players whose claimed information-gathering role could produce another useful result. A Tracker who has already named a target can expose future visits, so removing them promptly can prevent the town from building a stronger case.

Track the Katana holder by the pattern of kills, not just by claims. When the same holder never moves the Katana and every attack succeeds, that holder is a Yakuza suspect, and the holder's teammates are whoever shares private messages or nomination pushes with them. Write this down each night.

Do not stall for hard data when none is coming. Our Day 2-3 'no nomination without new results' stance let the Katana kill a claimed investigator every night. When two days pass with no new result, nominate the best-supported lead, even on a soft read, instead of waiting again.

Read the public private-message ledger as a bloc signal. A burst of PMs from one player to two others right before a nomination, with all three then pushing the same nomination, is a coordination tell. Ask each of them publicly what was said, and check it against their votes.

applies_to: everyone (any role that can be puppeted)
tip: If the moderator tells you that you are being puppeted, say so publicly on that Day at once. Otherwise Puppeteer-written claims made in your name (here a false Lookout result) stand as yours and sway trials until someone corrects them, as ours did for a full day.

applies_to: Profiler, Tracker, Sheriff and other investigators
tip: Claiming a role publicly with tokens left makes you a Katana target: the Yakuza killed every claimed investigator on the following night. Post exact results once, and stop repeating them daily, since the repetition adds nothing and draws the kill. Spend the last tokens on the player you can't otherwise check.

Count how far you are from the vote lock every Day. If one more night kill puts the Yakuza at half the living players, hang your best lead today rather than 'wait for results'. Results that arrive after the lock can't be turned into a hang.
evidence: On Day 2 the town was 4v3. Every Villager repeated 'no nomination without new data' for about 8 rounds. Frank died on Night 2, it became 3v3, and on Day 3 the nominations of Grace (3 Yes) and Carol (2 Yes) both failed to the Yakuza bloc. Grace (a Guilty vote on Dave and an unverifiable Sheriff claim) and the never-claiming Carol were both reasonable Day 2 hangs.

tip: When a second player 'independently' confirms a result the same Day and then nominates straight away, consider that they may be puppeted. Once a player says they were puppeted, look through every profile, survey or role list for 'Puppeteer' and press whoever it points to.
evidence: Puppeted Alice backed up Frank's track with a fake Lookout result and nominated Dave at once. On Day 3 Alice reported the puppeting. Heidi's Night 1 profile of Bob already listed Puppeteer, and her Night 3 profile of Erin (Bloodhound/Puppeteer/Trapper) fit it, but the town never pinned the Puppeteer on Erin while it still had the votes to hang her.

tip: Put your trap or protection on the player most likely to be killed next: the claimed investigator who just posted a result. Don't leave it on an early guess. Move it as soon as someone claims.
evidence: Dave trapped Grace on Night 1 on a hunch and took no action on Nights 2 and 3, even though Frank publicly claimed Tracker on Day 2. The Katana then killed Frank and later Dave himself. A trap on Frank on Night 2 would have stopped Carol's attack and hit her back.

tip: Use checks on unclaimed or unverifiable players, not on claims that are already backed up. Combine results with how people died: a player killed by the Katana is almost certainly not Yakuza, so Yakuza options on their profile drop out.
evidence: Heidi spent her Night 2 token confirming Frank's already-backed Tracker claim. A profile of Grace (the unverifiable 'Sheriff') or Carol (no claim) could have caught a Yakuza before the lock. Her inference that Frank was the Tracker because he died to the Katana was right. Alice's 'correction' that it proved nothing muddied the discussion.

tip: When the town is falling behind or nearing the lock, your shots are its only way out: fire early at the best lead, and spend more tokens per shot once nominations can't pass. Tokens you're holding when you die are wasted.
evidence: Alice took no action on Nights 1 and 2. On Night 3, at 3v3 with no way to pass a nomination, she fired a single Basic shot at Carol, which Narrow Escape stopped. She was hanged on Day 4 still holding 2 tokens.

tip: A fake investigator claim that 'clears' a teammate is most believable when you point out its limits yourself (e.g. 'a Not Evil read doesn't clear a Katana holder'). Pair it with checks that can't be verified, on players nobody is suspecting.
evidence: Grace claimed Sheriff with Carol Not Evil (Night 1) and Alice Not Evil (Night 2), called her own reads weak, and was never seriously tested. Meanwhile Carol held the Katana all game.

tip: Keep a ready Village cover instead of refusing to claim forever. A player who never claims becomes the obvious Vigilante target and a nomination target.
evidence: Carol answered 'no claim' all game. Alice nominated her on Day 3 and shot her on Night 3 for exactly that reason. Only her hidden Narrow Escape kept her alive.

tip: After you reach parity, vote as a bloc against every Village nomination. Kill in the order that removes your threats: trackers and watchers first, then the protector or trapper, then hang whoever claims a killing role.
evidence: From Day 3 on, the Yakuza voted No together on Grace and on Carol. They killed Frank (the Tracker) on Night 2 and Dave (the Trapper) on Night 3, hanged Alice the moment she claimed Vigilante on Day 4 (3-2), then killed Heidi.

tip: After any trial, match each player's stated vote against the announced totals and keep the list. Once a player flips Yakuza, any non-Yakuza who sat in a small Guilty or Innocent minority with them is a strong teammate lead. Count claimed Zealot or Merciful votes when you do this.

A census never counts Neutrals, and a claimed Tracker or Lookout who only ever targets players with passive or non-visiting roles reports results that can't be checked. That is a classic Neutral-killer cover (here an Arsonist). Before the endgame, list every claim that no one else can confirm.

Claim and shoot on the same turn once you have a mechanical lead near the endgame. A shot that kills a Yakuza effectively confirms you, and your vote then steers the final hang. Don't save the shot past the point where the Yakuza could reach the vote lock.

When checking a Fortune Teller's visit counts, remember that the Katana holder can use their own role's action and also make the Katana visit. A gap of one in the visited count usually means a holder who visited two players, so look at whoever is the lone claimed visitor to the night's attack target.

An Archivist list gains credibility when roles on it are claimed later by players who couldn't have known. A role on the list that a suspect borrows after the list is posted (here Enforcer) should be treated as likely fake until it is checked.

Post your fake claim (role, target, result) early, in your first or second turn, before other people's results come out. If you hold it back and then claim a role from someone's posted list, on the one player who already has public data, it looks retrofitted. The whole town flags that, even if the claim is mechanically consistent.

Don't kill an investigator whose will already names tonight's check (for example 'Seer pair Bob+Carol'). The will is published on death, so the kill doesn't hide the check. It reads as the Yakuza fearing that result, and it points straight at the named player. Kill someone else, or a player whose plans aren't written down.

A player who pushes you hard from Day 2, threatens to nominate before there is data, and claims only late is often an Executioner whose target is you. If you're Yakuza and accused by that player, remember that a census ignores Neutrals. Framing them as 'the Evil one' in a Bob-or-them split collapses once they win and leave.

Don't rely on the Disguised trait to fool a Chronicler's death reveal. In this game the mark showed my true role, not my disguise. Assume a marked Yakuza flips true and plan the team's covers on that basis.

Each teammate's claimed nightly actions should account for the Katana visit in the Fortune Teller's visitor counts. A 'held my action' night from the holder leaves a visible gap in the count that the town will pin on them. Make your cover claim a visit to the same player as the Katana target.

Put your mark on the player most likely to be hanged next. A marked hang shows the true role publicly, so the vote either confirms a Yakuza or clears the suspect's accuser. That reveal settles census splits and fake claims in one step, so it's worth more than a mark on a random player.

When you argue from Fortune Teller visitor/visited counts, remember that the Katana holder can use their own role's action AND make the Katana visit. A Sleepwalker adds a random visit too. Before you nominate on a count, list every way it could still fit. I nominated Frank on a count that had three fits, and the trial wasted part of a Day.

Be suspicious of a 'Tracker' whose targets are always players who never visit (a Scout, passive claimants), because those results can never be checked. That pattern fits a Neutral killer such as an Arsonist, and Census Takers never count Neutrals, so their counts can't catch one.

A player who pushes one specific person relentlessly from Day 2, without data and without claiming, may be an Executioner. Hanging their target is still right if the target is Yakuza. But afterwards every Guilty voter is at risk of a Divine revenge. If you're Bonded, your partner's death kills you too, so keep the Guilty votes near a bare majority when the hang is already safe.

Once a hang reveals a Yakuza, re-examine every claim that player's lies had 'confirmed' or contradicted. Bob's fake Heidi visit propped up Grace's 'Heidi visited nobody' track. Both 'Trackers' (Frank and Grace) turned out to be fake.

If your trap goes off but nobody dies of the Strong hitback, the attacker probably had Strong Defense. A Yakuza Diviner who targets themself gets exactly that, and Narrow Escape also does it. Post this right away and look at whoever claims a visit to the trapped player. Don't treat it as a dead end.

Explaining a Day 2 visit as 'a protective action not active until N2' tells the Yakuza you are a Trapper. They will then plan around the hitback with self-defense or an Astral attack. If you have to explain a visit, give the target but not the mechanism, or have a cover ready.

Visit-count math (Fortune Teller, Cartographer) is wider than it looks. The Katana holder can use their own role's action AND make the Katana visit, so one claimed visitor can cover two visits. Use the counts only to rule out claimed non-visitors, never to pin one claimant.

An unclaimed player who keeps pushing one specific target, and threatens to nominate before there's any data, fits an Executioner. Executioner revenge hits a random Guilty voter, and Bonded pairs can then die of heartbreak. When the hang is clear anyway, keep the Guilty count near a bare majority so fewer key info roles are exposed.

A claimed Tracker whose tracks always land on players with passive or no-visit roles is giving results nobody can check. That fits a Neutral killer (Arsonist/Serial Killer), who reads Not Evil and is invisible to a census. Test them with a watch or a hang near the endgame.

applies_to: Village information roles (Scout, Seer, Census Taker, etc.)
tip: Don't be the Day 1 agenda-setter. Speaking first and steering everyone gets you marked as 'organizer, probably an investigator', and you become the first Katana target. Speak mid-round, keep it short, and let a non-info player lead.

Distrust a visiting claim whose results always land on players who never visit (a Tracker who only tracks passive claimers or a Scout, so it's always 'visited nobody'). Nothing can ever check it, and it's a natural cover for a Neutral who visits every night, like an Arsonist dousing. Push that claimant to target an active visitor, or list them as a Neutral suspect.

In Fortune Teller or visit-count arguments, the Katana holder can visit twice (the Katana visit plus their own role's action), and Sleepwalkers add random visits. A count only rules out players who visited nobody. Don't hang on 'the count leaves only X' without that correction.

An Archivist or role list that names roles before anyone has claimed them is strong evidence the list is real. A claim that matches the list but appears only after it was posted, especially after a holdout, is the weakest kind of claim. Test it, or hang that player if a census or Chronicler mark can settle it.

Spend Chronicler marks on the suspect in a live two-way split (for example a census that says 'one of Bob or Judy is Evil'). Hanging the marked suspect then reveals their role and resolves the split in public, whichever way it falls.

Douse players likely to live, not the obvious Katana target. A douse on someone who dies to another cause is wasted. Day 1's agenda-setter or a freshly claimed investigator often dies that night, so douse quiet or confirmed-looking townies the Yakuza will leave alone.

Once you've survived a trial, ignite the next night, even with only 1-2 players doused. Each extra night of dousing gives a Fortune Teller or Cartographer another count with an unexplained visitor in it. Killing the player who is tracking the counts removes your biggest threat.

applies_to: Neutral killers / anyone with a fake visiting claim
tip: A Tracker cover whose every result is 'visited nobody' on passive-role players gets called uncheckable and wasted. Pick tracks that could be checked but probably won't be, or claim a role whose visits match your real douse targets. Then visit counts and Lookouts back up your story instead of leaving an unexplained extra visit.

At 4-5 alive, a 'Yakuza cleared' census or a Village-only trait (Armed, a Sniper shot) makes that player near-confirmed. If you attack them, the others will side with them. Get yourself out of the top suspect spot before the final few. Kill the counter or claimer before you're the only one left unexplained.

An alignment census counts only Good or Evil, never Neutral. So 'Evil 0' clears a player of Yakuza but not of being a Neutral killer. Use the census's Good count, or other checks, to rule out Neutrals.

With small Guilty totals, your vote can be worked out. If teammates are known to vote Guilty (for example a self-declared Zealot), joining them on a trial that fails 3-9 tells the town exactly who the third Guilty voter was. On trials that are going to fail anyway, vote with the town majority.

Never claim that you 'held' your action on a night your team killed. A blank night is exactly the gap a Katana holder needs in visit counts like the Fortune Teller's. Claim a concrete result that can't be checked, on a target whose visits fit the counts, and post it before anyone asks.

Before you send the Katana, list where a claimed Trapper or protector has probably put their ward. A Trapper who says the trap is on 'another player, not Bob or Judy' almost certainly protected the town's top confirmed investigator. Hit someone else, or use a role whose attack isn't a visit (a Ritualist guess) on that player.

Killing an investigator doesn't erase a result if their will names their target. A Seer whose will says 'my pair is Bob+Carol; if I die, look at Bob' convicts Bob just by dying. Before killing them, weigh whether the kill confirms the very suspicion you're trying to bury.

In the endgame, check every surviving claim against the Fortune Teller's visited and visitor counts night by night. Look for a player whose track always lands on someone who never visits, or who claims nothing on the night the holder needed to be unaccounted for. Those claims can't be checked, so they deserve the most suspicion.

After you post the list, match every list role to a claimant. A list role that no living player claims (here Arsonist and Ritualist) almost always belongs to someone who claimed a role that isn't on the list. Name those claimants as the pool and keep pushing until someone owns each role. Don't settle for 'only half are real, so missing claims are fine.'

Once a Seer's 'different' pair has been settled by hanging the other member, the surviving member says publicly every Day that the pair is resolved and the hanged player's vote pattern backs it. If you don't, an Armed player or a Vigilante may still treat you as half of an open coin flip and shoot you.

Visitor and visited counts (Fortune Teller, Cartographer) only rule out people who visited nobody. A Katana holder can make the Katana visit and use their own action too, and a Neutral killer adds visits as well. Don't let a count argument clear a claimed visitor whose result can't be checked (for example 'tracked a passive role, it went nowhere').

A player whose every night result lands on someone who never visits (a Scout, a Fortune Teller, an Archivist) is giving results nobody can check. Treat that as a lead early, before it costs a Day. Here the Tracker who did this was the Arsonist.
When two players claim the same role, don't accept both because 'roles can repeat'. If neither claim can be checked and neither role is on a known-real list such as the Archivist's, test both.

Don't say publicly that you still have a chosen-pair token. It tells the Yakuza which check is coming and makes you the next Katana target. Spend it on the first night it can settle a live suspect, and say only 'I have a result' until you post it.

applies_to: Seer (and any checker with a pair or group check)
tip: Pair the suspect with a player who is already nearly confirmed Good, so SAME or DIFFERENT decides the suspect alone. Write the will to cover both outcomes ('if DIFFERENT, X is not Good'), because the result of the night you die never reaches your will. Even if you die that night, the will still sets the town's next hang.

Be suspicious of a claimed Tracker or Lookout whose every target is a player who never visits (a Scout, a passive Fortune Teller, a passive Archivist). 'They visited nobody' can't be checked, so it's the safest fake result. Two 'Trackers' with only uncheckable results are not shown real just because Trackers can repeat.

If someone pushes one player hard from the first day, with no data and no role claim, think of an Executioner. Hanging their target makes them win and sets up a Divine revenge on a random Guilty voter the next night. If that player is still the right hang, cap the Guilty votes at a bare majority, and keep confirmed investigators and Bonded players off the Guilty side.

Fortune Teller counts rarely single out one person. The Katana holder can visit two players (own action plus Katana), a Sleepwalker adds a random visit, and a Census 'Evil 0' still leaves Neutrals possible. List every assignment that fits the numbers before using the count to justify a hang.

Push your target in the town's own words: demand a plain claim, set a deadline ('if it's still missing on my next turn, I'll nominate'), and vote with the majority on everyone else. When your target holds back info, you look like a diligent villager, not a Neutral.

Pick an Astral, tokenless investigative cover (Juror, Oracle) and write a full fake result in your will early. It never shows up in Fortune Teller, Tracker or visit-group data, so nobody can mechanically break it, even if you only claim once you're under pressure.

A Census Taker's count never includes Neutrals. 'Evil 1 among X, Y and a known-Good' doesn't mean X or Y is the Yakuza when one of them could be Neutral. A Neutral in the group can steer the town at the other one. Check the unclaimed member's role before treating the census as a coin flip.

A hang that a quiet or late-claiming player pushed hard can be an Executioner's win. The revenge Divine Attack then lands on a random Guilty voter. If an Evil read is solid, keep Guilty votes near a bare majority so fewer villagers are exposed to Executioner or Jester revenge.

Killing an investigator doesn't stop their result if their will names tonight's target. Ivan's will named a Bob+Carol pair, and that alone condemned Bob. Kill the investigator the night before they commit to a target, or make sure the teammate in that check has an airtight cover.

applies_to: Ritualist (and any Yakuza with one-shot kill tokens)
tip: Use the ritual guess on Night 1 if there is any reasonable read, for example a Day 1 agenda-setter as an investigator, or a teammate's Diviner read on a player. Yakuza often get hanged on Day 2 from random Seer pairs or counts, and unused tokens die with you. Holding them 'until a solid read' usually means never using them.

When an Archivist-style list names roles before anyone claims them, and later claims match it, the town will treat it as proven. Don't attack its credibility to save yourself, because that only makes you look worse. Choose a cover role that is plausibly among the list's fakes, and argue instead about who the other half of the pair could be.

Announce your forced vote trait at your first trial vote, before you're ever in danger. If you claim it for the first time during your own trial, it reads as a convenient excuse. An early claim also makes the totals match your words later.

Your random visit counts in Fortune Teller, Cartographer and Scout numbers, so claim a role that visits exactly one player a night (Lookout or Tracker). Then the visitor count fits your claim. Pick a target nobody else is likely to report on.

Killing an investigator whose will names the check they just made (for example 'Seer pair on Bob') points the town right at that teammate. If a check on a teammate is already locked in, consider killing someone else and preparing the teammate's cover for the result.

applies_to: Fortune Teller / anyone using visit counts
tip: A count that matches the claims only shows the number of lies balances out, not that each claim is true. A Sleepwalker's hidden visit plus one invented target, or a holder making two visits, can still give the same totals. Before you act on a count, list every way it could fit.

Don't spend a one-shot kill on a chain of 'if X's claim is true, then Y is evil'. If Yakuza lie about visiting someone, that someone isn't evil. Take a lead and a sign that the target's own claim is real (an archive naming roles before anyone claimed them) as evidence for them, and fire only at a player whose own claim is broken.

In a Seer 'different' pair, the bad one is usually the player whose result can't be checked and who claimed only after being named. A player whose result has already been confirmed by later claims is usually the good one. Don't flip that read later on a teammate's theory.

A player who keeps tracking or watching people who never visit (passive claimers, a Scout) is giving results nobody can check. That's a classic cover for an Arsonist or a Yakuza. Also, an 'Evil 0' census doesn't clear Neutrals.

Someone who pushes one player hard from Day 2 and never claims a role may be an Executioner. When their target is hanged they leave, and a random Guilty voter dies that night. Keep Guilty votes at a bare majority, or keep your protected players' votes off that hang.

applies_to: everyone (especially Bonded players and key investigators)
tip: Before you vote Guilty on a hang that is already safe, think about Executioner and Jester revenge. If the nominee has been pushed hard by one player who has no checkable role, assume an Executioner may be targeting them. The revenge hits a random Guilty voter. When the Guilty total is well past the majority, a valuable or Bonded player can quietly vote Innocent to stay out of that pool. Votes are secret and only totals show.

A census never counts Neutrals. So when a group of three reads 'Evil 1' and one member is a dead Katana victim, the other two are not simply a 50/50 Yakuza split. One of them may be a Neutral who is framing the other. Say so publicly before the town hangs, and check whose push started the case.

applies_to: investigators who expect to be targeted
tip: Once you've publicly claimed and given useful results, expect the Katana and plan for your next result being lost. Post tonight's census target and the deductions each possible count would give (e.g. 'around Heidi: if Good 2 among Carol/Grace/Heidi, Grace is Yakuza') during the Day. Then even a will written before the result can still be read by town.

Don't put a suspicion in your will that a hang has already resolved. When one player of a Seer's 'different' pair is hanged, their earlier lies (such as a claimed Lookout visit that broke the visit count) strongly suggest they were the non-Good one. Pointing back at the other player of the pair just misleads town and can get a Good player shot.

Two players claiming the same no-token info role, with results that can never be checked (tracking players who never visit), make a strong lead. Ask each to track someone whose visits are known, and compare against the Fortune Teller's counts.

Post your cover claim and night target early, before other players' data comes out. A claim that arrives just after someone posts a role list or visit data, and fits it neatly, looks retrofitted. Most players will name it as the least trustworthy fit.
evidence: Bob held back his role and target all Day 2 while five players asked for them. He then claimed Enforcer, a role on Heidi's list, with a visit to Heidi, the only player with public visit data. Heidi, Ivan, Judy, Niaj, Olivia, Alice and Carol all called it the weakest fit. That made him the main suspect even before Olivia's census and Carol's mark confirmed him.

tip: Fortune Teller and Cartographer counts show where claims break. Remember that the Katana holder can also use their own role's action, so a count only rules out players who claim no visit at all. Don't hang on a count that fits several holders.
evidence: On Day 2 the 7 visitors / 4 visited count was first read as pointing only at Frank. Frank showed that Grace or Bob could fit too, Dave added the holder-also-acts point, and the Village wisely acquitted Frank 3–9. The count's real culprit was Bob's fake visit to Heidi.

applies_to: Village players with a one-shot kill (Armed, Vigilante, Sniper)
tip: Before shooting, check whether the suspicion has already been explained. A Seer 'different' pair is used up once its non-Good half has been hanged and confirmed by other evidence, and a Yakuza lying about visiting someone is no evidence against the person named.
evidence: Niaj shot Heidi on Night 3 because of Ivan's Mallory/Heidi pair and Bob's fake visit to her. Mallory had already been hanged as Yakuza, and Heidi's list had named unclaimed roles correctly. Niaj killed a Good Archivist and wasted the gun.

tip: Use stated votes against the announced totals to find the hidden partner of a Yakuza already exposed. Anyone who publicly voted with known Yakuza on a failed trial that the rest of town opposed is a strong lead.
evidence: Frank's trial on Day 2 ended 3 Guilty, and Bob, Grace and Mallory had each said Guilty. Once Bob and Mallory were confirmed Yakuza, Alice named Grace as the only Guilty vote left. She also pointed to Grace's 'held track' gap on Night 2, then sniped her with a Strong shot on Day 4. Grace was Yakuza.

tip: If you fake an investigative role, sometimes give results that can be checked. Tracking only players who never visit, so every result is 'visited nobody', becomes its own tell over several days.
evidence: Frank (Arsonist) 'tracked' Erin (Scout), Niaj (Fortune Teller) and Heidi (Archivist), and every result was 'visited nobody'. On Day 4 Niaj and Alice both named this pattern when they hanged him.

tip: Ignite while your doused targets are still alive. Dousing players the Katana or gunmen kill wastes nights, and an Arsonist who never ignites is usually hanged with nothing to show for it.
evidence: Frank doused Erin (killed that night), Niaj, and Heidi (shot that night). He never ignited, and at the end only Niaj was still doused when Frank was hanged at 4 players.

tip: Yakuza: if you expect a trap, give the holder Defense (a Diviner on itself, a Kitsune charm) so it survives the hitback. Trapper: put your trap on the claimed investigator most likely to be killed next. It arms one night later, so place it early.
evidence: Dave moved his trap to Olivia (Census Taker) on Night 2, and on Night 3 it stopped Grace's Katana. Grace had used her Diviner action on herself for Strong Defense, so the trap's Strong hitback failed and she survived.

tip: A trap protects the player it is placed on; it triggers on an attack aimed at that player, not when that player attacks someone else. It arms the following night, so choose a likely attack target and make the timing clear.
A clash between role claims is not proof when that role can repeat. Only Smuggler and Vulture are unique; look for independent evidence before treating a duplicate claim as impossible.

Test claims against visit-based mechanics: for example, a Sheriff’s check requires a visit, and an alerted Veteran attacks visitors. Treat that as a strong contradiction, but consider defenses and other rules that could explain survival before voting.

Alert gives only Standard Defense, so it can't stop a Serial Killer's Strong attack. Spend alert tokens on nights you expect a real visitor or a Katana, not on quiet nights; a token spent on a night with no visitors gains nothing and is gone.

A Standard Attack (Stolen Blade, Katana, Medic-less shot) cannot kill a Serial Killer or Arsonist, who have Standard Defense. Reserve Standard attacks for Yakuza or other targets; a failed hit on a suspected SK only reveals that you attacked.

Once two or three players are alive, a player with Standard Defense can vote No on every nomination and stall the game. Hang the strongest suspect while there are still three or more living voters, not after a late elimination argument that depends on an unverifiable role claim.

An elimination argument ('only X and I were alive, so X is the killer') only proves something if every living player's role is known. Check each claim against a mechanical result before using it to justify a vote or a private appeal.

Post a nomination's reason as a checkable contradiction (a visit to an alerted Veteran, a Katana victim with no matching visit) and ask each claimant for a single verifiable result. Vague defenses and claim-switching are themselves evidence.

A trap arms only on the following night, so one placed on a player who dies that night does nothing. Trap a living player who is likely to be attacked or to visit someone, not the player you are most suspicious of on Day 1. My Night 1 trap on Heidi was wasted when she died that night.

applies_to: Village roles that claim a checkable role
tip: Publicly claiming a role that kills or protects at night (such as Trapper) can make you the next Katana and Serial Killer target. I was killed the night after I claimed. Claim when the claim can change a vote or when it has already been revealed, not in a loop of repeated 'no nomination' posts.

A Day 1 private message between two players is a real lead, not noise. Heidi and Erin were the Yakuza pair, and the Heidi-Erin PM was flagged early. The town instead spent Day 2 pushing Grace, a Juror who was actually Village, and lost her as a checker. Chase the pair before the loud claimant.

Pressing an uncheckable claimant to a nomination mostly helps a Serial Killer. Frank pushed Grace to a failed vote, then used the same method on Erin. Demand a result that can be tested tonight, such as a Medic stop or a trap going off, before a nomination, not just 'explain yourself'.

A Standard Defense (a Serial Killer, or a Medic's self-protection) stops Standard attacks such as a Veteran's Stolen Blade. A failed Standard hit proves little. Against a suspected Serial Killer, use a Strong attack or a Strong alert instead of relying on a Standard shot.
Treat “Not Evil” as a limited appearance result, not a town clearance. A Serial Killer or Arsonist can read Not Evil to a Sheriff, and a Yakuza holding the Katana also reads Not Evil that night.

Check whether a claimed action would actually create a visit or trigger another role’s ability. A claimed Sheriff check must visit its target, but treat a resulting contradiction as evidence to investigate, not automatic proof: hidden survival effects can explain some apparent impossibilities.

At two players, a nomination needs both Yes votes and execution needs both Guilty votes. An opponent can agree to trial and then vote Innocent, making conviction impossible; account for this before treating a trial as a path to victory.
Do not wait indefinitely for a perfect target: a one-use attack dies with you. Set a clear trigger for using it, while still requiring enough evidence that a blind shot is worth the risk.
A Yakuza voting Guilty on a doomed teammate can look like honest prosecution and shape the next day's suspicion. Evaluate the vote alongside the player’s earlier pushes, claims, and night choices.

Choose a cover that fits your actual night actions and the public mechanics. A claim like “I checked the alerted Veteran” creates a visit that can be challenged if no attack or visit evidence supports it; a late hidden-trait explanation is much less persuasive.

Before spending a vote-manipulation token, consider whether your target is likely to survive until the trial. If your faction is also targeting them for a kill that night, the token may be wasted before they cast a vote.
A trial requires strictly more than half of all votes counted. With two players, both must vote Guilty to execute the accused; one Guilty and one Innocent is not enough.

A failed attack identifies neither the target’s role nor the source of their survival by itself. Check attack level against the highest Defense: a Standard Attack cannot beat Standard Defense, and protections do not stack.
Keep teammate coordination in night chat where possible. Even when private-message contents are hidden, the public ledger reveals who messaged whom and can make the connection a focus of questioning.

Recalculate majority thresholds as the living player count changes. With two players, both must vote Yes to pass a nomination and both must vote Guilty to execute; a defendant who votes Innocent can prevent a hang from a single Guilty vote.
Keep a precise private record of the claim you have made, including targets and results. Changing a claimed night target after someone challenges it gives opponents a concrete inconsistency to press.

Treat a failed attack as evidence, not an exact-role result: defense, protection, and hidden traits can all explain survival. Likewise, a death's cause can narrow the killer down without proving which living player caused it.

applies_to: Serial Killers and other solo killers
tip: Keep prioritizing your actual win condition in the endgame. Appeals to stall or spare someone are not a substitute for checking whether removing the last opponent wins immediately.

Don't spend alert tokens on nights with no credible threat. Bob went on alert N1, N2 and N3 with no visitors and was dead of a Serial Killer by Night 4 with zero tokens left. Save alerts for nights when the Serial Killer or Katana holder is likely to visit, and say so only after the fact if it matters.

A claimed alert with no visitors only contradicts a Sheriff's visit if the visitor is shown to be alive afterward. Erin survived, which pointed at a faked claim, but a one-use Narrow Escape could also explain it. Look for a second independent break before convicting on one contradiction.

Once a Serial Killer is alive, a Not Evil or Good read doesn't clear anyone. Only a Serial Killer's kills (who died to it) and the number of living players narrow the field. Track which deaths were Serial Killer kills versus Katana kills, since a Katana death implies a Yakuza holder and a Serial Killer death implies a Neutral.

With an even number of living players, a trial needs every Guilty vote to pass in a two-voter trial, and ties count as Innocent. A Village player with two survivors cannot hang anyone unless the other survivor agrees, so the Village has to win before the last two remain. Check the lock count before the 3-player stage, not after.

Spend Juror checks on pairs that include a player you need cleared or convicted, and check trial votes rather than nomination votes once trials exist. Nomination-vote agreement was almost always 1 of 1 or 2, so it told me very little. My two checks (Erin/Frank, Bob/Frank) both pointed at Frank without settling anything.

Any Day 1 private message between teammates is visible as a sent PM, and its wording can leak. My 'coordinate the Katana plan' PM to Erin became the town's first lead. Keep teammate contact to the night chat and use neutral wording if you must PM.

I died on Night 1 holding two Ritualist tokens and never used them. A one-shot guess is worth spending on the first suspect who looks like a Village Katana or killing target, since unused tokens die with you.

With two players alive, a trial needs both votes Guilty (1 of 2 is not a majority). A lone Village player can't hang a Neutral killer in a two-player endgame, so the Village has to hang the last Neutral before the count reaches two.

A dead Medic/Veteran-style claim can't be checked after death. Vote on mechanical breaks (a visit to an alerted Veteran, a trap going off, a Katana death), not on whose story sounds consistent. Erin was hanged on a Veteran claim that no one could verify.

Serial Killers win only alone, so the Village will not hang on appeals. Appealing to the killer by PM (as Bob did three times) did nothing. Make your pressure public and about checkable claims, not about the killer's motive.

Whenever someone claims a night result, check the visit it implies against what you know yourself, right away: your own alert, your trap, whether you were role-blocked, your own role. If a claim visited you on a night you know nobody did, say so in that same message and nominate. A contradiction you hold yourself is the strongest break in the game.
evidence: On Day 2 Erin claimed she checked Bob as Sheriff on Night 1. Bob then claimed Veteran with an alert and no visitors on Night 1, and also heard Frank say he had protected Bob. Nobody connected these until Grace did on Day 3. By then Carol was dead and Frank had become unbeatable.

tip: When there are Yakuza and a Neutral killer at about 5 players, up to two people die each night. 'Wait for tonight's results' costs a Villager every night. If you have one real break, hang it that Day. If you have none, push the shakiest claim to trial so a Day isn't wasted.
evidence: On Day 2 Bob, Carol and Grace each said several times that they would vote only on a checkable break. They passed no nomination even though Erin and Frank both had broken claims. That night Erin and Frank both killed Carol, leaving the Village unable to deal with both killers.

applies_to: Village players with a one-shot attack (Stolen Blade, Armed), and Vigilante
tip: If you privately know a claim is false, shoot the liar that night. Don't hold the shot or use your night on defense. Remember that Standard and Basic attacks can't kill a Serial Killer or Arsonist (Standard Defense), so aim them at a suspected Yakuza or an undefended liar.
evidence: From Day 2 on, Bob knew Erin's Sheriff check on him was a lie. On Night 2 he alerted instead, and his Standard Stolen Blade would have killed her. He used it on Night 3 against Frank, the SK, and it failed against Standard Defense.

tip: Don't announce which nights you will alert or how many tokens you have left. Killers just go around a known alert, which wastes your tokens and steers kills onto your allies. Once you've posted your count, they wait until you're out. Uncertainty is what makes an alert dangerous.
evidence: Bob announced alerts for Night 2 and Night 3 and posted his remaining tokens. Frank never visited him on an alert night, killing Carol and then Grace instead. He attacked Bob only on Night 4, after Bob had said he had no tokens left.

tip: Pick a fake claim that fits your token count, and don't invent a result on a living player who might contradict it with a Veteran alert, a trap or their own claim. If you must claim a result, name a dead player or claim a role whose results nobody can check. Give your excuses up front; a late 'Narrow Escape' reads as made up.
evidence: Erin, a Fixer with 2 tokens, claimed Sheriff, a role with no tokens, while Dave was counting her tokens. She said she had checked Bob, who turned out to be an alerting Veteran. She brought up Narrow Escape only after Bob nominated her, and she was hanged 3-1.

tip: Never PM a teammate on Day 1. With 8 players, the one visible PM becomes the whole town's lead and draws traps, checks and kills from Neutral killers too.
evidence: Heidi's Day 1 PM to Erin was the only data that Day. Carol trapped Heidi because of it, Frank (the SK) killed Heidi on Night 1, and Alice and Frank kept the PM in play against Erin.

applies_to: Juror, and everyone reading secret votes
tip: Nomination votes are secret, so a Juror check on the nominator and a suspect can expose a hidden ally. Point it at the pair who pushed a no-data nomination, and post the result with what it implies.
evidence: Frank nominated Grace for not claiming, and the nomination got 2 Yes votes. Grace checked Erin and Frank and got 1 of 1 agreement, which proved Erin had voted Yes with Frank. That backed up the Day 3 case against Erin.

tip: Claim a protective role that explains surviving an attack, kill whoever is collecting vote and pairing data, and stay away from anyone who has announced a defense until they're out of it. In a two-player trial, remember that both votes are needed to execute, so you can safely vote Yes on your own nomination and still vote Innocent.
evidence: Frank claimed Medic and explained surviving the Katana on Night 3 as self-protection. He killed Grace, the Juror, on Night 3 and avoided Bob's alerts. On Day 4 he correctly pointed out that a single Guilty vote couldn't hang him, then killed Bob to win.

tip: A 'no attack' result clears a player only for that one night, because the Yakuza move the Katana. Spend the second-target token to re-check someone you 'cleared' earlier while you test a new suspect. On N3 Bob made no attack, but on N4 he held the Katana and my hit on him killed him.

Before you act, write tonight's targets in your will, plus how to read each outcome (e.g. 'if X dies to Enforcer, X was the holder'). If you die that same night, the cause of death and your will can still prove a Yakuza even though your result never arrives.

Check every Tracker or count-style claim against the wills of the dead and the role each will claims. A Tracker whose 'new' information only ever goes against Village claimers' wills, and whose 'confirmations' only repeat claims already public, is probably a fake. So is a counter whose numbers back that Tracker.

Every trial vote you cast counts as Guilty, so never be one of the players the town expects to vote Innocent. When you read the totals, remember your vote is fixed: a lone Innocent can't be yours, which narrows down who cast it.
A Yakuza teammate's last will or fake counts pushing a suspect is weak evidence against that suspect. If anything, it points toward whoever the dead Yakuza backed.

Never give a fake result that contradicts something a Villager can still back up: a will, an action they announced earlier, or a later result. A dead player's will can say 'audited X'. If your track says he visited no one, the clash stays on record, and once a teammate is exposed it becomes the case that hangs you. If you have to contradict someone, do it only to a living claimant whose action nobody else can check.

Look at whom a living Enforcer (or Vigilante, Veteran and so on) has actually visited on past nights, not whom they 'cleared'. An Enforcer who checked you twice will often check you again. Give the Katana to the teammate that killer has never visited, or kill or block the killer before moving the Katana. A dead holder killed by an Enforcer is proof of Yakuza, and every claim they backed falls with them.

applies_to: Yakuza with a passive-counter cover (Fortune Teller, Cartographer)
