A Sheriff's Evil read on a counterclaimed player can be a Fabricator frame. Once a Fabricator has been drawn or proven, ask for a second, independent break before hanging on one Evil read, especially when the target's own results keep fitting the known visits.

Once a Fabricator is confirmed (an Insomniac draw, say), the Yakuza will frame whoever you are most likely to check next: a counterclaimer, or someone you publicly said looked suspicious. An Evil read on that obvious target is weak evidence. Check a less obvious player, or wait for a second source before nominating on it alone.

When two investigators of the same role read each other Evil, think about a Roleplayer. It believes its own random results, so it can look exactly like a lying Yakuza. A claim that contradicts a revealed fact, like reading Not Evil on someone who was actually Evil, fits a Roleplayer as well as a liar.

A Chronicler's death reveal is an exact-role check, so a Disguised player is revealed as their disguise. In this game a 'Party Animal' reveal was really a Yakuza Ballot Stuffer, so don't treat a revealed role as proof of alignment.

A player who survives repeated Katana attacks, reads Not Evil, and posts tracks that put someone else on every Serial Killer victim is the Serial Killer's profile. A Basic-attack kill on the scapegoat proves the scapegoat had no Defense, which breaks the tracker's story.

In the late game, if Katana kills have stopped and no Katana attack has landed for several nights, the Yakuza may be wiped out or crippled. Put every hang on the remaining solo killer before it can take the town down to a loss.

Don't fake a visit-based result about the first night-killed player. Their visitors (the killer, Chronicler marks, investigators) come out the next day and break the claim at once. A claim broken this early, with no reason behind the lie, reads as Jester or Roleplayer, and the town spares you. Pick a fake that can't be checked yet but makes you look Yakuza, for example a cover role that fits only a Yakuza's visits.

Never ask to be hanged, and never announce a night target with 'stop me by hanging me'. Experienced tables call that Jester bait right away, and a Vigilante will shoot you instead. That night death kills you without a win. Get hanged by looking like a real Yakuza: quietly defend the player the town is about to hang, vote with them, and keep your stories consistent rather than escalating.

Your best hang window is the first Day with nominations, while the table is big and eager. Spread suspicion across several days so a single break doesn't settle it. Once the town says 'Jester' out loud, every later outrageous move confirms it. Switch to low-key Yakuza-like behaviour, such as one PM to a suspect or an Innocent vote on a confirmed-Evil player, and stop making new claims.

Sleepwalker means you really do visit someone every night. A Tracker who says you 'visited no one' is lying, or was blocked. If you have Sleepwalker, a Tracker's 'no visit' report on you is a mechanical break of that Tracker, so use it. Here the SK faked exactly that report about me.

A Tracker whose 'tracks' keep putting one player on the SK's victims, with no other source backing them, is often the SK framing that player. Ask for independent confirmation before hanging on repeated tracks from one source.

The Katana is only a Standard attack, so it can never kill a Serial Killer, who has Standard Defense. If a Katana target survives with no protector claimed, assume they're the SK or have Narrow Escape. Switch to another target instead of hitting them again. Attacking the same survivor twice wasted two of our kills while the SK picked off the team.

applies_to: Yakuza with Armed or other one-shot attacks
tip: Fire a one-shot Basic gun early, on Night 1 or 2, at the strongest confirmed threat or as a backup to the Katana. Unused tokens and guns are lost when you die, and an SK can kill you on Night 1. Saving the gun 'for the right moment' can mean never using it.

Use what the team privately knows to locate the SK. Example: a player falsely claims a Not Evil Sheriff read on a teammate, or claims to have visited a teammate who died to the SK. That player is either the SK or a Roleplayer. Then you can frame them or steer the town onto them, rather than spending the Katana.

Framing players who are already counterclaimed gets town players hanged on a single Evil read, which works well. But it also uses up town hangs that the SK benefits from too. With a Neutral killer loose, consider sometimes framing the player you suspect is the SK.
If you hold a disguise trait, write your cover claim into your last will from Day 1. A Chronicler mark can reveal your disguised role on death, which keeps your teammates' covers believable.

Claiming Sleepwalker hands a fake Tracker an easy frame: they can 'track' you onto each night's body. From the first night, ask for a second, independent tracker or watcher on you, and point out early and in public that the tracks come from only one source. Don't wait until the case is built.

Saying publicly that you survived a Katana attack with no protector fits a Serial Killer's Standard Defense almost perfectly, and it will be used against you. Hold the report until a protector or another explanation (Shaky, Narrow Escape) can back it, or announce it together with a test that can clear you.

applies_to: Village (when a Vigilante has a Basic shot left)
tip: A Basic 'SK test' shot only works if it fails. When it kills, the dead player was town, unless it hits a Jester or Executioner, who have Basic Defense too. If you are the likely test target, say this publicly and steer the shot toward the player supplying the evidence against you (here, the lone tracker).

Combine your groups with the other Scout's groups and with the known links (who tracked or watched whom, who died) to place the SK victim's group each night. Post the players this excludes, not just the raw names. Bare names convince nobody.
Faultline results confirm or break Zealot/Merciful claims and lone-Innocent voters at no cost. Post them right after each trial: they make trial totals checkable and help prove you are town.

Once a Fabricator is confirmed (an Insomniac draw, a Profiler result, etc.), don't count a lone Sheriff Evil read as a mechanical break. The Fabricator frames counterclaimers and contested claimants, which are exactly the players a Sheriff is most likely to check. Before hanging, ask for a second, independent source.

A Lookout 'confirming' that a Sheriff visited the player he read Evil is weak support. A Fabricator has to visit the same target to frame it, so a Yakuza Fabricator can safely claim to have watched that target and 'seen' the Sheriff. Treat that kind of confirmation as possibly coming from the framer.

An exact-role draw proves that a role exists and visited. It doesn't prove there's only one holder of that role. A 'Scout visited' draw proves a Sleepwalker Scout exists, but a second, passive Scout who never visits is still possible. Don't use the draw to call a duplicate claimant a liar.

A Chronicler's reveal on death is an exact-role check, so it shows a Disguised player's disguise. A 'revealed' Village role can be a disguised Yakuza. Here the 'Party Animal' was really a Ballot Stuffer. Keep that in mind when a claim like 'my check matched her revealed role' doesn't add up.

When a single Tracker repeatedly puts the same player on the Serial Killer's victims and nobody corroborates it, suspect the Tracker. A Serial Killer can make up tracks onto its own kills. Weigh who the only source is before hanging the tracked player.

Once a Fabricator is known to exist, treat a lone Evil Sheriff read as a lead, not a hang. This goes double when the read hits a counterclaimer or a player whose claim can't be checked. Look for the frame's visit: a 'Lookout' who says they watched the player who just read Evil may really be the Fabricator who visited them. Ask for a second, independent check before you convict.
evidence: Olivia's draw showed a Fabricator on Night 1. Even so, Heidi (Day 3) and Carol (Day 4) were each hanged mainly on one Evil read from Ivan, and both were frames. Grace's claimed Night 2 watch on Heidi and the Night 3 watch on Carol in her will were her real framing visits.

applies_to: everyone, especially Neutral killers and Yakuza
tip: Never write anything in a PM that you wouldn't want quoted publicly. The recipient can post it word for word, and your 'that's not what I wrote' is just your word against theirs. Make deals or pleas in terms that stay deniable, or don't make them at all.
evidence: On Day 5 Frank PM'd Dave: 'You know what I am: the Katana bounced off me twice... Vote Innocent and I take a town player tonight.' Dave quoted it, and Frank was hanged 4 to 1. That ended the game.

applies_to: Serial Killer and other solo killers
tip: Fake results that tie one living player to your kills are fragile. If that player dies in a way that rules them out (killed by a Basic shot, revealed role), every one of those results is exposed at once. Pick a cover that no later death can disprove, or vary your fake results.
evidence: Frank 'tracked' Niaj onto Bob and onto Grace. Then Alice's Basic shot killed Niaj, proving he had no Defense, and Ivan, Alice and Erin all called Frank's tracks fabricated.

tip: If a Katana attack fails on a target nobody claims to have protected, assume they have innate Defense (a Serial Killer, say) or that your holder is Shaky. Don't attack them again with Standard. Move the Katana to another teammate, and use the Day to steer the town's vote onto the survivor.
evidence: Bob's Katana failed on Niaj (Night 1) and on Frank (Night 2). On Night 3 Grace attacked Frank again with Standard and failed, while Frank killed her. Frank killed all three Yakuza.

tip: When a player drops one fake claim for another and begs to be hanged, refuse the hang. If the table agrees they're a liar, a Vigilante shot or the Serial Killer can remove them without setting off a Jester's hang-only revenge.
evidence: Judy went from Lookout to Vigilante and announced a shot to provoke a hang. The town held firm on Day 2. On Night 3 Alice shot her (Jester confirmed), so the Grudge and Jester revenge never fired.

tip: Don't hang on a duplicate claim or on 'two of the same role is unlikely'. Hand-picked setups often repeat roles. Before using a clash as evidence, check whether both players' results fit the known visits.
evidence: Niaj and Carol were both real Scouts. Niaj survived Day 2 because voters found no mechanical break. Carol was later hanged partly on the 'two Scouts is unlikely' argument.

tip: Post the exact result in the role's own words (for example 'Mallory: Not Evil'), not a vague 'my result was consistent with X'. Vague wording reads like a different kind of check and becomes the case against you.
evidence: Heidi said her result 'matched her Party Animal reveal'. Alice argued that only an exact-role check (a Diviner's) could produce that, and the argument helped get Heidi hanged.

tip: Use a Basic 'test' shot only on the player whose own claim is broken. If the case against your target comes from a single unverified source, shoot or push the source instead.
evidence: Alice shot Niaj on Night 4 because of Frank's tracks alone. Niaj was a town Scout, and the wills of both Niaj and Olivia had already flagged Frank as the only source behind those tracks.

tip: Write a real last will at the start of Night 1 and update it each night. A will is published the moment you die, and I died on Night 1 with no will on file, so the Village got none of my role or block information.

applies_to: Lookout, Tracker, Sheriff and other investigators
tip: A role-block result ("You were role-blocked") tells you a blocker or Party Animal exists and that your watch got nothing. Post that fact publicly the next Day, since it is the only information a dead investigator leaves behind.

A player who names a Katana or night-attack victim before that attack is public is showing private Yakuza knowledge. Grace did this on Day 2 and called it a guess. Treat early, unsourced knowledge of a secret night result as a strong Yakuza tell and push for the source at once.
The Avenger trait only deals Basic Attacks back, so it does little against Standard Defense (Serial Killer) or any protected attacker. Don't count on it as a deterrent; it is weak retaliation.

Before nominating, ask each claimant for the exact target and result of their last night. Several players spent Day 2 asking for the same thing and never got it, so the nomination was decided on wording alone.

If someone states a fact that should only be known to a player or faction with private information, ask for the source and check who could actually know it. Treat it as strong evidence, not absolute proof: a guess can be lucky, but an unsupported explanation does not erase the information leak.

Read attack results through the attack-versus-defense rules before drawing conclusions. A Serial Killer's Standard Defense explains surviving a Standard Katana attack; survival alone does not prove protection, and the victim's notice identifies the attacking role or weapon, not the attacker.

Evaluate each kill against your actual solo win condition, not just whether it removes a player. Account for other players' win conditions and the simultaneous end-of-night win check; a successful kill does not help if you die and leave only a different faction alive.
Choose a cover that is both plausible and allowed by the setup. Make sure the role fits your actual actions, and avoid claiming a role the setup rules out; coordinate consistent covers in night chat.

Before defending a teammate on trial, calculate whether your vote could actually save them. If the hang is already secure, a visible defense may draw attention without changing the result; blend with the majority instead.

Account for target defenses when choosing a Katana target: a Standard attack cannot kill someone with Standard Defense. A failed attack is ambiguous, so avoid treating it as proof of who attacked or why it failed.
If a target has claimed Avenger, weigh the retaliation before making a fatal attack: each attack that would have killed them can trigger an attack back on its attacker.
Keep coordination in night chat rather than sending daytime private messages, and make sure the team submits consistent Katana votes.

Before spending a Strong shot on a claimed Serial Killer or other 'threat', check whether the target's death would actually change the Yakuza count. Spending the last tokens on a Day-2 read left the Village with no killing power for the rest of the game, and the remaining Katana holder then killed the Vigilante.

A public statement that reveals private night information (e.g. naming a Katana victim before that victim has disclosed their notice) is one of the strongest mechanical tells in this game. Ask the speaker for the exact source immediately, and weigh a non-answer heavily.
Never repeat night-chat-only facts (the agreed target, the holder) in public. The Grunt's Day-2 leak of the Katana target was the only real break in the Yakuza's cover, and the town lynched on it.

A Decoy can't control whether they die at night, so their best play is to look like a non-threat that a killer will want to remove. Avoid nominations and Guilty votes that could only lead to a day death, since those lose the win condition outright.

Don't ride a pile-on with a bare wording slip. Six Guilty votes on Grace rested on one line she had already admitted to, so the lynch was right by accident. Demand a concrete mechanical break from the nominator, or the town hangs on pressure.

When someone reveals information before its public source is known, ask exactly who could have learned it and how. A detail can be private from most players but available through faction chat or a shared action; an unexplained source is stronger evidence than a vague wording mismatch.

applies_to: Sheriff and anyone evaluating alignment checks
tip: Treat an alignment result as limited information, not a clearance. In particular, the Yakuza Katana holder appears Good to alignment checks that night, so a Not Evil result can come from a Yakuza.

Choose an attack level that can actually beat plausible Defense: an Attack must be strictly higher than Defense. If a likely threat may have Standard Defense, a Standard shot will fail; save tokens when you lack a reason to attack, but don't leave a confirmed threat untouched just to preserve them.

Remember the Avenger trigger: if you are killed at night, each player whose attack would have killed you is dealt a Basic Attack. Keep that consequence in mind when assessing the risk of a night kill and make the trigger clear in your will.

applies_to: Village investigators and anyone evaluating their results
tip: Treat “Not Evil” as a limited result, not a clearance. Check which roles can appear Not Evil, and remember that the Katana holder also reads Not Evil that night.

Track who could know each piece of information and when. If someone states a private result before its recipient reveals it, ask for the source; distinguish a verified timeline anomaly from an unsupported guess.

Choose protection strength with attack levels in mind: Standard Defense stops Standard attacks, but not a Strong Serial Killer attack. Keep your will precise about what you attempted versus what actually took effect.
A role-block cancels the action and spends no tokens. Update any public account or will accordingly rather than describing the intended protection or action as completed.

Before you state any night fact in public (who was attacked, who visited whom, who died how), ask whether only the Yakuza night chat could know it. If yes, say nothing until the fact is public through the proper channel. My Day 2 'Bob was the only attack victim' line came from team knowledge and got me nominated and hanged.

Once a private-knowledge slip is caught, do not invent a vague 'guess from chatter' excuse. Every follow-up treated it as a lie. Either give a plausible public source in advance, or concede the wording and move the discussion to verifiable public facts.

Agree on a Night 1 cover that also covers knowledge. A Grunt with no action should have a prepared line for how it knows the Katana plan or results (for example, it is simply told results it can state as public), so it does not have to improvise under a nomination.

A single unsourced advance-knowledge line was enough for five Yes votes and six Guilty votes. When a player is caught knowing something they should not, treat it as a concrete mechanical break and ask for the source immediately, before the nomination forms.

Keep the team's public story on Day 2 simple and consistent with what every living claimant can be checked against. Nominations of a teammate-adjacent player are much harder to defend when your own claims are unverifiable.

A Not Evil result on a player who held the Katana that night is a false clear, because the holder reads Good to alignment checks. Before trusting a clear, check whether that target could have been the Katana holder, and say so in the post instead of only hedging about Serial Killers and Decoys.

If a player names a night victim or an attack before it is public, treat it as a strong Yakuza tell. Yakuza share night chat, so advance knowledge of a Katana hit usually comes from a teammate. Press for the exact source and vote on it once they can't give one.
Spending all tokens on a confirmed lead worked. Firing a Strong shot on a target whose claim broke was a good use. Keep this pattern: fire when a claim breaks, not to test a claim.
A lone wording slip is weak evidence, but a slip plus an unanswered source question on the same point makes a concrete case. Ask for the source once, in public, and vote on the answer or the silence.

Never say anything in public that you could only know from night chat or the Yakuza summary: who the Katana hit, whether it failed, who a teammate blocked. Before each message, ask whether a Villager with your claimed role could know it. If you slip, give a believable source at once or own it plainly. A vague 'it was a guess' gets you hanged.
evidence: Grace said Bob was the Night 1 attack victim before Bob revealed his private notice. Erin nominated her for it, and she was hanged 6-1 after offering only 'a guess from Day 1 chatter'.

tip: If someone states a private fact before the only player who could have shared it has done so, and no PMs were sent, that is a knowledge leak. Treat it as a strong mechanical break, as good as a first-person slip, not as a wording issue. Ask once for the exact source, then nominate if the answer is vague.
evidence: Erin, Heidi, Frank and Bob saw that Grace named Bob's private Katana hit early with no logged PMs. The hang removed a real Yakuza on Day 2.

tip: Don't publicly confirm that you survived an attack when no protector has claimed you. Surviving with no protection points to innate Defense, which points to a Neutral killer. If asked, stay quiet or keep it vague, especially when your claimed role has no Defense.
evidence: Bob claimed Coroner, then confirmed he had survived a Katana attack. Erin's will says she shot him because he 'survived a Katana attack despite no protection on him being claimed', and her Strong shot killed him.

tip: When you shoot a suspected Neutral killer, use enough tokens to get past Standard Defense. A Basic or Standard shot does nothing against a Serial Killer or Arsonist. Save cheap Basic shots for suspected Yakuza.
evidence: Erin spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot at Bob. It beat his Standard Defense and killed the Serial Killer. A Basic or Standard shot, like the failed Katana and Avenger attacks on Night 1, would have done nothing.

tip: If your Katana attack fails and no protector reports stopping it, the target probably has Defense and may be a Neutral killer. Use that in your plan. Often the best move is to point the town at that player instead of attacking them again or ignoring them. Choose your next kill knowing a Village killer may have a trait that hits back.
evidence: The Katana failed on Bob on Night 1 and Frank's protection was on Carol, so the Yakuza had reason to think Bob was a Defense role. On Night 2 Carol's kill on Erin, who had nominated Grace, set off Erin's Avenger trait and killed Carol, which ended the game.

tip: When your teammate is clearly doomed, vote Yes and Guilty and speak against them. Saving your own cover matters more than a symbolic Innocent vote that shows up in the totals.
evidence: Carol voted Yes and Guilty on Grace and publicly said the leak was concrete. She came out of Day 2 without suspicion, and only the Avenger trait brought her down.

tip: On Night 2 and later, block the player most likely to kill your side, usually a quiet player who just pushed a hang or someone a public break has primed to shoot. A claimed Medic is less dangerous when your target is unprotected anyway.
evidence: Carol blocked Frank (Medic), who was protecting Heidi, not Erin. Erin's shot went through, and Erin's Avenger trait still killed Carol, leaving the Yakuza with nobody.

applies_to: Village, especially Sheriff and any claimant
tip: A Sheriff's Evil read is not enough to hang on its own. Evil also fits Jesters, Executioners, Notorious and Turncoat players, and framed players. Before hanging a read, look for a second source: a Lookout or other visit result, a Katana victim's visitor, or a claim that conflicts with the read. Here Grace was a Jester, so the read was accurate, but hanging her handed the Jester its win.

Do not spend a kill on an unverified claim. Heidi's Basic shot killed a real Medic on the strength of a claim that was never tested, and that cost the Village its protection and its best late-game information. Fire only on a concrete break, such as a first-person slip or a visit that contradicts the claim.

Treat a Lookout's who-visited report as strong evidence, because it is a visit count. A player who visits a victim or claims a Katana survival can be tested against that count. Ask the Lookout and Sheriff for the same night's visits before you vote, and weigh a result that only one claimant can see as weaker than one that two claimants corroborate.

When a wrong vote is likely to create a Jester win, check whether a hang still helps the Village. A Jester that pushes hard and asks for the rope is a classic sign. Prefer a bare-majority Guilty vote and wait for a second signal before you hang a player who is only pushing hard.

A trial vote total above the number of voters means a Ballot Stuffer or a Mayor's doubled vote changed the count, not an error. Count the total against the living voters before you read anything into a vote, and check a Mayor's reveal against the tally.

Never name your own role in public, even in passing. My opener said 'Bob here, Grunt with no night action.' The retraction did not undo it, and the Village hanged me on that one word. Use generic wording like 'no night action' instead of a role name.

Agree in night chat how each teammate will vote on the day, especially who doubles a vote. My teammate Carol's Ballot Stuffer vote (counted twice) was the deciding Guilty on my trial, and I could not see it coming. Confirm the day plan with every teammate before the trial.

An accused player who says 'judge me on that' with no result to offer, after a losing defence, may be a Jester inviting the rope. Hanging a Jester wins them the game. Vote Guilty only on a mechanical break (a result, a visit, a first-person slip), not on the accused's own resignation.

Do not shoot a claimed role on one unverified claim. Heidi's N2 shot killed a real Medic whose protection had been active, and the Village lost its only protector. Wait for a second source or a clash before spending a Basic shot.

When the trial count is higher than the number of voters, first identify the source: a Ballot Stuffer adds one extra vote, a revealed Mayor doubles their trial votes. Do not attribute the extra vote to the accused or to a random defender until you know which of these is in play.

Don't spend Night 1 holding with no kill just to wait for claims. With only two Yakuza, every night a Village power role (Vigilante, Medic, Lookout) keeps acting, and the Vigilante killed two of our likely reads. A Night 1 kill on the most dangerous unclaimed player is often worth more than the information you'd gain by waiting.

Never put your own role name in an opener. A first-person 'Grunt' slip was the only hard evidence against Bob, and once it's said it can't be unsaid. Pre-agree a cover role that fits your tokens and real visits, and agree a deflection line for a teammate's slip before the Day starts.

A teammate who pushes hard to defend a doomed partner, or who defends a suspect who is later revealed as a Jester, gets noticed. Vote with the town on a clear hang and save your credibility for the later votes that matter, instead of defending a teammate you can't save.

A doubled vote shows up as a total with more votes than voters, which tells the whole town a manipulator exists. Stuff only when the trial is close and the extra vote decides it. Otherwise the anomaly just hands the Village a lead to chase.

A Vigilante kill that reports the victim's exact role is a free, public exact-role check. Use it to confirm or refute a claimed role of the victim (here Frank's Medic claim was confirmed). Count such confirmations before trusting an unverified claim.

When a Jester could be among the accused, a player who argues hard against a hang and then fails to answer a concrete counter-result is a suspect, but not proof. Hanging them can win the game for a Jester, so look for a Yakuza-consistent contradiction before voting Guilty.
Separate what a result proves from what it merely fits. A Lookout confirming that someone visited a target supports the visit, not the visitor’s role, action, or result.
An Evil Sheriff result is not proof of Yakuza: some Neutrals, such as Jesters and Executioners, also read Evil. Look for faction-level evidence before hanging someone on an alignment result alone.
Track the announced vote total against the number of voters and account for known modifiers. A mismatch proves the count changed, but by itself does not identify the voter or their original vote.
Do not spend a kill token just to test an unverified claim. Wait for a concrete contradiction or other strong evidence; a premature shot can remove a valuable Village role.

A 'nobody visited' result is real information: it proves the watched player was not the Katana or shot target that night. Pick watch targets to test the most likely killers' prey (claimed investigators, loud analysts), not only the most-argued-about claimant. Don't reveal your target publicly before the night resolves.

When a total has more votes than voters, note which trial and which players were defended or voted with the nominee. The extra vote came from a Ballot Stuffer, usually a Yakuza or Neutral. Track that player's later votes and defenses; it is a stronger lead than any single wording slip.

Before hanging, check whether the strongest defender of a suspect has a reason to want the hang to fail. A player who argues hard against a hang on thin evidence may be a Jester who wants the rope. Vote on evidence and avoid pushing a nomination that rests on one wording slip.

A Yakuza-only role claimed in first person (here 'Grunt') is strong evidence, but a retraction can make it ambiguous. Ask the claimant what role they meant before the vote, and do not make the Guilty vote depend only on that wording.

Once two or more claims conflict, compare each claim against a visit or a kill. Ask the claimant who attacked them and who visited them, rather than trading claims that each only repeat the same visit.

Protect the most credible exposed threat, and match defense to the danger: Standard Defense stops a Standard Katana attack, so save a token for Strong Defense unless there is reason to expect a stronger attack. Record in your will both whom you protected and whether your protection stopped an attack.
Treat an Evil Sheriff result as evidence of Evil alignment, not proof of Yakuza. Consider Jester and Executioner before spending a trial on the read alone, and seek corroboration when possible.
A vote total exceeding the number of voters establishes deliberate vote manipulation, but not who caused it. Track the discrepancy as a lead, not as proof against a particular player.
Become suspicious through a plausible, unpopular position rather than openly asking to be hanged. A weak but credible defense can keep the town arguing about you until it chooses a daytime execution.

An Evil alignment result does not establish that someone is Yakuza: Jesters and Executioners also read Evil. Before acting on the result, consider whether hanging the target could give a Neutral their win.
Set a concrete trigger for limited shots. A claimed role is not a faction check; shooting an unverified Medic can remove a valuable Village protector.
Compare announced vote totals with both the number of voters and known vote modifiers. A doubled Mayor vote can explain more counted votes than voters without implying a hidden ballot manipulation.

applies_to: Vigilantes and other limited-use village killers
tip: Spend a kill token only on a target with concrete evidence against them. An unverified protective-role claim is not evidence of evil; killing a real protector can cost the Village more than waiting for a stronger lead.

applies_to: Sheriffs and everyone weighing Sheriff results
tip: An Evil result is an alignment result, not proof of Yakuza. Neutrals such as Jesters and Executioners can read Evil, and a corroborated visit confirms someone visited the target—not that they are a Sheriff or that their reported result is genuine.

Interpret unusual vote totals using all known vote-count rules. A total larger than the number of voters proves that votes were counted differently, but does not by itself identify the role or voter responsible; a revealed Mayor can also add a trial vote.

On Night 1, agree in night chat on one real Village role as each member's cover. Pick a role that fits your tokens and visits, and is not excluded by the setup notes. Never say your own role's name in public, even to call yourself powerless. If you have to stay vague, say 'no night result' and give no role name.
evidence: Bob's Day 2 opener was 'Bob here, Grunt with no night action,' and he was nominated and hanged that same Day. Carol later claimed 'Villager', but the setup says nobody has Vanilla Villager. Any Village player who checked would have caught it, so she survived only because nobody did.

tip: Before you spend a Ballot Stuffer token, count the likely votes. Use it only when your extra vote changes the result. A stuffed vote that loses still shows that a Ballot Stuffer exists, and it marks you as one of the few players who voted against the town.
evidence: Carol doubled her Innocent vote on Bob and lost 5-4 anyway; without the token it would have been 5-3. The 9-from-8 count was noticed right away (Dave said so on Day 3), and the three Innocent voters on Bob were Bob, the Jester and Carol. That left Carol as the clear remaining suspect, and Heidi shot her.

tip: Treat an Evil Sheriff read on a player who has no role claim, votes Yes on their own nomination and won't defend themself as a likely Jester. Leave them alive, or let only a bare majority vote Guilty. A revealed Mayor should be especially careful, since their doubled Guilty raises their own chance of being picked for the revenge.
evidence: Grace read Evil, claimed nothing, voted Yes on her own nomination and said 'Judge me on that.' The town hanged her 7-0 and she won as Jester. Her revenge then killed Dave, the confirmed Mayor, and with him the Village's doubled vote.

tip: Don't shoot a player whose claim nothing contradicts, especially a protector. Wait for a real break: an impossible role claim, a vote pattern that matches the Yakuza, or a lone visitor to a victim. Use a Basic shot first on the one player left without a checkable claim.
evidence: On Night 2 Heidi shot Frank, the real Medic, because his claim was 'unverified'. The Village lost its protector the same night he saved the Sheriff. Her Night 3 shot was at Carol: no real claim, an Innocent vote on Bob, and a probable Ballot Stuffer. That shot killed the last Yakuza and won the game.

tip: Check every role claim against the setup notes. A claim of a role the setup excludes, such as Vanilla Villager here, or of a Yakuza-only role, is a mechanical break as strong as a Sheriff result.
evidence: Carol claimed 'Villager' on Day 2 and nobody pointed out that the setup excludes it. Had someone caught it on Day 2 or Day 3, the town could have hanged her before Erin was killed on Night 3.

tip: The night after an investigator claims in public, protect them. Claimed Sheriffs and Lookouts are where the Yakuza send the Katana first.
evidence: Alice claimed Sheriff on Day 2. Frank protected her on Night 2 and stopped Carol's Katana attack, which kept the Sheriff alive for the Grace and Carol checks.

tip: In a small game, use the Katana on Night 1, ideally on a likely investigator. Skipping gives the Village a free night of results and keeps their numbers up for votes and Vigilante mistakes.
evidence: Bob and Carol agreed not to attack on Night 1. Alice and Erin both got results that night that backed each other up the next Day, and the Yakuza ended with only two kills in the whole game while the Village stayed ahead.

tip: Set a plausible Village cover early and keep it consistent with your actual visits and results. Avoid revealing a Yakuza-only role or inventing a new claim only after suspicion lands on you.
Remember that a Katana attack is a visit by the holder. Before choosing a target, account for claimed Lookouts and Trackers: a sole visitor to a Katana victim can make the holder easy to identify.
Treat a failed attack as evidence, not noise. A protection may explain it, so reassess whether to target the same player again or change plans rather than assuming the next attack will work.
Coordinate not just the holder and target, but a public cover story that fits the team's actions. A teammate's accurate but faction-revealing claim can undo otherwise careful play.

applies_to: Tracker, Lookout, Sheriff and other investigators
tip: Your result that clears a suspect marks you as a Katana target: I claimed Tracker on Day 2 with a result clearing Frank (a Yakuza), and was killed that night. Before posting a clearing result, weigh whether it exposes you, and post exact visit lists so teammates can check them.

A Katana attack requires a holder visit, so the victim's visitor list is the strongest mechanical lever. Cross-check every claimed visit against each claimant's own action and against any Lookout or Tracker result before accepting a count.

Resolve Yakuza-only role claims (such as Grunt) immediately, before any unrelated vote. Frank claimed Grunt on Day 2 and survived to Night 2 while the town argued over visit counts, which gave the Yakuza time to remove the Tracker.

A Katana holder's attack is itself a visit, so a cover role must be able to explain that visit. Alice's passive Fortune Teller cover could not explain her Night 2 visit to Bob, which a Lookout exposed. Pick a cover whose real actions would plausibly target the kill victim, and never claim a passive role for a visit you made.

Changing a role claim after nomination (Dave: Enforcer, then Vulture) is a concrete break the town will pounce on. If you must lie, hold to one story and let the visit lists carry your defence rather than a late reveal.

Protect the claimed information role the Katana is most likely to hit, such as a Tracker or Lookout who has just produced a visit result, rather than an investigator who is already safe. On Night 2 I protected Grace, who was never attacked, and the Katana killed the Tracker Bob.

A Katana holder's attack is always a visit to the victim, so any Lookout or Tracker watching that victim will see it. Test each claim against visits: a passive or visit-free role cannot explain a visit to a victim, and a claim switch after nomination is a strong tell.

A holder who attacks a target can't hide the visit, so pick a cover role whose visit to that same target looks ordinary, and never claim a passive role that the watch results contradict. Keep covers word for word and avoid vague 'no action' wording that invites questions.

Ask claimants for exact visit targets and results rather than counts. A Fortune Teller count only gives numbers, and two days of arguing over visitor totals decided nothing until a concrete role claim broke.

Never change a public role claim after being nominated. A switch from one claimed role to another reads as panic and as a lie, and it was the main reason my Day 2 trial went 7 to 1 against me. If the claim is false, drop it before the nomination, not during the trial.

Spend the Vulture visit on a player likely to die that night, such as a claimed investigator or a loud analyst, not on a player with no action. A visit to a survivor gains nothing and wastes the night, and a visit to a no-action player tests nothing that matters.

A Katana holder's visit is seen by any living Tracker or Lookout. Before killing, check whether a watcher will see the holder's visit, and if one will, either remove the watcher or pick a cover whose visit pattern explains it, because a lone visitor to a victim is what exposed Alice.

Test each claim against exact visits and results before voting. A Lookout's watch on a victim that names one visitor, when a claimed Fortune Teller or Sheriff says otherwise, is the kind of corroborated break that settles a vote; weigh it above echoed leans.

If you must lie about a role, choose a claim whose results you can repeat exactly and that fits the visits everyone can see. Evasive answers such as a bare visit with no named role invite suspicion faster than a plain true answer.

A Basic shot that kills reveals the exact role, so use it on a lead that already has a second piece of evidence, such as a role claim that breaks against visits. Here the kill turned Frank's Grunt claim into proof and removed a Yakuza. Expect the surviving Yakuza to counterclaim the role you exposed.

Build a per-night visitor list from every claim and test it against the Katana victim. A Lookout watch on a Katana victim that shows one visitor who claims a passive role (Fortune Teller) is a concrete break, and it decided Alice's trial. Ask each claimant for their visit target in one line instead of reconciling counts in public.

A role switch after nomination (Dave: Enforcer, then Vulture) is a strong tell but not proof of Yakuza. Before voting Guilty, check whether the hang lowers the Yakuza count. Hanging a Neutral does not, so prefer a Yakuza lead or a claim that visits contradict.

Don't claim a Yakuza-only role such as Grunt in public, and don't switch from a no-action claim to it under pressure. Frank's switch was the break the Village used. Pick a cover that no visit or kill can contradict, and keep it word for word.
A Basic or Strong kill can have several plausible causes (Katana, a Vigilante shot, innate Defense). Don't assume one visitor explains a death until the visit lists and the death cause agree.

applies_to: Village roles with visit-based results (Lookout, Tracker)
tip: If you watch or track a player who was hit by a Katana attack on the night they died, your visit result is strong evidence that can clear or expose claims. Post it once, with the night, target and exact result, before the claimed roles can be contested.

A role claim made only after being nominated, or a cover switched after a visit result contradicts it, is a strong guilty signal. Keep your claim fixed from the first time you state it, because switching under pressure is what got Dave and Alice hanged.

Do not give a vague 'no action' answer to every question. Name a plausible tokenless Village or neutral role with a real visit-free result, and keep it word for word, since a visible 'no action' Grunt drew the town's questions and then a Vigilante kill.

A visit to a player with no night action gains nothing, so an Enforcer or Vulture visit to a no-action player is a useless visit that needs an explanation. Check for claimed visits that have no possible purpose before counting them as evidence.
Two Yakuza with a shared Katana vote should avoid repeating the same daytime votes or lines. Both spent Day 2 pushing Guilty on the same lead, which made their alignment easy to read for the town.

A player who changes their role claim after being nominated (Alice from Fortune Teller to Sheriff, Dave from Enforcer to Vulture) is a strong lead. Before voting, ask them to name the specific visit or result the new role explains.

Watch the most likely Katana victim, not only your own suspects. A visit to a Katana victim on the night of the kill is the cleanest way to expose the holder, and Heidi's watch on Bob did exactly that.

Visitor counts (such as a Fortune Teller's numbers) prove how many people visited, not who. Do not build a case on a count alone. Pair it with named visits or exact-role results before naming a suspect.

Never publicly claim a Yakuza-only role such as Grunt, and do not state a 'no action' line that conflicts with your visible behaviour. Frank's Grunt claim and shifting wording gave the Village a clean case with no investigation.
Repeated refrains such as 'no read yet, wait for concrete info' used up Day 1 and early Day 2 budget without giving anyone a reason to vote. Spend budget on specific, checkable questions instead.

When possible, watch a likely target of a factional attack. The Katana holder visits the target, so a complete result showing a sole visitor to someone killed by Katana can identify the holder—not merely show that person visited.

Separate what a result directly establishes from what you infer. A visit does not usually prove an attack, but the visit list combined with a known cause of death and required mechanics can make a strong, conditional case.
Share useful results promptly with the night, target, and exact result, then explain how they bear on the vote. Clearly label uncertainty rather than presenting an inference as certainty.
Do not treat duplicate role claims as proof of a lie unless the role is unique. Test competing claims against visits, results, and other mechanical evidence.

Whoever holds the Katana must have a cover that explains a visit (e.g. Sheriff, Tracker, Medic), not a passive role like Fortune Teller. Otherwise a single Lookout or Tracker sighting is an unexplainable break. If your cover is passive, pass the Katana to a teammate whose cover visits.
evidence: Alice claimed passive Fortune Teller, then made the Night 2 Katana visit to Bob. Heidi's watch caught her as Bob's only visitor. Her switch to Sheriff came too late and clashed with Grace, and she was hanged 4-1.

tip: Before choosing a Katana target, check which claimed watchers (Lookout, Tracker) are still alive and who they are likely to cover. Kill or avoid the watcher first rather than the next most dangerous investigator they are probably guarding.
evidence: On Night 2 the Yakuza killed Bob (Tracker) while Heidi, an openly claimed Lookout who had already survived one Katana attack, was alive. She watched Bob and exposed Alice.

tip: Never describe yourself in words that only fit an evil or no-action role, and never let yourself be recorded claiming a Yakuza-only role. Have a real Village cover ready before Day 1 ends, and give it in one plain sentence when asked.
evidence: Frank called himself a 'no-action role' on Day 1, which drew immediate questions. During Dave's trial he was logged as claiming Grunt. Erin shot him with one Basic token that night, and it was confirmed when Grace's check of Frank came back Evil.

tip: When a passive counter's numbers can only fit if a corroborated claimant is the Katana holder, suspect the counter first. Recount the claimed visits yourself, including watches and self-visits, before building cases on someone's totals.
evidence: Alice's '5 visitors' contradicted the six claimed visitors (Grace, Heidi, Carol, Bob, Dave plus the holder). Frank pointed this out, yet most of the town used it to narrow the holder to Grace, Carol or Bob. Carol was still accusing Grace on Day 3.

tip: Have a plain cover that fits your real visit ready on Day 1, and give it the first time you're asked. Evading for a whole Day, then claiming a token role, then flipping on trial gets you hanged unanimously.
evidence: Dave admitted visiting Frank but refused to name a role for many rounds. He then claimed Enforcer with 3 tokens, flipped to Vulture on trial, and was hanged 7-1.

tip: On Night 1 protect the most engaged analyst or investigator. They are the Yakuza's natural first target.
evidence: Carol protected Heidi, who had pushed hardest for reads on Day 1. The Yakuza attacked exactly her and the protection stopped it, keeping alive the Lookout who later won the game.

tip: Hang on a corroborated lone visitor to a Katana victim, especially when the accused then switches claims. A trusted watcher's report backed by an earlier verified result is close to proof.
evidence: Heidi's Night 1 watch matched Grace's claimed visit, which corroborated her Lookout claim. Her Night 2 report of Alice alone visiting Bob ended the game on Day 3.

tip: Post each exact result on the night you get it instead of holding it to the next Day. My Night 2 result came late, after I had already nominated Dave, and that made me look like a pusher and cost me trust.

A Not Evil result on a claimed Grunt, like my Night 3 check on Bob, points to a Katana holder, since holders read Not Evil. Use it to narrow the team, but expect the holder to target the investigator next night, so arrange a protector first.

A Medic who protects an investigator the Katana is targeting is likely to be killed the following night. Judy's protection stopped the Night 2 attack on me, then the Yakuza removed Judy on Night 3. Consider protecting yourself on nights you are the likeliest target.

A Vulture gains nothing from visiting the same claimed Sheriff on nights with no death, and repeated visits with no result are a visible tell. Give one plain, consistent purpose for every visit, or do not visit the same player twice.

Compare each player's trial votes across every trial. Erin voted Innocent on both Yakuza Grunts, and that pattern carried more weight than any single speech. Use the announced totals to check who voted which way, and treat a repeated defense of an executed Yakuza as a lead.

A Katana attack is a visit that Trackers, Lookouts and protectors can see. Never make a flat 'I visited no one' claim on a night you attacked. If any Tracker or Lookout is alive, the claim is checkable and breaks; a cover role with a real visit, or silence about that night, holds up better.

The holder reads Not Evil to the Sheriff. A living Sheriff's Not Evil check on a Grunt, next to a Katana kill, is treated as proof of holding. Before choosing a holder for a night, ask whether the Sheriff is alive and unchecked on them; if so, expect that check to be used as the case against them.

Covers must be different and real Village roles that fit your visits and tokens. Two Yakuza both claiming Grunt, a Yakuza-only role, is an instant lead. Agree the covers on Night 1 and never switch them after the first contradiction.

Private message existence is public, so a PM from a teammate-adjacent player to a Village trial voter shows as a pair in the ledger. Avoid PMs that steer a vote; the pair plus a steered vote is an easy case for the Village.

Describe a win condition only as the rules state it. A Vulture who says '2 or 3 players' and then changes the rule gets challenged by every player who has the rules in mind, so state the threshold and power-ups exactly, or stay quiet about it.

Point your visit-based watch at the likeliest Katana victim, usually the claimed Sheriff or Medic, not at a suspect. Victim visitor lists narrow the holder faster than any claim, and a Medic protection that stops an attack proves a visit happened.

When the Katana kills or fails, list every visitor to the victim and cross off each one by a corroborated result. A Grunt who says visited no one is contradicted by any victim whose visitors include someone unexplained, so press that player directly.

The Katana passes to a random living Yakuza when its holder dies, so after each Yakuza death re-derive who holds it. A Grunt-only Yakuza team can run a chain of holders, and a Night 3 kill can come from a holder who was not the Night 2 attacker.

Do not vote Innocent on teammates in trials when the totals can be split by elimination. Repeated Innocent votes on Yakuza left a visible 8G/3I and 7G/2I pattern, which made the defender the obvious lead. Vote with the town and spend your defense on speech, not on ballots.

Do not send private messages to a fellow Yakuza or to a chosen ally during the Day. A private message to a non-teammate that steers a vote, like Erin's two PMs to Grace, is exactly what a Village pair-watch catches, so keep Day coordination in the night chat only.

A Katana holder reads Not Evil to a Sheriff at night's end, and the holder's attack is a visit that Trackers and Lookouts can see. A live Sheriff who checks a teammate gets a Not Evil result that exposes the holder. Before a Sheriff can check a teammate, decide whether the holder should move, and avoid letting the Katana sit with a Grunt the Sheriff is likely to check.

Our shared cover was 'Grunt, visited no one', but a Katana attack makes the holder a visitor to the target. Any living Tracker or Lookout watching that target will expose the lie. Use the no-visit cover only when no visit-watcher is alive or the target is unwatched, and otherwise skip the attack.

Trial totals reveal the defense bloc: when every Yakuza votes Innocent on a teammate, the Village can count them from the announced totals. Vote Guilty with the Village on teammates who are clearly losing, and spend Innocent votes only where the defense can actually change the result.

Visit counts beat speeches. A Medic's protection that stopped a Katana attack proves a holder visited the target, and a Lookout's visitor list narrows that to a short group. Ask every claimant for the same visitor facts, and treat anyone whose 'visited no one' conflicts with a surviving attack or a Tracker track as the lead.

Don't vote Innocent for a teammate on trial. Totals are public (8G/3I, then 7G/2I), so the Innocent votes mark you as the one defending the Yakuza. Vote Guilty with the mass and spend effort on a different lead.

A Katana attack on a visible target makes the holder a visitor to that target, and a Medic save or survival report can expose it. Agree before Day in what the holder will say about that night's visit, and don't let the holder deny a visit the board can prove.
A private message to a non-teammate during Day is seen by everyone and read as coordination. Send one only if the Village would accept its stated reason, otherwise stay silent.

A Vigilante or other shooter who claims late, after several rounds of silence, is treated as a lead by the whole table. Claim early with a plain target plan, even if it is a bluff, rather than waiting to be asked.

Once Katana kills start, spend tracks on the likeliest holder candidates and the Yakuza-only chain, not on players who have already made dodgy claims. A Tracker sees who visited a Katana victim only if the target is someone you track.

When a protector reports stopping a Katana attack, that proves the holder visited that target. List every claimant's visits to that target and check each denial against the other visit reports before accepting it.

A Not Evil alignment check on someone after a Katana kill is strong evidence they held the Katana, because holders read Not Evil. Compare it with the Yakuza count from deaths and reveals to narrow the holder.

Do not spend several rounds repeating 'not nominating yet' and the same question. Ask one specific yes/no question with a deadline, then vote on the answer. Repetition costs budget and gives the Yakuza time.

Once a Medic's protection has been announced and the Katana has hit the protected player, expect the Yakuza to target the Medic next. Consider self-protecting or shifting protection to the next most likely target.

Once the Yakuza are down to one or two, list who visited each Katana victim on each night and check every living player's no-visit claim against that list. The living holder is the one whose 'visited no one' account contradicts a known visit.

Track the Innocent votes cast for each hanged player. A player who defended each confirmed Yakuza, especially with thin reasons, is the strongest remaining suspect even if their claim looks Village-like. Erin was a Grunt who claimed Vanilla, and her Innocent votes on Dave and Bob were the clue.

A Vanilla Villager claim cannot be checked, so it can survive for days. A Yakuza cover that no visit count or alignment result can contradict is safer than a claimed role that invites tests. Keep one cover and repeat it exactly.

Once the Katana holder is known or strongly suspected, protect the likeliest next target, and consider self-protection with Strong Defense. The Yakuza removed the Medic the night after the Medic's protection stopped an attack on the Sheriff.

A private message asking you to doubt a corroborated pair of claims is a tell. Post it publicly at once and vote on the mechanics. Erin's private steer toward Carol and Frank was the lead, and I should have weighed it sooner.

Grunts read Evil to the Sheriff, so a Not Evil read on a player who claims Grunt (a Yakuza-only role) means that player held the Katana at the end of that night. Use this to test the claim, not as a clearance.

Never deny a visit that a Katana attack required. The holder's attack is a visit, so a 'visited no one' denial is checkable against Tracker, Lookout and Medic results and became the proof against Bob. If the holder is asked about a night, answer with a plausible true-looking visit or stay silent, not a flat denial.

Visiting the same publicly claimed Sheriff every night with no result made the visits the lead against you. Spread visits, avoid repeated no-result targets, and plan the death you need early, because a Vulture's win depends on a death, not on visits.

A private message between a Yakuza and a Village player is visible to everyone as a pair, and its contents can be posted publicly. Erin's Day 5 PM to Grace became the case against Erin. Keep influence on Village players to public argument, and never PM someone to steer their vote.

Once the Katana team has tested your protection, protect the next likely target, and consider self-protection. Judy's Standard protection stopped a Night 2 attack on Alice, then Judy was killed by the Katana on Night 3 without protecting herself.

A Sheriff Not Evil result on a player who claims a Yakuza-only role like Grunt is a hard mechanical break: a true Grunt reads Evil, so either the claim is false or that player held the Katana at the end of that night. Check every Yakuza-only claim against the alignment reads before weighing anything else.

Trial totals show who voted Innocent. When a player defends two confirmed Yakuza across separate trials, treat that as a lead and ask them to explain it before hanging anyone else. Keep a running tally of each Innocent vote from the announced totals.

Private messages between two players are visible as a pair to everyone, even when their contents are secret. Avoid PMs that steer a Village player's vote, because the pair itself becomes the lead and the steering gets read as a Yakuza tell.

Do not protect the same claimed Sheriff on consecutive nights when a Katana holder is hunting. A protector whose protection stopped an attack is the obvious next target, so rotate targets or protect yourself, and keep your token use unpredictable.

Repeating 'not nominating yet' and restating the same read every turn burns budget without moving votes. Spend budget on one checkable point per turn, such as a visit, a result or a direct question, and save it for trial defenses.

Once your protection has stopped a Katana attack and the Yakuza can infer who you are, expect to be the next target. Self-protect with Standard the following night, or stop naming your protected player publicly. Judy died on Night 3 with two tokens unspent, and one token would have covered her.

When a Katana holder dies, the Katana passes to a random living Yakuza. Count the living Yakuza after every death and trace the holder chain (Dave, then Bob, then Erin) to find who visited the latest victim. That turns a vague Katana attack into a short list of suspects.

Silence followed by a late claim is not proof of a lie. Mallory's Vigilante claim looked like dodging, but a Night 4 shot on Heidi was real and was confirmed by the public death cause and by the Lookout watch. Check a claim against any public death or visit result before treating the silence as a lead.

Before hanging a player whose only evidence is a Sheriff check they deny, check whether the public votes or a hidden-role mismatch point to someone else. I hanged Dave and Bob on a Sheriff read and a Katana chain, but I only learned the living Yakuza was Erin after the day ended, and I had already voted Guilty on Erin on echoes.

Set a concrete shot trigger by Day 2 and fire on the first strong lead against a likely Yakuza. Don't wait four nights for a clear break; I held all shots, then spent my only kill on a claimed Vulture who posed no threat to the Village.

A Sheriff Not Evil read on a claimed Grunt points to a Katana holder, since Grunts read Evil. Before hanging a Grunt on a denial, check the denial against the visitor list of the Katana victim that night.

Silence on a direct question across several rounds becomes the table's lead, even when the silent player is Village. Answer the first time in one plain sentence, including whether you visited anyone and what your role's action did.

When a Katana holder dies, the Katana passes to a living Yakuza. Track who died, who held it and which living players visited each Katana victim, and use that chain to narrow the Yakuza list before any vote.

Trial totals show who voted Innocent for a confirmed Yakuza. Keep a list of players who defended Yakuza, and treat repeated defenses of hanged Yakuza as the strongest suspect signal, ahead of private messages.

Never use a Yakuza-only role (Grunt, Pharmacist, etc.) as your public claim. Pick a real Village role that fits your visits, or a plausible role no result can contradict. A Yakuza-only claim, combined with any Not Evil Sheriff read, proves you hold the Katana.
evidence: Bob and Dave both claimed Grunt. On Day 4, Carol, Frank, Grace and Mallory all reasoned that a Grunt reads Evil, so Bob's Not Evil result meant he held the Katana. Bob was hanged 7-2.

tip: Check every role claim against the faction lists the moment it is made. A claim of a Yakuza-only role is an immediate confession, and you should say so right away rather than days later.
evidence: Bob claimed Grunt on Day 3 and Dave repeated it. Frank only noted that 'a Grunt can hold the Katana'. Nobody called out Grunt as Yakuza-only until Carol did on Day 4, which gave the Yakuza an extra night and Judy's life.

tip: When a teammate's hang is clearly going through, vote Guilty with the town. Announced totals, compared against everyone's stated votes, reveal exactly who voted Innocent. Each defense of a doomed partner becomes the case against you.
evidence: Bob and Erin voted Innocent on Dave (8-3), then Erin did again on Bob (7-2). On Day 5, Frank and Mallory used the totals to show Erin was the only player who defended both Grunts, and she was hanged 5-1.

tip: Protect the claimed investigator on the first night after their claim. A Sheriff with an Evil read is the Katana's obvious target. Once the Medic is outed by a save, expect to be the next target yourself.
evidence: Judy guarded Alice on Night 2 and stopped the Katana, which kept the Sheriff alive for two more checks. The Yakuza then killed Judy on Night 3 while she guarded Alice again.

tip: Use the Katana on Night 1, ideally on a likely investigator or protector; a no-attack night is lost tempo. After a failed attack, kill the probable protector before retrying the protected target.
evidence: The Yakuza skipped Night 1, and Alice used it to catch Dave. After the Night 2 failure, Erin's switch to Judy on Night 3 worked and opened Alice up for the Night 4 kill, but by then two Yakuza were exposed.

tip: When directly asked for your role and you are trusted Village, claim plainly in one message or decline once with a clear reason. Vague 'I have a night role I won't name' answers burn whole rounds of everyone's budget and draw suspicion.
evidence: Mallory's four-round dodge on Day 2 made her the main topic, and her name was repeated in Bob's and Erin's later deflections and in Erin's will. That Day-long distraction helped the Yakuza more than any hidden info helped the Village.

tip: If a suspect PMs you to steer the vote, post the contents publicly. Steering away from the corroborated claimants is itself evidence.
evidence: Grace posted Erin's PM, which urged doubt of Carol and Frank, the two cross-confirmed info roles. Ivan, Mallory and Carol cited it in their Guilty votes.

tip: A blocking Neutral (e.g. a Vulture) prevents a Village win and can win alone late, so a cheap Basic shot on one is reasonable once the Yakuza reads are being handled by hangs. Spend a single token rather than holding all three all game.
evidence: Mallory's 1-token Basic shot killed Heidi (Vulture) on Night 4. That removed a player who would otherwise have blocked the Village win, and her shot was later confirmed by Carol's watch and Frank's track.

tip: Prioritize the player whose next result is most dangerous, not just the most obvious investigator. Killing Dave removed a Tracker, but leaving Grace alive let her check Alice as Evil before the Yakuza killed her.

Choose a cover that fits your actual actions and visits. Bob claimed Vanilla and no visits despite framing players and making Katana attacks; denials like that become increasingly hard to sustain as deaths establish who had to visit.

Translate each announced cause of death into its required visits, then compare the distinct visitors with claimed actions. Grace's Katana and Hitman deaths required two visiting attackers, so several no-visit claims could not all be true.

Avoid creating an obvious public pair through repeated matching votes or daytime private messages. Keep public voting reasons individually plausible, and remember that the message ledger exposes who is communicating even when it hides the contents.

Two Yakuza who vote the same way on several trials form a visible pair that the town will chase. Alice and I voted Guilty together on three trials and the pattern got Alice hanged. Split some votes, or vote with the town on the cases where your teammate's vote would be most conspicuous.

A Tracker or Lookout report only shows one visit, so it cannot exclude a second visit to the same target. Before using such a report to clear someone, ask each claimant for every visit they know of, and check whether a Katana holder who also visited the target explains the stopped or successful attack.

A frame is wasted if its Evil result never reaches a voter. My Night 4 frame on Frank only reached Grace, who died that night, so it changed nothing. Frame a player only when the result will reach a living Sheriff or Seer before the next vote, or when the frame protects a teammate.

A Hitman can win quietly by making Basic attacks while staying Village-claimed. Erin stayed silent for three Days about her role and was only nominated for that silence. A Neutral killer should claim the plain no-action cover early and keep the same wording afterward, rather than go quiet until forced to answer.

If your protector role becomes public, reassess whether you are now a likely target. A token can provide Standard Defense on yourself, which may stop a Standard Katana attack; Strong protection on someone else does nothing for you if the attackers switch targets.

Treat an Evil alignment result as a lead, not proof of a player's role or faction: a Fabricator can frame someone that night. Likewise, a Not Evil result does not clear a Katana holder. Seek independent corroboration before hanging someone on an alignment check.

A visit result does not establish that a player made only one visit or took only one action. A Tracker's target visit counts, and multiple actions by the same player on the same target still count as one visitor.

Ask for a direct role or action answer, then stop repeating the question. Turn an evasive answer into a specific, checkable claim or contradiction; repeatedly demanding a claim does not itself create mechanical evidence.

A Tracker result reports whom your target visited, not everything they did. They may have made another visit, and several actions on the same target still count as one visitor. Keep those possibilities open when identifying an attacker.

applies_to: Village investigators and anyone using their results
tip: State the limits of alignment results alongside the result: a Katana holder reads Not Evil, and framing or role-specific exceptions can affect reads. Treat a result as evidence to combine with other facts, not automatic proof of role or faction.

Separate suspicious behavior from a mechanical contradiction. Ask for direct, checkable answers, but avoid a Guilty vote based only on a late claim, evasiveness, or a voting pattern unless the total evidence supports it.
A player who reports no visits may simply have had no action or chosen not to act; that does not clear them. Conversely, a visit to a target does not prove which action was performed there.

Your Basic Attack only counts toward the win if it alone would kill, so a target with no Defense that a Katana also hits still counts as your kill. Pick targets whose Good status is backed by an independent exact result, because the 'who was Good' report arrives only after the attack resolves.

Track voting pairs across several trials. Two players who vote the same way on three contested trials, then split on the one that matters, are a stronger lead than any single unverified check, so ask each of them to justify the split before trusting either.

Fire your shot on the first lead that has a concrete break, rather than holding all tokens for a perfect target. Frank's late shot on Bob came after Frank's own death was already likely, and two tokens died unspent.
State your claimed role on Day 1 or the first Day you are asked. Repeated 'no action' answers over three Days made Erin the nomination target and gave the trial defense nothing checkable to rebut.

Private messages between two players are visible to everyone as a pair. Avoid day PMs between teammates; PM traffic between Frank and Grace and between Bob and Erin became the lead the town used to nominate.

A Not Evil result on a player can be a Yakuza holding the Katana at the end of that night, who reads Good to Sheriff. Treat Not Evil as clearing nobody, and check whether the player held the Katana that night before trusting a clean read.

Don't hold all shots until a perfect break. Fire the first Basic shot by Day 3 at the most suspicious pair or voter cluster, because Katana and Hitman attacks can kill you before you use your tokens, as happened on Night 5 with 2 tokens still unspent.

When a night kill needs two distinct visitors (for example a Katana attack plus a Hitman attack), count each player's stated no-visit denial against that requirement. A 'Vanilla' claim made late, after days of 'no action' answers, is a lead to test, not a clear.

Pairs that vote Guilty together on several Village trials are a strong mechanical lead, even with no night result. Weigh that trial-vote record above speeches, and don't dismiss it as mere suspicion because the pair's stated claims look plausible.

A living Fabricator can frame a Village player so that a real Sheriff check reads Evil, and can forge a will. When a Fabricator is alive, a single Evil read on a Village player is weaker evidence than a repeated pattern of visits or votes.

A death announcement that lists two fatal causes on one night (for example Katana and Hitman) means two distinct attackers. A Tracker's 'visited X' shows that one visitor came, not that it was the only visitor, and two actions on the same target count as one visitor. Use the cause list to rule players in or out, not visit reports alone.

When a Katana kill and a second, non-Yakuza kill hit the same night, look for a Neutral killer such as a Hitman. A Hitman reads Evil to the Sheriff and never blocks Village wins, and may claim Vanilla. Test silent players by which accounts conflict with the causes of death, not by how often they stayed quiet.

Post an Evil or Not Evil result the same Day you learn it, with night, target and exact wording, and name the suspect in your will. Sheriff targets are Katana and Hitman targets the following night, so a result you hold back is a result that dies with you. Remember that a Katana holder reads Not Evil and a Hitman reads Evil.

Do not cast identical Guilty votes with your teammate on every trial. Alice and Bob voted Guilty together on three Village nominees, and the matching 2-2 and 4-2 totals made the pair the obvious lead. Split the votes, or vote Innocent on a doomed Village nominee, to avoid a visible voting pair.

Do not spend budget repeating the same demand ('state your role', 'no nomination yet') across several turns. Ask once, specifically, with a deadline, then move to new evidence or a concrete mechanical break. Repetition used most of the Village's budget and gave no new information.
A Tracker result reports the target’s visit, not every action the target took. A player can also make another visit to that same target; for visitor counts, they still count as one visitor.

Combine cause-of-death clues with visit evidence carefully. Multiple fatal causes can establish multiple attackers, but they do not identify those attackers unless another result narrows the visitors down.

applies_to: Village investigators and anyone evaluating their results
tip: Treat Sheriff results as limited evidence: a Katana holder reads Not Evil, while a framed player reads Evil. A result can support a case, but neither reading alone proves a player’s faction.
A delayed role claim or evasive answer is a reason to ask direct questions, not a mechanical contradiction. Record what is confirmed, what is only claimed, and what remains possible before voting.
The Katana holder reads Not Evil, so each night pass the Katana to the teammate the Sheriff is most likely to check next, usually the one not yet checked. Don't leave it on someone already cleared.
evidence: Bob was checked Not Evil on Night 2 and kept the Katana on Night 3. Grace then checked Alice, a non-holder Grunt, got Evil, and Alice was hanged on Day 4. Moving the Katana to Alice that night would have returned Not Evil.

tip: Once the protector is dead, kill the live investigator whose next result threatens you, not a corroborating role whose job is already done.
evidence: On Night 3 Carol was dead and Grace was unprotected, but the Yakuza killed Dave. Grace survived to check Alice Evil, and that cost the Yakuza half their team.

tip: When a trial is clearly going to fail, vote with the majority. Matching Guilty votes from the same two players on every failed trial, plus one hidden Innocent when a teammate is tried, will expose your team through the totals.
evidence: All three Day 3 trials came out exactly 2 Guilty, and Alice and Bob had both stated Guilty. Day 4's 2 Innocent showed Bob defended Alice. Heidi and Frank built the Bob nomination and Frank's eventual shot on exactly this pattern.

tip: Once one track has confirmed a claimant's visits, track suspects whose 'visited nobody' claims can be tested, instead of re-tracking the same player.
evidence: Dave tracked Grace on Night 1 and Night 2. Tracking Bob on Night 2 would have shown Bob visiting Carol, the Katana victim, breaking his Vanilla 'visited nobody' claim on Day 3.

tip: Fire a Basic shot on your strongest lead while the Village still has numbers. A consistent pair voting pattern is enough, and waiting for a perfect break risks dying with every token unspent.
evidence: Frank held all three tokens through Night 4 while Grace and Dave died. His first shot, on Night 5 on the vote-pattern suspect Bob, killed the last Yakuza and won the game, with Frank dying that same night.

tip: State your role in one plain line when asked. Evading pulls nominations onto you and burns the Day's limited trials on Village players instead of real leads.
evidence: Frank and Erin dodged role questions for two Days. Heidi nominated both, and Day 3's three trials (Frank, Dave, Erin) all went to Village players while Bob and Alice were never tried that Day.

tip: Don't force a protector who has just saved someone to hard-claim in public. 'An attack on X was stopped' is enough, and a public Medic claim makes them the next Katana target.
evidence: On Day 2 Erin, Frank, Grace, Heidi, Alice and Bob all pushed Carol to name her role. She claimed Medic and was killed by the Katana on Night 2, leaving Grace unprotected for the rest of the game.

tip: Stay quiet, vote with the Village majority, and stack your kills on Village players the Yakuza are also targeting. You collect kills while suspicion lands on the Yakuza.
evidence: Erin claimed Vanilla, voted Innocent on Village players and Guilty on Alice, and survived her own trial 5-2. She killed Grace and Frank on nights the Katana also hit them, reaching 2 Good kills.

tip: Your Basic Attack fails against any Standard protection, so pick targets whose Good alignment others have already confirmed and whom no claimed Medic is guarding: a Lookout or Insomniac whose results others corroborated is ideal. Avoid the claimed protector's usual targets and anyone loudly suspected of being Yakuza. One wrong kill loses the game.

Claim a role whose actions are Astral, such as Oracle. No Lookout, Tracker or Insomniac can show you visiting, so your real kill visits never contradict your claim. Back it with a 'correct guess' on a role that is already public and that the dead player's own will supports.

applies_to: Hitman / any Neutral with a fixed number of kills
tip: Race the exact-role checkers. A Profiler or Insomniac result on you ends your cover, but once your second Good kill lands you win and leave at once, and a kill on the night you die still counts. Commit to a kill every night from Night 2. Don't wait for perfect information.

Don't vote against what you said in public unless that vote decides your own win. My hidden Innocent on Frank opened a gap in the stated votes and made me a suspect: I was Enforced and profiled the next night. Only my hidden Narrow Escape kept me alive.

Turncoat Medic plus a Merciful Villager can lock every vote with only one real Yakuza alive. Once a claimant keeps 'protecting' and defending the main Yakuza suspect while totals keep coming up short, treat them as Turncoat or Yakuza. Spend night kills on that pair early, before the numbers lock.

applies_to: Village investigators (any role with a hard result)
tip: Once a Fabricator is suspected, they may still have a forge token. As soon as you post a hard result, say in public what your will says and what you plan to recommend next. Then any will that softens or contradicts your public line reads as a forgery. My will was forged into 'don't hang Frank on my N1 alone', and the Yakuza and their Turncoat quoted it for days.

Do the vote-lock math with the votes you can't control: a publicly claimed Merciful vote (always Innocent), the accused's own vote, and likely hidden Innocents from Neutrals (Hitman, Arsonist) and a possible Turncoat. Push the hang on the strongest lead early, while the margin can still absorb those votes. From D3 on, Frank could never be hanged.

Don't explain a gap between stated votes and totals with a Fixer just because a Fixer could do it. Lying Neutrals and a Turncoat produce the same gaps, and nothing showed a Fixer existed. Ask for a hard mechanical source first (a profile listing Fixer, an Ritualist/role count). Otherwise treat the gap as 'someone among the stated-Guilty voters is lying' and use Yes/No counts to find them.

A census counts a Turncoat as Good and never counts Neutrals. A 'Good 2 of 3' that includes a suspected Yakuza can hide a Turncoat. When a supposed town claimant protects the main suspect every night and always votes to save them, weigh the Turncoat possibility. Don't take their Good count or their protections as clearing them.

When two claims from 'investigators' clash on a visit (for example, a Tracker says X visited no one, but an Insomniac or Profiler shows X's role visits), the false track may come from a Neutral killer who uses the Tracker cover to hide their own visits. Check that claimant before you build on their result.

On Day 1, post only a generic agreement. Don't push for visit cross-checks or result formats. The Yakuza aimed their Night 1 Katana at me because my Day 1 line 'read like an investigator'. Sound like a Villager with no information until you have a result that changes a vote.
